Respiratory muscle training significantly improved six-minute walk distance (mean difference [MD] = 34.09 m, 95% confidence interval [CI] 9.71-58.47), forced expiratory volume in one second (MD = 0.32 L, 95% CI 0.16-0.49), forced vital capacity (MD = 0.31 L, 95% CI 0.20-0.41), maximum inspiratory pressure (MD = 14.16 cmH₂O, 95% CI 6.93-21.38), and Trunk Impairment Scale scores (MD = 2.27, 95% CI 1.12-3.43). Respiratory muscle training also reduced pneumonia incidence (risk ratio = 0.41, 95% CI 0.24-0.72). Heterogeneity was substantial for maximum inspiratory pressure (I2 = 89.9%), moderate-to-high for forced expiratory volume in one second (I2 = 62.4%), and moderate for Trunk Impairment Scale scores (I2 = 56.0%); forced vital capacity showed no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%). Sensitivity analyses indicated that the six-minute walk test and Trunk Impairment Scale findings were sensitive to individual trials, whereas forced expiratory volume in one second, forced vital capacity, and maximum inspiratory pressure estimates remained statistically significant after leave-one-out analyses. Egger's test for maximum inspiratory pressure was not significant (p = 0.097), but trim-and-fill analysis suggested potential missing studies for forced expiratory volume in one second, forced vital capacity, and maximum inspiratory pressure.
CONCLUSION: In patients with subacute stroke, respiratory muscle training is associated with improvements in respiratory function and functional outcomes and with a reduced risk of pneumonia. However, some pooled estimates were sensitive to individual trials and the evidence remains limited by heterogeneity, indicating a need for further large randomized trials.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261482562, Identifier, CRD420261482562.

Title: A prognostic inflammation-nutrition reserve index for 180-day functional-survival outcomes after acute ischemic stroke in patients aged 80 years or older.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients aged 80 years or older with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) have heterogeneous functional-survival outcomes despite similar clinical severity. We evaluated whether a routine laboratory-derived Prognostic Inflammation-Nutrition Reserve Index (PINRI) was associated with the 180-day ordinal functional survival state.
METHODS: This single-center cohort study screened consecutive patients admitted with suspected AIS from January 2021 through December 2024. Admission PINRI combined an internally standardized logarithmic C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio, the logarithmic systemic inflammatory response index, and the inverse of the prognostic nutritional index; no transportable clinical threshold was proposed. The primary outcome was 180-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 0-2, mRS 3-5, or death.
RESULTS: Among 278 analyzable patients, 111 (39.9%) achieved mRS 0-2, 114 (41.0%) had mRS 3-5, and 53 (19.1%) died; 167 (60.1%) experienced dependency or death. Each 1-SD increase in admission PINRI was associated with a worse functional survival state after adjusting for selected clinical covariates (adjusted common odds ratio [aOR], 1.98; 95% CI, 1.48-2.65; p < 0.001). The aOR for the highest versus lowest tertile was 3.43 (95% CI, 1.74-6.74; p < 0.001). The first-week PINRI burden remained associated with a worse outcome among 241 day-7 landmark survivors (aOR, 1.80; 95% CI, 1.19-2.72; p = 0.005). Adding PINRI improved the internally optimism-corrected C-statistic for dependency/death from 0.810 to 0.834 (difference, 0.024; p = 0.033). Comparator single-marker C-statistics were 0.821-0.825; none differed significantly from PINRI after false discovery rate (FDR) control.
CONCLUSION: Higher admission PINRI and first-week PINRI burden were associated with a worse 180-day functional survival state and provided modest incremental information beyond the clinical model. Multicenter validation and local calibration are required before implementation.

Title: Short-term effects of ambient PM₂.₅ exposure on cardiovascular mortality in Almaty, Kazakhstan.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ambient fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) is an established environmental risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet evidence regarding its short-term effects on cardiovascular mortality remains limited in Central Asia. This study investigated the short-term association between PM₂.₅ exposure and cardiovascular mortality in Almaty, Kazakhstan.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective ecological time-series study using daily cardiovascular mortality and environmental data collected between January 1, 2017 and December 31, 2025 (3,287 days). Distributed lag nonlinear models within a generalized additive model framework with a quasi-Poisson distribution were used to estimate lag-specific (0-7 days) and cumulative associations between daily PM₂.₅ concentrations and cardiovascular mortality while adjusting for long-term trends, day of the week, and nonlinear temperature effects. Stratified analyses were performed by age and sex.
RESULTS: During the study period, 43,095 cardiovascular deaths were recorded. The mean daily PM₂.₅ concentration was 36.9 ± 33.3 μg/m3. Neither lag-specific nor cumulative associations between PM₂.₅ exposure and cardiovascular mortality reached statistical significance. Relative risk estimates increased after exposure, peaking approximately 2-4 days later before declining. The cumulative relative risk for the overall population was 1.011 (95% CI, 0.837-1.222). Adults aged ≥65 years exhibited the highest cumulative relative risk estimate (RR 1.174, 95% CI, 0.926-1.489), although all subgroup confidence intervals included the null value.
CONCLUSION: Short-term PM₂.₅ exposure was not significantly associated with cardiovascular mortality in Almaty; however, the observed delayed temporal pattern was biologically plausible and suggested greater susceptibility among older adults.

Title: Metabolic abnormalities in pediatric pulmonary arterial hypertension: a narrative review of direct evidence, mechanistic boundaries, and a validation-focused research agenda.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Metabolic reprogramming has been proposed as a major mechanism of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), but evidence from adult patients, experimental models, and children is uneven. This distinction is especially important in pediatric disease because congenital heart disease (CHD), developmental syndromes, identifiable genetic disorders, and treatable metabolic conditions are more prominent than in adult-onset PAH. This narrative review evaluates what has been measured directly in children, defines the boundaries of extrapolation from adult and experimental studies, and identifies priorities for pediatric validation.
METHODS: PubMed-indexed literature and reference lists were searched from database inception through July 2026 using terms related to pediatric PAH, metabolomics, proteomics, biomarkers, mitochondria, glycolysis, pyruvate dehydrogenase, right-ventricular metabolism, CHD, genetics, and cobalamin C deficiency. Priority was given to original pediatric cohorts and biospecimen studies, followed by adult human mechanistic studies with perturbation or rescue and experimental studies that directly measured metabolic function.
KEY CONTENT AND FINDINGS: Direct pediatric studies document severe and heterogeneous disease, a substantial burden of genetic diagnoses, clinically informative but mechanistically nonspecific circulating biomarkers, and exploratory serum and bronchoalveolar-lavage metabolomic signatures in CHD-associated PAH. These studies do not establish a shared pulmonary vascular metabolic mechanism. Cobalamin C (cblC) deficiency provides the clearest evidence that a defined metabolic disorder can cause severe pediatric pulmonary hypertension and that targeted biochemical treatment can normalize pulmonary pressure in many affected children. Adult human and experimental studies support candidate roles for pyruvate dehydrogenase regulation, mitochondrial redox signaling and fission, endothelial and fibroblast glycolysis, inflammation, and right-ventricular lipid handling, but these pathways remain candidates for pediatric testing rather than established pediatric targets.
CONCLUSIONS: No metabolism-directed therapy has demonstrated efficacy and long-term safety in children with idiopathic, heritable, or CHD-associated PAH. Clinical practice should prioritize phenotype-directed screening for defined metabolic or nutritional disorders. Research should use pediatric subgroup-specific sampling, direct flux measurements, causal perturbation and rescue, independent replication, and prospective linkage to clinical outcomes.

Title: Evaluation of a postpartum cardiovascular risk clinic after hypertensive disorder of pregnancy: First-year experience.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy increase future cardiovascular risk. The Clinique Santé Globale PostPartum (CSGPP) was created to assess risk, provide lifestyle counseling, and inform primary care providers. This study was meant to assess its relevance, efficacy, and women's satisfaction to optimize the clinic.
METHODS: This descriptive, single-center prospective cohort study was conducted at the Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Sherbrooke. Women were recruited at their first CSGPP visit. Data on attendance, lifestyle behaviors, motivation, follow-up with primary care providers, and satisfaction were collected at baseline and 12 months postpartum.
RESULTS: Of 104 referrals, 84 women (80.8%) attended the first visit, 65 agreed to participate, and 47 completed follow-up. Belief in the health benefits of lifestyle changes increased (P = .007), and satisfaction with the clinic was high.
CONCLUSION: Given the high adherence and satisfaction with the clinic, these findings support expanding access to the clinic to all conditions increasing CVD in this young population.

Title: Heart Failure Mortality Before and After COVID-19: Demographic Variations and Urbanization Patterns in the United States (2018-2023).
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Contemporary evidence on heart failure (HF) recorded as the underlying cause of death remains fragmented across demographic groups and levels of urbanization. The 2018-2023 interval includes two years before the emergence of COVID-19 (2018-2019) and four years after its emergence (2020-2023).
OBJECTIVE: We aim to characterize the national underlying cause of HF mortality among US adults aged 45 years or older from 2018 through 2023; describe differences by sex, age, race, and Hispanic origin; and quantify changes in absolute death counts across the six National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) urbanization categories.
HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that the national age-adjusted HF mortality rate would increase and that demographic differences and variation in geographic death counts would persist.
METHODS: This retrospective, population-based, serial cross-sectional study used Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) Underlying Cause of Death data (International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) I50). Age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs) per 100,000 were evaluated overall and across demographic groups; age-specific crude rates were used for age groups. Zero-joinpoint log-linear models estimated annual percent change (APC) for the overall population, race categories, and Hispanic-origin categories. Race and Hispanic origin were analyzed separately and may overlap. Urbanization analyses used death counts and percentage changes; urbanization-specific population-adjusted rates were not estimated. Deaths listing HF only as a contributing cause were outside the case definition.
RESULTS: There were 512,960 deaths with HF as the underlying cause; the aggregate AAMR was 59.6 per 100,000. No statistically significant overall temporal trend was detected (APC: 0.59%; 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.37 to 1.57; p = 0.227). Men had a higher aggregate AAMR than women (68.1 versus 53.0), and Black adults had the highest racial AAMR (70.9). Asian adults had a lower aggregate AAMR than White and Black adults (22.9); Hispanic adults had a lower AAMR than non-Hispanic adults (35.2 versus 61.9). In their respective analyses, Asian and Hispanic groups had increasing trends at the nominal 0.05 significance level (APC: 1.30%, p = 0.047, and 1.96%, p = 0.030, respectively). Age-specific mortality increased sharply with age. Death counts increased across all six urbanization categories, most in Medium Metro counties (+11.0%).
CONCLUSIONS: No statistically significant national trend was detected during 2018-2023, while descriptive demographic differences and nominally significant increases in the Asian race and Hispanic-origin analyses were observed. These separate analyses do not establish differences between subgroup slopes or narrowing mortality gaps. Geographic findings describe absolute burden, not population-adjusted risk. The results concern HF as the underlying cause and do not measure total HF-associated mortality.

Title: Validating Acute Coronary Syndrome ICD Codes as Training Labels for Clinical AI.
Abstract: Artificial intelligence models may improve emergency department (ED) screening for acute coronary syndrome (ACS), but such models often rely on International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes as training labels, whose accuracy in contemporary ED populations is uncertain. In this 10-year retrospective study of 619,599 adult ED encounters, we compared ICD-coded ACS against a chart-reviewed reference standard defined as the treating team's documented diagnosis. Sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value were 94.4%, 99.7%, and 72.4%, respectively. Disagreement occurred in 0.31% of encounters. Among false positives (n=1,647), the leading reason was ACS suspected but later ruled out (80.3%); among false negatives (n=257), coder omission of documented ACS (86.0%). ACS ICD codes are suitable training labels for screening models where missing ACS is more consequential than over-identification, and the observed error patterns are systematic and interpretable rather than random.

Title: Multi-omics integration explores shared transcriptomic and immune signatures between pediatric Kawasaki disease and asthma.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Kawasaki disease (KD), the most common acquired heart disease in children with rising global incidence, significantly increases risk for later allergic diseases. KD-asthma comorbidity escalates medical needs and treatment complexity, necessitating a deeper understanding of their relationship. Therefore, this study aimed to explore shared transcriptomic profiles, immune cell landscapes, and key susceptibility genes between pediatric KD and asthma through multi-omics integration.
METHODS: This study retrospectively analyzed allergic disease incidence in KD patients at the Department of Cardiology, Shanghai Children's Hospital, School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and recruited 13 KD-asthma children for single-cell RNA sequencing. Common susceptibility genes were identified through literature mining and differential analysis of public datasets. Bioinformatics methods explored immune cell landscapes, gene expression profiles, and functional characteristics.
RESULTS: Retrospective analysis of 222 pediatric KD patients revealed that 47.74% later developed allergic diseases. A systematic review of nearly 5,000 articles identified shared susceptibility genes significantly enriched in immune processes and signaling pathways. Single-cell RNA sequencing of 13 children showed distinct immune cell compositions and expression profiles versus controls. Both diseases exhibited enrichment of inflammatory and extracellular vesicle-related genes. Molecular function analysis showed that asthma differentially expressed genes primarily involved antigen binding and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II protein complex binding, while KD genes involved Toll-like receptor binding and calcium-dependent protein binding.
CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests a potential immunological link between KD and subsequent allergic conditions. Shared susceptibility genes and transcriptomic profiles are significantly enriched in inflammatory and vesicle-related pathways, providing insights into the biological overlap between these conditions.

Title: Association of Diet Quality and Physical Activity through Young Adulthood With Mid-Life Cardiovascular Health Trajectories: The Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) Study.
Journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Young adulthood is a critical life course window during which cardiovascular pathophysiology develops, yet diet quality and physical activity (PA) are typically studied as separate, static exposures. We examined joint associations of diet and PA across young adulthood with midlife cardiovascular health (CVH) patterns.
METHODS: Among 2,806 participants in the biracial Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) cohort, group-based dual-trajectory modeling identified latent classes of joint Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) score and PA from exam Year 0 to Year 20 (mean age range at each exam 25-45 years). Group-based trajectory modeling defined midlife CVH trajectories using Life's Essential 8 (LE8) scores (5 physiologic components) from Year 20 to Year 35 (mean age range at each exam 45-60 years). Multinomial logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, race, and education, related young-adult behavioral groups to midlife CVH status (high ≥80, moderate 50-79, or low <50).
RESULTS: Four joint diet/PA groups from young adulthood behaviors were identified: low DASH/very low PA (Group 1; 10.9%); low DASH/moderate-declining PA (Group 2; 25.6%); moderate DASH/high-declining PA (Group 3; 41.5%); and high DASH/high-declining PA (Group 4; 22.0%). Three non-overlapping midlife CVH trajectories (low, moderate, high) emerged. Compared with Group 1, participants in Groups 2, 3, and 4 had 4.8-, 8.6-, and 21.7-fold higher odds of high versus low CVH. The joint odds ratio (21.7) exceeded those for high diet quality (7.2) or high PA (10.3) individually. Associations persisted after adjustment for baseline LE8 score.
CONCLUSIONS: Sustained simultaneous adherence to high-quality diet and high PA through young adulthood was strongly and synergistically associated with high midlife CVH, supporting early, comprehensive, and sustained lifestyle prevention.

Title: ECG-Derived Synthetic Left Ventricular Mechanics Predict Mortality After Acute Myocardial Infarction and Fatal Myocardial Infarction in the General Population.
Journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular (LV) mechanical function predicts outcomes after acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Recovering these parameters from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) could enable point-of-care risk assessment wherever an ECG is acquired.
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether ECG-derived synthetic LV mechanics predict all-cause mortality after AMI and myocardial infarction (MI)-specific mortality in the general population and add information beyond the GRACE score and ejection fraction.
METHODS: Synthetic peak systolic (s') and early diastolic (e') mitral annular velocities and mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE) were derived from the 12-lead ECG by a previously validated generative adversarial network, applied without retraining and blinded to outcome. Associations were assessed in an AMI cohort (n=1,065) by Cox regression and a population cohort (n=219,564) by Fine-Gray models. Incremental value was tested against GRACE, three AI-ECG reduced ejection fraction (EF) models, and measured LVEF.
RESULTS: In the AMI cohort (109 deaths; median follow-up 1.44 years), all three parameters predicted all-cause mortality (each P<0.001). Synthetic e' was the sole independent predictor after adjustment for clinical covariates (HR=0.90 per 1 cm/s; 95% CI 0.84-0.98) and for GRACE (HR=0.90; 0.83-0.97; P=0.006). In the post-discharge cohort (n=1,017; 61 deaths), synthetic e' improved discrimination beyond GRACE (C-index 0.67 to 0.70; HR=0.84 per 1 cm/s; 95% CI 0.76-0.93; P=0.001) and remained independent of AI-ECG-predicted and measured LVEF (HR 0.84-0.86 per 1 cm/s; all P≤0.004), contributing 28-46% of each model's prognostic information. In the population cohort (817 MI deaths; median follow-up 3.42 years), all three predicted MI-specific mortality after adjustment for age, sex, and ECG abnormalities, MAPSE showing the largest effect (sHR=0.49; 95% CI 0.37-0.65), with s' (sHR=0.78; 0.72-0.84) and e' (sHR=0.87; 0.82-0.93) also predictive (each P<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: ECG-derived synthetic LV mechanical parameters predict all-cause mortality after AMI and fatal MI in the general population, adding information beyond the GRACE score and LVEF.

Title: Early antithrombotic therapy improves 90-day functional outcomes in patients with postinterventional cerebral hyperdensity after mechanical thrombectomy: a retrospective cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Postinterventional cerebral hyperdensity (PCHD) is a specific type of hyperdensity commonly observed on computed tomography (CT) scans of the head after mechanical thrombectomy (MT). This study aimed to investigate the association between early antithrombotic therapy (EAT) and 90-day functional outcomes in anterior circulation acute ischemic stroke (acAIS) patients with PCHD.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 141 consecutive acAIS patients with PCHD after MT. EAT was defined as antithrombotic therapy administered within 24 h post-MT. The primary outcome was a favorable 90-day functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0-2). The secondary outcomes included 90-day mortality, ΔmRS (defined as the mRS score before MT minus the 90-day mRS score), enlargement of cerebral hyperdensity, and persistent hyperdensity on the 24-h follow-up CT graded by the European Cooperative Acute Stroke Study (ECASS III) morphology. Baseline and outcome data were compared between the EAT and non-EAT groups. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to assess the association between EAT and favorable outcomes. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness and internal consistency of the results.
RESULTS: Of the 129 patients with complete 90-day mRS data, 59 (45.7%) received EAT. The EAT group had a higher proportion of favorable outcomes (59.3% vs. 37.1%, p = 0.019). A multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that EAT remained significantly associated with favorable outcomes (Model 1: odds ratio (OR) 2.469, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.195-5.104, p = 0.015; Model 2: OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.02-7.20, p = 0.045; Model 3: OR 3.68, 95% CI 1.32-10.30, p = 0.013), and the results were consistent after imputation based on discharge data and multiple imputation. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses showed consistent results, with no significant interaction effects observed.
CONCLUSION: EAT is associated with improved 90-day functional outcomes in acAIS patients with PCHD, warranting further investigation in larger prospective studies.

Title: Association of the triglyceride-glucose index with the severity of lower extremity arterial disease across glucose metabolic states: a single-center cross-sectional study of 656 patients with angiographically confirmed disease.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine the cross-sectional association between the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index and the severity of lower extremity arterial disease (LEAD) in hospitalized patients with angiographically confirmed LEAD, to test whether this association differs across Glucose Metabolic States, and to quantify the ability of the TyG index to discriminate prevalent ischemic tissue loss (Rutherford grades 5-6).
METHODS: This single-center, retrospective, cross-sectional study included 656 consecutive patients with angiographically confirmed LEAD who were hospitalized in the Department of Vascular Surgery at the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University from January 2023 through December 2024. Diagnosis was confirmed by digital subtraction angiography (DSA). Patients were classified into four groups according to their Glucose Metabolic States: normal glucose tolerance (NGT, n = 150), impaired glucose regulation (IGR, n = 148), diabetes with a duration of <10 years (DM<10y, n = 174), and diabetes with a duration of ≥10 years (DM≥10y, n = 184). Glucose and lipid parameters and LEAD severity (Rutherford classification) were assessed during the same hospitalization. Spearman correlation, multinomial logistic regression (with grade 1 mild claudication as the reference), ordinal logistic regression with a TyG × Glucose Metabolic States interaction term, proportional-odds assessment by cumulative binary splits, ROC analysis with bootstrap internal validation (1,000 resamples), and decision-curve analysis were performed. Sensitivity analyses used continuous glycemic measures instead of the categorical groups, excluded implausibly low fasting glucose values, and added liver enzymes to the adjustment set. The primary outcome was ischemic tissue loss, defined as Rutherford grades 5-6 (n = 205, 31.2%).
RESULTS: The TyG index increased progressively across Glucose Metabolic States categories (8.79 ± 0.51, 9.15 ± 0.48, 9.57 ± 0.56, and 9.67 ± 0.52 for NGT, IGR, DM < 10 years, and DM ≥ 10 years, respectively; P < 0.001) and was strongly correlated with Rutherford grade (Spearman r = 0.677, P < 0.001). In a multinomial logistic regression model adjusted for age, sex, smoking, hypertension, BMI, and fatty liver disease (all variance inflation factors < 1.5), the TyG index remained associated with each severity category above the reference, with adjusted odds ratios per 0.5-unit increment of 2.51 (grade 2), 2.83 (grade 3), 7.56 (grade 4), 9.62 (grade 5), and 20.45 (grade 6). The interaction between TyG and Glucose Metabolic States was statistically significant (likelihood-ratio χ² = 95.63, df = 3, P < 0.001); stratum-specific odds ratios per 0.5-unit increment were 1.51 (95% CI 1.07-2.13) in IGR, 2.50 (1.90-3.29) in DM < 10 years, and 8.14 (5.23-12.67) in DM ≥ 10 years, whereas the NGT-stratum estimate was unstable (quasi-complete separation) and could not be interpreted. When the categorical groups were replaced with a continuous glycemic measure, the interaction with fasting plasma glucose remained significant but was in the opposite direction (χ² = 9.36, df = 1, P = 0.002): the TyG-severity association was stronger at lower fasting glucose levels (OR per 0.5 unit 4.81 at 4.8 mmol/L) than at higher fasting glucose levels (3.46 at 8.3 mmol/L). For discriminating Rutherford grades 5-6, the AUC was 0.833 (95% CI 0.796-0.870); the Youden-optimal cutoff was 9.42 (sensitivity 85.9%, specificity 71.0%, positive predictive value 57.3%, negative predictive value 91.7%, LR + 2.96, LR- 0.199), and this cutoff was stable across bootstrap resamples. Decision-curve analysis showed a positive net benefit relative to treat-all or treat-none strategies across threshold probabilities of approximately 0.09-0.57.
CONCLUSION: In this cohort of patients with angiographically confirmed LEAD, the TyG index was independently associated with LEAD severity. The strength of this association appeared to vary across Glucose Metabolic States, but the apparent gradient from normal glucose tolerance to long-standing diabetes was not reproduced when glucose was modelled continuously, suggesting that part of the categorical pattern is attributable to the grouping itself (i.e., mathematical coupling and range restriction). The TyG index showed moderate ability to discriminate prevalent ischemic tissue loss. Because exposure and outcome were assessed during the same hospitalization, these findings represent a cross-sectional association rather than a predictive one; the proposed cutoff values were derived from the same sample in which they were evaluated and require external validation before they can be considered for clinical use.

Title: Added value of brain perfusion ultrasound to prehospital stroke scales-a secondary analysis of the SONAS trial.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Accurate prehospital identification of acute ischemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion (LVO) is critical to guide selection of an optimal target hospital for either intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) alone and/or mechanical thrombectomy (MT). The novel portable non-imaging brain perfusion ultrasound (BPU) device SONAS(TM) indicated similar sensitivity and specificity as prehospital stroke scales. In this study, we reanalyzed data from the original 20 patient cohort to evaluate whether combining BPU with prehospital stroke scales (ph-SS) can further improve LVO detection.
METHODS: Clinical data and NIHSS scores of all patients suffering from acute ischemic stroke with and without proven LVO in the SONAS trial were collected and applied to 16 different phSS. As an exploratory analysis we also applied a prehospital score for intracerebral hemorrhage (ph-ICH) to this cohort. The positive and negative predictive values as well as sensitivity and specificity were analyzed retrospectively for both methods.
RESULTS: The best performing phSS, CG-FAST, and RACE, showed comparable performances to BPU, but still misdiagnosed patients. However, in our specific cohort, the combination of both methods allowed for a reliable classification into three groups: (A) "highly probably LVO", (B) "highly probable non-LVO" and (C) "not assessable" (including all patients misdiagnosed by one method alone). The addition of BPU resulted in shifts towards higher sensitivity and NPV. When using the ph-ICH score three patients were classified as ICH (false positive), and all of them showed severe perfusion deficits in BPU indicating LVO.
CONCLUSION: The combination of BPU with phSS may hold the potential to enhance prehospital triage of acute stroke patients selecting patients to (A) endovascular-capable centers, (B) the nearest stroke unit for, i.e., IVT or (C) either depending on other clinical factors and local circumstances. However, validation is critical in stroke-call patients in the prehospital setting including application by paramedics with/without emergency physicians or telemedical support, and compared to other prehospital point-of-care diagnostics both in respect to sensitivity/specificity, timeline and, ultimately, costs. In the future, the addition of serum biomarkers for ICH may open new opportunities for early ICH treatment or even enable prehospital IVT, and/or streamline direct to angio-suite approaches in confirmed LVO.

Title: Association between mean ocular perfusion pressure and proliferative diabetic retinopathy in a northern Chinese population.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: To evaluate the associations of mean ocular perfusion pressure (MOPP), pulse pressure (PP), and systolic blood pressure (SBP) with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) among patients with type 2 diabetes in a northern Chinese population.
METHODS: A retrospective cross-sectional study included 1,323 participants, comprising 1,119 patients from the Beichen Eye Study and 204 patients identified from electronic medical records at the Tianjin Medical University Eye Hospital. The participants were categorized into no diabetic retinopathy (NDR), non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), and PDR groups. SBP, diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and intraocular pressure (IOP) were measured. PP was defined as the difference between SBP and DBP. MOPP was calculated using the formula: MOPP = 2/3 (DBP + 1/3 PP) - IOP.
RESULTS: With PDR as the reference category, higher MOPP was associated with PDR relative to both NDR (OR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.89-0.95) and NPDR (OR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.91-0.98). SBP and PP showed similar patterns in their respective adjusted models and tertile analyses. Exploratory analyses showed evidence of nonlinear associations for PP (P for likelihood test = 0.046) and IOP (P for likelihood test < 0.001), but not for SBP or MOPP.
CONCLUSIONS: Higher MOPP was associated with PDR relative to both NDR and NPDR, suggesting that MOPP may provide complementary hemodynamic information in relation to DR severity.

Title: Maternal E-cigarette Exposure Augments Murine Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm.
Journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Smoking and family history are major risk factors for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). Smoking and nicotine are modulators of DNA methylation, capable of causing heritable epigenetic alterations. Nicotine infusion and e-cigarette (e-cig) vaping augment murine AAA. We investigated the effects of murine maternal e-cig vaping on offspring experimental AAA, and impacts on transgenerational DNA methylation and accessibility.
METHODS: We performed perinatal e-cig nicotine vaping in two strains of adult female mice (ApoE-/- and C57BL/6J). Mice were mated to control males, and treated through gestation. A parallel group were instead sacrificed after treatment, for DNA analysis. Offspring were aged to adulthood, and AAAs were then induced by elastase (C57BL/6J) or angiotensin-II infusion (ApoE-/-), and ultrasound-tracked for 4 weeks. In a second cohort, parental and offspring aortic tissue and blood DNA underwent RRBS and ATAC-seq analysis respectively. Offspring abdominal aortic anatomy was examined, and stiffness was assessed with ex vivo arterial myography.
RESULTS: Maternal e-cig exposure increased offspring AAA growth in both models and genders. AAA incidence was increased in ApoE-/- males, and observed effects were overall more pronounced in males. Maternal vape exposure altered aortic DNA methylation and blood DNA accessibility in mothers and offspring, with differential sites in numerous genes identified, including AAA-related genes and pathways. Pathways were enriched for transcription factors, inflammation/immune-related genes, and angiogenesis genes, with similar changes identified in exposed mothers. Male offspring displayed more differential genes. Significant changes were located in genes known to harbor AAA risk loci in humans, and overlapped with published epigenetic alterations in human smokers. Differences also occurred in offspring aortic structure and stiffness.
CONCLUSIONS: Maternal e-cig nicotine exposure augments AAA growth in multiple models across generations. These effects are accompanied by broad epigenetic DNA reprogramming of key AAA modulator genes and pathways.

Title: Spatial Patterns of White Matter Hyperintensities and Cognitive Function in Older Adults: A Community-Based Study.
Journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are associated with cognitive decline in older adults. We examined whether anatomically defined spatial WMH patterns are associated with cognitive performance and subsequent decline in a large community-based cohort with approximately six years of follow-up.
METHODS: We analyzed 1,667 participants (mean age 76 years) from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study. WMH were segmented from FLAIR images and mapped to 112 white matter regions using deep-learning-based parcellation. Principal component analysis identified dominant WMH distribution patterns; candidate components were selected by Horn's parallel analysis and retained if stable across resampled split samples. Linear mixed-effects models examined associations between WMH patterns and cognitive performance at baseline and follow-up, adjusting for demographic, genomic, and vascular risk factors. Robustness was assessed using analyses accounting for total WMH burden, study center, and selective attrition.
RESULTS: Of 14 candidate principal components (PCs) identified by parallel analysis, eight met the resampling stability criterion and were retained, together explaining 42% of the variance. Three components were associated with cross-sectional or future cognition. PC3, characterized by deep white matter burden in the corpus callosum and anterior corona radiata with relative preservation of superficial white matter, showed no cross-sectional association at baseline but was associated with accelerated decline across multiple domains.
INTERPRETATION: A deep spatial pattern of WMH loading on the corpus callosum and anterior corona radiata was associated with subsequent cognitive decline in the absence of a cross-sectional association at baseline, independent of total lesion burden.

Title: David vs supracoronary with non-coronary sinus replacement in acute type A aortic dissection: 5-year outcomes.
Abstract: BackgroundAcute aortic dissection complicated by severe aortic regurgitation (AR) requires urgent surgical intervention. The optimal root management strategy remains controversial. This study compared the long-term outcomes of the Tirone David procedure and supracoronary aortic replacement with non-coronary sinus replacement in patients with acute type A dissection.MethodsThis retrospective observational study included 80 consecutive patients with acute aortic dissection type A (AADA) and severe AR who underwent surgery between October 2015 and February 2020 at the University Hospitals, with a 5-year follow-up. Patients were divided into two groups: valve-sparing reimplantation (Tirone David, n=40) and supracoronary repair with non-coronary sinus replacement (n=40). Outcomes included operative data, postoperative complications, mortality, and echocardiographic assessment of AR immediately postoperatively, at 6 months, and at 5 years.ResultsThere were no significant differences in age, cross-clamp time, bypass time, intensive care stay, hospital stay, or early mortality between groups (p>0.05). Immediate postoperative AR occurred significantly more frequently in the supracoronary group (57.5% mild AR) compared with the Tirone David group (5.0% mild AR; p<0.001). At 6 months and 5 years, the incidence of AR remained significantly lower in the Tirone David group (10% and 15%) versus the supracoronary group (65% and 75%, respectively; p<0.001).ConclusionsIn this selected cohort of relatively stable patients with AADA and severe AR, the Tirone David procedure was associated with better long-term aortic valve competence than supracoronary aortic replacement with non-coronary sinus replacement, without an observed increase in major perioperative complications.

Title: Feasibility and acceptability of prenatal parental palliative care in congenital heart disease: a pilot study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ductal dependent congenital heart disease (ddCHD) is associated with significant parental anxiety, yet palliative care (PC) support is rarely offered in the prenatal period. While prior studies have evaluated PC postnatally, little is known about feasibility and acceptability of prenatal PC interventions for this population. The purpose of this study is to assess feasibility and acceptability of prenatal PC support sessions (PCSS) for parents whose fetus has been diagnosed with ddCHD requiring neonatal cardiac intervention.
METHODS: This prospective single-center feasibility study enrolled English-speaking parents referred to a pediatric cardiology clinic after fetal echocardiographic diagnosis of ddCHD. Eligible participants were offered monthly prenatal PCSS, in person or via videoconference, led by a dual-certified pediatric critical care and hospice/palliative medicine physician. Feasibility was defined as ≥75% session attendance and very/extremely easy scheduling and attendance ratings; acceptability was defined as ≥75% satisfied/very satisfied ratings.
RESULTS: Of 26 eligible parents, 15 (58%) (10 mothers, 5 fathers) consented to participate. Sixteen sessions were scheduled; 14 (87.5%) were attended, with median duration of 42 min. Most sessions (75%) occurred via videoconference. Thirteen participants (86.7%) rated scheduling and attendance as "very easy" or "extremely easy." All attendees rated the sessions as "satisfied" or "very satisfied."
CONCLUSION: Prenatal PC support for families facing a ddCHD diagnosis may be feasible and acceptable, with high rates of participation and satisfaction at a single tertiary care hospital. Larger, multi-center studies are warranted to assess outcomes and develop sustainable models for integrating prenatal PC into congenital heart disease care pathways.

Title: Explainable machine learning for predicting 28-day mortality in ICU patients with stroke complicated by chronic kidney disease.
Journal: BMC medical informatics and decision making
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with stroke complicated by chronic kidney disease (CKD) face high mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU) due to complex "brain-kidney crosstalk." We aimed to develop and externally validate an explainable machine learning (ML) model based on routine bedside indicators to predict 28-day all-cause mortality, in strict adherence to the TRIPOD-AI reporting guidelines.
METHODS: Clinical data were extracted from the MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-III (external validation) databases. To prevent data leakage, the internal cohort was partitioned into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets before any preprocessing. Class imbalance was addressed using the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) exclusively within the training set. Core predictors were identified using a dual dimensionality-reduction strategy that combined LASSO regression and the Boruta algorithm. Thirteen ML algorithms were evaluated, and the optimal model's discriminative performance was formally compared to traditional severity scores. The Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) framework was utilized for clinical interpretability.
RESULTS: A total of 1,550 eligible patients were included. The feature selection pipeline identified 14 primary physiological and biochemical baseline indicators. The Random Forest (RF) model demonstrated stable generalizability, yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.654 in the internal testing set and 0.672 in the external validation cohort. SMOTE application substantially improved the sensitivity for identifying non-survivors (66.7% and 55.6% in the respective cohorts), albeit with an expected trade-off in specificity. DeLong's test confirmed that the RF model performed comparably to complex clinical scores (e.g., SOFA, SAPS II) with no statistically significant difference (all P > 0.05). SHAP analysis identified creatinine, white blood cell count, anion gap, heart rate, and respiratory rate as the top five drivers of mortality, elucidating critical non-linear pathological thresholds.
CONCLUSION: By relying solely on 14 easily accessible routine clinical indicators, the proposed RF model offers a streamlined and transparent alternative to complex traditional scoring systems. It offers data-driven, non-linear insights for early high-risk screening and individualized clinical decision-making in critically ill stroke patients.

Title: The associations between job stress and physical and mental health in firefighters: a systematic review.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Firefighters are exposed to psychosocial stressors including interpersonal conflict, organizational injustice, and discrimination. This systematic review investigated the associations between work-related psychosocial stress and physical and mental health outcomes among firefighters.
METHODS: A comprehensive search was performed in PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from inception to May 2026. Original cross-sectional, longitudinal, and cohort studies examining associations between job stress and health outcomes in firefighters were included. The review focused on six outcome domains: (1) depression and suicidality, (2) non-depressive mental health problems (PTSD symptoms, anxiety, burnout), (3) alcohol use disorders, (4) sleep quality, (5) somatic disorders (cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal), and (6) physical performance. Quality assessment was conducted using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). A thematic narrative synthesis was employed due to methodological heterogeneity. Findings were synthesized narratively, with key odds ratios (ORs) extracted and presented in summary tables.
RESULTS: Thirty-four original studies involving 87,242 firefighters across Asia, North America, Europe, and South America were included. The strongest associations were observed for organizational system stress with self-reported depressive symptoms (OR = 8.03 in the longitudinal study), discrimination and harassment with self-reported PTSD symptoms (OR = 2.21) and anxiety (OR = 2.56) in female firefighters, and lack of reward with gastrointestinal disorders (OR = 2.17-2.39) and musculoskeletal disorders (OR = 2.39). Protective factors including social support, self-efficacy, and resilience consistently buffered stress-related health outcomes. Physical performance declined with age (12-13% decrease in strength and power), and less experienced firefighters demonstrated greater physiological stress responses.
CONCLUSION: Job stress is associated with pervasive and clinically significant adverse health outcomes in firefighters. The available evidence, predominantly cross-sectional, suggests associations rather than causal effects. Organizational interventions targeting workplace fairness, conflict reduction, and anti-discrimination policies, alongside individual-level resilience training, are warranted. Protecting firefighter health through evidence-based stress prevention is an occupational health priority.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD420261417550.

Title: Game-based learning in cardiology: assessing the effect of puzzle games on medical students' perceptions and clinical reasoning.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Developing clinical reasoning for diagnosing cardiovascular diseases is a major challenge in undergraduate medical education because learners must integrate fragmented clinical information into coherent diagnostic hypotheses. Puzzle game-based learning (GBL) has the potential to facilitate this process by promoting evidence integration, collaborative reasoning, and illness script development. This study evaluated the effect of a puzzle-based GBL intervention on undergraduate medical students' learning outcomes and perceptions in cardiovascular disease diagnosis.
METHODS: A quasi-experimental study with a non-equivalent post-test-only control group was conducted among 206 undergraduate medical students undertaking their cardiology clerkship at Shahid Sadoughi University of Medical Sciences, Iran, during the 2024-2025 academic year. Students were recruited through cluster sampling and allocated to intervention and control groups using sequential temporal cohort allocation. The intervention consisted of a collaborative board-based puzzle game in which students reconstructed authentic cardiovascular cases by integrating patient history, physical examination findings, chest radiographs, and electrocardiographic data through stepwise clinical reasoning. The control group received conventional lecture-based instruction supplemented with illustrative clinical cases. Learning outcomes were evaluated using a structured scenario-based clinical reasoning examination, and students' perceptions were assessed using a validated 10-item questionnaire. Between-group differences were examined using independent-samples t-tests and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusted for age and gender. Effect sizes were reported using Cohen's d and partial eta squared.
RESULTS: Students receiving puzzle-based GBL achieved significantly higher learning scores than those in the control group (69.21 ± 11.15 vs. 66.07 ± 10.83). After adjustment for age and gender, participation in the puzzle-based GBL intervention remained significantly associated with higher learning outcomes (adjusted mean difference = 3.07, 95% CI: 0.01-6.13; F(1,202) = 3.91, p = 0.04; partial η² = 0.019). The unadjusted effect size was small (Cohen's d = 0.29). Among intervention participants, formative puzzle performance demonstrated a moderate positive correlation with final examination scores (r = 0.35, p < 0.001). Overall, 76.2% of students reported positive perceptions of the puzzle-based GBL experience.
CONCLUSIONS: Puzzle-based GBL was associated with modest but statistically significant improvements in learning outcomes and was well accepted by undergraduate medical students. The findings suggest that its educational benefits may extend beyond learner engagement by supporting the progressive integration of fragmented clinical evidence, collaborative diagnostic reasoning, and the construction of illness scripts. Given the quasi-experimental post-test-only design and the small effect size, these findings should be interpreted with appropriate caution. Nevertheless, puzzle-based GBL may serve as a promising complementary instructional strategy for strengthening clinical reasoning in undergraduate cardiology education.

Title: Investigating predictive value of Q-waves and inverted T-waves in anterior STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI: a prospective cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study investigated the prognostic role of pathological Q waves and T-wave inversions (TWI) in patients with anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
METHOD: Prospective cohort study of 658 anterior STEMI patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was conducted. Participants were divided into four categories based on the presence of pathological Q waves and TWI presence on initial ECGs: Q + TWI+ (n = 34), Q + TWI- (n = 132), Q-TWI+ (n = 81), and Q-TWI- (n = 411). The primary endpoint was a composite outcome, which includes cardiovascular death, newly developed or aggravated New York Heart Association (NYHA) class IV heart failure, recurrent myocardial infarction, and cardiogenic shock. The secondary outcome was all-cause mortality, and the total study period was one year. Survival differences and hazard ratios among groups were assessed using log-rank tests and Cox regression analyses.
RESULTS: Patients had significant baseline differences in age, gender, and clinical parameters. Survival analysis revealed significantly higher mortality risks in Q + TWI+ (aHR: 7.2, 95% CI: 1.80-28.83), Q + TWI- (aHR: 2.46, 95% CI: 1.1-5.5), and Q-TWI+ (aHR: 4.28, 95% CI: 1.31-13.89). In isolated analyses, both T-wave inversion (aHR: 3.08, 95% CI: 1.15-8.21) and Q waves (aHR: 1.99, 95% CI: 1-3.96) were independently associated with increased mortality. For secondary outcomes, only Q-TWI+ showed significantly elevated risk (aHR: 3.73, 95% CI: 1.01-13.77).
CONCLUSION: In anterior STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI, Q waves predicted short-term risk, while TWI strongly associated with long-term risk; their combination conferred the highest risk. Unadjusted for door-to-PCI time, these hypothesis-generating findings may reflect ischemic duration. Ultimately, they validate prior reports in a Middle Eastern cohort and support dynamic risk stratification.

Title: Physiological reserve and cardiometabolic burden in relation to functional decline in older adults: a multicohort study.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: Activities of daily living (ADL) disability is a clinically important manifestation of functional decline in later life. It remains unclear whether peak expiratory flow (PEF), a simple marker of respiratory physiological reserve, and cardiometabolic burden provide complementary information for identifying older adults at higher risk. We examined their separate and joint associations with incident ADL disability across three ageing cohorts.
METHODS: We conducted harmonized prospective analyses of adults aged > 60 years who were free of ADL disability at baseline in CHARLS, HRS, and SHARE. Low PEF was defined using cohort- and sex-specific lowest-quartile thresholds, and high cardiometabolic burden as two or more of hypertension, diabetes, lipid disorder, and obesity. We fitted cohort-specific Cox models and pooled estimates by random-effects meta-analysis. We evaluated multiplicative and additive interaction, between-cohort heterogeneity, multiple imputation, and proportional hazards assumptions.
RESULTS: Among 43,285 participants, 11,315 developed incident ADL disability. Higher PEF was associated with a lower risk, whereas greater cardiometabolic burden was associated with a higher risk. Participants with both low PEF and high cardiometabolic burden had the highest relative hazard (pooled HR 1.73, 95% CI 1.54, 1.95). The multiplicative interaction estimate was statistically significant but small in the complete-case analysis (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.01, 1.19; P = 0.029). It was similar in the multiple-imputation analysis (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.02, 1.17; P = 0.008) and heterogeneous across cohorts. Pooled additive interaction estimates were close to the null.
CONCLUSION: The combination of low PEF and high cardiometabolic burden identified an older subgroup at elevated risk of incident ADL disability. However, the small and heterogeneous multiplicative interaction and near-null additive interaction estimates did not support a consistent interaction beyond the separate associations.

Title: EXPRESS: Associations of the triglyceride/HDL-cholesterol ratio and triglyceride-glucose index with malnutrition risk and other geriatric parameters in older adults: a retrospective cross-sectional study.
Journal: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
Abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate the association of the triglyceride/HDL-cholesterol ratio (THR) and the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index with malnutrition risk and other geriatric parameters among patients attending a geriatric outpatient clinic.
METHODS: A total of 355 patients aged ≥65 years who presented to the geriatric outpatient clinic and completed a comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) were retrospectively evaluated in this study. Patients were divided into tertiles according to THR and TyG values. Mini Nutritional Assessment-Short Form (MNA-SF) and CGA parameters were recorded and compared between groups. Malnutrition risk was defined as MNA-SF <12.
RESULTS: The median age of patients was 79 years (59.7% female). Regarding comorbidities, TyG and THR values were higher in the presence of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and malignancy (all p<0.05). In unadjusted analyses, gait speed was positively correlated with both TyG and THR (both p<0.05). Higher THR and TyG values were correlated with higher MNA-SF scores, and MNA-SF score remained associated with both indices in multivariable linear regression analyses. In binary logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and diabetes, both indices were associated with malnutrition risk (MNA-SF <12; present in 69.6% of patients) and with impaired Timed Up and Go test performance; the association with malnutrition risk persisted after additional adjustment for basic activities of daily living, instrumental activities of daily living, depression, and comorbidity burden, in which higher THR was also associated with higher odds of Clinical Frailty Scale >4. After multiple-testing correction, only the association of THR with malnutrition risk remained significant. THR and TyG had limited discriminative power for malnutrition risk (area under the curve 0.601 [95% CI 0.535-0.667] and 0.592 [95% CI 0.526-0.659], respectively).
CONCLUSION: Within the observed range, higher THR and TyG values were associated with lower malnutrition risk in older outpatients. Because their discriminative power is limited, these indices should not be considered independent screening or diagnostic tools; reverse causality cannot be excluded, and prospective studies are needed.

Title: EXPRESS: Air pollution increases cardiometabolic diseases in China: A nationwide longitudinal cohort study.
Journal: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the associations between long-term exposure to multiple ambient air pollutants (PM1, PM2.5, PM10, O3 and NO2) and the incidence of cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) in middle-aged and older Chinese adults, and to identify potential effect modifiers.
DESIGN: Nationwide longitudinal cohort study.
SETTING: The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), covering 28 provinces in China.
PARTICIPANTS: A total of 8,725 participants aged 45 years and older from the CHARLS 2011 baseline, free of pre-existing CMM, defined as having two or more of the following four conditions: hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and stroke, with complete follow-up data through 2020. Participants with only one of these conditions at baseline were retained.
PRIMARY AND SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was incident CMM. Secondary outcomes included pollutant-specific hazard ratios and effect modification by education level and sleep duration. Sensitivity analyses using multiple imputation were performed to assess the robustness of the associations for all five pollutants.
RESULTS: Long-term exposure to PM1, PM2.5, PM10, O3 and NO2 was significantly associated with an increased risk of incident CMM. Stronger associations were observed among participants with lower educational attainment and shorter sleep duration.
CONCLUSIONS: Long-term exposure to ambient air pollutants is associated with a higher risk of CMM in the Chinese middle-aged and older population. These findings highlight the importance of air quality improvement and targeted public health strategies for socioeconomically disadvantaged and sleep-deprived subgroups.

Title: Colchicine in chronic coronary artery disease: effects on vascular glucose uptake, inflammation, remodeling and blood pressure.
Abstract:
AIMS: The mechanisms underlying colchicine's cardiovascular benefits in patients with coronary artery disease remain unclear and warrant further translational investigation.
METHODS AND RESULTS: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 111 patients with chronic coronary artery disease and aortic or carotid target-to-background ratio ≥1.6 were assigned to colchicine 0.6 mg daily (n=55) or placebo (n=56) for 24 weeks. Arterial inflammation was assessed using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) of the ascending aorta. The primary endpoint was the change in mean maximum target-to-background ratio over 24 weeks. Secondary and exploratory objectives included evaluation of systemic inflammatory markers and blood pressure. To support interpretation of the clinical findings, a complementary hypertensive rodent model, the spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR), was treated with colchicine for 4 weeks to explore vascular and inflammatory pathways potentially influenced by colchicine using immunohistochemistry, myography and proteomics.Colchicine did not reduce aortic FDG uptake compared with placebo (adjusted mean change 0.05 [95% CI -0.02 to 0.12] vs 0.01 [95% CI -0.06 to 0.08]; p=0.38). In secondary and exploratory analyses, colchicine was associated with a reduction in neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (adjusted mean change -0.36 vs -0.08; p=0.033), a trend toward lower high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (adjusted geometric mean percentage change -28.2% vs -5.8%; p=0.060) and attenuation of increases in systolic (adjusted mean change 0.88 mmHg vs. 4.94 mmHg; p=0.046) and diastolic (1.41 mmHg vs. 4.35 mmHg; p=0.048) blood pressure. In SHRs, colchicine had no effect on the aorta but attenuated the progression of hypertension and reduced inflammation and extracellular matrix remodelling in mesenteric resistance arteries, while enhancing vasodilator responses. Reductions in CXCL10, CXCL2, NLRP3 and IL-18 expression were observed in mesenteric arteries from the SHR following colchicine treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the hypothesis that vascular effects of colchicine likely extend beyond large conduit arteries, while the specific pathways and relevance to coronary atherosclerosis require further investigation.

Title: First-time incidence of ischemic heart disease among immigrants in Sweden: variation by country of origin, duration of residence, and immigrant generation in a nationwide cohort study.
Abstract: As Sweden's immigrant population has become increasingly diverse and many countries of origin have undergone an epidemiological transition with rising cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors, understanding disparities in ischemic heart disease (IHD) among immigrants and their descendants has become increasingly important. This nationwide registry-based cohort study included over 8.5 million individuals aged 35-85 years [50.1% women; 18.2% first-generation (G1) and 9.4% second-generation (G2) immigrants] who followed from 1993 to mid-2023. Adjusted Cox regression models were used to examine associations between migrant-related factors-including country of origin, duration of residence, period of immigration, and immigrant generation-and first-time IHD incidence. During follow-up, 703 212 first-time IHD events occurred. Compared with Swedish-born individuals, G1 immigrants from the Nordic countries, the Middle East, and selected Asian countries (Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, and Sri Lanka), as well as G2 individuals with Finnish parental origin, had a higher risk of IHD. The highest risks were observed among recent immigrants from the Middle East and among immigrants with the shortest duration of residence. Risk generally declined with increasing duration of residence and became lower than that of the reference population in many immigrant groups. Although age-standardized IHD incidence rates declined over the past three decades, the pace of decline varied across immigrant groups and was slowest among Asian immigrants. In conclusion, most immigrant groups, particularly recent immigrants from the Middle East and immigrants with the shortest duration of residence, had a higher risk of IHD. Tailored cardiovascular prevention strategies are essential to reduce these disparities among immigrants in Sweden.

Title: Comparative validation of standard screening tools and an exploratory model for detecting obstructive sleep apnea in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Abstract:
STUDY OBJECTIVES: Despite representing a highly prevalent comorbidity, standard screening tools for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) lack validation in the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) population. We sought to prospectively evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of three widely used screening tools against gold-standard polysomnography in an HCM cohort and to explore the potential for a tailored predictive model.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, patients with HCM completed the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Berlin (BQ) and STOP-Bang questionnaires before undergoing inpatient overnight polysomnography.
RESULTS: Of 159 participants (median age 60; 64% male), 90 (57%) had OSA (46% mild, 26% moderate, 28% severe). Standard tools yielded modest performance: STOP-Bang [AUC 0.59 (0.50-0.68), sensitivity 77% (68-86), specificity 40% (28-52)]; ESS [AUC 0.58 (0.49-0.67), sensitivity 24% (15-33), specificity 92% (86-98)]; and Berlin [AUC 0.62 (0.53-0.71), sensitivity 65% (55-75), specificity 57% (45-69)]. In contrast, an exploratory model incorporating age, BMI, and waist-hip ratio showed promising preliminary results [AUC 0.82 (0.74-0.88), sensitivity 60% (48-72), specificity 84% (75-91)].
CONCLUSIONS: This study underscores the high prevalence of OSA in patients with HCM and demonstrates that standard screening tools developed for the general population perform poorly in this cohort, complicating clinical triage when polysomnography is delayed. While the derived exploratory model may represent an improvement in risk stratification, these findings require extensive external validation. Targeted screening strategies tailored to the unique pathophysiology of HCM remain necessary to improve OSA identification and management in this high-risk population.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Validation Study; Comparative Study

Title: Association of pre-transplant right ventricular function parameters with long-term cardiovascular outcomes following kidney transplantation.
Journal: The international journal of cardiovascular imaging
Abstract: The hemodynamic effects of end-stage kidney disease and associated pulmonary hypertension may impair right ventricular (RV) function and influence cardiovascular (CV) outcomes after kidney transplantation (KT). We aimed to evaluate the association between pre-transplant echocardiographic RV function parameters, including RV strain, and long-term CV outcomes following KT. In this retrospective cohort study, we included adult KT recipients at a single Midwest academic center from 2015 to 2024 who had adequate-quality pre-transplant echocardiograms and follow-up at our institution. RV function parameters included tricuspid annular systolic velocity (S'), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), fractional area change (FAC), RV index of myocardial performance (RIMP), and RV free wall strain measured by two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as a composite of CV death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular accident, heart failure hospitalization, coronary revascularization, or sustained ventricular arrhythmias. Among 371 patients (mean age 53.5 ± 13.1 years; 56% male) followed for a median of 4.9 years (IQR, 3.1-6.4), 79 (21.2%) experienced MACE. On univariable Cox analysis, RIMP and RV strain parameters were associated with MACE, whereas S', TAPSE, and FAC were not. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower MACE-free survival in patients with abnormal mid and apical RV strain, whereas the basal and dichotomized average-strain comparisons were not significant. In multivariable models, only average, mid, and apical RV strain remained independently associated with MACE. Pre-transplant RV strain was independently associated with long-term MACE after KT and may aid CV risk stratification. Further studies are needed to validate these findings.

Title: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance feature-tracking strain characterization across phenotypic spectrum of danon disease.
Journal: The international journal of cardiovascular imaging
Abstract: To characterize atrial and ventricular strain across the phenotypic spectrum of Danon disease (DD) and explore their relationships with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) extent. This retrospective case-control study included 27 DD patients (median age 17 [range 10-50] years; 15 males) and 32 healthy controls. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging was performed at 3-T with cine and LGE. Structural, functional, and LGE parameters were assessed. Kruskal-Wallis H test with Dunn's test and Bonferroni correction was used for intergroup comparisons; Mann-Whitney U or t-test for two-group comparisons; Spearman's correlation; and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis were used. Left atrial (LA) and right atrial (RA) strain were impaired across all DD subgroups versus controls, with LA strain impairment evident even in the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) subgroup with preserved LVEF. LV global longitudinal strain (LV-GLS) was reduced across all subgroups, whereas global circumferential strain (GCS) and global radial strain (GRS) impairment were confined to hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy (HCM-DCM) and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) subgroups. Mid-ventricular longitudinal strain was relatively preserved (P = 0.062). LGE extent correlated with GRS (all P < 0.01). Left atrial conduit strain rate (LASRe) demonstrated the best diagnostic performance (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.981; sensitivity 88.9%, specificity 100%). CMR feature-tracking revealed phenotype-specific bi-atrial and biventricular strain abnormalities in DD. Atrial strain impairment was detectable even in HCM with preserved LVEF, suggesting early mechanical dysfunction. LASRe showed promising discrimination and warrants validation. HCM-DCM may represent a possible transitional phenotype; longitudinal validation is required.

Title: Systematic review of pulmonary and cardiovascular disease among asphalt pavers.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Asphalt pavers may be exposed to a wide range of potentially hazardous substances, and an annual decline in lung function among asphalt pavers has been reported. Studies reporting a modest increase in lung cancer mortality among asphalt workers have been thoroughly summarized and reviewed.
AIMS: The aim of this paper was to systematically review and meta-analyse mortality from non-malignant pulmonary diseases and cardiovascular disease (CVD) associated with asphalt paving (PROSPERO Nr CRD42022341463).
METHODS: A librarian conducted a literature search in February 2024. We included human studies, assessed risk of bias, conducted meta-analysis and assessed confidence in effect-estimates using GRADE. We included cohort studies reporting estimates on mortality from non-malignant pulmonary disease and CVD among asphalt pavers compared with referents.
RESULTS: We included 10 cohort studies (3714 to 248 087 participants). Asphalt paving was associated with standardized mortality ratio (SMR) from all causes of 0.94 (95% CI 0.81-1.07), SMR from non-malignant pulmonary disease was 1.19 (95% CI 0.95-1.42), whereas SMR from CVD was 0.88 (95% CI 0.75-1.02).
CONCLUSIONS: Our study gave no support to the hypothesis linking asphalt work to excess mortality from cardiovascular or non-malignant pulmonary disease. The studies were not adequately adjusted for confounders. Healthy worker bias may have affected the results. From the GRADE assessment we are uncertain (very low confidence) about the association between asphalt paving and mortality from cardiovascular or non-malignant pulmonary disease. New studies, especially on non-malignant pulmonary disease with better control of confounding factors are warranted.

Title: Autopsy findings after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination: a German national registry study.
Journal: Virchows Archiv : an international journal of pathology
Abstract: Autopsies are the foundation of evidence-based medicine and gold standard for determining causes of death. A potential causal relationship between COVID-19 vaccination and death remains a subject of debate, however multidisciplinary, multicentric national autopsy studies are missing. N = 486 eligible SARS-CoV-2 vaccinated autopsy cases from 14 German pathology, neuropathology and legal medicine university centres between 2021 and 2024 were available via the German National Autopsy Registry. For comparison COVID-19 autopsies were included (n = 385 cases, all performed before the vaccination campaign in Germany started). A previously established causality algorithm was applied in a consensus assessment of potential causality between vaccine administration and an adverse event following immunization (AEFI). N = 176 cases with a post vaccination interval ≤ 28d were included into analyses. In a single case of allergic reaction, in 5/8 cases of either myocarditis (n = 4 cases) or perimyocarditis (n = 1 case), and 9/26 cases of thromboembolism, the consensus process resulted in a potential AEFI in these cases, but no definite causality. In n = 3 cases in which the cause of death remained unclear after autopsy, no potential AEFI could be established. In SARS-CoV-2 positive autopsy cases without vaccination, thromboembolism was documented as cause of death in 18/385 cases and myocarditis in 2/385 cases. In conclusion, autopsies are a valuable tool to assess adverse effects. Currently, post vaccination autopsy numbers are too low to draw conclusions on the general population or to identify rare AEFI signals. As part of pandemic preparedness, international guidelines for post vaccination autopsy procedures, diagnostics and interpretation are necessary. Autopsy registries can support this collective effort.

Title: Blood pressure control assessed by clinic and home blood pressure measurements among hypertensive patients in India: results from the GRAND study.
Journal: Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension
Abstract: Hypertension is a prevalent non-communicable disease and a significant cardiovascular risk factor in India, affecting 25% of adults. Among those treated, only 52.5% achieved controlled clinic blood pressure (CBP). We investigated blood pressure (BP) control in India using CBP and home BP (HBP). This multicenter, cross-sectional study across 18 centers in 12 states within 7 regions enrolled hypertensive participants aged 20-70 years receiving antihypertensive medications for ≥3 months who regularly visited their clinic. A background survey and four CBP readings were collected at baseline ("Clinic Visit 1") and Clinic Visit 2. Participants underwent HBP monitoring for seven days. Based on average CBP across the two clinic visits and average HBP, participants were classified as having well-controlled hypertension (CBP < 140/90 mmHg and HBP < 135/85 mmHg), white-coat uncontrolled hypertension (WUCH; CBP ≥ 140/90 mmHg and HBP < 135/85 mmHg), masked uncontrolled hypertension (MUCH; CBP < 140/90 mmHg and HBP ≥ 135/85 mmHg), or sustained uncontrolled hypertension (SUCH; CBP ≥ 140/90 mmHg and HBP ≥ 135/85 mmHg). Among 1920 participants, 1578 with appropriate CBP and HBP readings were analyzed. Of these, 55.9% had well-controlled hypertension, 5.1% had WUCH, 21.8% had MUCH, and 17.2% had SUCH. The proportion classified as controlled was 77.7% using clinic BP alone versus 55.9% using both clinic and home BP, a difference of 21.8 percentage points. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating HBP alongside CBP for comprehensive assessment of BP control and identification of BP control phenotypes. Clinical trial registration: Registered at Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI) under CTRI/2023/02/049486 on 06 February 2023.

Title: Integrated clinical, biochemical, cardiac imaging, and transcriptional changes under MEK inhibition in complicated Noonan syndrome.
Journal: European journal of human genetics : EJHG
Abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in Noonan syndrome (NS), with a high risk of heart failure and arrhythmias. Lymphatic dysplasia represents another clinically significant manifestation often associated with significant morbidity. Emerging evidence suggests that MEK inhibitors may target these severe complications. Seven pediatric patients with molecularly confirmed NS and severe, treatment-refractory HCM and/or lymphatic effusions received oral trametinib treatment under compassionate use. Clinical, biochemical, and echocardiographic parameters were longitudinally assessed to evaluate efficacy and safety. Transcriptomic analysis of RAS/MAPK pathway-related gene expression was performed in a subset of patients at baseline, one week after treatment initiation, and during prolonged therapy. Trametinib treatment was maintained at doses ranging from 0.0075 to 0.033 mg/kg/day for 3-45 months. All patients showed a rapid decrease in NT-proBNP levels, followed by significant reductions in interventricular septal thickness and, when present, left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. In patients with lymphatic dysplasia, trametinib was associated with sustained reduction of pleural effusions and improved respiratory status. Treatment discontinuation led to progressive clinical and biochemical worsening, with improvement after reintroduction, when performed. Transcriptomic analysis demonstrated early modulation of RAS/MAPK pathway signatures in most patients. Adverse events were mild (grade 1), predominantly dermatological, and manageable with dose adjustments. These findings provide additional clinical and molecular evidence supporting trametinib treatment as a targeted therapeutic strategy for cardiac and lymphatic manifestations in NS. Prospective studies are needed to define long-term safety, optimal dosing, and treatment duration of MEK inhibition in NS and other RASopathies.

Title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase for acute basilar artery occlusion with sufficient recanalization after thrombectomy: the INSIST-IT randomized clinical trial.
Abstract: The clinical effect of adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase after successful recanalization in acute basilar artery occlusion (BAO) remains uncertain. In this prospective, randomized, adaptive-enrichment, open label, blinded-end point, multi-center trial, patients with BAO within 24 h of estimated symptom onset who achieved successful reperfusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) were randomized (1:1) to intra-arterial tenecteplase (n = 75) or control (only received standard medical therapy, n = 69). The primary efficacy outcome was independent ambulation (modified Rankin Scale 0-3) at 90 days; the primary safety outcome was symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH). The trial was stopped early due to safety concerns and lack of efficacy per Data Safety and Monitoring Committee recommendation. Among 144 randomized patients, 143 (99.3%) completed follow-up. At 90 days, independent ambulation was achieved in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 50.0% in the control group (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.34-1.29; P = 0.23). sICH occurred in 6.2% versus 4.8% (OR 1.31; 95% CI 0.28-6.89; P = 0.73). All-cause mortality at 90 days was 41.3% versus 26.5% (OR 1.96; 95% CI 0.97-4.03; P = 0.063). In this prematurely terminated trial, adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase did not improve functional outcomes in patients with BAO.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Randomized Controlled Trial; Multicenter Study; Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't

Title: Applicability of cognitive decline risk scores in a high socioeconomic preventive medicine cohort.
Abstract: BackgroundValidated cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease risk scores (CAIDE, ANU-ADRI, LIBRA, LIBRA2) were developed in general-population cohorts; how they behave in the high-socioeconomic, health-selected populations typical of preventive-medicine programs and over-represented in ageing cohorts is undescribed.ObjectiveLacking a cognitive outcome, we did not test predictive validity but described score distributions, inter-score concordance, the components driving variance, and complementary biological data.MethodsFour scores were computed for 895 participants aged ≥45 years in the Zoī cohort, a self-referred, self-funded preventive-medicine sample. Concordance was assessed by Spearman correlations and, after dichotomization, by pairwise agreement (percentage agreement, Cohen's κ). Principal component analysis identified components accounting for most between-person variance. Complementary data (DEXA body composition, HbA1c, erythrocyte omega-3) were cross-tabulated with score-derived risk categories.ResultsConcordance was moderate (ρ = 0.39-0.60), and dichotomized categories were fairly-to-moderately concordant across families (Cohen's κ 0.33-0.52). Protective variables showed ceiling effects (education ≥10 years, 86%; social/cognitive activity, 100%), leaving cardiovascular factors (BMI, hypertension, coronary heart disease) to account for most variance.
