METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of Science, and LILACS up to June 2025. Studies in adults with CS that measured NT-proBNP, BNP, or MR-proANP, and that used electrocardiographic monitoring as a reference standard, were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool, and data were meta-analyzed using a bivariate model and a hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic model. Certainty of the evidence was assessed in accordance with the GRADE methodology.
RESULTS: Eight observational studies involving 1616 patients were included, with an overall PAF prevalence of 19%. For NT-proBNP and BNP, respectively, pooled sensitivity was 78% (95% CI, 63%-87%) and 75% (95% CI, 56%-87%); specificity, 64% (95% CI, 53%-73%) and 67% (95% CI, 45%-84%); and diagnostic odds ratio, 6.18 (95% CI, 3.94-9.70) and 6.10 (95% CI, 4.42-8.42). The certainty of the evidence was low for NT-proBNP and moderate for BNP. Heterogeneity was associated with selected cutoff values, analytical platform, and reference-standard monitoring.
CONCLUSION: NPs are potentially useful adjunctive biomarkers to support PAF risk stratification in patients with CS. However, the certainty of evidence for NT-proBNP was low, and for BNP moderate. Incorporating them into stepwise strategies may help stratify patients, but their incorporation requires prospective validation. NPs alone should neither guide anticoagulation nor replace rhythm monitoring.
Publication Types: Systematic Review; Journal Article; Meta-Analysis; Review

Title: Prognostic Implications of High HFpEF Probability in Patients With Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) and left heart disease, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), show overlapping clinical features despite distinct pathophysiology.
OBJECTIVES: The HFpEF-ABA algorithm (age, body mass index, atrial fibrillation) was used to characterize HFpEF pretest probability in patients with CTEPH and evaluate its association with left heart disease and clinical worsening.
METHODS: Among 466 patients with CTEPH stratified by HFpEF-ABA score (low < 25%, intermediate 25%-74%, high ≥ 75%), Spearman's correlation assessed associations with common left heart disease comorbidities. Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression evaluated associations with clinical worsening, with restricted cubic splines assessing the dose-response relationship and non-linearity. Subgroup analyses by sex, smoking, alcohol use, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and obstructive sleep apnea assessed the consistency. We also evaluated whether adding the HFpEF-ABA score improved COMPERA 2.0 discrimination for clinical worsening.
RESULTS: Intermediate and high HFpEF probability was found in 52.4% (n = 244) and 9.0% (n = 42), respectively. After adjustment, each standard deviation increase in HFpEF probability was associated with an approximately 73% increase in clinical worsening (p < 0.001). Results were consistent for HFpEF probability (p < 0.05), with no significant subgroup interactions. Adding HFpEF-ABA with COMPERA 2.0 improved discrimination, increasing the C-index increasing from 0.532 to 0.634 (p = 0.012).
CONCLUSIONS: Assessing HFpEF probability in patients with CTEPH identifies those at high risk for this comorbidity and improves the precision when integrated with existing risk models.

Title: Inflammatory and Insulin Resistance Indicator for Predicting Repeat Revascularization and In-Stent Restenosis in Patients With Chronic Coronary Syndrome Undergoing Percutaneous Coronary Intervention.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The C-reactive protein-triglyceride glucose index (CTI) has been associated with cardiovascular risk. This study evaluated its prognostic value for repeat revascularization and in-stent restenosis (ISR) in patients with chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).
METHODS: A total of 2147 CCS patients undergoing PCI were stratified into CTI tertiles. The primary endpoint was a composite of repeat revascularization and ISR. Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank tests was used to compare event rates. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic spline analyses were applied to assess associations. Predictive performance was evaluated using time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves.
RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 60 months, 992 patients (46.2%) experienced the primary endpoint. Event rates increased progressively across CTI tertiles. After multivariable adjustment, CTI remained independently associated with the primary endpoint (HR 1.11; 95% CI 1.01-1.22; p = 0.028). Compared with the lowest tertile, the highest CTI tertile was associated with a 31% higher risk (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10-1.55; p = 0.002). A linear dose-response relationship was observed (p for non-linearity = 0.172; p overall = 0.040). The multivariable model incorporating CTI showed modest discrimination, with AUCs of 0.627 (95% CI 0.602-0.651) at 3 years and 0.651 (95% CI 0.627-0.674) at 5 years.
CONCLUSIONS: CTI is independently associated with increased risks of repeat revascularization and ISR after PCI in patients with CCS. However, its incremental predictive value beyond conventional risk factors appears limited and requires further validation.

Title: Comparative outcomes of endovascular versus synthetic bypass for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions: A 3-year single-center cohort study.
Abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) ranges from intermittent claudication to critical limb‑threatening ischemia (CLTI), with <3% of intermittent claudication cases progressing to CLTI. This study aimed to compare the outcomes of percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with stenting (PTAS) and synthetic graft femoropopliteal bypass (FPB) in a homogeneous PAD cohort. A subgroup analysis of TransAtlantic Inter-Society Consensus (TASC) B and C lesions, which lack standardized treatment algorithms, was also performed. We retrospectively analyzed 88 patients with no prior history of vascular interventions in the same limb who were treated for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions between 2016 and 2020 (29 underwent PTAS and 59 underwent FPB). Primary outcomes were reintervention, limb amputation, mortality, and vessel patency (primary, assisted primary, and secondary) over a 3‑year follow‑up. Subgroup analysis was performed to assess differences in treatment outcomes. No statistically significant differences were detected in reintervention, limb amputation, mortality, or patency between the two treatments. For loss of primary patency, the hazard ratio (HR) for FPB versus PTAS was 1.89 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.76-4.69; log-rank p = 0.146) and 1.23 (95% CI, 0.45-3.38) after adjustment for lesion length and TASC grade. In the TASC B and C subgroup, no significant differences were observed in primary, assisted primary, or secondary patency (log-rank p = 0.809, 0.302, and 0.135, respectively). The study was underpowered to detect modest effects (post-hoc power for primary patency, 34.4%). In this small single-center cohort, no statistically significant difference in 3-year outcomes was detected between PTAS and FPB for isolated superficial femoral artery lesions; clinically meaningful differences cannot be excluded, and the findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating.

Title: Clinical outcomes in various coronary artery bypass grafting techniques: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: There are different coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) techniques, conventional (C-CABG), minimally invasive (MI-CABG), and robotic (R-CABG), each with its respective advantages and drawbacks. This study aimed to compare all three techniques and their nine sub-technique variations to provide a reference for the clinical selection of the most suitable surgical approach.
METHODS: A systematic search was applied to seven databases to find observational studies or randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared outcomes between CABG techniques in patients. Critical appraisal of observational studies (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale) and RCTs (Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0) was performed. We used frequentist network meta-analysis to rank and analyze the pooled odds ratios and mean differences of each intervention. Primary outcomes were mortality and complete revascularization, while the rest were secondary outcomes. The protocol was registered with the ID CRD42023480325.
RESULTS: A total of 132 studies with 779,773 patients were included. All three techniques were associated with comparable revascularization rates. However, in the comparison of the nine sub-techniques port access (PA)-CABG was associated with a significantly higher rate compared to C-ONCAB. R-CABG demonstrated the most favorable outcomes in terms of ICU stay, overall hospital stay, mortality, and ventilation time compared to MI-CABG and C-CABG. Additionally, R-CABG was associated with lower rates of wound infection, cerebrovascular accident, and renal failure. Both R-CABG and MI-CABG were associated with lower rates of non-sinus rhythm compared to C-CABG. While MI-CABG was associated with the highest reoperation rate.
CONCLUSION: R-CABG suggested promising outcomes over MI-CABG and C-CABG. However, as this exploratory NMA was predominantly based on observational data, these findings should be regarded as a hypothesis-generating framework for future research. Clinicians should interpret results cautiously, prioritizing patient-specific factors and institutional experience until higher-level evidence emerges.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Systematic Review; Network Meta-Analysis

Title: Nomogram for Postoperative Permanent Neurologic Dysfunction Following Acute Type A Aortic Dissection Surgery: A Multicentral Retrospective Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Permanent neurologic dysfunction (PND) often complicates following surgery for acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) and is strongly correlated with unfavorable outcomes. Consequently, developing an effective diagnostic method to identify high-risk patients is of considerable importance.
METHODS: This retrospective study, covering 2022 to 2024 across two centers, ultimately included 117 ATAAD patients with Supra-Aortic Branch Vessel (SABV) dissection from our center (2022-2023) as the training set and 52 ATAAD patients with SABV dissection from a secondary center (2024) as the validation set. We used logistic regression to identify predictors and developed a nomogram, which was assessed using the area under the ROC curve, calibration and decision curve analysis. External validation was conducted using the validation set.
RESULTS: In this study, 169 cases were finally collected (117 in the training set and 52 in the validation set), of whom 64 patients developed postoperative PND. Four risk factors were identified: brachiocephalic trunk dissection at the bifurcation plane, chronic kidney disease, age over 50, and cross-clamp duration over 168 min. The AUC was 0.809 for the training set and 0.736 for the validation set. The nomogram model demonstrated acceptable predictive performance, and decision curve analysis potential clinical utility for predicting postoperative PND risk for thresholds of 1%-90% in the training set and 3%-75% in the validation set.
CONCLUSIONS: This study developed and validated a predictive model for assessing the risk of postoperative PND in patients undergoing ATAAD surgery, which may assist clinicians in individualized risk assessment.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Validation Study

Title: Effectiveness of nurse-led hypertension interventions on retention, adherence, and blood pressure control among adults in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension affects more than 1.28 billion adults globally and remains the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, renal failure, and premature death. This burden is inconsistently distributed across Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), where nearly three-quarters of adults live with hypertension. This gap is largely driven by poor adherence and low retention. This systematic review aims to assess the effectiveness of nurse-led interventions on retention in care, medication adherence, and blood pressure among adult patients with hypertension in primary health care settings in LMICs.
METHODS: The protocol was registered (PROSPERO CRD420251136515) following the PRISMA guidelines. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane for articles published between 2000 and 2026. Eligibility criteria included: adults (≥18 years) with hypertension receiving care from primary care clinics; nurse-led interventions; usual care as comparator; primary outcome: retention rates; secondary outcomes: medication adherence, blood pressure (BP) control. Inclusion: experimental, quasi-experimental, and prospective cohort studies. Dual independent screening and data extraction were performed. Quality assessment was performed using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2(RoB2) for randomized controlled trials and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) tools for quasi-experimental and observational studies. Due to heterogeneity in intervention duration, outcome measures, and follow-up periods, a narrative synthesis was employed.
RESULTS: Eleven unique studies (n = 19,005) were identified: 63.6% RCTs, 18.2% quasi-experimental, and 18.2% observational. Seven studies were conducted in Africa and four in Asia. The mean age range was 52.0-67.4 years; 51.3%-76.0% were female. Risk-of-bias assessment revealed high or unclear risk in the missing outcomes data domain for most RCTs. Ten studies used multicomponent interventions. Retention rates varied with appointment attendance (12.6-96.5%), routine clinical retention (27.0-62.8%), and study completion of follow-up (83.8% to 97.2%). Four studies reported medication adherence with varying effects in the intervention group compared to the control or baseline. Ten studies reported systolic blood pressure (SBP) outcomes; 9 reported mean SBP after intervention; the majority reported the mean reduction of SBP was greater than 10 mmHg. Nine studies reported diastolic blood pressure (DBP) outcomes; all studies reported a reduction in DBP after the intervention, with a range of -1.8 mmHg to -20.6 mmHg. Reported SBP and DBP reductions included both within-group controlled estimates; these should not be interpreted as a pooled effect.
CONCLUSION: This systematic review included 11 studies that showed nurse-led interventions improved blood pressure control in primary health care facilities of LMICs. But retention in care showed substantial variability in nurse-led interventions in primary health care facilities of LMICs. Nurse-led interventions in LMICs are a promising strategy for improving blood pressure control. However, retention in care was substantially and variably due to heterogeneous definitions and evidence on medication adherence was limited. Future research should prioritize standardized outcome measures and robust study designs to strengthen the evidence base and inform sustainable scale-up of these models in LMICs.

Title: Evaluating nursing performance during heatwave simulations: Protocol for a repeated measures cross-over study.
Abstract: This study protocol combines clinical simulations with climatic chamber experiments, to evaluate 1) the impact of heat stress on hospital nurses' physiological strain, physical and mental fatigue, vigilance, and clinical performance; and 2) the efficacy of a practical cooling intervention (i.e., electric fan) in mitigating the negative impact of heat stress. UK-based, registered adult nurses working in hospital settings will be recruited to partake in a repeated-measures cross-over design study, consisting of five separate 3-hour experimental sessions simulating clinical work, and taking place within a climatic chamber at Southampton General Hospital (UK). Sessions will differ by ambient temperature and cooling intervention as follows: 1) control (CTR; 18°C, 50% relative humidity [RH]); 2) warm (WARM; 26°C, 50%RH); 3) warm with electric fan (WARM+FAN; 26°C, 50%RH); 4) hot (HOT; 34°C, 50%RH); 5) hot with electric fan (HOT + FAN; 34°C, 50%RH). This study has been registered on a publicly accessible clinical trial registry (ISRCTN45793399). During each session, participants will first complete a standardised fatigue-induction protocol simulating shift work (i.e., low-intensity cycling with cognitive tasks); followed by a simulated hospital ward round involving six simulated patients and two simulated cardiac arrest scenarios. Nursing cognitive and physical performance will be assessed using a standardised observational assessment battery, along with objective cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) performance metrics. Physiological responses will be assessed by monitoring changes in core temperature (Tcore), skin temperature (Tskin), heart rate, and whole-body sweat loss (WBSL). Fatigue and vigilance will be measured using the Swedish Occupational Fatigue Inventory (SOFI) and Brief Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT-B), respectively. Baseline (i.e., prior to fatiguing protocol) to post simulation changes in 1) vigilance assessed via the PVT-B (i.e., a determinant of role-specific cognitive performance); 2) CPR quality score (i.e., a determinant of role-specific physical performance); and 3) Tcore (i.e., a determinant of thermo-physiological state); will be analysed using linear mixed models to determine the effects of ambient temperature and cooling intervention on nurses' clinical and physiological performance. By providing a controlled methodological framework for assessing the effects of heat exposure on hospital nurses' physiological, perceptual, and clinical performance, this study will provide empirical evidence on air temperature-related changes in nursing performance and physiological strain and the role of cooling interventions in modifying these responses. This will support the development of evidence-based climate adaptation strategies to protect healthcare staff wellbeing and maintain patient safety during periods of extreme heat.

Title: Study on Wall Shear Stress Changes in the Aortic Arch and Isthmus in Fetuses With Aortic Coarctation Using Vector Flow Mapping.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate segmental peak systolic wall shear stress (WSSmax) in the aortic arch and isthmus of fetuses with coarctation of the aorta (CoA) and to explore its relationships with conventional anatomical and hemodynamic parameters.
METHODS: This prospective study included 58 CoA fetuses and 58 gestational age-matched normal controls. Vector flow mapping measured WSSmax at the inner and outer curvatures of the aortic arch and isthmus. Within the CoA group, Spearman correlation was used to assess relationships between isthmus WSSmax and the isthmus Z-score, PA/AO, TV/MV, isthmus Vmax, and RV/LV. Multivariable linear regression was performed using the isthmus Z-deficit (-Z), PA/AO, and isthmus Vmax.
RESULTS: Arch WSSmax did not differ between groups (all p > 0.05). Isthmus WSSmax (general, inner, and outer curvature) was significantly higher in the CoA group than in controls (all p < 0.05). Within the CoA group, isthmus WSSmax was lower than arch WSSmax (all p < 0.05). Isthmus WSSmax was correlated with the isthmus Z-score, PA/AO, and isthmus Vmax. In multivariable regression, isthmus Z-deficit (B = 0.271, 95% CI 0.031-0.510, p < 0.05) and isthmus Vmax (B = 0.01, 95% CI 0.001-0.020, p < 0.05) were independently associated with isthmus WSSmax, whereas PA/AO was not significant (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Isthmus WSSmax is elevated in fetuses with CoA and is independently associated with greater isthmus hypoplasia and higher isthmus flow velocity, suggesting a role in CoA pathophysiology. Its incremental diagnostic value could not be assessed because the control group consisted of normal fetuses. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ABOUT THIS TOPIC?: Prenatal diagnosis of aortic coarctation (CoA) has a high false‑positive rate. Hemodynamic changes in CoA include increased velocity and turbulence, but biomechanical assessment in fetuses is limited. WHAT DOES THIS STUDY ADD?: This study uses VFM to quantify WSSmax in the fetal aortic arch and isthmus. Isthmus WSSmax is significantly elevated in fetuses with CoA and is independently associated with greater isthmus hypoplasia and higher isthmus flow velocity, providing mechanistic insights into the biomechanical alterations of fetal CoA.

Title: Advanced Echocardiographic Phenotyping of Myocardial Recovery During VA-ECMO-A Scoping Review.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) provided temporary circulatory support in refractory cardiogenic shock but substantially altered ventricular preload, afterload, and native ejection. Consequently, conventional echocardiographic measurements obtained during support did not necessarily represent intrinsic myocardial contractility. This scoping review mapped conventional and advanced echocardiographic approaches used to characterize myocardial recovery and guide VA-ECMO liberation.
METHODS: PubMed, OpenAlex, and Crossref were searched from inception through September 20, 2026. Eligible studies included adults receiving VA-ECMO in whom echocardiography was used to assess myocardial recovery, flow-dependent cardiac performance, weaning readiness, decannulation outcomes, or transition to durable mechanical support. Citation searching supplemented the database searches. Study selection was reported according to PRISMA-ScR, and the search process was documented according to PRISMA-S. Data were synthesized descriptively because of substantial heterogeneity in populations, imaging protocols, flow-reduction strategies, and outcome definitions.
RESULTS: The searches identified 3,912 records, of which 2,834 remained after duplicate removal. Thirty-nine full-text reports were assessed, and 35 studies were included. Conventional measures, particularly left ventricular ejection fraction and left ventricular outflow tract velocity-time integral, were frequently associated with successful weaning but were strongly influenced by ECMO-related loading conditions. Flow reduction commonly improved ejection fraction, longitudinal strain, native stroke output, and annular velocities without representing immediate biological myocardial recovery. Advanced phenotyping incorporated left ventricular global longitudinal strain, mitral annular plane systolic excursion, cardiac time intervals, left atrial reservoir strain, right ventricular free-wall strain, three-dimensional right ventricular ejection fraction, and right ventricular-pulmonary arterial coupling. Serial and flow-challenge assessments provided greater prognostic information than isolated measurements under full support. Distinct trajectories included coordinated biventricular recovery, isolated left ventricular recovery, persistent biventricular failure, and refractory systolic stagnation. Successful decannulation did not consistently predict sustained recovery or survival, and integrated models combining echocardiography with pulsatility, filling pressures, vasoactive requirements, and end-organ recovery showed the greatest clinical utility.
CONCLUSIONS: Echocardiographic assessment of myocardial recovery during VA-ECMO had evolved from static ventricular thresholds toward dynamic, multiparametric phenotyping. No single parameter reliably established decannulation readiness. Standardized serial imaging and controlled flow-reduction protocols that integrated biventricular function, deformation, native forward flow, ventricular-vascular coupling, filling pressures, and clinical stability were required. Prospective multicenter validation and harmonized definitions of sustained myocardial recovery remained necessary.

Title: Effects of upadacitinib on lipid profiles and their relationship with inflammation in patients with inflammatory bowel disease: a real-world longitudinal cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Upadacitinib (UPA), a selective Janus kinase 1 inhibitor, is approved for moderate-to-severe inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). JAK inhibitors affect lipid metabolism, but longitudinal real-world data on lipid changes during UPA therapy, and their relation to inflammatory activity, are scarce.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective cohort study, patients with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease treated with upadacitinib were followed for up to 2 years. Serial fasting lipid profiles and inflammatory markers (fecal calprotectin, C-reactive protein [CRP], high-sensitivity CRP) were collected at baseline, end of induction (weeks 8-12), 1 year, and 2 years. Lipid trajectories were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models; paired changes were compared with paired t-tests.
RESULTS: Among 159 patients (mean age 43.3 ± 14.0 years; 62.3% male), total cholesterol (TC) rose from 4.19 ± 0.87 mmol/L at baseline to 4.92, 5.03, and 5.21 mmol/L at the end of induction, 1 year, and 2 years (mixed-effects estimates +0.70 to +0.90; all P < .001). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) rose in parallel, and the LDL-C/HDL-C ratio did not increase. CRP reductions correlated with lipid rises (Spearman rho = -0.45 to -0.47; all P ≤ .02). No cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke occurred (0/159); one venous thromboembolism and 3 hypertension cases were recorded.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with IBD treated with UPA, TC and LDL-C rose modestly alongside the resolution of inflammation; HDL-C improved and the LDL-C/HDL-C ratio did not increase. Lipid monitoring and individualized cardiovascular risk assessment are warranted during UPA therapy.

Title: Coronary angiography in heart transplants from donors older than 40: a Eurotransplant study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The increasing age of heart donors in Europe raises concerns about undetected coronary artery disease (CAD), a contributor to early graft dysfunction and long-term complications. This study examined the association between donor coronary angiography (CA) and heart transplant utilization, particularly in donors aged >40 years.
METHODS: A total of 20 681 donor heart offers reported to Eurotransplant between 2004 and 2020 were analysed. The use of CA, donor characteristics, and acceptance rates were assessed. CAD status was imputed for donors without angiography using logistic regression based on clinical risk factors. Transplantation probabilities were modelled using observed and imputed CAD severity to explore potential differences under a scenario of broader CA availability.
RESULTS: CA was performed in 23.5% of cases, predominantly in older donors and those with cardiovascular risk factors. Among donors with CA, 37.5% had CAD, which was significantly associated with age, male sex, hypertension, and smoking. Donors with normal CA findings had lower odds of rejection compared with those without CA (odds ratio 0.36, P < .0001). In a counterfactual model, broader CA availability in donors aged >40 years was associated with a higher estimated transplant utilization (56.4%-67.1%), corresponding to a model-based increase of ∼535 transplants.
CONCLUSIONS: In this observational cohort, CA availability was associated with differences in donor heart utilization, particularly when findings were normal or showed non-significant CAD. These findings suggest that angiographic information may reduce diagnostic uncertainty and support clinical decision-making in older donors. A risk-adapted, resource-sensitive approach to CA use is warranted.

Title: Beyond blood: a narrative review of advancements in saliva-based diagnostics.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Human whole saliva is an accessible, noninvasive biofluid reflecting systemic and oral physiology, offering a viable alternative to invasive venipuncture and its associated pre-analytical vulnerabilities (e.g. ex vivo glycolysis).
AREAS COVERED: This narrative review synthesizes salivary biomarkers across major clinical domains, focusing on glycemic control (glucose, 1,5-anhydroglucitol, α2-macroglobulin), cardiovascular risk indices (cTnI, hs-CRP, sAA), critical care and sepsis surveillance (IL-10, acute-phase proteins), endocrinology (free steroid hormones), infectious diseases (HIV, HCV, SARS-CoV-2), oncological liquid biopsy (exosomal miRNAs, ctDNA), and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (Aβ42, p-tau181, lactoferrin). Analytical modalities - ranging from high-sensitivity immunoassays to wearable electrochemical biosensors and mass spectrometry - are critically evaluated. Furthermore, this review delineates regulatory-cleared diagnostic platforms (FDA PMA/510(k), EUA, CE-IVD, and SAMHSA-certified panels for viral antibodies, late-night salivary cortisol, and toxicology) from emerging discovery-phase panels.
EXPERT OPINION: Widespread clinical translation remains constrained by unstandardized collection protocols, oral matrix interference, and a lack of normative reference intervals. Transitioning salivary testing into mainstream diagnostics requires three priorities: (1) universal sampling standardization incorporating flow-rate normalization, (2) engineering matrix-matched biosensors tailored for sub-picomolar detection, and (3) rigorous multicenter prospective trials to validate definitive clinical cutoffs, dynamic blood-saliva correlation kinetics, and digital point-of-care integration.

Title: Indoor Radon and Incident Heart Failure Among Postmenopausal Women.
Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Evidence has shown an association of radon exposure with heart failure risk factors, but whether there is an association with heart failure remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To assess whether indoor radon concentrations are associated with incident heart failure among US postmenopausal women.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This prospective cohort study used data from the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) observational study and clinical trials. Participants were postmenopausal women from 40 US clinical centers who were aged 50 to 79 years and did not have self-reported heart failure at enrollment or randomization (September 1993 to December 1998) but had physician adjudication of heart failure during follow-up through February 17, 2024.
EXPOSURE: Geocoded participant address-based assignment of county-level, US Environmental Protection Agency-categorized indoor radon concentration (<2, 2-4, or >4 picocuries [pCi]/L).
MAIN OUTCOME AND MEASURE: Incident hospitalization for acute decompensated heart failure was ascertained through physician adjudication of medical records. Hazard ratios (HRs) for heart failure by indoor radon concentration were estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression models.
RESULTS: Among 43 188 postmenopausal women (mean [SD] age, 63 [7] years), 36% were exposed to a radon concentration less than 2 pCi/L; 41%, to a concentration of 2 to 4 pCi/L; and 23%, to a concentration of more than 4 pCi/L. Over a mean (SD) follow-up of 16.2 (8.4) years, 3446 incident heart failure events occurred. The fully adjusted HR for heart failure was 1.19 (95% CI, 1.07-1.33) at more than 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L, changing little in sensitivity analyses. The HR was higher for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (1.24; 95% CI, 1.04-1.49) and heart failure mortality (1.37; 95% CI, 1.12-1.69) at radon concentrations more than 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L, but these HRs were not different from the null at concentrations of 2 to 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L. The HR at concentrations greater than 4 pCi/L approximated that of a 16-mm Hg increase in systolic blood pressure or an increase of 4.8 in body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study of US postmenopausal women, higher indoor radon concentrations were associated with an increased risk of incident heart failure, suggesting that radon may be a modifiable environmental determinant of heart failure.

Title: Resistant hypertension and accelerated vascular aging: evidence for PTEN-AKT-associated cellular senescence.
Abstract: Resistant hypertension (RH) is increasingly linked to accelerated vascular aging and is particularly prevalent among older and obese individuals. Cellular senescence has emerged as a potential driver of vascular aging, but its contribution to RH remains unclear. We examined age and body mass index (BMI) in the WalkByLab cohort and assessed whether RH was associated with vascular features consistent with accelerated aging. Obesity-related transcriptomic datasets were integrated with a curated senescence-associated gene set to identify candidate regulators, followed by validation in an independent RH dataset, PBMCs, and human endothelial cells. An exploratory clinical-molecular nomogram was also developed. BMI and age increased progressively from normotension to RH. RH was characterized by reduced flow-mediated dilation, increased pulse wave index, and unchanged ankle-brachial index, consistent with endothelial dysfunction and arterial stiffness. Transcriptomic analyses identified enrichment of inflammatory, PI3K-AKT, and senescence-associated pathways. In PBMCs from RH patients, PTEN expression was reduced, AKT phosphorylation was increased, and p16/p21 levels were elevated, indicating a systemic senescence-associated molecular profile. In human endothelial cells, exposure to obese serum or pharmacological PTEN inhibition induced AKT activation and cellular senescence, whereas AKT inhibition attenuated these effects. Together, transcriptomic, clinical, and experimental findings indicate that RH is associated with vascular and molecular features consistent with accelerated vascular aging. Human data indicate a systemic senescence-associated molecular profile, whereas endothelial cell experiments support endothelial senescence as a mechanistically relevant cellular component. PTEN-AKT-associated cellular senescence may represent one mechanistically relevant component linking obesity to vascular dysfunction in RH.

Title: A critical appraisal of "Pre-emptive combined serratus anterior plane block and early recovery after minimally invasive direct coronary artery bypass: a retrospective cohort study".
Atrial Fibrillation Across the Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation Continuum: A Systematic Scoping Evidence Map.
Abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter (AF/AFL) are clinically relevant complications across the haematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) continuum, but evidence supporting phase-specific management and transitions of care remains fragmented. This review aimed to map direct HCT-AF evidence, broader HCT cardiovascular evidence, and relevant guidance; identify major evidence-to-care gaps; and define an evidence-informed framework for AF/AFL management across the HCT continuum.
RECENT FINDINGS: We conducted a systematic scoping evidence map of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, supplemented by a predefined closed hand-search of guidance sources. Twenty-seven clinical reports and 15 guidance documents were retained, yielding 42 evidence sources. Direct evidence was concentrated on AF/AFL incidence, timing, predictors, recurrence, and prognosis, whereas evidence for treatment selection, rhythm-surveillance strategies, anticoagulation during thrombocytopenia, and survivorship follow-up remained limited and frequently dependent on extrapolated guidance. The evidence map informed a phase-specific care framework spanning pre-HCT risk assessment, risk-adapted rhythm surveillance, structured acute AF/AFL assessment, dynamic anticoagulation reassessment, medication-safety review, and accountable discharge and survivorship follow-up. AF/AFL after HCT should be viewed as a longitudinal care challenge rather than an isolated inpatient arrhythmic event. The proposed phase-specific quality-of-care processes are hypothesis-generating and require prospective evaluation for feasibility, reproducibility, implementation, and association with clinical outcomes.

Title: Vitamin D receptor activator-associated calcium-alkali syndrome-like phenotype without calcium supplementation: a case series of seven patients.
Abstract: Vitamin D receptor activators (VDRAs) are widely prescribed for osteoporosis and CKD-mineral and bone disorder in Japan. Although hypercalcemia and acute kidney injury (AKI) are recognized adverse effects, metabolic alkalosis in these patients has received limited attention as a feature of calcium-alkali syndrome (CAS).We retrospectively reviewed patients with VDRA-associated hypercalcemia at our institution between April 2016 and June 2026, applying study-defined operational criteria for a CAS-like phenotype: hypercalcemia, elevated bicarbonate compatible with a metabolic alkalosis component (HCO₃⁻ ≥ 26 mmol/L), and AKI (KDIGO criteria). Seven elderly women fulfilled all criteria. Six received eldecalcitol (0.75 μg/day) and one received alfacalcidol (1.0 μg/day). Underlying CKD was present in six patients.Time from initiation to onset ranged from 1 to 120 months (median 18 months). Three cases had no identified exogenous alkali source. The serum Na-Cl difference was elevated in all patients (range 36-53 mEq/L). Renal outcomes were complete recovery in three patients, partial recovery in two, and non-recovery in one; one patient died of worsening heart failure.VDRA-associated hypercalcemia can present as a CAS-like phenotype even without calcium supplementation, and renal outcomes may be irreversible. Because the temporal relationship between hypercalcemia and metabolic alkalosis cannot be established from these retrospective data, the main clinical message is that elderly patients receiving VDRAs, particularly those with CKD or relevant concomitant medications, require periodic calcium monitoring and prompt evaluation when nonspecific symptoms, AKI, or an elevated Na-Cl difference are observed.

Title: Mitral valve disease in rheumatic heart disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome, and rheumatoid Arthritis.
Abstract: Mitral valve disease occurs in rheumatic heart disease (RHD) and selected systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases, but similar lesions may have different underlying mechanisms. This structured narrative review examines epidemiological, mechanistic, imaging, and management evidence, distinguishing established pathways from incompletely validated mechanisms and hypotheses. In RHD, post-streptococcal valvulitis leads to fibrotic remodeling, commissural fusion, and chordal shortening, producing mitral stenosis, regurgitation, or mixed disease. A meta-analysis of 215,552 children and adolescents in endemic settings reported echocardiographically detected RHD in 24 per 1000. In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), typical findings include leaflet thickening, Libman-Sacks vegetations, and regurgitation; embolic complications may occur despite mild valve dysfunction. Among 508 clinically selected patients with SLE undergoing echocardiography, 27.4% had heart valve involvement and 11.2% had mitral involvement. Immunothrombotic mechanisms may contribute to these lesions, but direct validation in human valve tissue remains incomplete. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a prospective cohort found an association with incident mitral regurgitation (adjusted hazard ratio 1.54, 95% confidence interval 1.32-1.81), but not mitral stenosis. Myocardial imaging findings do not establish a causal link to regurgitation. These findings support anatomy- and severity-based assessment in RHD, combined valvular and thromboembolic evaluation in SLE/APS, and assessment of conventional regurgitation mechanisms in RA. The framework informs clinical interpretation within existing guidelines, while proposed disease-specific mechanisms require further validation.

Title: Gene-metabolite-cardiac associations in the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Characterizing gene-metabolite-cardiac associations in childhood chronic kidney disease (CKD) has the potential to identify new research directions or therapeutic targets for mitigating the excessive cardiovascular risk in childhood CKD.
METHODS: The Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) is a prospective cohort that recruited children with eGFR 30-90 ml/min/1.73 m2 across 54 North American centers. Predictor and outcome variables included genotypes, metabolite levels, left ventricular mass index (LVMI) z-score, and left ventricular filling pressure (E/e'). Multivariable linear regression analyses assessed metabolite associations with either LVMI z-score or E/e', adjusting for age, sex, CKD duration, glomerular etiology, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system blockade, hypertension, anemia, dyslipidemia, eGFR, and proteinuria. Significance was based on the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate <0.05. Metabolites associated with cardiac markers were carried forward for a metabolite-genome-wide association study (mGWAS). Linear regression calculated the residual metabolite variability not explained by age, sex, and eGFR. Linear regression assessed metabolite residual variability versus genetic variant dosage at the Bonferroni-corrected genome-wide significance threshold (corrected for number of metabolites assessed).
RESULTS: 556 unique participants with 574 metabolites and ~8.4 million SNPs were included. Sphingomyelin (d18:2/d18:1) and hypotaurine were associated with LVMI z-score. Isobutyrylglycine and 3beta-hydroxy-5-cholestenoate were associated with E/e'. Multiple genetic variants associated with these metabolites at p < 1.25E-8 (p < [5E-8]/4, Bonferroni-corrected genome-wide significance threshold).
CONCLUSIONS: We identified metabolites associated with cardiac markers in children with CKD. We identified genetic associations with variability in these metabolites. Collectively, these gene-metabolite associations suggest roles for inflammation, increased oxidative stress, mitochondrial and energy dysmetabolism, and gut microbial dysbiosis in mediating cardiac pathology in childhood CKD. A higher resolution version of the Graphical abstract is available as Supplementary information.

Title: Cardiovascular Features of Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children and Kawasaki Disease.
Abstract: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) was a new condition with clinical features overlapping with Kawasaki disease (KD) observed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Differences emerged that supported distinguishing between the two conditions, including distinct cardiac presentations and sequelae. The study objective was to compare echocardiographic findings between MIS-C and KD utilizing prospectively collected longitudinal cohort data from a multicenter consortium and the Kawasaki Disease Research Center. Pre-COVID KD cases (2017-2019) and MIS-C cases (April 2020-March 2022) were analyzed for differences in coronary artery (CA) Z-score and left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) during admission and follow up. Relative risks (RRs) were calculated between disease category and cardiac presentation (diminished EF and aneurysm status). We analyzed 480 subjects (MIS-C n=262; KD n=218). KD subjects had a higher risk of CA aneurysm (RR= 1.86; 95% CI: 1.23, 2.79). Conversely, KD subjects had a lower risk of diminished EF (RR=0.09; 95% CI: 0.04, 0.18). Although most cardiovascular abnormalities resolved by follow-up, diminished EF persisted in 6 MIS-C patients (6%). None of the KD subjects had diminished EF at follow-up. CA Z-score ≥2.5 persisted in 3 MIS-C patients (10%) and 13 KD patients (25%). At follow-up, newly documented diminished EF was observed in 1 MIS-C subject, while a CA Z-score ≥2.5 was newly identified in 1 MIS-C subject and 2 KD subjects. MIS-C and KD demonstrate distinct cardiovascular phenotypes, with diminished EF more prominent in MIS-C and CA aneurysms more characteristic of KD. These findings support disease-specific approaches to cardiac monitoring and longitudinal follow-up.

Title: Structured variation in daily life experience within and across individuals.
Abstract: Human experience varies across contexts and individuals. Yet, psychological studies typically seek to constrain rather than discover structured variation. Here we leverage a powerful alternative approach to examine variability in emotional experience by sampling multimodally from individuals across a variety of contexts throughout their daily life and employing unsupervised machine learning to discover reliable, person-specific, multimodal patterns of experience. Healthy adults (N = 97) completed 14 days of biologically triggered experience sampling. Participants wore mobile cardiac monitors for 8 hr/day and reported their current valence, arousal, primary activity (e.g., relaxing), social context (e.g., alone), and emotional experience (via free report) when prompted. Prompts were initiated whenever a sustained change in cardiac interbeat interval was detected in the absence of gross bodily movements (and twice randomly each day). From each event (10,755 total, M = 110.9 events/person), we extracted cardiovascular, postural, affective, and contextual features, which were submitted to integrative clustering to derive reliable patterns for each individual. Clustering identified 313 multimodal patterns (M = 3.2 patterns/person). Multimodal patterns varied across people in number and, to varying extents, in nature. The features that best distinguished patterns from one another also varied by person. Critically, all participants mapped many emotion labels to a single multimodal pattern and a single emotion label to many patterns (i.e., a many-to-many mapping). Simulated data sets validated our novel analytic strategy. This comprehensive approach has broad utility for discovering structured variation in emotional experience "in the wild" and provides further evidence that emotions are diverse populations of instances constructed by a perceiver in context. Title: Hemodynamic changes during total-body cooling and rewarming phase in neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
Abstract: IntroductionNeonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality. Therapeutic hypothermia (TH) is the standard neuroprotective intervention; however, it significantly influences cardiovascular function, necessitating careful hemodynamic monitoring.AimTo evaluate hemodynamic changes in term neonates with HIE during therapeutic hypothermia and the subsequent rewarming phase using serial echocardiographic assessment.Materials and methodsThis prospective observational study included 32 term neonates with suspected perinatal or intrapartum hypoxia admitted within 6 hours of birth. All patients underwent whole-body TH followed by controlled rewarming. Hemodynamic evaluation was performed using serial echocardiography at predefined time points during cooling and after rewarming. Cardiac troponin I levels were measured at admission, during cooling, and after rewarming, and compared with levels in healthy neonates.ResultsSerial echocardiography demonstrated significant changes in cardiovascular function across the cooling and rewarming phases. Cardiac output, left ventricular output, fractional shortening, right ventricular output, and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion showed significant changes over time, with several measures of ventricular systolic function improving after rewarming. Myocardial performance indices also decreased over time, indicating changes in global ventricular performance. Superior vena cava flow and pulmonary artery pressure increased during cooling and remained elevated during the early post-rewarming period. Inferior vena cava collapsibility and right ventricular systolic/diastolic indices also showed significant changes across the study period. Cardiac troponin I levels did not differ significantly between the cooling and post-rewarming measurements (0.19 ± 0.02 vs. 0.20 ± 0.02 ng/mL, P = 0.825). Correlations between echocardiographic parameters and clinical severity markers, including pH, Apgar score, and Sarnat stage, were variable.ConclusionTH induces significant but reversible alterations in cardiac function in neonates with HIE. Serial echocardiographic assessment provides valuable insights into these dynamic changes and may support individualized cardiovascular management during both cooling and rewarming phases. Larger multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to determine their clinical significance and relationship with neonatal outcomes.

Title: Intramyocardial Granulomatous Histoplasmosis Presenting as Narrow-Complex Ventricular Tachycardia.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiac histoplasmosis is rare, typically manifesting as pericarditis or endocarditis; tissue-proven intramyocardial granulomatous histoplasmosis has not been previously described.
CASE SUMMARY: A 77-year-old man with immunosuppression presented with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and recurrent narrow-complex tachyarrhythmias attributed to supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Echocardiography showed a hyperechoic basal septal mass. Autopsy confirmed a 1.8 × 1.1 cm partially hyalinized necrotizing granuloma of the high interventricular septum containing Histoplasma on silver staining. Retrospective aVR algorithm analysis reclassified the arrhythmia as ventricular tachycardia (VT), anatomically concordant with the granuloma.
DISCUSSION: Granulomatous histoplasmosis of the upper interventricular septum can produce high septal VT mimicking SVT, expanding the differential of granulomatous myocarditis in immunocompromised hosts.
TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: Histoplasmosis should be included in the differential of granulomatous myocarditis, particularly in immunocompromised patients from endemic regions. Systematic use of the Vereckei aVR algorithm can prevent misclassification of relatively narrow-complex VT as SVT and guide management.

Title: Creation and verification of an interpretable machine learning model for forecasting in-hospital results in Cardiorenal syndrome patients in critical condition.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) encompasses a spectrum of disorders in which acute or chronic dysfunction of the heart or kidneys induces dysfunction of the other. The heart-kidney crosstalk underlying CRS has since been extended into the broader cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome by incorporating metabolic risk factors.CRS is associated with significantly increased mortality in intensive care unit (ICU) patients. However, dedicated tools for predicting short-term outcomes remain lacking, which limits timely risk stratification and treatment optimization.
METHODS: This multicenter cohort study enrolled 6,668 CRS patients from MIMIC-IV (v2.2) for model development and 3,602 from eICU-CRD (v2.0) for external validation. In patients remaining in the ICU for ≥24 hours, candidate predictors were ascertained within the first 24 hours, including early treatment exposures. Subsequent all-cause in-hospital mortality was predicted at this 24-hour landmark. Eleven machine learning algorithms were systematically compared after 1:1 random undersampling of the development cohort. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied to enhance interpretability and identify key prognostic features.
RESULTS: The artificial neural network (ANN) model performed best. The final model incorporated six readily obtainable variables: AKI stage, age, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor use, β-blocker use, and ACEI/ARB use. It achieved an AUC of 0.810 (95% CI 0.757-0.860) in internal validation and 0.704 (95% CI 0.679-0.729) in external validation, indicating good internal but moderate external discrimination.
CONCLUSIONS: We developed the first interpretable machine learning model specifically for predicting in-hospital mortality in critically ill CRS patients. SHAP provides transparent feature contribution analysis, and a web-based interface facilitates clinical implementation. When applied 24 hours after ICU admission, the model enables early identification of high-risk patients. It may also support risk stratification and resource allocation in the ICU.

Title: Efficacy of empagliflozin in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction according to the presence of echocardiographic features of diastolic dysfunction in the EMPEROR-Preserved trial.
Abstract:
AIMS: To define the impact of diastolic dysfunction (DD) on the response to empagliflozin treatment in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Diastolic dysfunction was defined by left atrial volume index ≥34 ml/m2, the ratio of early diastolic mitral inflow velocity to early diastolic mitral annular tissue velocity (E/e) ≥ 13 or left ventricular mass index >115 (males) or >95 (females). We created three categories of increasing DD (0, 1, or ≥2 DD criteria at baseline) to describe the effect of DD on response to empagliflozin therapy and adverse effects. Of 5988 patients in the EMPEROR-Preserved trial, 3766 (63%) had no documented baseline DD, 1619 (27%) had one, and 603 (10%) had two or more measures. Baseline DD was associated with sex, race, ethnicity, and region and was more common with lower heart rate, DBP, body weight, and eGFR. Despite baseline DD not being significantly associated with the primary endpoint of hospitalization for heart failure or cardiovascular death within the placebo group, a progressive treatment effect across the three DD categories was seen (trend test P-value .0014), with estimated hazard ratios of empagliflozin vs placebo of 0.91 (none present), 0.64 (1 present), and 0.49 (≥2). A significant treatment-by-subgroup trend test was also observed for the total number of hospitalizations for heart failure. Both Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score improvement at week 52 and safety profile were consistent across DD categories.
CONCLUSION: Baseline detection of echocardiographic DD predicted improved clinical response to empagliflozin in a graded fashion, but the reasons cannot be reliably determined from this analysis.

Title: Machine-Learning-Guided Identification of CCT245737 as a Functional Pan-G-Quadruplex Ligand for the Treatment of Multiple Myeloma.
Journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
Abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) still lacks curative therapies, creating an urgent demand for innovative agents targeting unique molecular vulnerabilities. G-quadruplex (G4) stabilization modulates oncogenic regulatory regions and displays potent preclinical antitumor effects. Nevertheless, most existing G4 ligands act on single G4 motifs. Pan-G4 agents capable of perturbing multiple oncogenic pathways are scarce, while conventional high-throughput screening is costly and labor-intensive. Herein, we constructed a repurposing-driven screening pipeline combining curated fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-derived melting-temperature shift (ΔTm) data sets, 1024-bit Chemistry Development Kit (CDK) molecular fingerprints, three machine-learning classifiers, and multi-G4 molecular docking. In nested cross-validation, our Random Forest (RF) classifier yielded a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC) of 0.840 and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.708, superior to label-randomized controls. Consensus screening of 4270 compounds from the TargetMol Anticancer Library yielded 812 high-confidence hits; the top-ranked 487 candidates underwent docking against four structurally diverse oncogenic G4s (c-Myc, c-KIT, Bcl-2, k-RAS). CCT245737 ranked in the top ten across all four independent docking analyses. Functional assays revealed that CCT245737 suppressed the viability of U266 and RPMI-8226 MM cells (IC50 = 0.58 ± 0.06 and 0.68 ± 0.04 μM) and enhanced nuclear BG4 signals. FRET-melting and NMM-displacement assays verified its concentration-dependent stabilization of the four G4s with minimal duplex-DNA interference. qPCR and immunoblotting confirmed downregulation of c-Myc, c-KIT, Bcl-2, and k-RAS at both mRNA and protein levels. In summary, CCT245737 is validated as a promising pan-G4 ligand, and our FRET-guided workflow offers a feasible repurposing strategy for discovering anti-MM G4-targeted therapeutics.

Title: Smart Devices-Based Longitudinal Assessment of Patterns of Insomnia (SLEEPI): Protocol for Large-Scale, Digital, Longitudinal, and Decentralized Clinical Trials.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Personalized medicine requires an understanding of health conditions in real-world settings, but traditional clinical tools are often poorly suited for longitudinal tracking due to logistical hurdles, high participant burden, and data quality issues. While consumer wearables offer a scalable alternative, decentralized clinical trials introduce new challenges in patient recruitment, sustained engagement, and data management. Insomnia serves as a suitable use case for this protocol due to its global prevalence, frequent underdiagnosis, and the well-documented discrepancy between subjective patient reports and objective physiological metrics.
OBJECTIVE: We present a research protocol for large-scale decentralized clinical trials and report its recruitment performance, applied to a longitudinal study on insomnia, called the SLEEPI (Smart Devices-Based Longitudinal Assessment of Patterns of Insomnia) study, using an established base of commercial devices with limited additional manual intervention. This study aims to develop a machine learning model classifying subjective insomnia presence at the participant level against DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision) criteria.
METHODS: Two data streams are collected: subjective, clinically anchored patient reports and objective physiological metrics (eg, heart and respiratory rates) captured via unobtrusive wearable and nearable sensors. This study is executed through a digital protocol designed to conduct a large-scale, longitudinal clinical trial. This protocol replaces the manual interventions of site-based studies with digital tools that manage the full participation process. We detail this protocol from initial recruitment through engagement, adherence, study monitoring, and data management to study completion or withdrawal. The data collected are intended to train and evaluate a machine learning model for subjective insomnia classification. The recruitment objectives were determined by using simulations to determine the minimal sample size for that purpose and by applying a prospective attrition model to calculate the initial contact volume needed to reach that targeted sample.
RESULTS: This protocol enables the continuous monitoring of over 10,000 individuals for 26 weeks. Enrollment metrics exceeded projections: initial survey response rates reached 16% (vs 10% projected), the consent rate was 96% (vs 77% projected), and the final inclusion rate was 90% (vs 81% projected). Recruitment opened in February 2025, and the initial wave closed 6 weeks later with 10,823 individuals included. Data collection is projected to end in June 2027. Preliminary analyses have been conducted, and the first results are expected in the summer of 2027.
CONCLUSIONS: This protocol uses preexisting user bases of connected devices to conduct the trial with limited additional manual intervention. Beyond insomnia, the protocol is intended as a model for generating large-scale, real-world clinical datasets, presenting new opportunities for research in other complex areas such as immunology, mental health, and cardiovascular diseases.

Title: Longitudinal Trajectories and Determinants of Post-Discharge Frailty in Older Adults Undergoing Cardiac Surgery: A 2-Year Cohort Study.
Abstract:
AIMS: To elucidate longitudinal changes in frailty and identify factors associated with its improvement or progression in patients undergoing cardiac surgery.
METHODS: This multicenter prospective cohort study used data from the Japanese Cardiovascular Physiotherapy Network registry. Patients aged 65-89 years who underwent elective cardiac surgeries between May 2021 and December 2022 were included. Frailty was assessed using the Kihon Checklist (KCL) preoperatively and at 6, 12, and 24 months after discharge. Group-based trajectory modeling identified distinct frailty trajectories over 2 years. Multinomial logistic regression examined factors associated with trajectory group membership. Longitudinal changes in KCL scores were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models.
RESULTS: Among 588 patients (mean age, 74.7 years; 41.0% female), three trajectories were identified. Group 1 (50.5%) showed persistently low and improving KCL scores, indicating favorable recovery. Group 2 (36.1%) exhibited moderate and stable frailty. Group 3 (13.3%) demonstrated persistently high and progressively worsening frailty. Compared with Group 1, membership in Group 3 was significantly associated with postoperative delirium, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lower hemoglobin levels, lower Barthel index scores, more advanced age, lower body mass index, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, and impaired renal function. Linear mixed-effects modeling confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction (p < 0.001), with sustained frailty increases occurring only in Group 3.
CONCLUSIONS: Frailty trajectories following cardiac surgery are heterogeneous; approximately one in eight patients experience persistent and progressive frailty over the first 2 postoperative years. Early identification of high-risk patients may enable targeted multidisciplinary interventions to improve long-term functional outcomes.

Title: Ethnic Differences in Clinical Manifestations of Behçet's Disease: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Turkic and Non-Turkic Patients.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Behçet's disease (BD) is a multisystem inflammatory vasculitis with clinical heterogeneity that may vary across ethnic groups within the same country. This study aimed to evaluate the influence of ethnicity on the clinical manifestations, immunogenic laboratory findings and disease course of BD by comparing Turkic and non-Turkic patients in a large Iranian referral cohort.
METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 2697 patients with BD followed at the BD clinic of Shariati Hospital in Tehran, Iran, from 2007 to 2019 were included.
RESULTS: Patients were stratified by ethnicity into Turkic (N = 1037; 38.5%) and non-Turkic (N = 1660; 61.5% [with Persian/Fars, N = 980 subgrouping]) groups, and demographic, clinical manifestations, and immunogenic laboratory findings were extracted from medical records. Mean age at BD onset was 25.72 ± 10.02 years in Turkic patients and 24.69 ± 10.23 years in non-Turkic patients, and males comprised 61.3% and 57.1% of the two groups, respectively. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B5 positivity was 55.1% in Turkic versus 53.1% in non-Turkic patients, and HLA-B51 positivity was 48.7% versus 46.5%, respectively. Most clinical manifestations showed similar prevalence across groups, including oral aphthous ulcers (98.7% vs. 99.0%), genital aphthous ulcers (60.5% vs. 62.0%), uveitis (50.1% vs. 53.2%), and deep vein thrombosis (5.3% vs. 5.1%). Superficial phlebitis was more frequent in Turkic patients (p = 0.02), and oral aphthous ulcers occurred earlier in Turkic patients (p = 0.023). A three-class latent class model demonstrated the best fit (BIC = 14,986.58). In multinomial logistic regression analysis, Turkic patients had slightly higher odds ratio of the ocular-predominant phenotype (OR = 1.10, 95% CI: 0.91-1.33; p = 0.320) and slightly lower odds ratio of the multisystem phenotype (OR = 0.94, 95% CI: 0.68-1.30; p = 0.692); however, neither association was statistically significant. Female gender was associated with higher odds ratio of the ocular-predominant phenotype than the mucocutaneous-predominant phenotype (OR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.14-1.67; p = 0.001).
CONCLUSION: In this large Iranian BD cohort, Turkic and non-Turkic patients exhibited broadly similar disease phenotypes and comparable HLA-B51 frequencies, with small but potentially relevant ethnic differences in the timing of oral ulcers and the frequency of superficial phlebitis. These findings suggest that ethnicity may influence BD phenotype through mechanisms beyond HLA-B51, possibly involving other immune-related genetic variants such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1(ERAP1), Interleukin (IL)-10. Of note, the significant differences observed in Turkic versus non-Turkic comparisons were not present in the Turkic versus Persian (Fars) comparison, indicating that the findings are not driven by a single ethnic subgroup.

Title: The Role of Cardiovascular Function in Endogenous Pain Modulation.
Abstract: Structural and functional overlap between the nociceptive and cardiovascular systems establish a bidirectional coupling that supports dynamic regulation across both systems. Disruption of this coupling could contribute to impaired endogenous pain modulation in chronic pain conditions. Thus, this study aimed to investigate the relationship between endogenous pain modulation and cardiovascular function in healthy participants. Thirty participants underwent assessment of pain modulatory capacity using offset analgesia (OA; 47-48°C-47°C) and conditioned pain modulation (CPM), with pressure pain thresholds as test stimuli and a cold pressor test (CPT) as conditioning stimulus. Resting heart rate variability (HRV) and baroreflex sensitivity (BRS) were derived from 5-min baseline recordings of continuous electrocardiography and beat-to-beat blood pressure. Blood pressure reactivity during the CPT was calculated as the relative difference between peak blood pressure during the CPT and baseline. Associations between pain modulation (OA, CPM) and cardiovascular function (HRV, BRS, blood pressure reactivity) were examined. In this healthy cohort (N = 30), participants exhibited pronounced pain inhibitory capacity, with OA at -85.7% ± 21.8% and CPM at -19.0% ± 14.7%. Higher resting BRS was related to higher OA (rho = -0.48, p = 0.030) and CPM capacity (rho = -0.52, p = 0.021). Moreover, higher CPM capacity was associated with larger blood pressure responses in both parallel (rho = -0.48, p = 0.021) and sequential designs (rho = -0.49, p = 0.033). Increased OA capacity was linked to higher HRV (rho = -0.50, p = 0.030) at rest. Using a multimodal approach, these findings support a functional coupling between endogenous pain modulation and cardiovascular regulation in healthy individuals, emphasizing the role of cardiovascular adaptability in shaping pain inhibitory processes. Understanding this pain-cardiovascular coupling may help explain interindividual variability in endogenous pain modulation in healthy individuals and might offer insight into its disruption in chronic pain conditions. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06443281.

Title: The role of the combined [18F]FDG PET/CT carotid artery and brain studies in stroke prediction: an AI-based prediction of stroke after a 10-year observation period.
Journal: Nuclear medicine review. Central & Eastern Europe
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Long-term (10-year) stroke risk may be assessed by integrating metabolic biomarkers from [¹⁸F]FDG PET/CT scans of carotid plaques and the brain using an artificial intelligence (AI)-based model.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: A prospective study enrolled 43 symptomatic patients (median age 66 years) with carotid plaques. Participants underwent Doppler ultrasound of carotid arteries and [¹⁸F]FDG PET/CT of the brain. A Bayesian network was developed to predict stroke occurrence, incorporating imaging (SUVmax) and clinical data. Model performance was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation and a 10-year follow-up.
RESULTS: During follow-up, 21 patients experienced a stroke. A statistically significant association was observed between increased metabolic activity (SUVmax) in the right common carotid artery and subsequent stroke (p = 0.03). The AI model achieved an overall accuracy of 77% and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.76.
CONCLUSIONS: This proof-of-concept study suggests that AI-integrated multimodal data, specifically [¹⁸F]FDG PET/CT imaging of carotid and brain metabolism, may provide useful exploratory biomarkers for long-term stroke risk assessment.

Title: Novel Metabolomic Signature as a Biomarker to Detect Subclinical Atherosclerosis in Individuals Traditionally Classified as Low Risk.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Standard modifiable risk factors such as age, hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol, and smoking contribute to coronary artery disease risk. However, up to 27% of first-time heart attacks occur in individuals without standard modifiable cardiovascular risk factors. As medical management can stabilize coronary atherosclerosis, there is a need for biomarkers to identify disease before symptoms or a heart attack.
METHODS: We performed targeted metabolomics, identifying 54 metabolites in 1212 adults undergoing coronary artery calcium score (CACS) from the BioHEART-CT Study. Individuals were classified as having clinically actionable CACS positive or not (clinically actionable CACS negative). Metabolite-to-metabolite ratios were then calculated to identify transferable biomarkers. Logistic regression models incorporating age, sex, and metabolite ratios were developed and classified as low risk by traditional scoring. The BioHEART Metabolite Risk Score (BioHEART-MRS) was derived from the best-performing model, trained in a Discovery cohort (n=635), adapted using transfer component analysis (n=266), and validated in an independent External cohort (n=311).
RESULT: A model including age, sex, and 5 metabolite ratios: histidine-kynurenic acid, histidine-riboflavin, citrullin-proline, kynurenic acid-phosphocholine, and arginine-dimethylguanidino valerate, referred to as BioHEART-MRS, demonstrated the best performance in younger individuals for predicting CACS. In the External cohort, BioHEART-MRS outperformed the traditional risk score (area under the curve=0.67 versus 0.55). The traditional risk score underperformed in the under-60 cohort, misclassifying 62% of those with clinically actionable CACS as low risk. Within this group, BioHEART-MRS identified 46 additional cases among low-risk individuals (n=495). As a triage tool, BioHEART-MRS reduced the number needed to scan to detect one true positive case to 7, compared with scanning all low-risk individuals.
CONCLUSIONS: In the External validation cohort, BioHEART-MRS showed greater discrimination than Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis risk score among traditionally low-risk individuals and enriched for clinically actionable CACS positive among those selected for imaging. These findings support prospective evaluation of metabolite-based triage for CACS, particularly in younger and SMuRFless individuals.

Title: Explainable machine learning with wavelet-enhanced multi-scale texture analysis of diabetes-related heel pad ultrasound texture differences.
Journal: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes is associated with structural and functional differences in plantar soft tissues, which may be reflected in ultrasound texture patterns. However, existing ultrasound texture studies are limited by single-scale feature extraction and limited feature-level interpretability.
PURPOSE: To develop an explainable machine learning framework incorporating a wavelet-enhanced multi-scale texture feature extraction module (WEMS-TFE), and to investigate whether heel pad ultrasound texture features differ between patients with diabetes without active foot ulcers and healthy controls.
METHODS: Heel pad ultrasonography was performed in 76 patients with diabetes (without active foot ulcers) and 47 healthy controls. Ultrasound images of the heel pad were analyzed at the microchamber and macrochamber levels. The WEMS-TFE module was proposed to extract multi-scale, multi-directional texture features via two-dimensional discrete wavelet decomposition combined with the gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM). Features with significant between-group differences were selected and evaluated across seven machine learning classifiers using repeated cross-validation with participant-disjoint data partitions. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used to interpret feature contributions in a representative XGBoost model.
RESULTS: The WEMS-TFE scheme achieved the highest cross-model composite performance and robustness among the five evaluated feature extraction schemes. Cross-classifier importance analysis identified 6 features that recurred across multiple classifiers. Consistently, most of these also ranked among the important features in the XGBoost SHAP analysis, and two representative features showed clear value-dependent contribution patterns. The identified features therefore reflected group-associated image-texture differences, although their associations may be affected by residual demographic confounding.
CONCLUSIONS: The proposed framework, with the WEMS-TFE module as its core component, enables quantitative characterization of group-associated differences in heel pad ultrasound texture features. The findings provide imaging-based evidence of group-level texture differences in the heel pad and support further investigation of plantar tissue characteristics in diabetes, while acknowledging that these differences may be affected by residual demographic confounding and do not establish diabetes-specific structural changes or causal tissue mechanisms.

Title: Decreased early bystander CPR initiation despite stable overall rates: a nationwide time-to-event analysis during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Timely bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BCPR) is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). While overall BCPR rates during the COVID-19 pandemic have been inconsistently reported, BCPR initiation timing has received limited attention. This study assessed BCPR initiation within 10 min after witnessed OHCA.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used the All-Japan Utstein registry. Adults with non-traumatic, layperson-witnessed OHCA during March 11-December 31 of 2019 and 2020 were included. The primary outcome was BCPR initiation within 10 min after witnessing. Kaplan-Meier and Cox models were used for time-to-event analyses. Exploratory logistic regression examined associations between BCPR timing and 1-month outcomes.
RESULTS: Among 56,082 eligible cases (27,770 pre-pandemic; 28,312 pandemic), overall BCPR rates were stable (58.7% vs. 58.6%, p = 0.759). However, time-to-event analysis detected a modest difference in early BCPR initiation (log-rank p = 0.010), with a lower hazard during the pandemic (aHR 0.96; 95% CI 0.93-0.98). Among BCPR recipients, earlier initiation was associated with higher odds of a favorable neurological outcome at 1 month (aORs 3.27, 2.66, and 1.68 for 0-3, 4-7, and 8-10 min, respectively; reference >10 min). The pandemic period remained associated with lower 1-month survival after adjustment for BCPR initiation timing (aOR 0.86; 95% CI, 0.80-0.92).
CONCLUSIONS: Although the overall BCPR rate remained unchanged during the pandemic, time-to-event analysis identified a modest reduction in early BCPR initiation. Earlier BCPR was associated with better outcomes, but differences in its timing did not fully explain the lower survival during the pandemic.
