Title: Efficacy and Safety of Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds Versus Contemporary Drug-Eluting Stents in Coronary Artery Disease: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Trial Sequential Analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to address some limitations associated with permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES), but the comparative safety and efficacy of these scaffolds remain uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and observational studies comparing BVS with contemporary DES in patients with coronary artery disease. The primary outcome was the composite clinical endpoint at 1-year. Secondary outcomes included mortality, myocardial infarction (MI), revascularization, thrombosis, and angiographic measures. Outcomes at 2, 3, and 5 years were analyzed separately. Trial sequential analysis (TSA) was used to assess the robustness of the evidence for the primary outcome.
RESULTS: A total of 51 studies (69 reports) were included. At 1 year, BVS was associated with a higher risk of the composite clinical endpoint than DES (risk ratio (RR) 1.11, 95% confidence interval (CI 1.00-1.22)), mainly driven by increased risks of MI, target lesion revascularization, and thrombosis. In contrast, all-cause and cardiac mortality did not differ significantly between groups. TSA showed that although the cumulative Z-curve reached the required information size, the Z-score did not cross the trial sequential monitoring boundary, indicating that the evidence for the primary endpoint remained inconclusive. During mid- and long-term follow-up, BVS remained associated with higher risks of ischemic events and repeat revascularization, without a survival benefit. Angiographic analyses showed greater late lumen loss, smaller minimal lumen diameter, and greater diameter stenosis with BVS.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with contemporary DES, BVS appears to confer a higher ischemic risk without a long-term mortality benefit. Contemporary DES remains the preferred revascularization strategy.

Title: Lipoprotein(a) in calcific aortic stenosis: mechanistic insights, clinical evidence, and emerging therapies.
Abstract: Calcific aortic stenosis (CAVS) is the most prevalent valvular heart disease affecting older adults, yet no validated pharmacological intervention can halt its progressive deterioration. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] denotes a genetically regulated low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-like particle, in which apolipoprotein(a) forms a covalent bond with apolipoprotein B-100. Cumulative genetic, epidemiological, imaging and mechanistic research supports a causal role for elevated circulating Lp(a) in the initiation, and suggests a contribution to the advancement, of calcific aortic valve lesions. Lp(a) mediates valve injury mainly via preferentially transporting oxidized phospholipids (OxPL), anchoring within aortic valve leaflets, triggering endothelial activation and inflammatory cascades, as well as stimulating the autotaxin-lysophosphatidic acid (ATX-LPA) axis; collectively these signals drive osteogenic differentiation and mineralization of valve interstitial cells (VICs). Higher Lp(a) levels correlate with incident aortic valve calcification, accelerated hemodynamic deterioration, augmented calcium deposition quantified by computed tomography (CT), and elevated risks of aortic valve replacement (AVR) or all-cause cardiac death. Conventional lipid-lowering agents fail to reverse disease trajectory in patients with established CAVS. Though proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors only modestly cut Lp(a) concentrations, exploratory analyses have delivered preliminary suggestive signals for cardiovascular protection. RNA-targeted therapeutics and oral agents blocking Lp(a) assembly can reduce circulating Lp(a) by 70% up to over 95%, as demonstrated in early- and mid-phase clinical trials. Most notably, the ongoing Lp(a)FRONTIERS CAVS randomized trial is directly testing whether pelacarsen can decelerate CAVS progression, and no completed trial has yet demonstrated that Lp(a) lowering modifies CAVS disease. This narrative review summarizes Lp(a) biological characteristics, causal evidence linking Lp(a) to CAVS, together with opportunities and unresolved uncertainties surrounding Lp(a)-targeted therapeutic strategies.

Title: Lipoprotein(a) and Prognostic Nutritional Index Levels Exhibit Interactive and Joint Effects on Mortality Risk in Patients With Coronary Artery Disease: Findings From a Real-World Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Abnormal lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) levels and malnutrition are independent cardiovascular risk factors; however, the associated combined effects on mortality in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) remain incompletely understood. Thus, this study aimed to evaluate the independent and joint associations of Lp(a) and the prognostic nutritional index (PNI) with all-cause and cardiovascular (CV) mortality in patients with CAD, as well as the associated combined interaction.
METHODS: A total of 47,482 patients with CAD from the Southern China multicenter Cardiorenal Improvement II cohort (2007-2020) were enrolled. Patients were stratified according to Lp(a) levels (low: <15 mg/dL; middle: 15 to <30 mg/dL; high: ≥30 mg/dL) and PNI (high: ≥45; low: <45). The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and CV mortality. Restricted cubic splines were used to assess non-linear associations, while multivariable Cox models and Kaplan-Meier analyses were used for risk assessment; receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to compare predictive performance, and additive interaction analysis was used to evaluate joint effects.
RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 5.2 years, 5229 patients (11.01%) died from any cause and 3698 died from CV causes. In fully adjusted models, high Lp(a) combined with low PNI was associated with the highest risk of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio (HR) 1.85, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.69-2.03) and CV mortality (HR 2.20, 95% CI 1.98-2.46), compared with the low Lp(a)/high PNI reference group. The combined model achieved a higher area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve for mortality prediction than either marker alone (p < 0.05). Significant additive interactions between Lp(a) and PNI were observed for all-cause mortality (relative excess risk due to interaction, RERI 0.30, 95% CI 0.14-0.43) and CV mortality (RERI 0.32, 95% CI 0.11-0.52).
CONCLUSIONS: Lp(a) and PNI are independently associated with increased long-term mortality in patients with CAD and demonstrate a significant additive interaction. Joint assessment of Lp(a) and PNI may help identify high-risk patients with CAD at hospital discharge and may inform clinical risk stratification, optimized management, and personalized follow-up.

Title: Salvaging the forgotten valve: T-TEER as the new frontier in torrential primary TR.
Abstract: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) has historically been considered the "forgotten valve disease", but growing evidence has established its independent prognostic impact and has driven the rapid expansion of transcatheter tricuspid valve interventions. While transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) has demonstrated safety and clinical benefit in patients with secondary functional TR, evidence supporting its use in primary TR remains scarce, and surgery continues to represent the standard treatment. However, many patients with primary TR are considered ineligible for surgery because of prohibitive operative risk, creating an important unmet therapeutic need. In this Perspective, we discuss the potential role of T-TEER in selected patients with primary TR through the paradigm of a patient who developed torrential TR following iatrogenic rupture of the septal papillary muscle-chordal apparatus during cardiac device lead extraction. Owing to multiple comorbidities and prohibitive surgical risk, the patient underwent successful transcatheter repair with two PASCAL Ace devices, achieving durable TR reduction and sustained clinical improvement at one-year follow-up. Building on this experience, we review the current evidence supporting transcatheter tricuspid interventions, discuss the anatomical and procedural considerations that may enable T-TEER in selected forms of primary TR, and highlight the limitations of the available literature. We propose that carefully selected anatomical subsets of primary TR may represent an emerging frontier for transcatheter therapies, bridging the gap between guideline-directed management and individualized treatment when surgery is not feasible. Prospective studies are warranted to define patient selection criteria, procedural feasibility, and long-term clinical outcomes.

Title: Long-Term Survival and Predictive Relevance of Nocturnal Ventricular Tachyarrhythmias Requiring Appropriate Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator Therapy.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether nocturnal ventricular tachyarrhythmias (VTAs) are associated with poorer long-term survival than daytime VTAs remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association between nocturnal VTAs and long-term survival, as well as the associated prognostic relevance.
METHODS: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) recipients from the Study of Home Monitoring System Safety and Efficacy in Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device-implanted Patients (SUMMIT) registry were retrospectively analyzed using data from home monitoring transmissions. Nocturnal VTAs were defined as episodes occurring between 22:00 and 05:59, whereas daytime VTAs were defined as those occurring during the remaining 16 hours (06:00-21:59).
RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 61.7 months, 102 cardiac deaths and 187 deaths from any cause were recorded. Among 730 patients, 422 experienced VTAs, of whom 231 (54.7%) had nocturnal VTAs. Compared with patients without VTAs, those with nocturnal VTAs had a 62% higher risk of cardiac death (hazard ratio (HR), 1.62; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.02-2.59; p = 0.041) and a 2.3-fold higher risk of all-cause mortality (HR, 2.30; 95% CI: 1.50-3.53; p < 0.001). Patients with nocturnal VTAs experienced more ICD shocks (77.9% [180/231] vs. 59.2% [113/191]; p < 0.001), more electrical storms (46.8% [108/231] vs. 9.4% [18/191]; p < 0.001), and a higher VTA burden (median, 1.36 [IQR, 3.44] vs. 0.59 [IQR, 1.01] episodes per year) than those with daytime-only VTAs. Elevated nighttime heart rate and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), as well as male sex and prior atrial fibrillation, were identified as independent risk factors for nocturnal VTAs.
CONCLUSIONS: Nocturnal VTAs were not uncommon. Patients experiencing nocturnal VTAs had a higher risk of cardiac death and all-cause mortality. Monitoring the occurrence and timing of VTA episodes may be a useful tool for identifying high-risk patients.

Title: Left atrial appendage occlusion versus antithrombotic therapy in nonvalvular AF with ASCVD and prior embolism.
Abstract: Managing nonvalvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and prior embolism is challenging. This retrospective study evaluated long-term outcomes of left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) compared with oral anticoagulation (OAC) and antiplatelet therapy (APT) in primary (n = 647) and external validation (n = 570) cohorts. The primary composite outcome included recurrent ischemic stroke or systemic embolism, major bleeding, and all-cause mortality. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), risks of the primary outcome, major bleeding, and mortality for LAAO were comparable with or lower than those of OAC and APT. For recurrent embolism, competing-risk analyses showed both OAC (SHR = 3.578, p = 0.003) and APT (SHR = 2.494, p = 0.040) carried a higher risk than LAAO. Results were consistent in the external validation cohort. These findings suggest LAAO may be a reasonable option for this high-risk population, offering a lower risk of recurrent embolism and comparable risk of major bleeding relative to pharmacological therapies.

Title: Clinical, Imaging, and Genetic Characteristics of Adult Left Ventricular Noncompaction: A Single-Center Registry Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC) is a heterogeneous cardiomyopathy characterized by excessive myocardial trabeculation and a variable clinical presentation. Although advances in multimodality imaging have improved diagnostic accuracy, prospective longitudinal risk stratification frameworks remain limited.
METHODS: This single-center registry study describes the baseline clinical, imaging, electrocardiographic, and genetic characteristics of adult patients with confirmed LVNC followed at a tertiary inherited cardiac conditions clinic, enrolled both prospectively and retrospectively. Baseline assessments included demographics, clinical history, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), electrocardiography, exercise stress testing, Holter monitoring, and genetic testing. This descriptive analysis does not include a formal time-to-event outcomes analysis, which is planned for future prospective follow-up of this cohort.
RESULTS: The cohort comprised 50 adults (34 women, 16 men; mean age at diagnosis 48.9 ± 13.4 years), enrolled prospectively (n = 38) and retrospectively (n = 12). Diagnosis was established by CMR in 80% of patients (n = 40), TTE in 18% (n = 9), and CT in 2% (n = 1). Presenting features included prior cardiac arrest (n = 3), syncope (n = 10), palpitations (n = 16), and a family history of sudden cardiac death (n = 9). Baseline TTE (available in 38 patients) showed a mean left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 51.8 ± 11.8%. CMR, available for 44 patients (88% of the cohort), confirmed LVNC in all cases, with the noncompacted-to-compacted ratio (NC:C) ranging from 2.8:1 to 6.3:1 (median 4.0:1); apical hypertrabeculation was universal, and lateral involvement was present in 72.7% (32/44) of CMR-imaged patients. Among 48 patients with electrocardiogram (ECG) data, T-wave abnormalities were present in 20.8% (10/48), left bundle branch block in 14.6% (7/48), and right bundle branch block in 6.3% (3/48). Genetic testing, performed in 32 of the 38 prospectively enrolled patients, identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 53% (17/32), most commonly in TTN (34%, 11/32); the remainder had variants of uncertain significance or no identified variant. Structured follow-up data were incomplete and variably attended, with follow-up 2 assessments available in 29 of 50 patients (58%); among those retested, LVEF remained preserved or only mildly reduced (mean 51.1% and 56% at follow-up 1 and 2, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS: This single-center registry demonstrates substantial phenotypic, morphologic, and genetic heterogeneity in adult LVNC, with CMR providing the most sensitive morphologic characterization and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants identified in approximately half of genetically tested patients. Since clinical outcome events and time-to-event analyses were not assessed in this baseline dataset, these findings are hypothesis-generating rather than prognostic. Thus, structured prospective follow-up of this cohort is needed to define arrhythmic and heart failure outcomes and to refine phenotype- and genotype-directed risk stratification.
