Title: Long-Term Survival Following Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Two-Center Five-Year Analysis.
Abstract: Randomized trials have shown short-term benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but the long-term durability of survival and neurological recovery after hospital discharge remains poorly defined. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA from two academic centers (University of Minnesota, USA, and Charles University, Prague) from January 2013 through December 2022. The primary outcome was 5-year survival. Secondary outcomes included neurological status by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) and associations of age and discharge disposition with long-term outcomes. Among 728 patients treated with ECPR, 211 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 138 from Minnesota and 73 from Prague. Median follow-up was 3.9 years; 68 patients (32%) completed 5 years. No patients were lost to follow-up. Among hospital survivors, 76.9% and 67.2% were alive at 1 and 5 years, respectively, with most deaths occurring within 90 days of discharge. CPC 1-2 was present in 78.7% at discharge and remained high among survivors beyond 1 year (93.4%-94.2%). Five-year survival declined by age from 91.6% for those between 18-39 years to 52.9% for >70 years. Discharge disposition also strongly stratified long-term prognosis. Among patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA, long-term survival was substantial, with approximately two-thirds alive at 5 years with favorable CPC in most. Younger age and discharge home or to acute rehabilitation identified subgroups with particularly favorable prognosis. These findings support the long-term durability of benefit among selected patients treated within established ECPR systems of care.

Title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Pediatric Perioperative Cardiac Arrest Survival.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Perioperative cardiac arrest (POCA) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Disparities in perioperative outcomes have been reported, but whether similar differences exist following pediatric POCA remains unclear. We evaluated racial and ethnic differences in 30-day mortality after pediatric POCA.
METHOD: Within the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program for Pediatrics (NSQIP-P) registry, we identified 2646 children under 18 who underwent inpatient, noncardiac surgery (2012─2024) and experienced POCA. Race and ethnicity were categorized as Hispanic, non-Hispanic Asian, non-Hispanic Black or African American, non-Hispanic white, or other. Crude and adjusted risk ratios for 30-day mortality following POCA were estimated.
RESULTS: Among 2646 children with POCA, 47.9% (n = 1268) were non-Hispanic white, 28.2% (n = 745) non-Hispanic Black, 4.0% (n = 106) non-Hispanic Asian, 16.2% (n = 430) Hispanic and 3.7% (n = 97) Other race. Overall, 30-day mortality was 32.9% (871/2646). Mortality was similar across racial or ethnic groups (P = .72). In adjusted analyses, mortality risk did not differ significantly for non-Hispanic Black (adjusted relative risks [aRR] 1.02, P = .80), Hispanic children (aRR 1.06, P = .43), or children of other race (aRR 1.02, P = .88) compared with non-Hispanic white children. Emergent surgery (aRR 1.62, P < .001) and preoperative inotrope use (aRR 1.41, P < .001) were independently associated with increased mortality.
CONCLUSION: We found no significant racial or ethnic differences in mortality risk following POCA among children undergoing inpatient surgery. Mortality was associated with clinical and perioperative factors, including emergent surgery and preoperative inotrope use. This suggests that efforts to identify drivers of disparities in pediatric postsurgical mortality must look beyond POCA outcomes alone.

Title: Net Clinical Benefit of Continuing vs Discontinuing Anticoagulation After Atrial Fibrillation Ablation: Results from a 280,000-Patient Meta-Analysis.
Abstract: Background Oral anticoagulation (OAC) in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) reduces ischaemic stroke (IS), but increases bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage (ICH). As catheter ablation reduces AF burden and IS risk, we evaluated the net clinical benefit (NCB) of continuing versus discontinuing OAC after AF ablation. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies comparing OAC continuation versus discontinuation after AF ablation. NCB was calculated as the reduction in IS with continued OAC minus 1.5 × the increase in ICH. Results Thirty-eight studies were included (3 RCTs, 35 cohort studies), enrolling 280,415 patients, with 2.7 years' follow-up. In RCTs, there was no difference between patients on-OAC vs. off-OAC for IS, major bleeding, ICH, or NCB. In cohort studies, IS was similar, but major bleeding (OR, 3.02; 95%CI, 2.06-4.42, p<0.001) and ICH (OR, 3.65; 95%CI, 2.31-5.77, p<0.001) increased, with net clinical harm (NCB -0.46; 95% CI, -0.82 to -0.10, p=0.012). Combining all studies, IS was similar, but major bleeding (OR, 2.93; 95% CI, 2.08-4.14, p<0.001) and ICH (OR, 3.63; 95% CI, 2.34-5.63, p<0.001) were increased with continued OAC, with NCB favouring discontinuation (NCB -0.46; 95% CI, -0.77 to -0.14, p=0.004). Conclusion The benefit of OAC thromboprophylaxis is attenuated after AF ablation but contributes to bleeding, supporting consideration of OAC discontinuation post-ablation. However, this cannot be extrapolated to the highest ischaemic risk patients and, as risks are dynamic and sinus rhythm maintenance is not guaranteed, close surveillance would be essential if considering this approach.

Title: [Venous thrombosis at unusual sites].
Abstract: Venous thrombosis at unusual sites such as the upper extremity, the splanchnic and cerebral veins, and rarer ovarian, renal and retinal sites has long been managed in analogy to lower-limb deep vein thrombosis because dedicated trials were lacking. This has changed substantially. The 2023 German S2k guideline now addresses these sites explicitly, and a growing body of randomized and prospective evidence supports the use of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). For upper-extremity thrombosis, therapeutic anticoagulation is first-line and is managed according to deep vein thrombosis. A functioning, still-needed catheter can remain in situ. For splanchnic vein thrombosis, anticoagulation reduces recurrence and mortality and improves recanalization, including in cirrhotic portal vein thrombosis (Child-Pugh A/B). In cirrhotic portal vein thrombosis DOACs are possible depending on the liver function (rivaroxaban/edoxaban in Child A, apixaban in Child B, low molecular weight heparin in Child C). A JAK2-V617F screen identifies an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm before blood-count changes appear and should be part of the etiological work-up of a non-cirrhotic splanchnic vein thrombosis. For cerebral venous thrombosis, DOACs have shown to be as effective as vitamin K antagonists with fewer major, particularly intracranial, bleeds, while vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT) requires non-heparin anticoagulation. For ovarian, renal and retinal veins, robust data remains absent. This article summarizes the practice-relevant advances for the general internist, focusing on the upper extremity and the splanchnic veins.

Title: Advances in research and clinical decision strategies for anticoagulation timing in acute ischemic stroke patients with atrial fibrillation.
Abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major risk factor for acute ischemic stroke (AIS), and oral anticoagulation is the cornerstone of secondary prevention. The optimal timing of anticoagulation initiation remains controversial because of the need to balance the risks of early ischemic recurrence and hemorrhagic transformation. Recent randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses indicate that early initiation of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) is generally safe in appropriately selected patients and may reduce recurrent ischemic events without increasing the risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. However, evidence remains limited in patients with severe stroke, hemorrhagic transformation, large infarcts, or recent reperfusion therapy, in whom the timing of anticoagulation should be individualized according to clinical and neuroimaging characteristics. The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline considers early oral anticoagulation reasonable in carefully selected patients with AIS and AF, particularly those with milder stroke severity, without specifying a uniform initiation window. Clinical decision-making should integrate stroke severity, neuroimaging findings, and individual thromboembolic and bleeding risks. Overall, current evidence supports a shift from fixed delay rules toward individualized anticoagulation strategies.

Title: Low-rank matrix features and quality-controlled RR-interval models in short multilead ECGs: Matched construct validation and external rhythm comparisons.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low-rank matrix features summarize multilead ECG structure, but their incremental value beyond RR-interval features and performance across competing rhythms remain uncertain.
METHODS: We analyzed a matched PTB-XL construct-validation cohort (250 development and 100 held-out pairs). Separate RR-only and RR-plus-static models were developed using 951 age- and sex-matched pairs from PTB-XL folds 1-8 and tested without refitting in the independent, multicenter PhysioNet ECG Arrhythmia release against seven rhythm groups.
RESULTS: In the PTB-XL construct-validation analysis, held-out AUROC was 0.692 for static, 0.604 for dynamic, and 0.958 for quality-controlled RR features. Development cross-validated AUROC was 0.989 for both RR-only and RR-plus-static models. In external matched comparisons, RR-only AUROC ranged from 0.527 for AF versus atrial flutter to 0.985 versus sinus bradycardia. Adding static features changed AUROC by -0.004 (95% CI, -0.006 to -0.002) for pooled competing rhythms and +0.089 (95% CI, +0.078 to +0.100) for supraventricular tachycardia.
CONCLUSIONS: Static features showed moderate construct validity but did not add discrimination consistently beyond RR features. External performance varied by competing rhythm, with poor separation from atrial flutter. The supraventricular-tachycardia increment is exploratory and requires confirmation.

Title: β-weighted admission ECG score for pre-angiographic prediction of high thrombus burden in young STEMI: Development and internal validation.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: High thrombus burden in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is associated with impaired reperfusion and adverse outcomes. We aimed to develop and internally validate an admission-only, β-weighted electrocardiographic (ECG) score for pre-angiographic identification of high thrombus burden in young patients with STEMI.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included 761 patients aged ≤45 years undergoing primary PCI. High thrombus burden was defined as TIMI thrombus grade 4-5. The 0-7-point ECG score comprised reciprocal ST-segment depression (1 point), terminal QRS distortion (2 points), fragmented QRS (2 points), and frontal QRS-T angle >90° (2 points). Internal validation was performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples.
RESULTS: High thrombus burden was present in 349 patients. The ECG score was higher in the high-thrombus-burden group than in the low-thrombus-burden group (3 [2-5] vs. 1 [0-2]; p < 0.001). The β-weighted ECG score showed an apparent AUC of 0.769 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.758. At a cut-off of ≥3 points, sensitivity was 65.6% and specificity was 80.1%.
CONCLUSION: An admission-only β-weighted ECG score provided useful pre-angiographic discrimination of high thrombus burden without requiring laboratory results. Prospective external validation is required before routine clinical implementation.
STUDY PERIOD: This retrospective observational study included young patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction who underwent emergent coronary angiography and primary percutaneous coronary intervention between June 2014 and June 2025.

Title: The Impact of Clinical and Biochemical Frailty on Outcomes following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Frailty results from declining reserve and function and is a modifiable cardiovascular risk-factor. Despite this, there is limited evidence surrounding its role in lower-risk TAVR cohorts.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate frailty among contemporary TAVR patients, delineate the impact of biochemical and clinical frailty, and understand its additive value to existing risk-prediction tools.
METHODS: Analysis of a multicenter Australian registry. Biochemical frailty (BF) was defined as serum albumin <35 g/L and clinical frailty (CF) as a Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale ≥5. Patients meeting BF or CF criteria were categorized as frail.
RESULTS: Of the 2,661 patients, the median age 82 (IQR: 77-86), 60% male, and median STS 3.3 (2-5.2), 920 patients (35%) were considered frail. A total of 171 (19%) of frail patients fulfilled both BF and CF criteria. The frail group was older (83 vs 81, P < 0.001), more females (43% vs 38%; P = 0.016) with higher STS scores (4 vs 3, P < 0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed a stepwise increase in 12-month mortality with increasing frailty (no frailty 4% vs BF or CF 7% vs BF + CF 16%, Log-rank P < 0.001). In Cox proportional hazards regression BF or CF (adjusted HR: 1.6; 95% CI: 1.0-2.4; P = 0.033) and BF + CF (adjusted HR: 3.3; 95% CI: 1.9-5.6; P < 0.001) independently predicted 12-month mortality. Addition of frailty to STS Score improved mortality prediction (area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve: 0.608 vs 0.664; DeLong's P = 0.021), with Shapley analysis demonstrating significant contribution from frailty.
CONCLUSIONS: Frailty is common with significant implications in TAVR. Patients with biochemical and clinical frailty criteria are highest risk. Development of strategies to address frailty is critical.

Title: Clinical profile, risk factors, and one-year outcomes of atrial fibrillation in a native West African setting: Insights from the Ibadan atrial fibrillation registry.
Journal: Journal of the National Medical Association
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: We sought to describe the clinical profile, risk factors, management, and one-year outcomes of atrial fibrillation in a tertiary hospital in Nigeria METHODS: The Ibadan AF registry enrolled consecutive patients with AF from January 1, 2016, to September 30, 2023, at Nigeria's oldest and largest tertiary hospital. The CHA2DS2VASC score was used for stroke risk classification. The participants were followed up for 12 months (at one month, 6 months, and 12 months) after enrolment through clinic visits or telephone calls, and supplementary data were obtained from medical notes. Stepwise multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to identify independent predictors of each of the study outcomes from the variables that were significant in univariable analyses.
RESULTS: Three hundred and fifty-seven patients were enrolled; median age was 65 years (25th and 75th percentiles = 61.6 and 64.6 years; minimum and maximum years = 19 and 95 years), and 52.9% were male. Hypertension was the most common risk factor (80.7%), and heart failure was the most common mode of presentation (70%). Sixty-one percent of patients had permanent AF, 25.0% had persistent AF, and 14% had paroxysmal AF. Most patients (78.4%) were on oral anticoagulants. Most received rate control with beta-blockers (75%) and/or digoxin (44%), and 70% achieved adequate rate control. At the end of one-year follow-up, 251 (70.3%) were alive, 31(8.7%) were hospitalized, and 88(24.6%) died. The independent predictors of composite outcomes (rehospitalization and/or all-cause mortality) were the Kanofsky score (aHR. 0.44, [95% CI: 0.21-0.92, p = 0.028] for score of 50-70 and (aHR. 0.26, [95% CI: 0.12-0.58, p = 0.001] for score of 80-100(Reference. 0-40), socioeconomic class (aHR. 0.54 [95% CI: 0.30-0.98),p = 0.041]) for middle socioeconomic class (Reference- low socioeconomic class) and use of amiodarone (aHR.1.77 [95% CI:1.00-3.13),p = 0.049]) CONCLUSION: Hypertension is the commonest risk factor for AF in this cohort, and >80% of study participants with AF require anticoagulation. Mortality at 12 months is high due to severe structural disease and high comorbidity burden. Efforts are needed to control and treat risk factors, heart failure, and comorbidities in AF management in our setting.

Title: Associations of depression and apathy with subjective and objective autonomic measures in early Parkinson's disease.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Neuropsychiatric symptoms and autonomic dysfunction are critical non-motor features of Parkinson's disease (PD). We aimed to investigate the differential association of depression and apathy with subjective and objective autonomic profiles in patients with early PD.
METHODS: This retrospective study analyzed data from 149 early-to-mid stage PD patients (Hoehn and Yahr stage 1-3) enrolled in the hospital's Parkinsonism Registry between 2022 and 2024. Participants were evaluated using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Apathy Evaluation Scale-Self (AES-S), Scales for Outcomes in PD-Autonomic (SCOPA-AUT) for subjective symptoms, and the Composite Autonomic Severity Score (CASS) for objective physiological deficits. Multivariable regression and ANCOVA were performed using a standardized set of covariates.
RESULTS: Both depression and apathy were associated with significantly higher total SCOPA-AUT and gastrointestinal scores after adjusting for common covariates. Depression exhibited a broader association, remaining linked to the cardiovascular, thermoregulatory, and pupillomotor domains. In multivariable linear regression, higher BDI scores were independent predictors of total subjective autonomic burden and multiple sub-domains, whereas AES scores did not show independent associations when adjusted for BDI scores. Regarding objective measures, no significant associations were observed for the total CASS scores or any sub-indices after controlling for clinical and medication-related factors. These findings suggest that subjective and objective assessment tools may capture distinct facets of the autonomic clinical profile in early PD.
CONCLUSION: Depression and apathy are differently associated with the perception of autonomic dysfunction in early PD, with depression associated with a wider range of subjective distress. Neuropsychiatric status is independently associated with subjective autonomic burden beyond measured physiological deficits, supporting multimodal assessments integrating patient-reported and physiological measures.

Title: Multicenter, retrospective study of balloon valvuloplasty-associated pulmonary artery dissection in dogs with pulmonary valve stenosis.
Journal: Journal of veterinary cardiology : the official journal of the European Society of Veterinary Cardiology
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Pulmonary artery dissection (PAD) is a rare complication in dogs with pulmonary valve stenosis (PS) that undergo balloon valvuloplasty (BVP). This study aimed to describe demographic, interventional, and survival data in a cohort of dogs with PS that experienced PAD during BVP.
ANIMALS, MATERIALS AND METHODS: Fifty-three dogs were included in this retrospective, multicenter study, with medical records and available stored images reviewed.
RESULTS: Dogs that developed PAD during BVP had a median body weight of 12.5 kg (range: 1.1-50.7 kg), median age of 0.8 years (range: 0.2-8.1 years), and 30/53 (56.6%) were male. Pit Bull terriers, Pit Bull terrier mixes, and 'Bully breeds' represented 23 of 53 dogs in the study (43.4%). The median angiographic balloon diameter to pulmonary valve annulus ratio of the largest balloon utilized during BVP was 1.4 (range: 1.0-1.58). High-pressure balloons (>6 atm) were utilized in 27 dogs (50.9%). Post-BVP transthoracic echocardiographic imaging clearly demonstrated the PAD in 62.2% of dogs, while 90.3% and 84.0% of available post-BVP angiography and transesophageal echocardiographic studies did, respectively. Forty-eight dogs (90.6%) survived to discharge. Median time from BVP to last follow-up or death (if applicable) was 2.0 years (range: 0.2-10.5 years), with all 27 dogs for whom ≥1 year of follow-up data were available confirmed alive at that time.
STUDY LIMITATIONS: Retrospective study design.
CONCLUSIONS: Dogs experiencing PAD during BVP have a high likelihood of survival in the immediate and long-term periods. Immediate post-BVP imaging with angiography or transesophageal echocardiography appears more sensitive than transthoracic echocardiography for diagnosis of PAD.

Title: Age-stratified risk of major adverse cardiovascular events with JAK inhibitors in rheumatoid arthritis: A nationwide cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The cardiovascular safety of Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) compared with biological disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) and conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remains debated. We aimed to evaluate the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) among patients with RA initiating these therapies.
METHODS AND FINDINGS: We conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Taiwan National Health Insurance Research Database (2010-2022). We matched adults with incident RA into JAKi, bDMARD, and csDMARD cohorts. The primary outcome was incident MACE. We used inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs). The weighted analytic cohort included 6856 patients (814 JAKi, 1613 bDMARD, and 4429 csDMARD users). Compared with csDMARDs, overall MACE risk was lower for JAKi (aHR 0.73, 95% CI 0.54-0.99) and bDMARDs (aHR 0.60, 95% CI 0.48-0.76). While the overall MACE risk did not differ significantly between JAKi and bDMARDs (aHR 1.22, 95% CI 0.87-1.72), JAKi initiation was associated with a higher MACE risk than bDMARDs among patients with at least one cardiovascular risk factor who were aged 50 years or older (aHR 1.80, 95% CI 1.13-2.89) and 65 years or older (aHR 4.45, 95% CI 2.30-8.63).
CONCLUSIONS: Initiating JAKi or bDMARDs lowers the overall risk of MACE compared with csDMARDs alone. However, JAKi therapy carries a significantly higher MACE risk than bDMARDs in older patients with existing cardiovascular risk factors, highlighting the need for age- and risk-stratified therapeutic selection.

Title: Hyperlipidemia Management in Primary Care: A Practical Review of Risk Stratification, Guideline Directed Therapy and Emerging Lipid Lowering Treatment.
Journal: Journal of primary care & community health
Abstract: Hyperlipidemia is a leading modifiable contributor to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Early identification and evidence-based management of dyslipidemia are essential components of cardiovascular risk reduction in primary care. Recent updates in lipid management guidelines including the 2026 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association have expanded risk assessment tools, emphasized earlier measurement of lipoprotein (a), apolipoprotein B (apo-B) and coronary artery calcium (CAC), and incorporated novel lipid lowering therapy (LLT). This review provides a practical framework for primary care physicians to evaluate and manage dyslipidemia through a stepwise approach that integrates lifestyle interventions, statins, non-statin therapies and emerging agents. We summarize current evidence regarding lipid physiology, risk stratification, diagnostic strategies and guideline directed pharmacologic therapy.

Title: Multiscale temporal deep learning for ECG waveform estimation from contactless radar signals.
Abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is widely used for monitoring cardiac activity and supporting the assessment of cardiovascularconditions. Conventional ECG systems require skin-contact electrodes, which may cause discomfort and limit their suitability forprolonged monitoring. Contactless radar sensing provides a non-contact approach for capturing chest-wall movements associatedwith cardiac activity. However, ECG waveform estimation from radar signals is challenging because radar measures mechanicalchest-wall motion, whereas ECG represents electrical cardiac activity. In addition, respiratory interference, motion artifacts, phasedistortion, and inter-subject variability can affect the relationship between radar and ECG signals. This study presents a multiscaletemporal deep learning framework for ECG waveform estimation from contactless radar signals. The proposed framework combinesradar signal preprocessing, feature extraction, multiscale residual convolutional learning, bidirectional long short-term memory(BiLSTM) networks, and multi-head attention to learn temporal and local signal representations from radar-derived features. Radarin-phase and quadrature (I/Q) signals are processed through phase extraction, denoising, and feature extraction to construct theinput representation for ECG estimation. The framework was evaluated using a publicly available synchronized radar-ECG datasetcontaining 30 subjects under the resting scenario. A subject-independent evaluation protocol was used, with separate participantsassigned to training, validation, and testing subsets. Across five repeated subject-independent randomized splits, the proposedframework achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.07584, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.14261 and Pearson correlationcoefficient (Pearson r) of 0.64459. These results demonstrate the feasibility of estimating the overall temporal structure of ECGwaveforms from contactless radar measurements under resting conditions.

Title: Outcomes Associated With a WhatsApp-Based Telehealth Education Program and Remote Follow-Up on Blood Pressure, Medication Adherence, and Self-Care: Formative Quasi-Experimental Pilot Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension is a common chronic condition associated with substantial morbidity globally. In Jordan, many patients struggle with sustained medication adherence and self-management, highlighting a need for accessible care strategies. Low-cost platforms such as WhatsApp may support telehealth education and remote follow-up, although formative pilot data are needed to assess feasibility in this context.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate within-participant changes in blood pressure, medication adherence, self-care behaviors, and hypertension-related knowledge from baseline to postintervention among adults with primary hypertension who participated in a formative WhatsApp-based telehealth education program with structured remote follow-up in Jordan.
METHODS: A quasi-experimental, single-group pretest-posttest pilot study was conducted. In total, 40 adults (aged 28-60 years) with primary hypertension were recruited from a university hospital. The 8-week hybrid mobile health (mHealth) intervention involved training participants in home blood pressure monitoring, delivering daily educational multimedia messages via WhatsApp (covering diet, exercise, and medication), and conducting biweekly structured telephone consultations with a nurse and dietitian. Validated tools (Hill-Bone Scale, Blood Pressure Self-Care Scale, and Blood Pressure Knowledge Scale) and electronic sphygmomanometers were used at baseline and after the intervention. Data were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
RESULTS: All 40 participants completed the 8-week pilot and contributed paired baseline and postintervention outcome data. Postintervention scores were higher for hypertension knowledge (r=0.840; P<.001) and self-care behaviors (r=0.524; P=.001); medication adherence scores were lower, indicating better adherence (r=0.805; P<.001); and systolic (r=.434; P=.006) and diastolic blood pressure (r=.684; P<.001) were lower than those at baseline.
CONCLUSIONS: This formative single-group pilot identified favorable pre-post differences in blood pressure, medication adherence, self-care behaviors, and hypertension-related knowledge among a selected sample of adults with primary hypertension. Because there was no control group, the findings do not establish intervention effectiveness or causality and should be interpreted as preliminary evidence supporting further controlled evaluation.

Title: TAVR in Patients with Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features.
Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: For patients with moderate aortic stenosis, current guidelines recommend clinical surveillance with echocardiographic assessment every 1 or 2 years. Whether transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) will improve outcomes in these patients remains unknown.
METHODS: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate whether TAVR will result in better outcomes than clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature (i.e., a symptom or structural or functional abnormality that has been shown to be associated with faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes). The patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance. The primary effectiveness end point was a composite of death from any cause or a heart-failure event with or without hospitalization at 2 years. Superiority testing was performed in the intention-to-treat population.
RESULTS: A total of 744 patients underwent randomization: 373 patients were assigned to the TAVR group and 371 to the clinical-surveillance group. The mean age of patients was 78 years, 39.1% were women, and 45.6% were at low surgical risk. The mean aortic-valve area was 1.2 cm2, and the mean aortic-valve peak velocity was 3.3 m per second. At 2 years, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients with a primary effectiveness end-point event was 16.7% in the TAVR group and 23.9% in the clinical-surveillance group (risk difference, -7.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -13.1 to -1.3; P = 0.02 for superiority). The Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients who died from any cause was 8.4% in the TAVR group and 7.3% in the clinical-surveillance group; the estimates for a heart-failure event were 10.8% and 19.0%, respectively. The incidence of procedure-related adverse events did not differ meaningfully between the patients in the TAVR group and those in the clinical-surveillance group who underwent aortic-valve replacement.
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with moderate aortic stenosis and at-risk features, a strategy of TAVR was superior to clinical surveillance in lowering the incidence of death or a heart-failure event at 2 years. (Funded by Edwards Lifesciences; PROGRESS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04889872.).

Title: BMI Category Mobility and Changes in Cardiovascular Risk Factors Among Career Firefighters: A 6-Year Cohort Study.
Journal: Journal of occupational and environmental medicine
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To characterize BMI category mobility among male career firefighters over 6 years and examine associations between baseline BMI category and odds of exceeding CVD risk thresholds.
METHODS: A cohort of 613 male career firefighters (2013-2018) undergoing annual fitness-for-duty exams was followed. Linear mixed-effects models tested changes in BMI, body fat %, and CVD risk factors. A cumulative-link mixed-effects model tested BMI category change. Logistic regression estimated odds ratios for CVD risk thresholds at baseline and Year 5.
RESULTS: At baseline, 12%, 47%, and 40% of firefighters were healthy-weight, overweight, and obesity category, respectively. BMI category changed significantly from baseline to Year 5, and within healthy weight and overweight categories.
CONCLUSION: Upward BMI mobility occurred across weight categories; the obesity category showed no reversals, supporting CVD surveillance from career entry regardless of baseline weight.

Title: Antithrombotic Therapy After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: The SIMPLAAFY Randomized Clinical Trial.
Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Following a left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) procedure, antithrombotic therapy is administered to safely allow time for device endothelialization. However, the optimal postimplant antithrombotic regimen is unknown.
OBJECTIVE: To determine if either reduced-dose non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs) or aspirin alone are noninferior to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for the composite clinical end point of death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding through 6 months post LAAC.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This open-label, 3-group, multicenter clinical trial randomized 1857 patients between October 2024 and December 2025 at 87 US investigational sites, with the final 6-month follow-up in July 2026. Enrolled patients had nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, underwent successful LAAC, and were eligible for all 3 regimens.
INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomly allocated 1:1:1 to DAPT for 6 months followed by aspirin (n = 624), a reduced-dose NOAC for 3 months followed by aspirin (n = 620), or aspirin alone for 12 months (n = 613).
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the 6-month composite of all-cause death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding. Noninferiority was tested in the primary analysis population with a 1-sided Farrington-Manning test (α = .025). Bleeding and 45-day device-related thrombus rates were exploratory without multiplicity adjustment.
RESULTS: The cohort had a mean age of 76 (SD, 8) years, 42.9% were female, the mean CHA2DS2-VASc score was 4.2 (SD, 1.3), and 68.0% had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. The primary outcome occurred in 41 patients (6.9%) with DAPT vs 31 (5.1%) with a reduced-dose NOAC (risk ratio, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.48-1.18]; risk difference, -1.7 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, 1.2) and 20 (3.3%) with aspirin alone (risk ratio, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.29-0.82]; risk difference, -3.5 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, -0.8). Both monotherapy strategies met noninferiority criteria (P < .001 for noninferiority for both). Major bleeding was 4.5% with DAPT, 2.7% with reduced-dose NOACs, and 1.7% with aspirin alone; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 8.7%, 4.8%, and 3.8%, respectively. Device-related thrombus was observed in 3.4%, 0.9%, and 2.7%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Both reduced-dose NOACs and aspirin alone were noninferior to DAPT for 6-month outcomes after uncomplicated LAAC.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06521463.

Title: Sickness Absence in Primary Aldosteronism and References: a Longitudinal Cohort Study.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Primary aldosteronism (PA) is a common cause of hypertension and is associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity. However, its impact on work capacity remains unknown. We investigated sickness absence and disability pension among patients with PA and in matched reference groups with and without hypertension.
METHODS: A nationwide eight-year longitudinal cohort study based on linked register data, including 838 individuals with PA aged 18-67 in 2019 and two matched reference cohorts with and without hypertension. Outcomes included annual proportions of individuals with sickness absence (in spells >14 days) or disability pension, mean annual net days, and trajectories of absence days.
RESULTS: Patients with PA had a higher mean annual proportion with sickness absence than individuals with hypertension (21% (range: 18-23%) vs 17% (range: 17-19%) and those without hypertension (10% (range: 9-12%)). Mean annual sickness absence days were 27, 20, and 9, respectively. The combined mean annual number of sickness absence and disability pension days was similar in PA and hypertension (54 (range: 40-66) vs 53 (range: 50-57), and higher than in those without hypertension (25 (range: 22-29)). Trajectory analysis identified four patterns of absence days; 12% of patients with PA had persistently high absence, significantly associated with female sex, higher age, lower education, unmarried status, rural residence, cardiovascular disease, and treatment with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
CONCLUSION: PA is associated with substantial and sustained sickness absence and disability pension, comparable to that observed in hypertension and higher than in individuals without hypertension. These findings extend the clinical impact of PA beyond cardiovascular morbidity and highlight the importance of considering work capacity in clinical management.

Title: Night-Shift Work and Incident Cardiovascular Disease in Adults With Depression Across Baseline Risk Profiles: A UK Biobank Study.
Journal: Journal of occupational and environmental medicine
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether night-shift work is associated with incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) across baseline CVD risk profiles among adults with depression.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, we analyzed 52,565 UK Biobank participants with baseline depression. Night-shift work was identified from baseline and employment-history data. Cox models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) across low-, intermediate-, and high-risk profiles.
RESULTS: Of 52,565 participants, 25,360 had a history of night-shift work. Compared with participants without night-shift work, those with night-shift work had higher CVD risk in the low-risk (aHR 1.33, 95% CI 1.20-1.49), intermediate-risk (1.25, 1.17-1.33), and high-risk (1.36, 1.23-1.51) groups (interaction P=0.016).
CONCLUSIONS: Among adults with depression, night-shift work was associated with higher incident CVD risk across baseline risk profiles.

Title: Engagement-Supportive Mechanisms in Stress-Focused Digital Mental Health Interventions With Adaptive, Conversational, and Context-Aware Systems: Narrative Review.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stress is a widespread public health concern associated with cardiovascular disease, depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs), delivered through smartphones, web platforms, and wearables, offer scalable support for stress management but often struggle to sustain user engagement. Evidence describing how adaptive, conversational, and context-aware mechanisms function together within stress-focused DMHIs remains fragmented.
OBJECTIVE: This review aims to synthesize evidence on engagement-supportive mechanisms in stress-focused DMHIs, with attention to personalization; biometric feedback; just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs); gamification; AI, including large language models (LLMs); and methodological approaches to studying engagement. It also examines methodological, motivational, and experiential dimensions of engagement.
METHODS: This narrative review was informed by a structured search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2018 and April 2025, followed by an evidence update through August 2026. Eligible studies described stress-focused DMHIs or related affective support interventions reporting at least 1 engagement-supportive mechanism. Randomized controlled trials, qualitative investigations, simulation or modeling studies, and implementation studies were included. Data were extracted using a structured form capturing study characteristics, engagement mechanisms, outcomes, and alignment with the review domains. Descriptive mapping summarized study types and mechanism frequencies, while a narrative synthesis integrated behavioral, experiential, methodological, and theory-informed findings.
RESULTS: Thirty-two studies met the inclusion criteria. Randomized or microrandomized controlled trials were the most common design (n=17), followed by qualitative investigations (n=6), design or implementation studies (n=3), mixed methods studies (n=3), simulation or modeling studies (n=2), and a quasi-experimental study (n=1). Dynamic adaptation was identified in 14 studies, conversational support in 10, static tailoring in 9, social or co-design mechanisms in 9, context-aware prompting in 7, gamified reinforcement in 5, biometric-responsive adaptation in 4, and narrative immersion in 2. These mechanisms frequently overlapped within layered adaptive architectures rather than functioning as isolated engagement features. AI-enabled systems included conversational agents, LLM-supported systems, recommender systems, reinforcement learning, and computational modeling approaches. Outcomes included behavioral indicators such as adherence, retention, and prompt receptivity, alongside experiential indicators such as perceived relevance, trust, emotional support, and immersion. Evidence strength varied substantially; many AI-enabled systems contributed feasibility, acceptability, or optimization-oriented evidence rather than definitive comparative effectiveness evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Stress-focused DMHIs are increasingly adopting adaptive, conversational, and context-aware engagement-supportive mechanisms, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous and methodologically uneven. Dynamic adaptation, conversational support, and static tailoring were most frequently represented, whereas biometric-responsive adaptation, narrative immersion, and deeply integrated gamified systems were less common. AI-enabled systems may support contextual responsiveness and personalized interaction but require transparent adaptive logic, privacy safeguards, and human-centered evaluation. Future work should prioritize longitudinal, mixed methods research capable of distinguishing behavioral engagement, experiential engagement, feasibility, acceptability, and sustained stress-related outcomes.

Title: Clinical and economic burden of major lower-limb amputations attributable to peripheral artery disease in Italy: A nationwide analysis.
Abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) represents a major cause of non-traumatic lower-limb amputation and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Despite advances in medical and revascularization therapies, major amputations remain frequent, and comprehensive nationwide estimates of their clinical and hospital-related economic burden within the Italian National Health Service (SSN) are limited. The objectives of this study were to estimate the hospital-related economic burden of major lower-limb amputations attributable to PAD in Italy and to assess revascularization patterns and in-hospital mortality within the SSN. We conducted a nationwide observational study using the Italian National Hospital Discharge Database. Acute hospital discharges between 2015 and 2021 with a major lower-limb amputation and Diagnosis Related Group 113 were identified. Inpatient volumes, length of stay, and costs were estimated by amputation level. A longitudinal cohort of patients amputated between 2015 and 2017 was followed for two years before and after the index hospitalization to assess prior revascularization and in-hospital mortality using age- and sex-adjusted Cox models. A total of 26,417 PAD-attributable major amputations were identified, 75.6% of which were above-knee procedures. Cumulative inpatient expenditure reached €294 million, corresponding to over 511,000 hospital days. Only 46.0% of patients underwent revascularization before amputation. In-hospital mortality increased steeply within the first six months post-amputation and remained higher after above-knee procedures and among patients with diabetes, reaching 16-25% at 180 days and 23-34% at two years. Major lower-limb amputation remains a severe and costly outcome of PAD in Italy. Improved implementation of guideline-recommended PAD management is needed to reduce avoidable amputations and their economic burden on the SSN.

Title: Compare 30-minute automated office blood pressure vs 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring: A prospective study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is the reference standard for diagnosing hypertension (HTN), but its use in routine practice remains limited because of cost, availability, and patient burden. Automated office blood pressure (AOBP) has been proposed as a practical alternative, although its performance relative to ABPM remains uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the agreement and diagnostic performance of 30-minute AOBP compared with 24-hour ABPM and to identify optimal cut-off values for detecting ambulatory hypertension.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, 79 adults undergoing ABPM also underwent 30-minute AOBP measurement with automated readings every 5 minutes. The mean of the final six measurements was analyzed. Agreement was assessed using paired comparisons and Bland-Altman analysis. Diagnostic performance using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and agreement statistics.
RESULTS: Thirty-minute AOBP values were consistently higher than ABPM measurements. Mean differences were +6.59/ + 7.27 mmHg for systolic/diastolic BP versus 24-hour ABPM and +3.73/ + 5.16 mmHg versus daytime ABPM (all p < 0.001). Bland-Altman analysis showed acceptable group-level agreement but wide limits of agreement. Sensitivity ranged from 84% to 96% and specificity from 28% to 79%. ROC analysis demonstrated good discrimination (AUC 0.77-0.87). The highest agreement with overall ABPM occurred at a cut-off of ≥140/84 mmHg (κ = 0.624).
CONCLUSIONS: Thirty-minute AOBP showed good discrimination for elevated ambulatory blood pressure but systematically overestimated BP relative to ABPM. It may serve as a practical screening tool, although normal AOBP values cannot reliably exclude ambulatory HTN and confirmation with 24-hour ABPM remains necessary.
CENTRAL ILLUSTRATION: Diagnostic Performance of 30-Minute Automated Office Blood Pressure Compared With 24-Hour Ambulatory Monitoring.

Title: Bringing Treatment Home: Daratumumab Administration by Danish Community Nurses in Multiple Myeloma-A Mixed-Method Study.
Abstract: The expansion of home-based cancer care aims to reduce hospital burden while supporting patient-centered treatment. For patients with multiple myeloma who require long-term therapy and frequent hospital visits, community-based treatment may improve flexibility and quality of life. This prospective mixed-methods study explored the feasibility of community nurses administering subcutaneous daratumumab in patients' homes or local healthcare clinics. Nineteen patients, nine community nurses, and four hospital healthcare professionals participated in interviews or focus groups. Patient-reported quality of life was assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30. Most patients preferred home- or local-based administration, citing greater comfort, reduced travel, and a greater sense of normalcy. Community nurses and hospital professionals considered the model feasible and safe when supported by structured training, clear guidelines, and effective communication. However, medication delivery and care coordination created logistical challenges that reduced flexibility for some patients. Quality-of-life scores showed no consistent differences between home- and hospital-based treatment. Home administration should consider clinical stability, cognitive function, patient preferences, and daily routines. Successful implementation requires standardized training, clear roles, reliable communication, and efficient workflows. Home-based daratumumab should be offered as an individualized option within integrated cancer care rather than as a universal replacement for hospital-based treatment.

Title: Preoperative screening for cognitive dysfunction including dementia among the elderly.
Journal: The National medical journal of India
Abstract: Background Neurocognitive disorders are common perioperative complications in older patients, leading to a higher incidence of mortality and morbidity. Pre-existing cognitive impairment is the strongest predictor. As patients who do not have documented dementia may have mild cognitive impairment, evaluating their cognitive status before surgery is important for risk stratification and for subsequent prevention and management. We aimed to assess the magnitude of cognitive impairment and dementia among the elderly and to find out any possible correlation between various sociodemographic factors and comorbid conditions. Methods In this hospital-based, observational, crosssectional study, patients 65 years or older were screened for cognitive dysfunction using the Mini-Cog and 4 'A's test during pre-anaesthetic check-ups. Information regarding sociodemographic profiles and clinical conditions was also collected. Data were analysed using standard statistical tests. Results Most study subjects were men aged 65-70. The prevalence of dementia was 40%, possible cognitive impairment was 43.43%, and delirium was 6.29%. As age increased, the prevalence of cognitive dysfunction also increased and was higher among men, and patients belonging to lower education levels and lower socio-economic status. Significant association of cognitive dysfunction was found with age, gender, socioeconomic status, level of education, past cerebrovascular accident (CVA)/transient ischaemic attack (TIA), and myocardial infarction (Ml). Conclusion There is a significant prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia among the elderly being assessed for surgery in eastern India.

Title: Expanding non-calcaemic roles of vitamin D in therapeutics and their mechanisms.
Journal: The National medical journal of India
Abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid that has a major role in calcium homeostasis in humans. The non-calcaemic roles of vitamin D have been extensively studied in the past few decades, and it is associated with various diseases, including cardiovascular, central nervous system, respiratory, infectious, autoimmune, metabolic disorders, and carcinomas. This review aimed to analyse the available evidence on non-calcaemic roles of vitamin D. We found that most observational studies concluded that low levels of vitamin D are associated with the incidence of many diseases, and some of the interventional studies supported this by positive outcomes after vitamin D supplementation. However, most of the systematic reviews and meta-analyses concluded that vitamin D supplementation has no therapeutic benefit, although these had limitations of heterogeneity of studies and inclusion of low-quality studies. We conclude that further high-quality randomized controlled trials with vitamin D supplementation should be conducted in diseases where there is a strong association between low levels of vitamin D and disease incidence in large observation studies.

Title: Effect of topical insulin in diabetic foot ulcer healing among patients with diabetes in Asia: a systematic review.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this systematic review is to provide a comprehensive understanding on the effectiveness of topical insulin in the healing of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) in patients with diabetes in Asian countries.
METHOD: A systematic review of both observational and randomised controlled trials evaluating insulin efficacy on DFUs-but which was limited to studies in Asian countries between 2016 and 2024-was conducted. Guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses were followed. Electronic databases including PubMed, Scopus, MEDLINE and Google Scholar were searched for studies comparing insulin interventions with standard of care or other interventions, based on specific inclusion criteria.
RESULTS: A total of 16 relevant studies (out of 1132 on initial search) reporting on 1056 patients were included. Of the studies, eight reported wound healing rates in terms of reduction in wound size. Data on days of hospitalisation, number of dressing changes and insulin applications, quality of life, cost-effectiveness, and the psychological parameters of anxiety and depression, were not considered by any of the included studies.
CONCLUSION: The findings of this review provide supportive evidence that insulin was an efficient adjunct for healing DFUs. The findings identified existing evidence and gaps within it that may inform future studies in other Asian countries and beyond.

Title: Age-specific respiratory support and monitoring for acute respiratory distress syndrome: a narrative review.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) causes inflammatory alveolar-capillary injury at different ages. Age-related differences in respiratory mechanics, airway anatomy, pulmonary vascular physiology, and disease etiology limit extrapolation of diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. This review compared respiratory monitoring and support strategies across adult, pediatric, and neonatal ARDS.
AREAS COVERED: We searched PubMed for English-language human studies published from database inception through 14 August 2026 and reviewed major society guidelines. This review covers age-specific ARDS definitions, epidemiology, pathophysiology, respiratory support, adjunctive therapies, and liberation from mechanical ventilation. Adult-derived evidence supports low-tidal-volume ventilation, prolonged prone positioning for severe ARDS, selective higher positive end-expiratory pressure, and early extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for refractory disease. Recommendations for pediatric ARDS often rely on consensus or observational evidence. Neonatal ARDS management remains largely extrapolated from neonatal respiratory disorders and must account for gestational age, surfactant biology, pulmonary hypertension, and etiology.
EXPERT OPINION: Respiratory support should be age-calibrated, phenotype-informed, and reassessed for gas exchange, respiratory effort, mechanics, hemodynamics, device performance, and clinical trajectory. Physiological improvements may not translate into positive outcomes. Noninvasive support should not delay intubation in cases of failure. Standardized interventions and prospective studies must be tailored to pediatric and neonatal populations.

Title: Proteomic markers of colorectal cancer risk: results from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition.
Journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Circulating proteins are promising biomarkers of colorectal cancer risk. Most studies combine colon and rectal cancer despite their biological differences.
OBJECTIVE: To identify proteins associated with colorectal, colon, and rectal cancer risk and triangulate findings using cross-cohort confirmation and Mendelian randomisation (MR).
DESIGN: We profiled 6,402 proteins, using the SomaScan 7K assay in a case-cohort study nested within the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC; 658 colon and 319 rectal cancers). Cox models identified proteins associated with cancer risk at a false discovery rate <5%. Findings were confirmed in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study (ARIC; SomaScan; 235 colon, 36 rectal) and UK Biobank (Olink Explore; 321 colon, 164 rectal). MR and genetic colocalisation evaluated potential causality.
RESULTS: We identified 36 proteins associated with colorectal cancer, 50 with colon cancer, and 2 with rectal cancer; 20 of the 36 were also associated with colon cancer and none with rectal cancer, and no protein was associated with both sites. Seven of the 40 colon cancer proteins available in ARIC were confirmed, including COMP, MIC-1/GDF15, TFF3, and THIK. Of these, MIC-1/GDF15 and TFF3 were also confirmed in UK Biobank. COMP was inversely associated with colon cancer risk observationally and in MR analyses.
CONCLUSION: Colon and rectal cancers have different pre-diagnostic proteomic profiles, underlining the need for site-specific analyses. COMP, MIC-1/GDF15, and TFF3 were the most robustly supported biomarkers of colon cancer risk. Future work should prioritise experimental validation of these associations and use of repeated measures to define timing.

Title: [Aortic root replacement with a stentless xenograft (Freestyle®) in Iceland - indications and outcome].
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Aortic root replacement (ARR) can be performed with a stentless porcine xenograft (Freestyle®) as an alternative to the conventional Bentall-procedure, where mechanical or stented bioprosthetic are sewn into a wov-en tube-graft. We examined early and late outcomes of Freestyle®-ARR in a whole-nation cohort, focusing on indications and surgical outcomes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective analysis that included 44 consecutive Freestyle®-ARR performed at Landspitali 2002-2018. Primary outcomes were 30-day and long-term survival (Kaplan-Meier), with a median follow-up of 111 months. Secondary outcomes included early postoperative complications and late reoperations.
RESULTS: A median of three cases was performed per year (range 0-5). The most common indication was dilated aortic root (70%), followed by Type-A aortic dissection (9%) and small aortic annulus during aortic valve replacement (9%). Average age was 62 years and 65% were male. Median EuroSCORE-II was 11% (range 3-71%), cardiopulmonary bypass time 234 min. and cross-clamp time 157 min. The most common postoperative complications were new-onset atrial fibrillation (51%) and perioperative myocardial infarction (14%). Postoperative length of stay was 12 days median and 30-day mortality 14% (n=6). At follow-up, 1- and 5-year survival rates were 81% and 74%, respectively. For patients surviving the first 30 days, 5-year survival was 86%, and at long-term follow-up only three patients (7%) had undergone reoperation.
CONCLUSIONS: Freestyle®-ARR is a technically challenging operation and is associated with high short-term mortality rates compared with regular AVR. However, long term survival was favourable, and reoperations were uncommon in those surviving to discharge.

Title: From liberal to restrictive and beyond: a narrative review of red blood cell transfusion strategies in the modern era.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion remains a cornerstone of modern medicine, yet optimal transfusion thresholds continue to be debated. Historically, liberal strategies -maintaining hemoglobin (Hb) concentration above 10 g/dL- predominated, but evidence from the 1990s onward has favored restrictive approaches (Hb threshold 7-8 g/dL). This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence on restrictive versus liberal transfusion strategies published between 2021 and 2026, evaluates population-specific considerations, and explores emerging ultra-restrictive thresholds.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A structured narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar with particular emphasis on evidence published between 2021 and 2026. Evidence from randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical practice guidelines is critically discussed.
RESULTS: The 2025 Cochrane update (48 trials, >20,000 participants) provided high-certainty evidence that restrictive strategies induce a reduction in the risk or proportion of patients receiving at least one RBC transfusion by 41% without increasing 30-day mortality or major morbidity. Restrictive thresholds are safe in stable critically ill patients, in those undergoing non-cardiac surgery, and in patients with acute gastrointestinal bleeding. However, important exceptions include: acute myocardial infarction (in which liberal strategies may reduce cardiac events), neurocritical care (conflicting evidence on neurological outcomes), chronic transfusion-dependent conditions such as thalassemia (liberal strategies are disease-modifying), and hematologic malignancies (individualized approach required). Ultra-restrictive thresholds (Hb <6-7 g/dL) have emerged as a potential blood conservation tool during shortages but require further safety validation.
DISCUSSION: Restrictive transfusion strategies are safe and effective for many stable adult hospitalized patients, reducing blood product utilization without compromising outcomes. However, individualized approaches remain essential for specific high-risk populations. Ultra-restrictive strategies are promising, but these approaches should currently be considered only in selected contexts pending further safety validation.

Title: Proteomic and Metabolomic Profiling in Moyamoya Disease: A Systematic Review.
Abstract: Moyamoya disease (MMD) is a progressive cerebrovascular disorder characterized by stenosis and occlusion of the internal carotid artery branches, leading to chronic ischemia and aberrant collateral vessel formation. Despite its clinical significance, the pathophysiology is not fully understood, and identification of MMD-related biomarkers may supplement invasive digital subtraction angiography, the current gold standard for diagnosis, as well as provide additional insights into prognosis and disease progression. High-throughput metabolomics and proteomics offer potential to elucidate disease mechanisms and identify diagnostic markers. Our goal is to systematically review the current literature on metabolomics and proteomics in MMD using high-throughput methods, identify candidate biomarkers, characterize implicated pathways, and assess the diagnostic and prognostic value of molecular signatures. We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus databases through April 13, 2026, for studies analyzing serum or CSF from MMD patients using mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic resonance, or immunoassays. Studies were included if they employed case-control, cohort, cross-sectional, or RCT designs in human subjects. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts, with disputes resolved by a third reviewer. Quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. We extracted the top differentially expressed proteins or metabolites, results of any enrichment pathway analyses, and demographics information from each study. From 3071 studies identified, 31 were included after removing 1558 duplicates and excluding 1482 irrelevant studies. Recurrent differentially expressed proteins implicated inflammatory signaling (CRABP-I, PDGF-BB, IL-7, complement proteins), angiogenesis (VEGF, Ang-2, MMP-9), and cytoskeletal remodeling (FLNA, ZYX, keratins), while consistent metabolomic signatures highlighted BCAA elevation, urea cycle disruption, and lipid remodeling. Pathway analyses recurrently implicated immune activation, endothelial dysfunction, cytoskeletal reorganization, hypoxia signaling, and metabolic reprogramming. Demographically, cohorts were predominantly adult, East Asian, and bilateral MMD, with a sample-size-weighted mean age of 40.0 years. High-throughput proteomics and metabolomics identified recurring molecular alterations in Moyamoya disease, commonly identifying inflammatory signaling, pathological angiogenesis, and cytoskeletal remodeling as potential pathophysiological mechanisms. Despite predominantly good-quality studies (mean Newcastle-Ottawa Scale 6.77 ± 0.67), major limitations included small sample sizes, single-center designs, and regional specificity. Validation in larger, ethnically diverse, multicenter cohorts is essential before clinical translation of candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

Title: Echocardiographic phenotypes of opioid-induced cardiotoxicity: a narrative review.
Abstract: Opioid cardiotoxicity is an increasing clinical concern, yet its echocardiographic manifestations are heterogeneous and poorly characterized. This narrative review synthesizes available evidence, maps the principal echocardiographic phenotypes of opioid-related cardiac injury, and identifies major knowledge gaps. A structured PubMed search (January 2014-December 2024) combined opioid and echocardiographic terms without language restriction. Human and animal studies of any design assessing cardiac structure or function by echocardiography after acute or chronic opioid exposure were eligible. Of 209 records, 41 were included and grouped by dominant phenotype. No formal protocol (e.g., PRISMA) or risk-of-bias appraisal was applied. Five distinct-and often conflicting-phenotypes emerged: (1) severe, potentially reversible global left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF as low as 20%), sometimes progressing to cardiogenic shock yet normalising within 48-72 h; (2) Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, classic after withdrawal and predominantly reverse after intoxication; (3) right ventricular dysfunction with pulmonary hypertension, usually secondary to hypoxia or left-sided failure but occasionally isolated; (4) consistent cardioprotection in animal ischaemia-reperfusion models, unsupported by any prospective human echocardiographic study; and (5) a mechanically normal profile despite QTc exceeding 610 ms and torsades de pointes. Phenotypes 1-3 rest largely on case reports, and many studies are confounded by co-administered cocaine, benzodiazepines or α2-adrenoceptor agonists. Opioid cardiac effects are context-dependent, and mechanical toxicity diverges from electrical toxicity: a normal echocardiogram does not exclude lethal arrhythmia, so echocardiography and serial QTc assessment are complementary rather than interchangeable. Prospective studies with advanced imaging are needed to establish phenotype frequency and determinants.

Title: Emerging BCR::ABL1 inhibitors in chronic myeloid leukemia: current advances and future directions.
Abstract: Treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) has evolved beyond survival prolongation toward deeper molecular responses, long-term safety, and treatment-free remission. However, many patients still experience resistance, particularly with T315I and compound mutations, or intolerance to current tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), including ponatinib and the allosteric inhibitor asciminib, and cumulative toxicity during prolonged therapy remains a barrier to deep and durable responses. This review summarizes the clinical development of four emerging BCR::ABL1 inhibitors: two ATP-competitive agents, olverembatinib (a third-generation TKI approved in China) and ELVN-001 (a highly selective active-site inhibitor), and two next-generation allosteric inhibitors of the ABL myristoyl pocket, TGRX-678 and TERN-701. The data range from phase 1 studies in heavily pretreated patients to a randomized registrational study of olverembatinib and show meaningful molecular responses, including in patients with T315I mutations and after ponatinib or asciminib. The selective agents have shown mainly low-grade toxicity, whereas cardiovascular events with olverembatinib require longer follow-up. We discuss how each agent may be positioned in T315I-mutated disease, after failure of current TKIs, and potentially in earlier lines, and outline the randomized trials (POLARIS-2, ENABLE-2, and pivotal studies of TERN-701 and TGRX-678) that will show whether these agents change the sequencing of CML therapy.

Title: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic outcomes in women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy at 12 months postpartum : The PreCareFem Cohort.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk factors for later cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease. Early postpartum trajectories of blood pressure and metabolic recovery in this high-risk population are still insufficiently defined.
METHODS: A prospective, single-center, observational cohort study was conducted in the Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Women's Healthcare Prevention Program (PreCareFem) at the University Hospital St. Pölten, Austria. Participants were enrolled on presentation between 1 June 2023, and 31 March 2025. Cardiovascular and metabolic surrogate parameters, including automated blood pressure measurement, anthropometric evaluation, cardiovascular, kidney and metabolic parameters, lifestyle assessment following the components of the "Life's Essential 8", and urine albumin-creatinine ratio were assessed peripartum and at 3-6 and 12 months postpartum.
RESULTS: A total of 91 women with preeclampsia (PE; n = 66) and gestational hypertension (GH; n = 25) were enrolled. At 12 months postpartum, 31% met the diagnostic criteria for arterial hypertension (PE 29%, GH 36%), 18% for prediabetes and 3% for diabetes. More than half (52%) had LDL levels > 100 mg/dL and 32% had low HDL levels. Obesity was diagnosed in 24% of participants, 8% of women were diagnosed with CKD 12 months postpartum. Low-grade albuminuria (uACR 10-30 mg/g) was observed in 21% of women with PE compared to 8% in women with GH.
CONCLUSION: A significant number of women were diagnosed with arterial hypertension, early kidney impairment and/or metabolic abnormalities 1 year following hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. These findings highlight the need for a structured, multidisciplinary postpartum follow-up to address an underutilized opportunity for prevention of cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease.

Title: Refining ECPR candidate selection: from fixed criteria to a dynamic probability-of-benefit framework.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a rescue strategy for selected patients with refractory cardiac arrest. However, identifying patients most likely to achieve neurologically meaningful survival remains challenging. Conventional selection criteria, including age, initial rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and no-flow and low-flow duration, are clinically useful but may be insufficient when interpreted as isolated thresholds.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative review of contemporary evidence on ECPR patient selection, incorporating randomized trials, observational studies, registries, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and current guideline and consensus recommendations. Evidence was critically evaluated with particular attention to patient-level prognostic factors, arrest setting, dynamic physiological and metabolic variables, ECPR logistics, and system-level determinants of outcome.
RESULTS: Current evidence supports a multidimensional rather than single-variable approach to ECPR candidacy. Favorable arrest characteristics, potentially reversible etiology, shorter low-flow duration, and preserved physiological reserve remain important; however, chronological low-flow time should be interpreted alongside the quality and effectiveness of ongoing CPR. Dynamic information-including transient return of spontaneous circulation, lactate kinetics, arterial pH, end-tidal carbon dioxide, and hemodynamic parameters-may further refine assessment of biological viability. Frailty, comorbidity burden, cerebral perfusion, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation-related contraindications should also be incorporated into decision-making. Importantly, selection cannot be separated from system performance: Cannulation strategy, transport logistics, institutional experience, and the ability to establish extracorporeal circulation rapidly may substantially modify the likelihood of benefit. Differences between out-of-hospital and in-hospital cardiac arrest further limit the universal application of rigid eligibility criteria.
CONCLUSION: Candidacy for ECPR should be viewed as a dynamic, probability-based assessment rather than a checklist of fixed thresholds. Integrating arrest characteristics, reversibility, evolving physiology, patient reserve, and system capability may provide a more clinically meaningful framework for identifying patients most likely to achieve neurologically favorable survival after ECPR.

Title: The efficacy of additional atrial driver ablation in persistent and long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Journal: The Egyptian heart journal : (EHJ) : official bulletin of the Egyptian Society of Cardiology
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) remains the primary ablation strategy for atrial fibrillation (AF), yet its success in persistent (PeAF) and long-standing persistent AF (LS-PeAF) is suboptimal. Adjunctive ablation targeting atrial drivers has been proposed to enhance outcomes. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared PVI alone with PVI plus atrial driver ablation in PeAF and LS-PeAF.
METHODS: Comprehensive searches of PubMed, Scopus, Europe PMC, and Cochrane Library identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) enrolling adults with PeAF or LS-PeAF undergoing first-time ablation. Eligible studies compared PVI alone versus PVI plus driver ablation and trials utilizing other adjunctive ablations were excluded. Outcomes included recurrence of AF and any atrial tachyarrhythmia (ATA) beyond the blanking period, procedural parameters, and complications. Pooled analyses employed random-effects models to measure risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: Seven RCTs met inclusion criteria. Adjunctive driver ablation modestly improved freedom from AF (RR 1.16; 95% CI, [1.03, 1.31]; p = 0.01; I²=61%). However, this finding was accompanied by substantial heterogeneity and was not robust to leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. Driver ablation failed to elevate freedom from any ATA (RR 1.09; 95% CI, [0.98, 1.20]; p = 0.11; I²=47%). Procedure duration (MD 37.81 min; 95% CI, [4.42, 71.20]; p = 0.03; I²=96%), fluoroscopy time (MD 4.25 min; 95% CI, [2.83, 5.67]; p < 0.00001; I²=0%), and ablation time (MD 10.01 min; 95% CI, [0.25, 19.77]; p = 0.04; I²=95%) were significantly longer with adjunctive driver ablation. Procedural complication rates were comparable among both groups (RR 1.65; 95% CI, [0.80, 3.43]; p = 0.18; I²=20%).
CONCLUSION: Additional atrial driver ablation modestly improves freedom from AF but does not reduce ATA recurrence, prolonging procedure time without increasing complications.

Title: Acupuncture for relief of gagging in patients undergoing transoesophageal echocardiography-a randomised placebo-controlled trial.
Journal: Clinical research in cardiology : official journal of the German Cardiac Society
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gagging during transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) can make the procedure distressing and even impossible to perform. Acupuncture is suggested to relieve the gag reflex during peroral endoscopic procedures. The aim was to test whether acupuncture is better than placebo for reducing gagging in patients undergoing elective ambulatory TEE.
METHODS: Sixty patients scheduled for ambulatory TEE were included according to eligibility criteria and received either fixed intradermal needles (N = 30) or placebo needles at acupuncture points CV24 and PC6 in a random order prior to TEE. Patients and practitioners, who performed TEE procedure and assessed the outcome measures were unaware of group (acupuncture or placebo) allocation. The primary outcome was the intensity of gagging, measured using verbal rating scale (VRS-11). Secondary outcomes included the use of rescue medication, the incidence of gagging, patients' satisfaction with relief of unwanted side effects during TEE procedure, success of patients' blinding, heart rate and oxygen saturation.
RESULTS: Median (IQR) of patient's reported gagging intensity in the acupuncture group was 4 (2-8) vs. 7 (5-8) in the placebo group (P = 0.13), the gagging intensity reported by TEE-examiner was 2 (1-5) among the patients from the acupuncture group vs. 4 (2-9) in the placebo group (P = 0.06). Six patients from the acupuncture group vs. 14 from the placebo group required sedative rescue medication (P = 0.03). All other measured outcomes were comparable between the study groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Acupuncture with indwelling fixed intradermal needles may reduce the need for sedative medication in patients scheduled for elective TEE. Larger trials with improved methodology are required to verify this finding.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT03821428; registration date: January 25, 2019.

Title: P-Wave indices in the presence of atrial myxomas: a retrospective cohort analysis.
Journal: Clinical research in cardiology : official journal of the German Cardiac Society
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac neoplasm, which may cause embolisms, obstruction, and arrhythmias. Whether electrocardiographic P-wave indices carry diagnostic information for detecting atrial myxomas has not been systematically examined.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 83 patients: 39 with histologically confirmed atrial myxoma (34 left, 5 right atrial) and 44 age- and sex-matched controls. Seven P-wave indices were derived from 12-lead ECGs: duration, morphology in V1, voltage in lead I, axis, area in lead II, morphology-voltage-P-wave duration (MVP) score and dispersion. Logistic regression was used to identify possible predictors for atrial myxoma, with adjustment for age, sex, coronary artery disease, dyslipidemia, and smoking.
RESULTS: Patients' median age was 60.0 [51.0-70.0] years; 77.1% were women. Atrial myxoma had a median size of 4.1 cm [IQR 2.5; 5.6]. Patients with a myxoma showed shorter P-wave duration (100 [80; 100] vs. 100 [100; 120] ms; p = 0.005) and lower lead-I voltage (0.07 [0.05; 0.08] vs. 0.09 [0.06; 0.10] mV; p < 0.001). On univariable analysis, both predicted tumor presence. Entered together, only voltage remained independently (OR 0.76 per 0.01 mV, 95% CI 0.63-0.91, p = 0.003) associated with atrial myxoma; duration became borderline due to collinearity (p = 0.078). After full adjustment, voltage remained robust (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.55-0.89, p = 0.004). Within the tumor group, a larger maximal tumor diameter was associated with lower lead-I voltage (Spearman ρ =  - 0.32; p = 0.044).
CONCLUSIONS: ECG analysis of patients with atrial myxoma revealed reduced P-wave voltage in lead I, with relatively short P-wave duration. Reduced P-wave voltage in lead I was an independent predictor after full adjustment for cardiovascular comorbidities and may serve as a novel, easily available diagnostic adjunct for atrial mass lesions.

Title: Development and Validation of a Nomogram for Predicting Preoperative Venous Thromboembolism in Patients With Lower Extremity Fractures: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
Journal: Clinical and applied thrombosis/hemostasis : official journal of the International Academy of Clinical and Applied Thrombosis/Hemostasis
Abstract: BackgroundPatients with lower extremity fractures (LEF) are at high risk of preoperative venous thromboembolism (VTE). However, existing risk assessment models are not specifically developed and validated for this population.ObjectiveTo develop and validate a prediction model for preoperative VTE in emergency LEF patients, and to compare the performance of traditional logistic regression (LR) with that of machine learning (ML) algorithms.DesignRetrospective cohort study.SettingPeking University Shenzhen Hospital, China.Participants486 patients with LEF admitted between January 2022 and July 2025.MethodsTwo modeling strategies were compared: 1) a traditional LR nomogram using backward stepwise selection, and 2) nine ML algorithms with Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO)-based feature selection.
