This study evaluates the effectiveness of U-Net architectures integrated with different pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) backbones for automated lung segmentation and lung cancer classification in chest CT images, with an emphasis on rigorous, leakage-free validation and cross-institution generalizability relevant to clinical practice.
METHODS: A balanced internal dataset of 832 chest CT images (416 cancerous and 416 non-cancerous cases, NIDCH, Bangladesh) was preprocessed using Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) and resized to 224 × 224 pixels. U-Net models with three CNN backbones (VGG16, ResNet50, and Xception) were implemented for lung segmentation, with pseudo-labels verified against expert-annotated masks. A standalone CNN and three hybrid classifiers combining CNN feature extraction with machine learning algorithms (Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting) were then evaluated, alongside a Vision Transformer baseline. All models were assessed using subject-level fivefold cross-validation, followed by fully independent external testing on a second, structurally distinct dataset (IQ-OTH/NCCD; 110 subjects) without retraining. Performance was measured using Dice coefficient, IoU, accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC, with 95% confidence intervals and statistical significance testing.
RESULTS: For segmentation, U-Net with the Xception backbone achieved the best overall performance (Dice: 0.9581 ± 0.0104; IoU: 0.9163 ± 0.0167). For classification, the CNN + SVM hybrid model achieved the highest internal cross-validation accuracy (98.21% ± 0.68%) and AUC (0.9881 ± 0.0041), significantly outperforming the standalone CNN (p = 0.041), and retained the strongest performance under external validation (92.73% accuracy), with the smallest accuracy drop among all evaluated models. Ablation analyses confirmed substantial contributions from CLAHE preprocessing and U-Net segmentation, and Grad-CAM analysis showed that segmentation constrains classifier attention to anatomically plausible lung regions.
CONCLUSION: Integrating U-Net segmentation with hybrid CNN-based classification provides an accurate and reasonably generalizable framework for lung cancer detection, offering a methodological foundation for future clinically oriented computer-aided diagnosis research, pending prospective, multi-institution validation.

Title: Sex-specific adverse neonatal outcomes and umbilical cord arterial ph at birth: a population-based cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Biological sex may influence neonatal vulnerability to adverse perinatal outcomes, but sex-related differences in these outcomes remain underexplored. Male neonates may be more susceptible to perinatal asphyxia, metabolic acidosis, preterm birth, and morbidity, possibly due to sex-specific placental differences and inflammatory responses. Umbilical cord arterial pH (UApH) < 7.05 is used in Sweden to define neonatal acidemia, associated with poor outcomes. This study aimed to investigate the association between neonatal sex and adverse outcomes, focusing on UApH.
METHODS: This retrospective multicenter cohort study used data from the Swedish Perinatal Revision South Register (1995-2015). The cohort included live-born, singleton, vaginal births. Neonatal and maternal data were extracted, and logistic regression models compared outcomes between male and female neonates, adjusting for maternal age, gestational age, and birth weight.
RESULTS: Among 87 840 neonates, 51.6% were male. Male neonates had significantly higher adjusted odds of adverse outcomes compared with females: UApH < 7.05 (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.07-1.30; P < 0.001), Apgar score < 7 at 5 min (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.14-1.56; P < 0.001), CPAP use (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.46-1.87; P < 0.001), NICU admission (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.43-1.60; P < 0.001), hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.29-3.90; P = 0.002) and central nervous system disease (OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.30-1.76; P < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Male neonatal sex was associated with several adverse perinatal outcomes, including acidemia and neurological complications. These findings contribute to the understanding of sex-related differences in neonatal vulnerability and warrant further investigation.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

Title: Primary care use and kidney transplant outcomes among patients on hemodialysis - a cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Kidney transplantation is the optimal treatment for kidney failure, but whether primary care use among those on dialysis is associated with increased rates of kidney transplantation is unknown.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using United States Renal Data System (USRDS) and Medicare Parts A, B, and D claims to estimate the association between any primary care use (vs none) and both kidney transplantation and "active" kidney transplant waitlisting. Primary care use was defined as ≥ 1 outpatient visit to a family, general, geriatric, or internal medicine provider from January 1st, 2018 to December 31st, 2018. Patients were followed January 1st2019 until December 31st2020.
RESULTS: We identified 74,028 (60%) and 48,794 (40%) Medicare beneficiaries with and without primary care use. After 2 years of follow-up, the sHR for kidney transplantation was 1.11 (95% CI 1.05-1.17; 2 year-incidence 5.3% vs 4.8%). Among patients not already waitlisted, primary care use was associated with increased "active" kidney transplant waitlisting (sHR 1.19, 95% CI 1.12-1.27; 2-year incidence: 4.3% vs 3.6%). Medical testing was also higher: mammogram sHR 1.30 (95% CI 1.25-1.35), colonoscopy sHR 1.28 (95% CI 1.22-1.33), and transthoracic echocardiography sHR 1.28 (95% CI 1.25-1.31). Among patients who ultimately underwent kidney transplantation, medical testing was similar between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: In US Medicare beneficiaries receiving hemodialysis, primary care use was associated with higher rates of kidney transplantation and medical testing. Because the completed medical testing was similar among all patients who ultimately received a transplant, these findings suggest that primary care use may be linked to more timely completion of transplant-related evaluation steps.

Title: Evaluation of plasma glucocorticoid receptor beta levels and intraocular pressure elevation during topical dexamethasone use after photorefractive keratectomy.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to investigate the association between plasma glucocorticoid receptor beta (GR β) levels and steroid-induced ocular hypertension in patients undergoing photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), along with selected autoimmune markers.
METHODS: Patients who underwent PRK and used topical dexamethasone were evaluated on the 21st postoperative day. Demographic data, medical history, preoperative and postoperative refractive values, pachymetry, and intraocular pressure (IOP) were recorded. Corrected IOP values after laser treatment were documented. 30 patients with ocular hypertension (Group 1) and 20 with normal IOP (Group 2) were compared for plasma GR β levels and autoimmune markers including rheumatoid factor (RF), antinuclear antibody (ANA), and anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and logistic regression analysis were performed to evaluate the discriminatory ability and association of GR β levels with postoperative ocular hypertension.
RESULTS: In Group 1, pre-laser IOP increased from 14.34 ± 2.64 to 20.10 ± 5.03 mm Hg post-laser. The mean cIOP, as per pachymetry post-laser, was 27.84 ± 4.5. Control group mean IOP values before and after laser were 13.42 ± 2.57 mmHg and 11.81 ± 2.52 mmHg, respectively. Corrected IOP, according to pachymetry post-laser, was 17.67 ± 3.14. Pre-laser IOP values did not differ significantly between the groups (p = 0.227), whereas both post-laser IOP and corrected post-laser IOP values were significantly higher in Group 1 compared to controls (p < 0.001 both). RF values were normal in both groups, and ANA/Anti-dsDNA levels showed no significant differences (p = 0.229, p = 0.28 respectively). GR β levels differed significantly (p = 0.003), with means of 38.32 ± 8.53 in Group 1 and 66.23 ± 37.91 in Group 2. ROC analysis showed moderate discriminatory ability of GR β levels (AUC 0.76), with an optimal cut-off value of 41.39 pg/mL providing 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity. In univariable logistic regression analysis, higher GR β levels were associated with a lower likelihood of postoperative IOP elevation.
CONCLUSION: Plasma GR β levels may be associated with steroid-induced ocular hypertension in patients using topical steroids. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, and larger prospective studies are required to confirm their clinical relevance, establish clinically relevant cut-off values, and determine whether GR β has predictive value.

Title: The application of brain-computer interface combined with neuromodulation for stroke upper-limb rehabilitation: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: In conventional rehabilitation, upper-limb recovery in patients with stroke is slow and limited. Motor Imagery-Based Brain-Computer Interface (MI-BCI) may promote cortical plasticity by translating brain signals into commands to control external devices; however, the effects of different intervention approaches remain unclear.
METHODS: This study followed the PRISMA 2020 statement and searched PubMed, EBSCO, Web of Science, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) reporting outcomes related to upper-limb function or activities of daily living. Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) and Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) were used to assess risk of bias and confidence in the evidence. Network meta-analysis was conducted using the network and mvmeta modules in Stata 18.0 to assess heterogeneity, network consistency, robustness of the results, and publication bias.
RESULTS: A total of 49 studies involving 2,209 participants and 13 intervention strategies were included. For the Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Upper Extremity (FMA-UE), interventions showing relatively favourable effects included MI-BCI combined with transcranial ultrasound stimulation and functional electrical stimulation (FES) (MD = 17.65, 95% CI: 6.88 to 28.43), MI-BCI combined with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and rehabilitation robotics (ROB) (MD = 14.22, 95% CI: 2.98 to 25.47), and MI-BCI combined with transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) and ROB (MD = 13.59, 95% CI: 6.90 to 20.28). For the Action Research Arm Test (ARAT), favourable interventions included MI-BCI combined with ROB and tDCS (MD = 17.26, 95% CI: 5.96 to 28.55) and MI-BCI combined with FES (MD = 14.94, 95% CI: 9.10 to 20.78). For the Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), MI-BCI combined with ROB showed the largest effect (MD = 10.72, 95% CI: 9.44 to 17.18). For the Modified Barthel Index (MBI), favorable interventions included MI-BCI combined with tDCS and ROB (MD = 20.40, 95% CI: 11.21 to 29.60), MI-BCI combined with rTMS and ROB (MD = 19.46, 95% CI: 9.33 to 29.59), and MI-BCI combined with intermittent theta-burst stimulation and ROB (MD = 18.24, 95% CI: 5.93 to 30.55). Overall, the network evidence showed no obvious inconsistency; between-study heterogeneity was within an acceptable range, and no clear publication bias was detected.
CONCLUSION: Some non-invasive MI-BCI combined interventions like neuromodulation, ROB, or FES might improve upper-limb function and daily activities in stroke patients. However, rankings don't imply clinical importance. Due to small samples, limited evidence, and differences, these findings need confirmation in larger trials.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Systematic Review; Network Meta-Analysis

Title: Physiological monitoring and physiology-informed strategies in cardiac arrest: current evidence and clinical translation.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite advances in cardiac arrest management, survival with favorable neurological outcomes remains limited. Physiological monitoring may complement standardized resuscitation by providing real-time information about circulatory effectiveness, reversible causes, and treatment responses. However, whether physiology-guided interventions improve patient-centered outcomes remains uncertain. This narrative review examines the current evidence and clinical applicability of physiological monitoring during resuscitation, physiology-informed rescue strategies, and individualized post-cardiac arrest care.
MAIN BODY: During cardiopulmonary resuscitation, invasive arterial pressure monitoring, waveform capnography, and echocardiography provide complementary information about the circulation generated by chest compressions and potential mechanisms of resuscitation failure. Although observational and experimental studies support their physiological relevance, no adult diastolic pressure target or pressure-guided vasopressor strategy has been validated to improve survival or neurological recovery. Recent randomized trials of transesophageal echocardiography have demonstrated physiological or procedural effects without establishing clinical benefit. Among rescue strategies, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation has yielded inconsistent results across randomized trials, with potential benefits dependent on patient selection, intervention timing, and system capabilities. Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta has not improved clinical outcomes in randomized evaluation, while head-up resuscitation remains investigational. Following the return of spontaneous circulation, randomized trials have challenged the benefits of uniformly higher blood pressure and oxygenation targets, mild hypercapnia, and deeper or prolonged temperature control. Individualized approaches incorporating cerebral autoregulation, venous congestion, and cardiopulmonary physiology are physiologically appealing but lack prospective validation.
CONCLUSION: Physiological assessment may complement established resuscitation algorithms by refining clinical decisions during and after cardiac arrest. However, improvements in physiological measurements should not be equated with improved patient outcomes. Future trials should determine whether predefined, physiology-guided treatment strategies improve survival and neurological recovery.

Title: Cardiovascular adaptation to spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension during scheduled cesarean section: the paradigm of ionized calcium and nitric oxide in a prospective cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Maternal arterial hypotension occurs in 55-90% of cesarean sections performed under spinal anesthesia. While sympatholysis and aortocaval compression are conventional explanations, refractory cases suggest possible biochemical contributors beyond sympatholysis. We hypothesized that an acute deficit in ionized calcium coupled with endothelial mediator overproduction may constitute a "double lock" mechanism that contributes to hemodynamic decompensation. This prospective observational study examined these associations.
METHODS: A prospective, single-center analytical study was conducted from June 2025 to February 2026 at the Centre Hospitalier d'Essos, Yaoundé, enrolling 80 ASA I-II parturients undergoing elective cesarean section under spinal anesthesia. Hemodynamic parameters (SBP, DBP, MAP, HR, SpO₂), plasma electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, iCa²⁺), and vasoactive mediators (nitric oxide [NO], prostaglandin I₂ [PGI₂]) were measured at baseline (T0) and 10 min post-induction (T1).
RESULTS: Hypotension was confirmed in 78% of participants. MAP fell by 23% (92.4 ± 8.1 to 71.2 ± 9.5 mmHg; p < 0.001). Ionized calcium dropped significantly below the critical threshold (1.18 ± 0.06 to 0.98 ± 0.04 mmol/L; p < 0.01), correlating strongly with SBP decline (r = 0.72; p < 0.01). NOₓ increased by 37.9% and PGI₂ by 25.3% (both p < 0.01). Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ remained stable.
CONCLUSION: Spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension in parturients was associated with concurrent acute ionized calcium reduction and elevated vasoactive mediators (NOₓ and PGI₂), consistent with a "double lock" hypothesis. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating. They support prospective interventional investigation of ionized calcium and vasoactive mediators as contributors to hemodynamic decompensation during spinal anesthesia for cesarean section.

Title: Association between PM2.5 and its chemical components exposure and heart disease risk: a longitudinal study from China.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Air pollution, particularly fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and its chemical components, poses a significant threat to public health. However, the association between these pollutants and heart disease risk, have not been thoroughly investigated, especially regarding differential effects across various populations and regions.
METHODS: we analysed 8,172 participants from 123 cities across China. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to assess the association between PM2.5 and its major chemical components (sulfate [SO₄²⁻], nitrate [NO₃⁻], ammonium [NH₄⁺], organic matter [OM], and black carbon [BC]) with heart disease risk. We constructed three progressively adjusted models, employed Weighted Quantile Sum regression to evaluate the composite effects of pollutant mixtures, used restricted cubic splines to explore dose-response relationships, and calculated Population Attributable Fraction. Additionally, stratified analyses were conducted to explore effect modification by age, gender, body mass index (BMI), residence, geographic region, smoking status, and drinking status.
RESULTS: The study found significant associations between PM2.5 and all its major chemical components with heart disease risk (p < 0.001). In the fully adjusted model (Model 3, adjusted for age, gender, body mass index, marital status, retirement status, residence, geographic region, education level, sleep duration, smoking, and drinking), each 1 µg/m³ increase in PM2.5 concentration was associated with a 2.7% increase in heart disease risk (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.027, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.022-1.032). Among the chemical components, BC showed the largest estimate per 1 µg/m³ increase associated with a 38.1% increase in risk (HR = 1.381, 95% CI: 1.266-1.506). All pollutants exhibited non-linear dose-response relationships with heart disease risk (p for nonlinear < 0.001). Geographic region and BMI were important effect modifiers, with southern residents and overweight individuals showing increased stronger associations to air pollution-related heart disease risks. The PAF of heart disease due to PM2.5 was 2.63%.
CONCLUSION: PM2.5 and its chemical components are significantly associated with heart disease risk, with notable differences in impact magnitude across components. BC showed the strongest association with heart disease risk. Southern residents and overweight individuals showed increased stronger associations to air pollution-related heart disease risks.

Title: Association of the C-reactive protein-triglyceride-glucose index with adverse cardiovascular outcomes in patients with acute coronary syndrome and type 2 diabetes: findings from an observational cohort study in China.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The C-reactive protein-triglyceride-glucose index (CTI), which integrates inflammation, lipid metabolism, and glucose metabolism, has emerged as a composite biomarker for metabolic and cardiovascular disease. This study aimed to evaluate the association between CTI and major adverse cardiovascular and cerebral events (MACCEs) in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and to determine whether CTI adds prognostic information beyond conventional clinical variables and its individual components.
METHODS: This single-center observational cohort study included 5,472 patients with ACS and T2DM treated at the Cardiovascular Centre of Beijing Friendship Hospital from January 2013 to January 2021. CTI was calculated as 0.412 × ln(C-reactive protein [mg/L]) + ln(triglyceride [mg/dL] × fasting plasma glucose [mg/dL]/2). The primary endpoint was MACCEs, defined as a composite of all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, and ischemia-driven revascularization. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox regression were supplemented by comparisons of CTI, the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, and ln(CRP), Harrell C-index, time-dependent area under the curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), calibration, decision curve analysis, ACS-subtype analyses, multiple imputation, proportional-hazards diagnostics, landmark analyses, and competing-risk analyses.
RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 3.04 (IQR: 1.07-5.02) years, 1,075 MACCEs occurred. In univariable Cox analysis, each 1-unit increase in CTI was associated with a higher risk of MACCEs (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.17-1.32; P < 0.001). After multivariable adjustment, CTI remained independently associated with MACCEs (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.17-1.36; P < 0.001). When analyzed by quartiles, compared with Q1, the multivariable-adjusted HRs (95% CIs) were 1.09 (0.90-1.33) for Q2, 1.44 (1.19-1.74) for Q3, and 1.75 (1.43-2.14) for Q4. Per 1-SD increase, the adjusted HRs were 1.27 (1.18-1.36) for CTI, 1.10 (1.02-1.17) for TyG, and 1.29 (1.20-1.39) for ln(CRP). Adding CTI to the clinical model increased the C-index from 0.688 to 0.694 and the 3-year AUC from 0.727 to 0.737, with an NRI of 0.293 and an IDI of 0.009. The corresponding ln(CRP) model achieved a C-index of 0.698 and a 3-year AUC of 0.744. Associations were consistent across UAP, NSTEMI, and STEMI (P for interaction = 0.59).
CONCLUSION: CTI was independently associated with an increased risk of MACCEs in patients with ACS and T2DM and provided modest incremental prognostic information beyond conventional clinical variables. However, its discriminatory performance was not clearly superior to ln(CRP) alone or to jointly modeled ln(CRP) and TyG. CTI should therefore be considered an adjunctive admission biomarker rather than a replacement for established clinical assessment.

Title: The effects of oral magnesium supplements on vascular and endothelial function: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Magnesium has been suggested to play a role in cardiovascular health through its effects on endothelial function, vascular stiffness, and blood pressure. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to update and evaluate the effect of magnesium supplementation on vascular function and cardiometabolic outcomes in adults.
METHODS: A systematic search based on PRISMA 2020 guidelines was conducted on PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov up to 23 April 2026 to include randomized placebo-controlled trials assessing the effects of magnesium supplementation on flow-mediated dilation (FMD), pulse wave velocity (PWV), and carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT), and as secondary outcomes for serum magnesium levels and systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Random-effect model, subgroup analyses (dose, duration, formulation), meta-regression, sensitivity analyses, and publication bias assessment were performed as well.
RESULTS: A total of twelve randomized controlled trials comprising 389 patients in the magnesium group and 276 patients in the placebo group were included in this study. Magnesium supplementation showed no significant overall effect on FMD (MD = 2.86; 95% CI: - 1.31 to 7.03; p = 0.18). However, doses > 400 mg/day significantly improved FMD (MD = 8.32; 95% CI: 3.45 to 13.19; p < 0.01), but it included 2 studies. CIMT was significantly reduced (MD = - 0.08; 95% CI: - 0.15 to - 0.01; p = 0.03), while PWV showed no significant change (MD = - 0.17; 95% CI: - 0.60 to 0.25; p = 0.43). Serum magnesium increased significantly (MD = 0.05; 95% CI: 0.02 to 0.07; p < 0.01) in overall and in subgroups, whereas blood pressure reductions were not statistically significant (p > 0.3). Meta-regression showed significant modifying effects of higher magnesium doses and higher baseline SBP on FMD, and a significant inverse correlation of baseline body mass index (BMI), baseline PWV, and baseline CIMT on FMD.
CONCLUSION: Magnesium supplementation may improve endothelial function and reduce CIMT, particularly at higher doses, although it should be interpreted cautiously because of limited studies and inconsistent effects on arterial stiffness and blood pressure. Further large-scale trials are required to confirm optimal dosing strategies and clinical benefits.

Title: Upregulation of miR-200b-3p serves as a diagnostic biomarker for coronary atherosclerosis and regulates the oxidized low-density lipoprotein cholesterol-induced dysfunction of vascular smooth muscle cells.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: MicroRNAs that are abnormally expressed in coronary atherosclerosis (CAS) have gradually been discovered due to their unique advantages.
OBJECTIVE: Assessing the value of miR-200b-3p in CAS.
METHODS: The level of miR-200b-3p and RAP1B in CAS (n = 103) and healthy (n = 77) subjects was analyzed by RT-qPCR. The role of miR-200b-3p in CAS was determined through the ROC curve, correlation, and multivariate logistic regression analysis. Downstream targets of miR-200b-3p were screened by online databases. A dual-luciferase reporter assay evaluated the regulatory relationship between miR-200b-3p and RAP1B. An ox-LDL-induced human vascular smooth muscle cell (HVSMC) model was used to explore the potential mechanism of the miR-200b-3p/RAP1B axis in CAS progression.
RESULTS: The expression of miR-200b-3p was upregulated in the CAS group compared with the HC group and showed a diagnostic value in distinguishing CAS from healthy participants. The miR-200b-3p expression was correlated with TG, TC, LDL-C, HDL-C, coronary artery stenosis and calcification, and predicted the risk of CAS development. RAP1B was a target of miR-200b-3p and negatively correlated with the level of miR-200b-3p. In ox-LDL-induced HVSMCs, upregulated miR-200b-3p expression and downregulated RAP1B expression were observed. The silence of miR-200b-3p mitigated the ox-LDL-treated HVSMC injury through suppressing cell proliferation, migration, inflammation (IL-6, TNF-α), and calcification (Ca2+, ALP activity) in HVSMCs by targeting RAP1B.
CONCLUSIONS: Upregulation of miR-200b-3p served as a biomarker in diagnosing CAS. Upregulated miR-200b-3p expression might be involved in CAS progression through promoting the ox-LDL-stimulated vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) injury via regulating RAP1B.

Title: Management and Outcomes in Traumatic Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Traumatic cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (tCVST) is a rare complication of head trauma associated with increased mortality. Unlike in non-traumatic CVST, there are no consensus guidelines to direct the management of tCVST. Anticoagulation is often used to prevent intracranial complications; however, concurrent traumatic brain injury (TBI) and other injuries complicate treatment decisions, and its clinical benefit remains uncertain. This study describes the epidemiology, management, and clinical and radiographic outcomes of tCVST.
METHODS: This is a retrospective single-center cohort study from a level 1 trauma center in Melbourne, Australia. Patients were identified from the Alfred Health Trauma Registry and hospital coding data between 1 January 2010 and 30 June 2024. Venous imaging was reviewed by two neuroradiologists to confirm tCVST diagnosis and thrombus characteristics. Primary outcomes were defined as discharge destination, with sinus recanalization on follow-up imaging as a secondary outcome.
RESULTS: tCVST was confirmed in 138 patients with an incidence of 0.9% in the TBI population and an all-cause inpatient mortality of 10.9% (15 patients). Anticoagulation was used in 78 patients (56.5%) and commenced a median of 5 days after diagnosis [interquartile range (IQR) 2-9]. Patients with anticoagulation generally had less severe traumatic injury, as measured by Injury Severity Score (ISS) and admission Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), but were more likely to have occlusive thrombosis. Among 123 patients who survived to hospital discharge, 93 underwent follow-up venous imaging from day 14, with complete recanalization in 57% by final available imaging. Occlusive thrombosis and multiple sinus involvement were associated with poorer recanalization, while no association between anticoagulation and recanalization was identified.
CONCLUSIONS: Traumatic CVST is a rare complication of head injury with multiple confounders influencing outcomes and uncertain optimal management. Clinical benefit of anticoagulation in this cohort requires further investigation.

Title: Efficacy and Safety of Alteplase Use for Venous Catheter Thrombosis in Pediatric Patients-a Single Center Study.
Journal: Pediatrics international : official journal of the Japan Pediatric Society
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Urokinase is used as a thrombolytic agent to treat catheter thrombosis. However, since 2022, the supply of urokinase has diminished, and we have been using alteplase as an alternative, although its use for treating catheter thrombosis is off-label in Japan.
METHODS: We performed a single-center, retrospective study on pediatric patients with central venous catheters (CVCs), peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs), and central venous ports (CVPs) who received alteplase for catheter thrombosis at our facility (May 2023-October 2025). Treatment involved filling the catheter (volume: 1-1.5 mL) with 600,000 U/mL (1 mg/mL) of alteplase solution and leaving it for approximately 40 min. Efficacy was evaluated as follows: (1) success on the first dose, (2) success after two or three doses, or (3) no success. (1) and (2) were defined as effective.
RESULTS: We evaluated 84 alteplase administrations in 31 patients (CVCs: 47, PICCs: 27, CVPs: 10). Success on the first dose was achieved in 55% of cases and success after two or three doses in 20% of cases, resulting in an overall efficacy rate of 75% (CVCs: 72%, PICCs: 93%, CVPs: 40%). No adverse events were observed.
CONCLUSIONS: Alteplase was generally effective for treating catheter thrombosis. However, results suggest that it is less effective in CVPs than in CVCs and PICCs, and a larger sample size is necessary for confirmation. We recommend that alteplase be approved for treating catheter thrombosis in Japan.

Title: Topographic and layer-specific mapping of anterior scleral complex thickness using anterior segment OCT: an anatomical reference with potential surgical relevance.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: To provide a layer-specific surgical atlas of the anterior scleral complex and link the AS-OCT anatomy to the tissue planes and entry zones used during glaucoma filtration surgery, scleral-fixated IOL implantation, intravitreal injection and ocular surface surgery.
METHODS: This prospective cross-sectional study included 120 healthy Turkish volunteers. Thicknesses of the scleral stroma, episclera, Tenon's capsule and conjunctiva were measured at 1, 2, 3 and 4 mm from the scleral spur in four quadrants using wide-angle anterior segment optical coherence tomography with rectus muscle visualization. Measurement reliability was assessed using the ICC, SEM, TEM and repeatability coefficient.
RESULTS: The mean age of participants was 42.74 ± 15.31 years; 72.5% were female. Layer-specific boundaries of all four tissues were feasible, with most parameters demonstrating good to excellent reliability. Notably, certain measurements of the thickness of the medial Tenon's capsule were significantly greater in females. Scleral stromal and episcleral thickness generally increased with age across most quadrants. The thickness of Tenon's capsule generally decreased with age. Conjunctival thickness changes were quadrant-specific, with a significant increases in the inferior and medial quadrants with age. Topographical analysis revealed that scleral stromal thickness progressively decreased toward the periphery, whereas episcleral thickness generally increased.
CONCLUSION: Beyond establishing normative AS-OCT measurements, this study introduces anterior scleral anatomy into a potential clinically relevant surgical reference framework. The layer-specific topographical atlas and age-related remodeling patterns describe the tissue characteristics encountered at commonly used surgical locations and may inform surgeons in selecting flap depth, fixation sites, dissection planes and injection zones according to patient age and quadrant-specific anatomy.

Title: Anticoagulation and All-Cause Mortality in Adults Aged 80 Years and Older with Atrial Fibrillation: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The benefits and risks of anticoagulation therapy in patients aged ≥ 80 years with atrial fibrillation (AF) remain underexplored, as this population is underrepresented in randomized clinical trials. We evaluated mortality and bleeding outcomes associated with anticoagulation use in this population.
DESIGN: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using MDClone, a synthetic electronic health record database from a large US health system, including 45,305 patients aged ≥ 80 years with AF after excluding those with mitral stenosis, mechanical heart valves, cirrhosis, or end-stage renal disease. Patients were categorized as continued, initiated, discontinued, or never anticoagulated. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 30 days, 6 months, 1 year, and 5 years; secondary outcomes were ischemic stroke, gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB), and intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). To address immortal time bias, the primary analysis used a time-varying Cox model, complemented by a 90-day landmark analysis and propensity score matching.
KEY RESULTS: Patients who continued anticoagulation had lower 1-year mortality than those never anticoagulated (8.7% vs 17.7%; p < 0.001). In the time-varying Cox model, anticoagulation was associated with a 25% lower hazard of mortality (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.71-0.79). Compared with continued anticoagulation, mortality was higher among patients who initiated (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.38-1.66), discontinued (HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.49-1.81), or never received anticoagulation (HR 2.22, 95% CI 2.05-2.41), and persisted after propensity score matching. At 5 years, mortality converged across groups. GIB was more frequent in anticoagulated patients (continued 13.0%, initiated 11.9%), whereas ICH rates were low and comparable across groups (1.3-1.6%, p = 0.129).
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients aged ≥ 80 years with AF, anticoagulation therapy was associated with lower all-cause mortality despite an increase in gastrointestinal bleeding. These findings support continued anticoagulation in appropriately selected elderly patients, rather than withholding therapy on the basis of age alone.

Title: When age matters: mortality and disability after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage in a cohort of elderly patients.
Abstract: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) in older adults is associated with high early mortality and substantial long-term disability. As referral patterns and neurocritical care have evolved, the age at which prognosis changes markedly remains uncertain, and longitudinal functional trajectories beyond discharge are poorly characterised in elderly patients. We retrospectively included consecutive patients aged 65 years or older admitted with confirmed aSAH to the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (London, UK) between February 2013 and August 2022. Primary outcomes were in-hospital mortality, all-cause mortality during follow-up, and functional disability (modified Rankin Scale, mRS) at discharge and last follow-up (unfavourable outcome defined as mRS 4-6). Age thresholds associated with mortality and disability were identified using receiver operating characteristic analysis with the Youden index and confirmed by maximally selected rank statistics. Predictors of in-hospital death, survival, and disability were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models. Functional trajectories were summarised using transition matrices and Sankey diagrams. Among 110 patients (median age 76 years; 80% women), in-hospital mortality was 18.2% and all-cause mortality during follow-up was 48.2% (median follow-up 24 months). Age independently predicted in-hospital death (odds ratio 1.19 per year, 95% CI 1.06-1.35) and long-term mortality (hazard ratio 1.16 per year, 95% CI 1.09-1.22). An exploratory, cohort-derived age cut point of 79.5 years delineated divergent trajectories: mortality increased from 10.4% in patients aged < 80 years to 36.4% in those aged ≥ 80 years, and median survival declined from 95 months to 3 months (log-rank p = 2.8 × 10⁻⁶). Among patients discharged alive, discharge mRS independently predicted post-discharge survival (hazard ratio 2.39 per point, 95% CI 1.60-3.56), including in those aged ≥ 80 years (hazard ratio 3.34, 95% CI 1.21-9.20). Functional trajectories showed frequent post-discharge recovery in patients aged < 80 years, whereas recovery was uncommon and progression to death frequent in those aged ≥ 80 years. In this cohort of elderly patients with aSAH, an exploratory, cohort-derived threshold of approximately 80 years identified patients with markedly lower survival and functional recovery. Longitudinal trajectory analysis suggests post-discharge improvement remains common in patients aged < 80 years but rare in those aged ≥ 80 years.

Title: UNICAL: Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Learning with MRI-Derived Synthetic Amyloid PET for Alzheimer's Disease Classification.
Journal: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
Abstract: Limited availability of amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) motivates imaging-informatics methods that derive complementary molecular-imaging representations from routinely acquired magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We developed UNICAL, an uncertainty-aware multimodal framework for Alzheimer's disease-spectrum versus cognitively normal classification that combines a self-supervised three-dimensional MRI encoder, Contourlet Wavelet Stationary Radiomics (CoWS-Rad) engineered MRI features, and MRI-derived synthetic 18F-florbetapir (AV45) PET. CoCoLIT generated four stochastic PET realizations per MRI; their mean and voxelwise variance were used for uncertainty gating before probability-anchored transformer fusion. Synthetic PET was validated in 228 paired OASIS-3 MRI-AV45 examinations, achieving a mean per-examination voxelwise Pearson correlation of r = 0.864 and strong cortical-composite SUVR agreement with acquired PET (Pearson r = 0.954). In the OASIS-3 development cohort (813 sessions from 811 participants), participant-grouped five-fold cross-validation repeated across 20 seeds yielded AUROC 0.868 and expected calibration error (ECE) 0.061. The OASIS-3 development endpoint used the manuscript's AD-spectrum reference standard, whereas ADNI3 used AD-versus-CN research-group labels, providing cross-dataset evaluation on a related but non-identical prediction endpoint. Without retraining, feature refitting, threshold optimization, or recalibration, the frozen framework was evaluated in an independent matched ADNI3 cohort of 261 participants (87 AD, 174 CN), achieving AUROC 0.836 (95% CI 0.791-0.876). ECE increased to 0.089 under external transfer, indicating that calibration was more sensitive to domain shift than rank discrimination. Ablation analysis and K-sample sensitivity supported the contributions of uncertainty gating, adaptive weighting, modality dropout, residual correction, and the K = 4 synthesis configuration. UNICAL therefore provides an uncertainty-aware MRI-derived multimodal representation for AD-spectrum classification that retains substantial cross-dataset discrimination while remaining distinct from acquired molecular imaging and not replacing amyloid PET as a clinical biomarker.

Title: Focal therapy vs radical prostatectomy for localized prostate cancer: a systematic review, meta-analysis, bayesian network, and trial sequential analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prostate cancer is a prevalent malignancy with procedural treatment strategies. These treatments are associated with significant quality of life impact, including erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence. Focal therapy (FT) has emerged as an option that may minimize treatment-related side effects. Its efficacy in cancer control compared to standard strategies, such as radical prostatectomy (RP), remains controversial. This systematic review and meta-analysis sought to compare the oncologic and functional outcomes of focal therapy versus radical prostatectomy (RP) for localized prostate cancer.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A comprehensive systematic search was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, and Google Scholar in October 2025. The study followed PRISMA guidelines and included prospective and retrospective observational studies comparing RP with FT. Eleven studies met inclusion criteria providing a total of 8399 patients of which 4498 underwent RP and 3901 underwent FT. The coprimary endpoints were salvage treatment-free survival and failure-free survival, with secondary endpoints including continence, erectile function, and complication rate.
RESULTS: Oncologic outcomes revealed a statistically significant overall difference in salvage treatment-free survival and failure-free survival between FT and RP, with a HR of 2.05 (95% Cl 1.29-3.26, p=0.002) and 2.68 (95% CI 1.04-6.93, p=0.04), respectively. Differences in overall survival were not statistically significant HR 1.71 (95% CI 0.75-3.90, p = 0.20). Subgroup analyses showed varied results across different focal therapy approaches, with cryotherapy and combined approaches demonstrating higher treatment failure rates. Functional outcomes strongly favored FT, with significantly higher rates of continence and erectile function across all measured time intervals. At 12 months post-treatment, FT patients demonstrated substantially better continence (OR 3.45, p<0.00001) and erectile function preservation (OR 6.43, p<0.00001) compared to RP.
CONCLUSION: FT offers substantial quality of life benefits, particularly within the first 12 postoperative months, compared to RARP, however, at the cost of decreased oncologic treatment effectiveness. Differences in oncologic outcomes become attenuated in propensity-matched studies and trial sequential analysis yielded inconclusive results. Careful patient selection is paramount, and patients should be thoroughly counseled about potentially reduced oncologic control effectiveness and increased post-ablation monitoring.

Title: Cardiovascular Effects of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Across Age Groups: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
Abstract:
AIMS: To evaluate whether cardiovascular effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) differ by age.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed and Embase were searched to 1 July 2026 for randomized placebo-controlled GLP-1RA trials in adults with type 2 diabetes or overweight/obesity reporting age-stratified major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke). Hazard ratios (HRs) for participants aged < 65 and ≥ 65 years were pooled using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Effect modification was assessed by pooling trial-specific ratios of HRs (RHRs) for ≥ 65 versus < 65 years. Where reported, effects were assessed across < 65, 65 to < 75 and ≥ 75 years.
RESULTS: Eight trials (SUSTAIN-6, EXSCEL, Harmony Outcomes, PIONEER 6, REWIND, AMPLITUDE-O, SELECT and SOUL) comprising 71 926 participants were included. GLP-1RAs reduced MACE at < 65 years and ≥ 65 years, with pooled HRs of 0.81 (95% CI 0.69-0.94; I2 = 64.1%) and 0.84 (95% CI 0.79-0.90; I2 = 0.0%), respectively. The pooled RHR showed no clear evidence of effect modification (1.03, 95% CI 0.85-1.25), although between-trial heterogeneity was high (I2 = 59.3%). Among trials reporting three age strata, RHRs showed no clear evidence of effect modification for 65 to < 75 or ≥ 75 years versus < 65 years, but data were available from only four trials, and the ≥ 75-year group was relatively small.
CONCLUSIONS: Across the included trial populations, GLP-1RAs lowered MACE in the age groups examined, with no clear evidence that relative cardiovascular effects differed by age.

Title: Comparison of rebleeding risk after navigation-guided catheterization and thrombolytic irrigation using tPA or urokinase in intracerebral hemorrhage.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Minimally invasive catheter-based evacuation is increasingly used for spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Urokinase and tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) are used for intracatheter thrombolytic irrigation; however, direct comparative data on their safety, particularly regarding rebleeding risk, remain limited. This study aimed to compare rebleeding risk and early outcomes between urokinase and tPA after navigation-guided catheterization.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed adults with spontaneous supratentorial ICH who underwent stereotactic, navigation-guided catheter placement followed by scheduled intracavitary thrombolysis between January 2018 and December 2023. Patients received either urokinase or tPA. The primary outcome was rebleeding, defined as hematoma expansion or recurrence on imaging with neurological deterioration. Secondary outcomes were hematoma volume change from baseline to day 4 and short-term changes in modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). Penalized logistic regression, multivariable linear regression, and ordinal logistic regression models were used to adjust for baseline imbalances and evaluate radiologic and short-term functional outcomes.
RESULTS: Eighty patients were included (urokinase, n = 35; tPA, n = 45). tPA-treated patients presented with higher initial systolic blood pressure and tended to have larger baseline hematoma volumes. Rebleeding occurred in 12/45 patients (26.7%) in the tPA group versus 2/35 (5.7%) in the urokinase group (p = 0.032), and the presence of concurrent intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) was a potent risk factor. After adjustment for concurrent IVH, symptom onset-to-surgery time, and baseline hematoma volume using a penalized multivariable model, tPA use remained associated with rebleeding (adjusted odds ratio,5.03; 95% confidence interval,1.12-22.64; p = 0.035). Mean hematoma volume reduction by day 4 was similar between groups, although volume change was more variable in the tPA group. Early shifts in mRS and GCS favored urokinase.
CONCLUSIONS: In catheter-based minimally invasive treatment of spontaneous supratentorial ICH, urokinase was associated with a lower risk of rebleeding and more favorable early neurological outcomes than tPA, despite comparable mean hematoma reduction.

Title: Contraindication-adjusted prescription omission patterns of RASi, beta-blockers, and MRAs in hospitalized heart failure: associations with 30-day and 1-year mortality.
Abstract: Guideline directed therapy is still underused in heart failure and little is known about how missing specific medications near discharge relates to survival. The aim of this study is to examine whether study-defined omission patterns of RASi (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or ARNIs), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) in the final 48 h before discharge were associated with short-term and 1-year mortality among hospitalized adults with heart failure. Adult admissions with a recorded heart failure diagnosis were identified using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes. The three classes were RASi, beta-blockers, and MRAs (SGLT2 inhibitors were not included). A contraindication-adjusted operational framework was used to identify admissions without selected laboratory or hemodynamic barriers to these therapies and to classify late-hospital prescription omission patterns. Final-48-h orders were a proxy for treatment near discharge, not a reconciled discharge list. This framework did not establish heart failure phenotype-specific guideline eligibility. Associations with mortality within 30 and 365 days after discharge were evaluated using multivariable regression models. The final analytic cohort included 57,098 admissions from 24,922 patients. The reference group with prescriptions for all three study classes was small whereas omission of 2 or 3 therapies was substantially more common across the cohort. Admissions with prescriptions for all three study classes had the lowest 365-day mortality (13.88%). Crude 365-day mortality was higher in all omission groups, reaching 30.84% when RASi and beta-blocker were omitted and 27.50% when all three classes were omitted. In adjusted analyses, omission of all 3 therapies was associated with higher 30-day mortality (OR = 1.67). For 365-day mortality, the strongest adverse association was observed for omission of renin-angiotensin system inhibitor plus beta-blocker (HR = 1.33). Late-hospital omission patterns involving RASi and omission of all three study therapies were associated with higher post-discharge mortality. As heart failure phenotype and left-ventricular ejection fraction were not incorporated into the eligibility definition, these findings should be interpreted as prognostic associations of prescribing patterns rather than causal effects of withholding guideline-indicated HFrEF therapy.

Title: Effects of External Trigeminal Nerve Stimulation on Neurocognitive Functioning in Children and Adolescents With ADHD: A Phase 2b Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with atypical cognition and related autonomic nervous system regulation. Trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS) received U.S. Food and Drug Administration clearance as neuromodulation treatment for ADHD based on findings of clinical improvements from a pilot trial that were not confirmed in the authors' larger multicenter UK trial. Effects of TNS on cognition in ADHD, however, are relatively unknown. The authors therefore tested secondary outcomes, that is, short- and longer-term effects of active versus sham TNS in youths with ADHD on a broad neurocognitive task battery, physiological indicators of autonomic nervous system regulation, and head motion.
METHODS: In the first confirmatory, multicenter, double-blind, parallel-group, phase 2b randomized sham-controlled trial, 150 youths with ADHD (ages 8-18 years) were assigned to 4 weeks of nightly active (N=75) or sham (N=75) TNS. Cognitive performance was assessed using a comprehensive battery of executive function and attention tasks (inhibition, sustained attention, time estimation, processing speed, and intrasubject response variability) at baseline, posttreatment, and 6-month follow-up. Autonomic nervous system regulation (heart rate, heart rate variability, and electrodermal activity) was measured via a wristband device and head motion with an eye tracker during rest or cognitive testing.
RESULTS: Intention-to-treat analysis showed no significant differential treatment effects between active and sham TNS on any cognitive or physiological outcomes after 4 weeks of treatment or on cognitive measures at 6-month follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: TNS does not appear to improve neurocognitive performance, autonomic regulation, or head motion in youths with ADHD, extending negative clinical findings. The findings do not provide evidence to support TNS as a viable treatment to improve cognitive or autonomic nervous system functioning in youths with ADHD.

Title: Extended Versus Short Dual Antiplatelet Therapy Duration After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention for Chronic Total Occlusion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Abstract: Chronic total occlusion (CTO) percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is associated with substantial ischemic risk, yet the optimal duration of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) after successful CTO-PCI remains uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing extended DAPT (>12 months) with short-term DAPT (≤12 months) following CTO-PCI. Four electronic biomedical databases were searched from inception to September 2026. Comparative studies evaluating adult patients undergoing successful CTO-PCI with drug-eluting stent implantation were eligible. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Three retrospective cohort studies including 3362 patients were identified, with 1761 receiving extended DAPT and 1601 receiving short-term DAPT. Extended DAPT was associated with a significantly lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared with short-term DAPT (RR 0.68; 95% CI 0.55-0.84; P = 0.0004). There was no significant difference in all-cause death (RR 0.25; 95% CI 0.04-1.41; P = 0.116), myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, major bleeding, or revascularization outcomes. However, extended DAPT was associated with a significantly higher risk of total bleeding (RR 2.34; 95% CI 1.31-4.20; P = 0.0043). Among patients undergoing successful CTO-PCI, extended DAPT was associated with lower major adverse cardiovascular events but increased total bleeding compared with DAPT ≤12 months.

Title: Home-based nurse-led self-management support for heart failure: a randomized controlled trial.
Abstract:
AIM: To evaluate the effect of a nurse-led, stage-tailored home-based self-management and follow-up programme on self-care behaviour in people with heart failure.
BACKGROUND: People with heart failure require ongoing education, symptom monitoring, and self-management support after specialist assessment. However, access to structured centre-based cardiac rehabilitation may be limited. A nurse-led home-based model may help bridge the gap between specialist cardiology care and community-based long-term support, particularly where rehabilitation services are unavailable.
METHODS: In this parallel-group randomized controlled trial, adults aged 40-75 years with New York Heart Association class I-III heart failure and ejection fraction >30% were allocated to a 12-week home-based programme or usual care. The intervention was delivered through nurse-led home visits and telephone follow-up for clinically stable patients who could not access structured centre-based rehabilitation. The intervention group received home visits and telephone follow-up (n = 32), while the control group received usual care (n = 31). The primary outcome was self-care behaviour. Secondary outcomes were quality of life, self-efficacy, and physical capacity. Exploratory clinical outcomes were body composition, ejection fraction, and HbA1c level.
FINDINGS: At 12 weeks, the intervention group had better self-care scores than the control group (17.78 ± 2.93 vs 40.00 ± 6.49). Secondary outcomes also favoured the intervention group, with better quality of life scores, higher self-efficacy scores, and greater 6-minute walk distance. Exploratory clinical outcomes showed changes in some parameters, including ejection fraction and body-fluid values. Most intervention participants reached the Transtheoretical Model action stage, and New York Heart Association class improved significantly. This primary health care-relevant home-based model was associated with improved self-care behaviour and may support continuity of care for people with heart failure after specialist cardiology assessment when centre-based rehabilitation is unavailable.
CONCLUSION: The programme improved self-care in people with heart failure and showed potential to support home-based self-management when centre-based cardiac rehabilitation was unavailable.

Title: Management and Outcomes of Bleeding Ectopic Varices in Patients With Liver Cirrhosis: A Systematic Review and Pooled Analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bleeding ectopic varices is a rare but life-threatening complication in patients with clinically significant portal hypertension and liver cirrhosis, with limited evidence available to guide treatment decisions.
AIM: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of current therapies for bleeding ectopic varices.
METHODS: A systematic review with pooled analysis was performed based on searches conducted in Embase, MEDLINE and Cochrane Library databases. Case series, retrospective and prospective studies including adults with a history of liver cirrhosis or portal hypertension presenting with bleeding ectopic varices were included. Individual patient data on interventions, rebleeding, complications and mortality were pooled and summarised using descriptive analysis. No conventional meta-analysis was conducted due to the heterogeneous nature of included studies.
RESULTS: 44 studies (15 non-consecutive case series, 25 single-arm retrospective cohort studies, 3 double-arm retrospective cohort studies and 1 single-arm prospective study) involving 458 patients met selection criteria. Alcohol-related liver disease (38.7%), viral hepatitis (18.8%) and primary sclerosing cholangitis (15.7%) were the most common aetiologies. Child-Pugh A, B and C cirrhosis accounted for 29.7%, 46.7% and 23.5% of patients, respectively, and the pooled median Model for End Stage Liver Disease score was 14.0 (IQR 10.0-20.8). The most reported sites of ectopic varices were duodenal (27.7%), rectal (27.3%) and stomal/peri-stomal (23.1%). Endoscopic sclerosant injection appeared to have a lower rebleeding rate than band ligation in the treatment of bleeding rectal varices (3.3% vs. 33.3%). Across variceal subtypes, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) combined with variceal embolisation, was observed to have a lower rebleeding rate than TIPS alone. The pooled all-cause mortality following small bowel, rectal and stomal variceal bleeding were 25.0%, 42.9%, and 66.6%, respectively, over a median follow-up period of 354 (IQR 120-780) days. Small sample sizes, missing data and significant heterogeneity between studies limited data quality.
CONCLUSION: Bleeding ectopic varices frequently recurs and carries high mortality. An individualised approach in conjunction with early multidisciplinary team discussions is essential in achieving favourable patient outcomes.

Title: Long-term variability of the blood pressure components and risk of mortality events and sudden cardiac death: a prospective cohort study (2002-2020).
Journal: Nutrition, metabolism, and cardiovascular diseases : NMCD
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: To evaluate the association between variability in systolic blood pressure (SBPV), diastolic blood pressure (DBPV), mean arterial pressure (MAPV), pulse pressure (PPV), and the risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality (CV mortality), and sudden cardiac death (SCD) in general population.
METHODS AND RESULTS: As many as 8479 participants (5425 women; mean age 49.0 years) underwent three visits between 2002 and 2011 at three-year intervals, then were followed up until 2020. Variability of the blood pressure components was assessed using standard deviation (SD) method. Underlying causes of mortality events were adjudicated by the outcome committee. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were applied and adjusted for a comprehensive set of confounders, including mean BP values and prevalent cardiovascular disease. During a median of 10.1 years, 681, 223, and 145 events of all-cause mortality, CV mortality, and SCD with incidence rates of 8.46, 2.77, and 1.80 per 1000 person-years occurred, respectively. In multivariable-adjusted analyses, hazard ratios (95% confidence intervals) for the association between 1-SD increase in SBPV, DBPV, MAPV, and PPV and all-cause mortality were calculated as 1.08 (1.02-1.15), 1.12 (1.05-1.20), 1.12 (1.05-1.19), 1.05 (0.99-1.11); for CV mortality were 1.15 (1.04-1.28), 1.17 (1.05-1.30), 1.18 (1.06-1.31), 1.12 (1.02-1.23); regarding SCD were 1.10 (0.96-1.25), 1.16 (1.01-1.33), 1.13 (0.98-1.29), and 1.10 (0.98-1.25), respectively. Compared to participants with low-SBPV/low-DBPV, their counterparts with high-SBPV/high-DBPV had 43% and 49% significantly higher risk of all-cause- and CV mortality, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: Higher SBP and DBP variability, independent of their mean values, was associated with mortality events, and the latter increased the risk of SCD.

Title: Cortisol in cardio-kidney-metabolic disease.
Abstract: Despite guideline-directed therapy, many patients with cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease remain uncontrolled due to therapeutic inertia, adherence barriers, and underrecognized secondary causes. Hypercortisolism, ranging from mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) to overt Cushing syndrome, is an increasingly recognized contributor. MACS is associated with a 2.5-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death and increased prevalence of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and kidney impairment. Cortisol excess promotes muscle insulin resistance, hepatic gluconeogenesis, β-cell dysfunction, sodium retention, and vascular remodelling, worsening glycaemia and blood pressure, leading to poor CKM outcomes. Recent prospective studies suggest that hypercortisolism is more prevalent than previously suspected in selected CKM phenotypes, including 24% in patients with difficult-to-control T2DM in CATALYST and 27% in patients with resistant hypertension in MOMENTUM. The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test remains the diagnostic test of choice. Therapeutic strategies include adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors, glucocorticoid receptor antagonists, and pituitary-directed therapies in selected cases, while surgery remains the first-line treatment for surgically remediable disease. This review summarizes the epidemiology and mechanisms linking cortisol excess to CKM dysfunction, and also highlights the need for clinical trials, standardized diagnostic thresholds, and assays to enable integration of cortisol-targeted therapies into management pathways to mitigate residual CKM risk. This review will serve as a practical guide for cardiologists to manage a potentially reversible contributor to poor CKM control.

Title: Helicopter and Fixed-Wing Air Medical Transport in a Resource-Limited Region of Eastern Anatolia: Epidemiological Patterns and Operational Challenges in Van Province, Turkey (2022-2025).
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Air ambulance services are essential for patient transport in geographically isolated and resource-limited regions. Van Province, located in the easternmost part of Turkey, features mountainous terrain, harsh winters, and frequent road closures. Despite the critical role of air medical transport in such challenging environments, epidemiological data from these regions remain scarce. This study aimed to characterize the distinct operational roles, patient demographics, and clinical indications for helicopter versus fixed-wing air ambulance transport in a geographically challenging, resource-limited region.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, descriptive epidemiological study analyzing all air ambulance transports (n = 940) coordinated by the Van Provincial Emergency Medical Services between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2025. Demographic, clinical, and operational data were compared between helicopter and fixed-wing transports. To address the well-known limitation that the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is not interpretable in patients who are pharmacologically sedated or intubated, the primary GCS comparison was performed in a subset of 738 patients after excluding 190 patients who were intubated, mechanically ventilated, or sedated at the time of preflight assessment; the excluded group is described separately.
RESULTS: Of 940 patients, 537 (57.1%) were transported by helicopter and 403 (42.9%) by fixed-wing aircraft. Helicopter patients were significantly older (38.4 vs. 18.4 years, P < .001) and predominantly adults (70.9%). Fixed-wing aircraft primarily transported neonates and children (71.0%), particularly those with congenital heart disease (n = 147, 92.5% fixed-wing). After excluding patients who were intubated, mechanically ventilated, or sedated (n = 190), mean preflight GCS was 14.7 ± 1.4 in the helicopter group versus 14.2 ± 1.6 in the fixed-wing group (P < .001); although this difference was statistically significant, the magnitude of this difference is unlikely to be clinically meaningful, as both groups were essentially alert. The geographically isolated Bahçesaray district accounted for 295 patients (31.4%), all of whom were transported by helicopter. All 52 scene responses were performed exclusively by helicopters.
CONCLUSION: Helicopter and fixed-wing aircraft serve distinct and complementary roles in the air medical system of eastern Turkey. These findings provide an operational reference for resource-limited regions and underscore the need for outcome-linked research to evaluate clinical effectiveness.

Title: International Fixed-Wing Air Ambulance Repatriation: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Analysis With Regression Modeling of Fox Flight Air Ambulance Inc. Patient Repatriation Characteristics 2009 to 2024.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: As international travel rises globally, particularly among older adults with chronic conditions, illness or injury abroad may require air medical repatriation. Contemporary data describing patient characteristics, transport practices, and in-flight events are limited. The objective of this study is to describe the patient demographics, clinical indications, transport characteristics, and in-flight events associated with international fixed-wing air medical repatriation by a single Canadian provider.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of all international repatriations completed by Fox Flight Air Ambulance Inc. between 2009 and 2024. Extracted chart data included demographics, diagnoses, transport modality, team composition, interventions, and in-flight events. Outcomes included repatriation completion, mortality, and in-flight events that required intervention. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with in-flight events.
RESULTS: A total of 3,905 transports were included. Patients were predominantly older adults (61.5 ± 21.5 years), with orthopedic/trauma, cardiovascular, neurovascular, and infectious disease diagnoses comprising most repatriations. In-flight events occurred in 26.7% of transports; major events represented 15.0% of all events (3.9% of transports). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant associations (P < .001) between in-flight interventions and mechanical ventilation, team composition, age group, and transport era. Over time, patients required stretchers and oxygen therapy more frequently, consistent with increasing acuity. In multivariable analysis, independent predictors of in-flight events included age, orthopedic/trauma and neoplasm-related diagnoses, oxygen therapy, invasive mechanical ventilation, and year of transport.
CONCLUSION: Serious in-flight events were infrequent and occurred within transports staffed by experienced teams, although causality cannot be inferred. The findings support risk-informed planning, team composition decisions, and operational strategies to optimize safety and resource utilization.

Title: Myocardial bridge impacts septal radiofrequency ablation safety in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Up to 30% of patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have the myocardial bridge (MB) mainly in the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. Given the close anatomical proximity between percutaneous intramyocardial septal radiofrequency ablation (PIMSRA) targets and the LAD, we investigated the impact of MB on the safety and efficacy of PIMSRA in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) patients.
METHODS: This single-centre retrospective study enrolled HOCM patients who underwent PIMSRA between January 2020 and June 2021. Patients were divided into MB and non-MB groups based on preoperative coronary CT angiography (CCTA). Clinical, echocardiographic and CCTA characteristics were collected at baseline and 1 year after PIMSRA.
RESULTS: 126 patients (mean age 45.11 years; 89 male) were included and 45 (35.7%, all localised to the LAD) had MB. New-onset angina occurred only in the MB group (13/45, 28.9%). Postoperatively, MB depth and systolic stenosis increased significantly (from 2.15±2.02 mm to 2.64±2.46 mm, median: 15.8%–17.1%, p<0.001), while MB length showed no significant change (p=0.286). Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis revealed that preoperative MB depth predicted new-onset angina (area under the curve=0.886, cut-off 2.7 mm). Left ventricular outflow tract pressure gradient and maximal septal thickness were significantly reduced from baseline in both cohorts (p<0.001).
CONCLUSION: MB does not affect PIMSRA efficacy but increases postoperative angina risk. Preoperative CCTA assessment of MB may identify high-risk patients and guide treatment.

Title: Obstructive sleep apnoea and cardiovascular risk in atrial fibrillation: a health system-based cohort study.
HIDDEN2: a prospective longitudinal observational study of the prevalence of deep vein thrombosis in patients with cancer receiving palliative care upon admission to hospital.
Positive Impact of Hypertension in Patients with Early-stage Lung Cancer Treated With Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIM: This study aimed to analyze the effect of hypertension on recurrence and progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with early-stage lung cancer who underwent curative stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This study included 100 patients with T1-T3N0M0 lung cancer who underwent lung SBRT using CyberKnife or volumetric-modulated arc therapy at Inha University Hospital between July 2008 and June 2025. Recurrence rates and PFS were analyzed. Data on hypertension and specific types of antihypertensive medications were retrospectively reviewed from electronic medical records.
RESULTS: The median follow-up period was 31.0 months (range=0.7-136.7 months). Of the 100 patients, 52 had hypertension. Recurrence occurred in 38 patients, including 25 with locoregional failure and 13 with distant metastases. Recurrence rates were significantly lower in patients with hypertension (p=0.015), with reduced locoregional recurrence (p=0.022), whereas distant metastasis showed no significant correlation with hypertension (p=0.315). Hypertensive drug users (n=37) had lower recurrence rates (p=0.003). Recurrence was higher in male patients (p=0.049) and lower in those aged >70 years (p=0.033). Patients with hypertension showed significantly improved PFS (p=0.010) but no difference in overall survival based on hypertension status (p=0.319). Other factors that positively affected PFS included female sex and age >70 years. Patients actively receiving antihypertensive medication showed greater PFS than those who did not (p=0.016). In particular, those using beta-blockers showed a low recurrence rate (0%, p=0.033).
CONCLUSION: The therapeutic effects of lung SBRT appear more pronounced in patients with hypertension. This favorable outcome may be related to the administration of antihypertensive medications, suggesting the need for further investigation into the underlying mechanisms.

Title: Impact of BMI on Perioperative Complications Following CRS and HIPEC for Appendiceal Cancer.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIM: Obesity is considered a risk factor for poorer postoperative outcomes. Its effect in the context of cytoreductive surgery (CRS) and heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) is less well understood. This study examined the effect of body mass index (BMI) on postoperative surgical outcomes in patients with appendiceal cancer who underwent CRS/HIPEC.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: A retrospective analysis performed including adult patients with appendiceal cancer who underwent CRS/HIPEC between 2021 to 2023 and grouped into weight ranges based on body mass index (BMI). Intraoperative and postoperative outcomes were recorded. Continuous variables were compared using Kruskal Wallis tests while categorical variables were compared using Chi squared tests. Multivariate regression analysis was performed and models controlled for age, sex and peritoneal cancer index.
RESULTS: A total of 130 adult patients who underwent CRS/HIPEC for appendiceal cancer were included in the analysis. Intraoperative outcomes were not significantly different between weight range groups. Wound complication rates were higher among patients with BMI >30 (p=0.014). The mortality rate and rate of complications were not statistically different between BMI groups. In the adjusted model, patients with higher BMI were more likely to develop cardiovascular complications [odds ratio (OR)=1.092, p=0.018] but were less likely to develop obstruction or ileus postoperatively (OR=0.911, p=0.045).
CONCLUSION: Surgery is a key component of the management of peritoneal surface malignancies but patients with higher BMI may be at increased risk of perioperative complications, potentially altering the perioperative management of this patient cohort. However, it is unclear what specific risks obesity confers to morbidity and mortality or oncological outcomes. In our study, when stratified by BMI, there was a significant difference in wound-related complications and increased likelihood of cardiovascular complications in patients with higher BMI who underwent CRS/HIPEC for appendiceal malignancy. There were no other significant differences in intra-operative or morbidity outcomes. These findings would suggest that high BMI should be considered but not prohibit patient selection for operative management. In such patients, BMI and cardiovascular risk profile should be optimised to improve perioperative outcomes.

Title: Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease in Hungary: multimorbidity and 11-year survival in a nationwide retrospective study.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the prevalence in Hungary of selected cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) conditions (type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease (CVD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD)) and their combinations and to assess 11-year overall survival (OS) by baseline disease status.
DESIGN: Nationwide, retrospective, population-based cohort study.
SETTING: Hungarian National Health Insurance Fund database; follow-up up to 132 months from 1 January 2013.
PARTICIPANTS: Patients aged ≥20 years with International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision codes for T2DM, CVD or CKD recorded between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2012 and alive on 1 January 2013.
INTERVENTIONS: Not applicable (observational study); the exposure was baseline disease status.
PRIMARY AND SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES: Point prevalence of T2DM, CVD, CKD and their combinations by age and sex on 1 January 2013, OS by baseline disease status (Cox proportional hazards models, with disease status fixed at baseline throughout follow-up) and longitudinal changes in health status within each baseline cohort.
RESULTS: On 1 January 2013, 1 059 087 patients (13.4% of the population aged ≥20 years) had a T2DM, CVD or CKD diagnosis recorded in the previous 2 years; 211 549 (20%) were multimorbid. At 132 months, patients with stand-alone T2DM, CVD or CKD had age- and sex-standardised OS rates of 54.2%, 53.8% and 44.3%, respectively. Coexistence of all three conditions was associated with an 11-year OS of 21.0% (median OS: 62 months). Male sex, older age and additional comorbidities were associated with significantly higher risks of death.
CONCLUSIONS: A substantial proportion of patients with T2DM, CVD or CKD, alone or in combination, developed additional comorbidities or died during follow-up, including in younger age groups. The frequent coexistence of these conditions and the steep survival gradient across them support the rationale for the CKM syndrome framework.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: Not applicable.

Title: PREGnancy, HEART Health and Cardiovascular Disease (PREG-HEART): protocol for a national, direct-to-participant prospective cohort study.
Abstract:
ABSTRACT: 
INTRODUCTION: Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality in the UK. Its prevalence in pregnancy continues to rise, driven by both improved survival of women with congenital and inherited heart disease into reproductive age and an increasing burden of acquired cardiovascular risk factors. However, its natural history and optimal management remain poorly defined. Current research is limited by small sample sizes, drawn from highly selected patient cohorts from individual units. The aim of the PREGnancy, HEART Health and Cardiovascular Disease (PREG-HEART) study is to develop a patient-driven, clinically relevant digital platform to understand the epidemiology of cardiovascular disease in pregnancy and support clinical trials of management strategies. This paper provides the protocol for PREG-HEART which will start with a 6-month pilot study.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: PREG-HEART will use an online, direct-to-patient platform to enrol patients with cardiovascular disease in pregnancy alongside healthy pregnant controls. Enrolled women will be invited to provide self-reported demographic and clinical data and consent to linkage with national health records for long-term follow-up. We will also seek consent for storage and analysis of leftover clinical biosamples and to re-contact participants, enabling recruitment into sub-studies and clinical trials. Planned analysis for the pilot study at 6 months will assess feasibility, including recruitment rates, case-mix of cardiovascular diagnoses, and participant geographical, socio-economic and ethnic background, compared with the UK general pregnant population. Findings from the pilot study will inform subsequent phases of PREG-HEART, which will explore associations between different cardiovascular diagnoses and adverse cardiovascular, obstetric and neonatal events. We will work closely with patients and clinicians to define priority research questions and use the PREG-HEART platform to support a range of observational and interventional studies to address these.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Approved by the West Midlands Solihull Research Ethics Committee (IRAS 349694; REC 25/WM/0142). Findings will be returned directly to participants, disseminated to clinicians through professional societies and the National Institute for Health and Care Research-British Heart Foundation Cardiovascular Partnership, and to the public through partner charities, as well as by peer-reviewed publication.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ISRCTN11700499.

Title: Improving cardiovascular population risk in primary care: protocol for the PROSPERA cluster-randomised controlled trial of a complex multilevel intervention.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The growing burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD) threatens the sustainability of our healthcare systems. In the Netherlands, two-thirds of CVD-related healthcare is delivered in primary care practices.
