Title: Clostridioides difficile Infection in a Romanian Tertiary Care Hospital: Epidemiology, Comorbidity Burden, Treatment Patterns, and Mortality Outcomes (2023-2025).
Abstract: Background: Real-world outcome data on Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) from Eastern Europe are scarce, and partly digitised hospital records make surveillance laborious. We characterised the epidemiology, comorbidity, treatment and in-hospital mortality of CDI in a Romanian tertiary hospital and validated a rule-based pipeline for extracting surveillance variables from free-text records. Methods: Retrospective two-period cohort (1 September 2023 to 31 December 2025) of 295 CDI episodes at the Pius Brinzeu County Emergency Clinical Hospital, Timisoara. Thirty variables were extracted from narrative records with a lexical algorithm applied identically to both periods and validated against manual coding (n = 144). Mortality predictors were analysed by logistic regression with LASSO selection, bootstrap-corrected discrimination and calibration testing. Results: Mean age was 69.2 years. Hypertension (76.6%), heart failure (46.4%), neoplasm (39.3%), ascites or pleural effusion (61.7%), sepsis (56.9%) and pneumonia (44.4%) were common; vancomycin was documented in 83.7% of episodes and non-CDI antibiotics in 85.8%. In-hospital mortality during the index admission was 33.6%. Sepsis (adjusted OR 2.68), pneumonia (2.53) and ascites or pleural effusion (2.32) independently predicted death (optimism-corrected AUC 0.75), whereas individual chronic comorbidities lost significance after adjustment; mortality rose from 6.8% with none of the three acute markers to 61.1% with all three. Toxin index magnitude was unrelated to death. The second period had a higher comorbidity score (3.1 vs. 2.5, p = 0.002). Extraction reached at least 90% accuracy for 15 of 22 variables (median kappa 0.89). Conclusions: Acute organ involvement, much more than underlying comorbidity, determines in-hospital CDI mortality in this setting. Rule-based extraction supports reproducible CDI surveillance in partially digitised hospitals when low-agreement variables are verified by hand.

Title: Risk Factors for Metastatic Infectious Complications in Patients with Catheter-Related Bloodstream Infection.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSIs) may lead to metastatic complications. However, risk factors for such complications remain insufficiently characterized. This study aims to identify risk factors associated with metastatic infectious complications in patients with CRBSI. Methods: This monocentric cohort study included adult patients with CRBSI due to Gram-positive cocci or Candida spp. (2015-2024). The primary endpoint was the occurrence of metastatic complications, including infective endocarditis, embolic events, bone and joint infections, and vascular graft infections. Results: A total of 1023 CRBSI episodes were included. Staphylococcus aureus was the most common pathogen (331 episodes; 32%), followed by coagulase-negative staphylococci (307; 30%), enterococci (175; 17%), Candida spp. (171; 17%), and streptococci (98; 10%). Metastatic complications occurred in 93 episodes (9%). In multivariable logistic regression, female sex (aOR 1.61; 95% CI 1.02-2.56), S. aureus infection (aOR 1.62; 95% CI 1.01-2.61), community-onset infection (aOR 2.23; 95% CI 1.26-3.95), septic deep vein thrombosis (aOR 2.19; 95% CI 1.04-4.58), and persistent bacteremia ≥ 48 h (aOR 4.54; 95% CI 2.78-7.44) were independently associated with metastatic complications. In the S. aureus subgroup, only persistent bacteremia remained significant (aOR 6.28; 95% 3.12-12.6). Conclusions: Metastatic complications occurred in approximately 9% of CRBSI episodes but were strongly associated with persistent bacteremia, particularly in S. aureus infections. Persistence of bloodstream infection and community-onset presentation should prompt evaluation for metastatic foci.

Title: The Relationship of Cyberchondria, Negative Affect, and Anthropometric Indices with Heart-Rate Variability Among Health Sciences Students: A Psychophysiological Study of Digital Health-Information Behavior.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: We examined whether cyberchondria was associated with resting heart-rate variability (HRV) in health sciences students.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional study of 600 students in Türkiye, we assessed cyberchondria using the 12-item Cyberchondria Severity Scale (CSS-12), negative affect using the 21-item Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21), self-reported screen exposure, anthropometry, and five-minute resting HRV. The root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) was the primary physiological outcome. A hierarchical model entered demographics, waist-to-height ratio, and physical activity, then screen exposure and anxiety, followed by CSS-12.
RESULTS: CSS-12 correlated inversely with RMSSD (r = -0.412). After covariate adjustment, CSS-12 was associated with lower RMSSD (β = -0.256; p < 0.001), adding 4.9% to explained variance (final adjusted R2 = 0.272). Waist-to-height ratio showed a smaller inverse association (β = -0.087). Overall, the four-factor CSS-12 model fit was good; comparisons between academic programs were unadjusted and exploratory.
CONCLUSIONS: Higher CSS-12 scores were associated with lower resting RMSSD after adjustment for measured general anxiety and total screen exposure. Health anxiety was not measured; therefore, the model cannot determine whether this association reflects cyberchondria-related behavior, overlapping health anxiety, or other unmeasured psychological and physiological factors. Prospective studies incorporating validated health-anxiety assessment and detailed digital-behavior and HRV measures are needed.

Title: From Monogenic Variants to Polygenic Risk Scores in Inherited Cardiomyopathies: Clinical Utility, Ancestry Gaps, and Future Implementation in Arab Populations.
Abstract: Inherited cardiomyopathies are major causes of heart failure, malignant ventricular arrhythmia, and sudden cardiac death, and they require lifelong surveillance of affected individuals and clinically at-risk relatives. Their clinical genetics has traditionally been organised around rare monogenic pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants, especially in sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), titin-related and other sarcomeric forms of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), nuclear-envelope DCM, and desmosomal arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM). This model remains indispensable, but it is incomplete: it does not fully explain genotype-negative disease, variable penetrance, age of onset, disease severity, or discordant phenotypes within the same family. Polygenic risk scores (PRS), which aggregate the weighted effects of common variants, offer a second layer of inherited susceptibility that may refine the interpretation of rare variants and borderline phenotypes. Current evidence is strongest for HCM, increasingly important for DCM, and still weak for ACM and restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM). The central limitation is equity and transferability. Most cardiomyopathy PRS discovery, calibration, and validation have been performed in European-ancestry datasets. At the same time, Arab and Middle Eastern populations remain underrepresented in GWAS, reference allele-frequency databases, longitudinal cardiac imaging resources, and clinical utility studies. Direct importation of European PRS into Arab cardiovascular genetics would therefore risk miscalibration, variant misclassification, false reassurance, overdiagnosis, and inappropriate counseling. This critical review evaluates PRS evidence across HCM, DCM, ACM, RCM, and related inherited cardiac diseases; explains why PRS is not a diagnostic test or replacement for monogenic testing; and proposes a phased Arab implementation framework based on local discovery cohorts, whole-genome sequencing, ancestry-aware calibration, family-based penetrance studies, harmonized imaging phenotypes, prospective outcome tracking, genetic counseling pathways, and governance safeguards. The future is not monogenic versus polygenic risk; it is integrated genomic risk, implemented only when clinically validated and equitable.

Title: ACTN3 Variants Beyond Performance: Metabolic and Inflammatory Implications.
Abstract: Background: Athletic performance is a result of interaction between genetic and environmental factors, including training, nutrition, rest, hormonal and psychophysiological status. Numerous genes and polymorphisms can influence key physiological processes, such as muscle contractility, energy metabolism, oxidative capacity, and cardiovascular efficiency. Among these, the ACTN3 gene, and in particular the polymorphism rs1815739 (NM_001104.4:c.1729C>T; p.Arg577Ter), is well known for its association with athletic performance, but emerging evidence suggests broader effects on metabolic and inflammatory phenotypes. Methods: For this study, 109 elite athletes were enrolled and genotyped for ACTN3 c.1729C>T by Sanger sequencing. Moreover, biochemical markers, such as creatine kinase (CK), C-reactive protein (CRP), lipid profile, adiponectin, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), were examined. Finally, to better investigate the association between genotype and athletic performance, the genotypes and the results of standardized physical tests were correlated in a small exploratory subgroup of 28 professional basketball athletes. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test; non-normally distributed variables were summarized as median [IQR] and analyzed with non-parametric methods. Genotype comparisons were adjusted for multiple testing using the Holm procedure, and principal biochemical models were adjusted for age, BMI, sex, and ancestry. Results: The c.1729C>T genotype distribution differed between the two ancestry groups (exact p = 0.049), and all three variants were compatible with Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium within the ancestry groups. No biochemical genotype association remained statistically significant after Holm correction. In the performance subgroup, no genotype-performance association remained significant after Holm correction. Conclusions: In this cohort, the corrected analyses did not provide robust evidence for genotype-dependent biochemical or performance effects. The results are exploratory and require replication in larger cohorts, considering ancestry and gender differences.

Title: NOTCH2 VUS Interpretation in Pediatric Cholestasis: A 365-Variant Landscape and Genotype-Phenotype Analysis of 7 Cases.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Interpretation of NOTCH2 variants of uncertain significance (VUSs) remains challenging in pediatric cholestasis and suspected Alagille syndrome (ALGS) due to incomplete penetrance, phenotypic variability, and extensive genetic variation. Although disease-specific variant classification criteria have identified pathogenic hotspots within epidermal growth factor (EGF)-like repeats 8-12 and ankyrin repeat domains 3-6, characterizing these VUSs requires a robust framework. Methods: We reviewed aggregate deidentified data from 519 multigene cholestasis panel entries and evaluated genotype-phenotype data from a consortium cohort of 7 pediatric patients with heterozygous NOTCH2 VUSs using a clinical-genomic prioritization framework informed by disease-specific ACMG criteria and domain location. Results: Across the 519 entries, 365 unique NOTCH2 VUSs were identified, none of which overlapped with 69 previously reported ALGS-associated variants or localized to established hotspots, with over 60% occurring outside recognized functional domains. Among the 7 consortium cases, one patient carrying a cysteine-altering variant (p.Cys593Arg) in EGF-like domain 15 demonstrated a strong ALGS-compatible phenotype, while alternative diagnoses in other cases included trisomy 21 and congenital hepatic fibrosis with polycystic kidney disease. Conclusions: Among 365 unique NOTCH2 VUSs identified through pediatric cholestasis panel testing, none overlapped with previously reported ALGS-associated variants or localized to established pathogenic hotspots. However, a cysteine-altering variant outside canonical hotspots occurred in a patient with a strong ALGS-compatible phenotype, highlighting the importance of integrating variant characteristics, domain location, detailed phenotyping, and alternative diagnoses when prioritizing NOTCH2 VUSs for further evaluation.

Title: Predicting miRNA-Disease Associations Based on Contrastive Learning of Linear and Nonlinear Features.
Abstract: Background: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate biological processes and are associated with human diseases. Computational prediction can prioritize candidate associations for experimental investigation, but many existing methods emphasize nonlinear representations and may underuse complementary linear information and interactions between miRNA and disease features. This study aimed to integrate these complementary representations for miRNA-disease association prediction. Methods: We developed Singular Value Decomposition and Graph Autoencoder for miRNA-Disease Association prediction (SGMDA). Singular value decomposition extracted linear representations from the association matrix, while graph autoencoders learned nonlinear representations from integrated miRNA and disease similarity graphs. Contrastive learning aligned the two representation spaces, and a highway network modeled interactions between the fused miRNA and disease features. A random forest classifier generated association scores. Evaluation included pair-wise five-fold cross-validation, global leave-one-out cross-validation, miRNA-wise and disease-wise cross-validation, ablation experiments, and case studies of lung and prostate neoplasms. Results: The reported comparisons showed competitive predictive performance across the evaluated settings, with lower performance under entity-wise cross-validation than under pair-wise cross-validation. Ablation experiments supported the complementary contributions of linear and nonlinear features, contrastive alignment, and highway-based feature interactions. Many highly ranked case-study candidates were supported by at least one external database. Temporal validation using different HMDD releases provided additional retrospective evidence for prioritizing subsequently recorded associations. Conclusions: Combining linear and nonlinear representations with contrastive alignment and feature-interaction modeling provides a useful framework for prioritizing potential miRNA-disease associations. Database support does not establish biological causality or constitute strict independent validation, and the predicted associations require further experimental investigation.

Title: Somatic Blood Mosaicism and Psychiatric Disease: Current Evidence and Causal Limits.
Abstract: Somatic blood mosaicism is an established feature of ageing and a heterogeneous marker of haematologic cancer and inflammatory and vascular risk, but its psychiatric evidence base remains small. This structured critical narrative review evaluates mutation-defined clonal haematopoiesis, clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), autosomal mosaic chromosomal alterations (mCAs), and sex-chromosome loss while separating probable developmental mosaicism from adult-acquired blood clonality. Direct human evidence comprises seven methodologically heterogeneous studies. Psychiatric CHIP findings rely mainly on one prospective UK Biobank cohort of 360,451 participants, in which CHIP was associated with any incident psychiatric disorder (hazard ratio 1.15), particularly major depressive and substance-use disorders. Separate studies report excess mosaic losses in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder and autosomal or X-chromosome mosaicism in suicide. Clone-size gradients and lesion-specific findings add biological structure, but do not provide independent replication. Most mechanistic support comes from cardiovascular, stroke and neurodegenerative research: mutant myeloid cells can alter inflammasome signalling, endothelial function, thrombosis and tissue macrophage behaviour. These pathways make indirect brain effects plausible without establishing a psychiatric mechanism. Blood detection also cannot date a mosaic event or demonstrate the same clone in neural tissue. Taken together, the available evidence supports somatic blood mosaicism as a potentially informative marker of psychiatric heterogeneity and shared inflammatory, vascular and ageing-related biology, but does not establish a causal blood-clone-to-brain pathway. Routine psychiatric screening for CHIP or mCAs is therefore not currently justified. The immediate research priority is independent replication in longitudinal cohorts with repeated sequencing, detailed exposure and treatment histories, and direct testing of inflammatory, vascular and neuroimaging intermediates capable of distinguishing cause, consequence and shared risk.

Title: Genetic Patterns in Familial Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Disease.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: We examined familial patterns and phenotypes of thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections (TAAD) in the 3746 patients currently populating our Yale Aortic Institute Database.
METHODS: Patient charts and electronic medical records were retrospectively reviewed for the entire cohort. TAAD disease was categorized as syndromic (with extra-aortic manifestations) or non-syndromic (without) for each patient. Family patterns and whole exome sequencing results were assessed. Family history was considered 'proven' when a patient's relative(s) had an arterial aneurysm or dissection confirmed by an imaging study, surgical treatment, or postmortem examination. Family history was termed 'likely' when at least one relative suffered sudden death at ages ≤50 for males and ≤60 for females, and 'possible' with a history of sudden death at any age.
RESULTS: Of the 3746 patients in the database, family history of aneurysm or dissection and connective tissue status was able to be determined for 3113 patients, divided into 109 (3.5%) syndromic and 3004 (96.5%) non-syndromic TAAD patients. Findings were as follows: (1) In the syndromic group, 46 (42.2%) patients had a 'proven' family history, 6 (5.5%) had a 'likely' family history, 4 (3.7%) had a 'possible' family history, and 18 (16.5%) had 'none'. For 35 patients (32.1%) their family history was unknown. (2) In the non-syndromic group, 587 (19.5%) patients had 'proven' family history, 147 (4.9%) had 'likely' family history, 210 (7.0%) had 'possible' family history and 1444 (48.1%) had no family history, thus representing sporadic TAAD. A total of 616 (20.5%) had an unknown family history. (3) There was a significant difference between the rate for 'proven' and 'none' family history between the syndromic and non-syndromic groups (42.2% vs. 19.5% and 16.5% vs. 48.1%, respectively; p < 0.001). (4) Syndromic patients presented at a significantly younger age than non-syndromic or sporadic patients (41.2 vs. 63.3 or 63.6; p < 0.001). (5) There was no significant difference in age of presentation between familial non-syndromic (patients with 'proven', 'likely', and 'possible' family history) and sporadic patients (63.3 vs. 63.6; p = 0.64). (6) Overall, of the 3746 patients in the database, 631 patients (25 syndromic, 552 non-syndromic, and 54 with unknown status) underwent Whole Exome Sequencing (WES). Sequencing revealed 170 disease-causing or suspicious variants [13 pathogenic, 16 likely pathogenic, 7 not classified, and 134 Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS)] found in the exomes of 141 (22.3%) patients (12 syndromic, 103 non-syndromic TAAD patients plus a remaining 26 of unknown connective tissue status). Seventy (49.6%) of these patients had a 'proven' family history. (7) Familial TAAD patients were more likely to find a variant in their WES result than patients without a family history (70 vs. 26; p < 0.001). Recognition of these strong familial patterns, even in non-syndromic cases, encourages intensive investigation of family in order to save lives by detecting silent TAA disease.
CONCLUSIONS: Our large-scale, clinical and sequencing-based study clearly demonstrates the strongly familial and genetically mediated nature of thoracic aortic disease. We vividly demonstrate and characterize this familial nature of TAAD, both clinically and by genetic sequencing. Our findings strongly support vigorous family investigation when a new patient is diagnosed with thoracic aortic aneurysm, as well as vigorous application of whole exome sequencing for these families.

Title: Early Amniocentesis Versus Transabdominal Chorionic Villus Sampling for Early Invasive Prenatal Diagnosis: A 15-Year Prospective Cohort Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Two sampling routes are available when definitive genetic testing is required in the first trimester: early amniocentesis (EA) and transabdominal chorionic villus sampling (TA-CVS). Direct comparisons of the two at 11 to 14 weeks of gestation are, however, few. Our aim was to place the techniques side by side in terms of the genetic information they yield, the chromosomal abnormalities they uncover and the pregnancy outcomes that follow them.
METHODS: This single-operator, prospective cohort study evaluated singleton pregnancies between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation across 15 years (2010-2024), comparing TA-CVS with EA. Fluid for EA was withdrawn by amniovacucentesis (3-5 mL of amniotic fluid) through a 22-gauge needle, while villus tissue was taken with a 20-gauge needle, both with the ultrasound image visible throughout. Color Doppler assessment of the uteroplacental and fetal vessels and of the fetal heart rate preceded and followed every procedure. Material obtained by either route underwent cytogenetic testing, and targeted copy-number variant (CNV) analysis was added whenever ultrasonography had shown a major structural abnormality.
RESULTS: Of 3238 singleton pregnancies, a cytogenetic result was achieved in 1611 of 1613 (99.9%) EA and in 1622 of 1625 (99.8%) TA-CVS cases. An abnormal chromosome finding was present in 138 cases (4.3%), while pathogenic CNVs emerged in 5 of 35 (14.3%) fetuses with structural abnormalities. Spontaneous abortion affected 4 of 1613 EA pregnancies (0.25%) and 3 of 1625 TA-CVS pregnancies (0.18%; difference 0.06%, 95% CI -0.32 to 0.47%; p = 0.73). Talipes occurred in two EA cases and none after TA-CVS, whereas hemangiomas occurred in two TA-CVS cases and none after EA. Premature rupture of membranes, preterm delivery, neonatal respiratory distress and neonatal anomalies did not differ between the groups. Doppler pulsatility indices were essentially unchanged after both procedures; small changes reached statistical significance only in the umbilical (p = 0.032) and middle cerebral (p < 0.001) arteries, and all were transient and unaccompanied by clinical complications.
CONCLUSIONS: Fetal-derived material adequate for first-trimester genetic diagnosis was obtained by both routes, with cytogenetic results in more than 99% of pregnancies. Beyond the conventional chromosomal abnormalities, targeted CNV analysis added clinically meaningful diagnoses in fetuses with structural anomalies. Invasive fetal sampling therefore retains a definite place in definitive prenatal genetic diagnosis in the era of NIPT.

Title: Artificial Intelligence in Acute Coronary Syndromes: From Early Diagnosis to Culprit Lesion Characterization, Coronary Physiology, and Risk Stratification.
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being investigated across the acute coronary syndrome (ACS) care pathway, including early diagnosis, coronary lesion characterization, procedural guidance, and risk prediction. This comprehensive review examines the current evidence across the entire ACS trajectory, with particular emphasis on clinically actionable and interventional applications. AI-enabled electrocardiography (ECG) may improve detection of myocardial infarction, including occlusion myocardial infarction (OMI) that does not meet conventional STEMI criteria. Models combining clinical data and high-sensitivity troponin may improve early rule-out and rule-in. In coronary imaging, AI can quantify plaque characteristics and assist with the interpretation of OCT and IVUS, while image-derived physiology may help assess non-culprit lesions. However, better diagnostic accuracy does not necessarily translate into better revascularization decisions. AI-based models can also estimate post-ACS ischemic, bleeding, and mortality risk, although evidence that their use improves treatment or outcomes remains limited. The next priority is prospective evaluation of whether these tools improve decisions, workflow, and patient outcomes across diverse clinical settings.

Title: CT Ventricular Volume Reference Percentile Curves Using Automated nnU-Net Segmentation: A Study with LLM-Facilitated Cohort Selection.
Abstract: Background: Age- and sex-specific CT reference percentile curves of ventricular volume may support objective assessment of ventricular enlargement. We aimed to generate such curves by combining a locally deployed large language model (LLM) for cohort curation with nnU-Net 12-subcompartment segmentation. Methods: This retrospective study did not require formal ethics approval under the Swiss Human Research Act. We screened 42,211 head CT reports from January 2019 to April 2024. A phrase prefilter identified 9622 candidates for German-tuned 70-billion-parameter LLM review of stroke, leukoencephalopathy, parenchymal defects, enlarged ventricles, and space-occupying lesions; 6516 remained. A second LLM workflow screened 210,761 clinical data warehouse summaries to exclude dementia, organic brain disease, or cognitive decline. After image-availability and series-mismatch exclusions, the final cohort comprised 2608 CTs from 2608 patients (1374 males, 1234 females; age 14-98 years). Ventricular masks were obtained using a validated nnU-Net tool integrated in TotalSegmentator. Results: LLM labelling accuracy in 471 blinded reports ranged from 0.966 to 0.992. CDW screening audit showed 91% agreement, sensitivity 0.96, and negative predictive value 0.96. Median total ventricular volume rose from 10.94 mL in young females and 13.42 mL in young males to 21.97 mL and 31.97 mL, respectively, in the 60-69 age group. Except for the fourth ventricle, compartments showed positive age correlations (r = 0.44-0.69); the fourth ventricle showed no relevant association (r = 0.01 males; r = 0.05 females). After adjustment for age, male sex remained associated with greater total ventricular volume (6.54 mL; 95% CI, 5.61-7.46; p<0.001). Conclusions: This study provides age- and sex-specific CT ventricular nomograms in a selected reference cohort. The LLM-assisted curation and nnU-Net segmentation workflow provides a feasible approach for large-scale cohort analysis.

Title: Multi-Platform Transcriptomic Classification of LUAD Driver Mutation Subtypes via Heterogeneous Ensemble Learning.
Abstract: Background: Accurate identification of EGFR-mutant, KRAS-mutant, and triple-negative (TN) LUAD driver mutation subtypes is essential for guiding targeted therapy, yet standard molecular testing is invasive and not always feasible. Gene expression-based machine learning offers an alternative that avoids additional invasive sampling; however, existing models are largely restricted to binary classification and lack cross-platform generalizability. Methods: We developed a multi-cohort, ComBat-harmonized pipeline integrating SHAP-driven feature selection and a Bayesian-optimized heterogeneous ensemble of five learners, extended with NSGA-II Pareto-optimal weight optimization under leak-free cross-validation. External validation used an independent RNA-seq cohort with reference-batch harmonization and threshold calibration. Results: ParetoVoting achieved the best internal performance (F1-macro = 0.736, AUROC = 0.877), statistically indistinguishable from SoftVoting (F1-macro = 0.735; Cliff's δ=-0.12), which was carried forward for external validation. On TCGA-LUAD (n=508), SoftVoting attained F1-macro = 0.700 and AUROC = 0.850, though this reflects an out-of-range KRAS threshold (representative value ∼0.66-0.68). Ablation analysis showed components contributed unequally within internal cross-validation, with ComBat's critical role instead emerging during cross-platform external generalization. SHAP analysis identified biologically coherent signatures consistent with known LUAD oncogenic signaling. Conclusions: This framework provides a reproducible, cross-platform approach to three-class driver mutation subtyping from transcriptomic data, offering benchmarks for this underexplored task and potential clinical utility where tissue-based profiling is infeasible.

Title: Assessing the Positive Predictive Value of International Classification of Diseases Code K55.0 for Identifying Acute Mesenteric Ischaemia.
Abstract: Background: Acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI) includes acute superior mesenteric artery (SMA) thrombosis and embolism, venous AMI, and non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (NOMI). Patients with AMI are identified using the International Classification of Diseases (tenth revision (ICD-10)) code K55.0 (acute vascular disorders of the intestine). Reporting of outcomes depends on reliable case identification. Methods: A retrospective review of all patients assigned with ICD-10 code K55.0 at a tertiary university hospital between 1st January 2023 and 31st December 2025 was performed. Medical records and imaging findings were scrutinized to validate the diagnosis. Results: Among 218 patients assigned ICD-10 code K55.0, 117 (53.7%) had confirmed AMI and 198 (90.8%) had acute gastrointestinal ischaemia. Patients with NOMI (n = 30, 53.3%) had a higher bowel resection rate than patients with embolic SMA occlusion (n = 21, 23.8%; p = 0.039) or venous AMI (n = 15, 6.7%; p = 0.012). The in-hospital mortality rate was lower in patients with venous AMI (6.7%) than in patients with NOMI (66.7%; p < 0.003) or thromboembolic SMA occlusion (42.9%; p = 0.015). Conclusions: The positive predictive value for AMI using ICD-10 code K55.0 was 53.7%, underscoring the need for validated case identification. The heterogeneity of diagnoses captured by this code supports consideration of a more granular ICD coding system. A conceptual proposal is presented for further discussion and validation.

Title: Association Between Local Ascending Aortic Elastic Properties and Left Ventricular Global Longitudinal Strain in Patients with Multiple Sclerosis: A Cross-Sectional Case-Control Echocardiographic Study.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS) has been associated with subclinical cardiovascular involvement, including impaired myocardial deformation and increased arterial stiffness. However, the local elastic properties of the ascending aorta and their relationship with subclinical left ventricular (LV) longitudinal dysfunction remain insufficiently characterized in MS. Methods: In this prospective cross-sectional study, 67 adults with MS and 67 age-matched controls without cardiovascular disease underwent standardized transthoracic echocardiography. Aortic strain, distensibility and stiffness index (β) were derived from M-mode ascending aortic diameters and simultaneous brachial blood pressure, and LV global longitudinal strain (GLS) was measured by two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography. Multivariable linear regression was utilized to assess associations. Results: LV ejection fraction was similar between groups, while LV GLS was less negative in MS (-17.49 ± 1.81% vs. -19.85 ± 1.80%, p < 0.001). Patients with MS had lower aortic strain (7.54 ± 3.66% vs. 12.91 ± 3.84%) and distensibility (3.81 [2.23-6.06] vs. 5.95 [4.90-9.26] × 10-3 mmHg-1) and a higher stiffness index (4.77 [3.10-7.10] vs. 3.44 [2.31-4.05]) (all p < 0.001). After adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index, MS remained independently associated with aortic strain, distensibility, and stiffness index. Within the MS group, aortic strain was independently associated with LV GLS after adjustment for age, sex, body mass index, Expanded Disability Status Scale score and LDL cholesterol (B = -0.276, standardized β = -0.558, p < 0.001). LV GLS was independently associated with log-transformed distensibility (B = -1.021, p = 0.011) and stiffness index (B = 1.095, p = 0.014). Conclusions: Patients with MS show concurrent, inter-related impairment of local ascending aortic elasticity and LV longitudinal deformation despite preserved ejection fraction. Further studies are needed to establish the temporal sequence and prognostic relevance of these findings.

Title: Generative Forecasting of Longitudinal 3D-OCT Under Anti-VEGF Therapy for Diabetic Macular Edema.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Forecasting the individual anatomical response to anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy from optical coherence tomography (OCT) could support the management of diabetic retinal disease. Direct volumetric generation is difficult because treatment-associated change is local while most of the retina is stationary, so generative models regress to the mean and blur retinal layers. Methods: We propose a two-stage framework that decouples baseline anatomy from longitudinal change in 3D-OCT. A Retinal Response Tokenizer compresses the latent residual between baseline and follow-up volumes into discrete action tokens via Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ), and a conditional decoder renders the follow-up volume from baseline features and these tokens. An Action Transformer predicts the tokens from the baseline scan, the follow-up interval, and baseline covariates. Results: On the OLIVES trial cohort (diabetic retinopathy and macular edema; 738 test pairs from five held-out eyes), our method achieved the highest structural similarity in every test eye (SSIM 0.657 vs. 0.543-0.623) and tracked the central subfield thickness (CST) change measured by a frozen regressor (Δ-r=0.88). In a five-fold cross-validation over 52 eyes, it improved PSNR over an identity copy by 1.27 dB (95% CI 0.93-1.57) and reduced the CST change error by 10.5 μm (95% CI 3.1-19.4). Conclusions: Prospective validation is required before clinical use.

Title: Prospective External Validation of the HFA-ICOS Baseline Cardiovascular Risk Classification in Women with Breast Cancer Receiving Anthracycline-Containing Therapy in a Central Asian Cohort.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: The HFA-ICOS baseline cardiovascular risk classification was developed to standardize pretreatment risk stratification before potentially cardiotoxic cancer therapy, but its external performance across diverse populations remains incompletely characterized. We prospectively evaluated its performance in women with breast cancer receiving anthracycline-containing therapy in Central Asia. Methods: This prospective single-center external validation study used data from the PREDICATE cohort (ISRCTN12628444). Participants were classified at baseline as being at low, moderate, high, or very high cardiovascular risk according to the HFA-ICOS classification before treatment and outcome ascertainment; the high- and very-high-risk categories were pooled for analysis because of small numbers. Participants underwent serial cardiovascular surveillance, including echocardiographic assessment of left ventricular ejection fraction and global longitudinal strain, together with serial cardiac biomarker measurements. The primary outcome was cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD), defined according to the 2022 ESC cardio-oncology criteria. Results: The analysis included 108 participants. CTRCD occurred in 43 of 108 participants (39.8%). The observed proportion of participants who developed CTRCD increased from 30.0% in the low-risk group to 47.5% in the moderate-risk group and 75.0% in the high/very-high-risk group (p = 0.026). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated significant separation of CTRCD-free survival across HFA-ICOS risk categories (log-rank χ2 = 10.12; p = 0.006). Compared with the low-risk group, the hazard of CTRCD was higher in the moderate-risk group (hazard ratio [HR], 2.16; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.13-4.13) and high/very-high-risk group (HR, 3.59; 95% CI, 1.42-9.11). Discrimination was modest (area under the curve, 0.630; 95% CI, 0.530-0.724). Conclusions: The HFA-ICOS classification demonstrated a clear ordinal gradient in CTRCD risk and significant time-to-event separation but showed limited discrimination at the individual-patient level. It may guide initial risk stratification but should be complemented by longitudinal cardiovascular surveillance rather than used as a stand-alone predictor.

Title: Survival Outcomes in Transthyretin Cardiac Amyloidosis in the Tafamidis Era: Real-World Evidence from Greece.
Abstract: Background: Diagnoses of transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) have increased in recent years, with a growing proportion of patients being identified at earlier disease stages. However, temporal trends in ATTR-CM diagnosis and survival during the tafamidis era in the Greek population remain largely unknown. Methods: This retrospective study included 75 patients with ATTR-CM treated with tafamidis. Baseline demographic, clinical, laboratory, and echocardiographic characteristics were assessed, and survival outcomes were subsequently evaluated. Results: Among 75 tafamidis-treated patients, 14 deaths (19%) occurred during a median follow-up of 20 months [IQR 10.0-30.5] with an estimated 30-month survival of 75%. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated significantly poorer survival among patients aged ≥80 years (log-rank p = 0.013), those with NYHA class III-IV (log-rank p = 0.018), and across progressively more advanced NAC stages I-III (global log-rank p < 0.001). In contrast, survival did not differ significantly according to LVEF <50% versus ≥50% (log-rank p = 0.863) or maximal wall thickness ≥15 mm versus <15 mm (log-rank p = 0.801). After Holm correction across five comparisons, only NAC stage remained statistically significant (adjusted p < 0.001). Conclusions: In this real-world Greek cohort of patients with ATTR-CM treated with tafamidis, the estimated 30-month all-cause mortality was 25% and more advanced NAC stage was associated with poorer survival.

Title: Subclinical Cardiovascular Adaptation in Uncomplicated Monochorionic Twin Pregnancies: Echocardiographic and Cardiac Biomarker Findings.
Abstract: Background: Although cardiac involvement is well characterized in complicated monochorionic (MC) pregnancies, whether subtle cardiovascular changes occur in uncomplicated pregnancies remains unclear. We characterized fetal and neonatal cardiovascular adaptation using echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers. Methods: In this prospective longitudinal cohort, 76 dichorionic (DC) and 68 uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) twins underwent fetal echocardiography at 28 weeks and neonatal echocardiography within 72 h after birth. Cord blood N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) and heart-type fatty acid-binding protein (H-FABP) were assessed at delivery. Analyses used generalized estimating equations to account for within-pregnancy clustering and Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Associations between cardiac biomarkers and fetal echocardiographic parameters and interactions with chorionicity and gestational age at birth were also evaluated. Results: MCDA fetuses showed trends toward a higher cardiothoracic ratio, lower right ventricular fractional shortening and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, and a higher prevalence of tricuspid regurgitation (TR) compared with DC fetuses. In the early neonatal period, nominal differences in interventricular septal thickness and tissue Doppler indices did not persist after FDR correction. Cord-blood hs-cTnI (21.83 vs. 12.29 pg/mL; p = 0.015, FDR-adjusted p = 0.027) and NT-proBNP (1327.6 vs. 887.6 pg/mL; p = 0.018, FDR-adjusted p = 0.027) concentrations were higher in MCDA twins. After gestational age adjustment, the association with hs-cTnI remained relatively stable, whereas that with NT-proBNP was attenuated; neither remained significant after FDR correction (p = 0.116 for both). The TR-hs-cTnI association differed by chorionicity (p for interaction < 0.001, FDR-adjusted p < 0.004) and persisted after adjustment for gestational age at birth. Conclusions: Conventional echocardiographic measures of cardiac structure and function appear to be largely preserved in uncomplicated MCDA twins during fetal life and the early neonatal period. Higher cord-blood hs-cTnI and NT-proBNP may suggest subclinical myocardial stress associated with monochorionicity, although gestational age-adjusted findings warrant caution.

Title: Association Between Admission Calculated Serum Osmolality and New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation in Patients with Non-ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction Undergoing Percutaneous Coronary Intervention.
Abstract: Background: New-onset atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common complication of non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and is associated with adverse outcomes. We evaluated whether admission calculated serum osmolality is associated with new-onset AF in NSTEMI. Methods: This retrospective study included 656 eligible NSTEMI patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) between March 2021 and April 2022. Only patients in sinus rhythm at admission whose blood sample preceded any AF episode were analyzed. Osmolality was calculated as 2 × sodium + glucose/18 + blood urea nitrogen/2.8. Prespecified logistic models were assessed for discrimination, bootstrap internal validation, calibration, and incremental value. Results: New-onset AF developed in 136 patients (20.7%). Osmolality was higher in patients with AF (297.4 ± 8.9 vs. 291.6 ± 15.7 mOsm/kg, p < 0.001). In the complete-case model (n = 570; 130 events), osmolality was associated with AF (adjusted OR 1.565 per 10 mOsm/kg, 95% CI 1.102-2.223; p = 0.012). Adding osmolality increased the AUC from 0.927 to 0.933 (DeLong p = 0.081; likelihood-ratio p = 0.012; optimism-corrected AUC 0.924). The association was attenuated without renal-function adjustment (p = 0.060). Conclusions: Admission calculated serum osmolality was associated with new-onset AF in NSTEMI patients undergoing PCI, but its incremental predictive value was modest. External validation is required.

Title: Multimodal Cataract Severity Classification from AS-OCT Examination Reports: Analyzing the Complementarity of B-Scan Images and A-Scan Profiles.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Deep learning on anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) has been applied mainly to nuclear cataract. This study evaluated whether the A-scan profile in Anterion reports adds information to the B-scan image for classifying nuclear (N), cortical (C), and posterior subcapsular (P) cataract severity. Methods: B-scan images and A-scan profiles were extracted from 1416 reports of 691 patients. LOCS III grades were converted into three levels (None/Mild, Moderate, Advanced); inter-observer agreement was excellent (weighted κ 0.84-0.97). Image and profile encoders were combined using five fusion strategies and evaluated with patient-level 5-fold cross-validation. Results: Adding the A-scan profile improved F1 for N (+0.030) and P (+0.094) but not for C (-0.002). All fusion strategies outperformed single-modality models and performed comparably (average F1 0.514-0.531). For P, the gain was largest at the Moderate grade (F1 0.183 to 0.336), and masking the profile segment containing the posterior capsule caused the largest drop. B-scan line profiles could not replace the device-provided profile, and most misclassifications occurred between adjacent grades. Conclusions: The A-scan profile provided a useful incremental contribution, particularly for N and P, in this single-center dataset. The approach may be useful in retrospective and multi-center settings, but this remains to be demonstrated.

Title: Biomarkers in Acute Mesenteric Ischemia: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Performance and Injury-Related Signals.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: We examined nine biomarkers for acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) detection, necrosis and postoperative prediction. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library and indexed citation links were searched on 10 October 2026 without a lower publication-year limit. PubMed and citation searches used an October 2026 publication cutoff. English- and Russian-language clinical reports with at least 10 participants were eligible. Narrative synthesis used QUADAS-2 and diagnostic GRADE. Results: Twenty-nine primary reports were included, with reported cohorts of 18-1479 participants. Cohort overlap and varying tested denominators precluded an unduplicated participant total. Among 28 diagnostic reports, 22 had high index-test risk and 25 had high flow/timing risk. Certainty was very low for eight markers. I-FABP, α-GST and citrulline findings depended on population, assay and timing. D-dimer, lactate, procalcitonin and ischemia-modified albumin lacked intestinal specificity. Urinary I-FABP estimates were imprecise. SM22 supplied association data without diagnostic-performance estimates. Conclusions: No evaluated marker supports reliable stand-alone exclusion of AMI or determination of bowel viability. Complementary panels require prospective validation. The injury diagrams are unvalidated research models.

Title: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy-Guided Selective Distal Perfusion in Femoral Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: A Feasibility Study.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: We evaluated the feasibility of a near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS)-guided selective strategy based on a single absolute regional tissue oxygen saturation (rSO2) threshold and described clinically overt limb ischemia. Methods: This single-center retrospective study included 110 adults receiving femoral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation between April 2020 and December 2024. All underwent bilateral lower-extremity NIRS monitoring. In 83 patients, distal perfusion catheter (DPC) placement was triggered by rSO2 < 40% in the cannulated limb or clinically evident limb ischemia; 27 received routine prophylactic DPC placement at cannulation. Primary endpoints were DPC avoidance and clinically overt limb ischemia. Results: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) accounted for 64.5% of patients. Under the selective strategy, 45/83 patients (54.2%; exact 95% CI, 42.9-65.2%) avoided DPC placement, with no clinically overt limb ischemia (0/45; exact 95% CI, 0-7.9%). Limb ischemia occurred in 2/83 versus 2/27 patients (2.4% versus 7.4%; risk difference, -5.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -21.1 to +3.0; p = 0.252). Because threshold crossing triggered DPC placement, the reported threshold characteristics reflect the operation of the management protocol rather than independent diagnostic accuracy. Conclusions: A single-threshold NIRS-guided selective strategy was feasible in this ECPR-dominant population, allowing just over half of patients to avoid prophylactic DPC placement. No clinically overt limb ischemia was observed in this subgroup, but the upper 95% confidence limit of 7.9% precludes a definitive safety conclusion. Prospective studies are needed to assess limb ischemia risk and refine selection criteria.

Title: Uterine Fibroids in Pregnancy: Maternal, Obstetric, and Neonatal Outcomes in a Retrospective Cohort Study.
Abstract: Background: Uterine fibroids are the most common benign tumors in women of reproductive age, and their coexistence with pregnancy is becoming increasingly frequent as maternal age at first pregnancy rises. Objective: The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of uterine fibroids on obstetric and neonatal outcomes and, secondarily, the effect of pregnancy on fibroid growth. Study Design: This retrospective observational study included 1512 pregnant women, 136 of whom had uterine fibroids, who were followed at a university hospital. Ultrasound examinations were performed before pregnancy (T0) and during the first (T1), second (T2), and third (T3) trimesters. Fibroid number, size, location, and ultrasound characteristics according to FIGO classification were recorded. Obstetric complications, mode of delivery, and neonatal outcomes were analyzed according to fibroid type and size. Fibroid growth throughout pregnancy was also evaluated. Results: Among 1512 pregnant women followed between 1 January 2024 and 30 November 2025, 136 patients (9.0%) had uterine fibroids. A positive family history of fibroids was identified in 36% of cases. Gestational complications were infrequent overall, although gestational hypothyroidism was significantly more common among women with fibroids, whereas preeclampsia and postpartum hemorrhage were significantly less frequent in univariable analysis. Vaginal delivery was less frequent in the fibroid group, while operative vaginal delivery and cesarean section were significantly more common. Fetal growth restriction (FGR) and umbilical venous pH also differed significantly between groups. In multivariable analysis adjusted for maternal age, BMI, parity, ART, smoking, chronic hypertension, and diabetes, the association with cesarean section was attenuated (aOR 1.47, 95% CI 0.93-2.32), whereas lower PPH rates persisted (aOR 0.34, 95% CI 0.14-0.84) and a slight inverse association with umbilical venous pH remained detectable (β -0.01, p = 0.01). Exploratory stratification according to FIGO classification (3-4 vs. 5-7) showed significant differences in PPH, cesarean section, FGR, and LGA. Repeated-measure analysis demonstrated progressive fibroid growth in maximum diameter during pregnancy compared with preconceptional measurements (T0) (p < 0.001), with substantial enlargement already observed by the second trimester and fibroids ≤5 cm exhibiting greater relative growth at T2 compared with T0 than larger lesions (+18% vs. +7%; p = 0.03). Conclusions: Uterine fibroids were not consistently associated with adverse obstetric or neonatal outcomes, although careful obstetric surveillance remains warranted. Pregnancy was associated with progressive fibroid growth, particularly in smaller lesions and during early gestation.

Title: Aortic Endograft Infection After COVID-19: A Single-Centre Case Series and a Proposed Descriptive Clinical-Radiological PET/CT Staging Framework.
Abstract: Background: Aortic endograft infection (AEI) after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) is rare but life-threatening. The Management of Aortic Graft Infection Collaboration (MAGIC) criteria define infection, but there is no standard way to report the extent of infection. We describe patients who developed AEI after coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and propose a descriptive clinical-radiological PET/CT staging framework. Methods: Retrospective, single-centre case series of EVAR patients who underwent [18F] fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG PET/CT) between 2020 and 2023. Six index patients (Group A) were managed for AEI after PCR-confirmed COVID-19. Five reference patients without COVID-19, imaged during the same period for suspected infection at another site (Group B, n = 2) or malignancy (Group C, n = 3), were included to describe endograft uptake in the absence of AEI; they were not matched controls. Each patient was classified according to MAGIC, with the finding supporting each criterion recorded. Each endograft was assigned a descriptive clinical-radiological stage (0-III): Stages 0-II were defined by PET/CT uptake pattern and anatomical extent, and Stage III by an additional imaging-defined (e.g., endograft limb thrombosis) or clinical (sepsis) complication, recorded separately. Results: Mean age was 76 years (9 men). Of the six index patients, one (Case 6, organism cultured from the explanted endograft) met the MAGIC definition of diagnosed AEI and five met that of suspected AEI. All six presented with fever, and every index patient had at least one additional source of bacteraemia or cause of immunosuppression, including corticosteroids given for COVID-19 pneumonia. Five had iliopsoas abscess. Four index endografts were classified as Stage III (clinical complication, sepsis, in all four; imaging-defined complication, endograft limb thrombosis, also in one) and two as Stage II; all five reference endografts were Stage 0. The median interval from COVID-19 to AEI diagnosis was 14 months (IQR 10-16), and from EVAR to PET/CT 15 months (IQR 4-35). Three index patients died (two infection- or aorta-related), and all three Group C patients died of malignancy progression. Conclusions: This case series describes late AEI, frequently with iliopsoas involvement, in patients with prior COVID-19 and multiple other risk factors. The design does not permit any conclusion as to whether COVID-19 contributes to endograft infection. The proposed descriptive clinical-radiological PET/CT framework may help standardise the reporting of disease extent alongside MAGIC-based diagnosis but requires validation in larger, independent cohorts before any diagnostic or therapeutic use.

Title: Premature Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in a Middle Eastern Cohort: A Risk-Accumulation Perspective on Shared Determinants and Temporal Exposure Patterns.
Abstract: Background: Premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) represents a growing clinical and public health concern, particularly in regions with a high burden of modifiable risk factors. Whether premature ASCVD reflects a distinct pathophysiological entity or an earlier manifestation of shared risk exposures remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize the clinical profile of premature ASCVD and to examine its relationship with conventional cardiovascular risk factors within a Middle Eastern cohort. Methods: This pooled observational analysis included 2763 adults with established ASCVD derived from multiple cardiovascular registries and a prospective cohort. Premature ASCVD was defined using sex-specific age thresholds (<55 years in men and <65 years in women). Multivariable logistic regression analyses, including sex-stratified models, were performed to evaluate associations between premature presentation and cardiovascular risk factors, including smoking, family history, lipid parameters, and cardiometabolic comorbidities. Results: Among 2763 participants in the pooled clinical cohort, 1335 (48.3%) met the study definition of premature ASCVD. Compared with later-onset disease, premature ASCVD was strongly associated with current smoking, family history of premature cardiovascular disease, and a more atherogenic lipid profile, including higher levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides, and non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. In contrast, later-onset ASCVD was characterized by a higher prevalence of hypertension and diabetes mellitus. These patterns were consistent across sex-stratified analyses. Despite high rates of secondary prevention therapy use, a substantial residual atherogenic burden was observed among patients with premature ASCVD. Conclusions: In this predominantly coronary cohort, the findings suggest that premature and later-onset ASCVD occur within a broadly overlapping risk-factor landscape, but that the relative distribution of these factors differs according to age at first clinical presentation. The greater prevalence of smoking, family history, and atherogenic lipid abnormalities among younger patients may reflect earlier or greater exposure to these factors, whereas the greater burden of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and other chronic comorbidities among older patients is consistent with their progressive accumulation with age. These cross-sectional associations should not be interpreted as demonstrating distinct causal mechanisms or age-independent risk profiles.

Title: MicroRNAs as Diagnostic Biomarkers for Deep Vein Thrombosis.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: In patients with suspected acute deep vein thrombosis (DVT), new blood biomarkers with high specificity for DVT could potentially lower the proportion of patients requiring imaging. The plasma microRNAs (miRs) miR-134-5p, miR-103a-3p and miR-210-3p have been proposed as diagnostic biomarkers of venous thromboembolism, but their diagnostic accuracy for acute DVT has not been investigated. We aimed to assess the diagnostic performance of miR-134-5p, miR-103a-3p and miR-210-3p for DVT in patients with suspected first-lifetime acute lower-extremity DVT. Methods: This prospective cross-sectional study consecutively included outpatients with suspected first-lifetime acute lower-extremity DVT. Plasma levels of miRs were measured using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. DVT status was determined by whole-leg duplex compression ultrasonography. Diagnostic test performance was assessed by the area under the curves (AUCs) from receiver operating characteristic curves with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). The diagnostic accuracy of D-dimer was also assessed for comparison. Results: Among the 360 patients included in this study, 28% had a first-lifetime acute lower-extremity DVT. The AUCs for miR-134-5p, miR-103a-3p, and miR-210-3p ranged from 0.53 to 0.57, with 95% CIs overlapping 0.50. D-dimer had a sensitivity of 97% and specificity of 41% using the cut-off value of 0.5 µg/mL. Conclusion: Plasma miR-134-5p, miR-103a-3p and miR-210-3p showed poor diagnostic test performance for DVT. Our findings suggest that these miRs would not be helpful in discriminating between patients in whom DVT can be safely excluded and those who require imaging.

Title: Intraoperative OCT-Based Stromal Topography in Phototherapeutic Keratectomy.
Abstract: Objectives: This study aims to investigate whether anterior corneal curvature can be reliably measured by combined Placido-optical coherence tomography (OCT) during phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) despite intraoperative stromal swelling, and to quantify the immediate smoothing effect of PTK on anterior stromal higher-order aberrations (HOAs). Methods: In this prospective study, 20 eyes with epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD) undergoing PTK were examined using the MS-39© (CSO©) at four timepoints: preoperatively (t1), after epithelial debridement (t2), after PTK ablation (t3), and at 3-month follow-up (t4). Anterior curvature, corneal and stromal thickness, and epithelial thickness were analyzed across 17 corneal sectors within an 8 mm zone using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) (timepoint × sector). Anterior Zernike HOAs were computed globally, and the smoothing effect of PTK ablation was assessed by paired comparison of t2 and t3, both obtained on de-epithelialized stroma. Results: Mean central sagittal anterior curvature remained stable across intraoperative timepoints (t1: 44.27 ± 2.32 D; t2: 44.83 ± 2.75 D; t3: 45.01 ± 2.48 D; p = 0.490), despite substantial stromal swelling: Central corneal thickness increased by 114.4 ± 53.0 μm from t2 to t3 (p < 0.001), exceeding preoperative values. At 3-month follow-up, a significant flattening of -1.13 ± 1.38 D was observed (t3→t4; p = 0.002). Stromal HOA analysis revealed a significant smoothing effect of PTK ablation: total HOA root mean square (RMS) decreased from 2.28 ± 2.14 to 0.99 ± 0.46 μm (t2→t3; p = 0.001), with coma RMS showing the most consistent reduction (Δ = -0.38 ± 0.33 μm, p < 0.001; 19/20 eyes). Epithelial thickness distribution narrowed at t4 (interquartile range (IQR) -52.2%), consistent with epithelial remodeling after stromal surface regularization. Conclusions: Anterior corneal curvature remains stable during PTK despite intraoperative stromal swelling, supporting the feasibility of OCT-based intraoperative topographic assessment. In contrast, pachymetric readings are rendered unreliable by stromal hydration. Anterior stromal HOA, particularly coma RMS, may serve as a quantitative intraoperative marker of the smoothing effect achieved by PTK.

Title: Heart Failure Beyond the Heart: Digestive-System Involvement and Its Diagnostic and Prognostic Implications-A Systematic Review.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Heart failure (HF) is a systemic syndrome in which congestion, hypoperfusion, inflammation and neurohormonal activation may affect the liver, splanchnic circulation, intestinal barrier, pancreas, biliary system and nutritional state. This systematic review synthesised clinical evidence on digestive-system involvement in adults with established HF and examined its diagnostic and prognostic implications within a cautious cardio-gastrointestinal syndrome (CGIS) framework. Methods: The structured synthesis was based on an audited historical review register. The original project record reported 815 records before deduplication, although source-specific yields and the citation-level deduplication trail could not be reconstructed from the preserved files. A reproducibility-validation rerun was executed on 8 August 2026 in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection, targeting literature through 1 July 2026; exact day-level cutoff reproducibility differed by database. The rerun recovered all ten benchmark reference-set reports but was not used to redefine the historical corpus and does not establish search exhaustiveness. The final 29-report register was re-audited for eligibility, design, analysed sample, principal findings and cohort overlap. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. Results: 29 eligible reports represented approximately 26 cohort families. Hepatic and splanchnic involvement was the most mature evidence cluster, followed by intestinal congestion/barrier dysfunction. Pancreatic, biliary, microbiota and nutritional findings were less independently replicated. Liver biochemistry, composite hepatic scores and venous Doppler phenotypes showed marker-specific prognostic associations. Intestinal oedema was associated with impaired oral diuretic response. Direct pancreatic exocrine-insufficiency evidence was limited to faecal-elastase assessment. Conclusions: Digestive involvement in HF is clinically coherent but unevenly evidenced. CGIS is best regarded as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than a validated diagnostic entity, and prospective standardised studies are required before organ-specific biomarkers or imaging thresholds enter routine algorithms.

Title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Renal Safety of Carbon Dioxide Angiography in Lower Limb Angiography: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Iodinated contrast media (ICM) used in lower limb angiography carry risks of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) and allergic reactions, particularly in patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and renal dysfunction. Carbon dioxide (CO2) angiography offers a potential non-nephrotoxic alternative. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and renal safety of CO2 angiography compared with ICM in patients undergoing lower limb angiography for PAD. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science was performed from inception to 4 September 2025. Studies comparing CO2 angiography with ICM in adult PAD patients were included. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies and RoB 2 for randomised trials, and the methodological quality of comparative observational studies with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, adverse events, CIN, contrast volume, serum creatinine, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were analysed using random-effects models. Results: Nine studies (527 patients) were included. In three studies (111 patients) with extractable diagnostic accuracy data, CO2 angiography showed pooled sensitivity of 0.89 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78-0.95) and specificity of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.85-0.99). Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups (four studies; risk ratio [RR] 0.63, 95% CI: 0.15-2.71), but discomfort during CO2 injection was common. CIN risk was lower with CO2 (two studies; RR 0.31, 95% CI: 0.14-0.73; p = 0.007), and contrast volume was reduced by a mean of 80.71 mL (two studies; p < 0.00001). Pooled serum creatinine and eGFR estimates showed extreme heterogeneity (I2 = 98-99%), with the two contributing studies reporting effects in opposite directions. Conclusions: In a small number of comparative studies, CO2 angiography showed pooled sensitivity and specificity compatible with clinically useful diagnostic performance, although these exploratory estimates derive from three studies with unblinded reference standards. The lower risk of CIN with CO2, observed in two studies, is hypothesis-generating, and CO2 has adverse effects of its own, principally discomfort during injection. These findings should be confirmed in larger prospective trials before CO2 can be regarded as an established alternative for patients at risk of CIN or iodine allergy.

Title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Cardiac Magnetic Resonance in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Diagnosis, Phenotypic Characterization, and Risk Prediction.
Abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous myocardial disease associated with a broad spectrum of clinical outcomes, including heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) plays a central role in the comprehensive assessment of HCM by enabling integrated evaluation of myocardial morphology, ventricular and atrial function, tissue characterization, myocardial deformation, and longitudinal disease progression within a single comprehensive imaging modality. However, conventional CMR interpretation remains limited by manual post-processing, interobserver variability, sequence-dependent measurements, and reliance on a relatively restricted set of predefined imaging parameters. These limitations may hinder the full exploitation of the rich multidimensional information contained in CMR datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, particularly machine learning and deep learning, together with radiomics-based quantitative image analysis, provide new opportunities to extend the diagnostic and prognostic value of CMR to extract high-dimensional and quantitative information from cine imaging, late gadolinium enhancement, parametric mapping, and feature-tracking-based deformation analysis. Emerging evidence suggests that AI-enhanced CMR may facilitate automated image analysis, improve diagnostic classification, support differentiation of HCM from phenocopies, enable tissue- and deformation-based phenotypic characterization, and enhance individualized risk prediction. Although several studies have included independent or external testing, many remain retrospective, rely on selected populations or internal validation, and lack prospective assessment of clinical utility. High discrimination performance should not be interpreted as established clinical utility, because calibration, decision-curve analysis, clinically relevant thresholds, and prospective clinical impact remain insufficiently evaluated. In addition, interpretability and clinical generalizability remain important challenges for translation into routine practice. This review summarizes the current role of CMR in HCM and discusses emerging applications, methodological challenges, and future directions of AI-enhanced CMR for diagnosis, phenotypic characterization, and risk stratification.

Title: Regional Perivascular Space Burden in Pediatric Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension: A Case-Control MRI Study.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Altered perivascular fluid dynamics and glymphatic function have been implicated in the pathophysiology of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), but data in pediatric patients remain limited. Our aim was to evaluate MRI-visible perivascular space (PVS) burden in pediatric IIH and investigate its relationship with conventional MRI findings, transverse sinus stenosis (TSS), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure. Methods: In this retrospective case-control MRI study, 46 pediatric patients with clinically confirmed IIH and 46 controls frequency-matched by age and sex were included. PVS burden was independently assessed by two pediatric radiologists on axial T2-weighted images using the Potter grading system. Conventional MRI findings associated with IIH and TSS were evaluated. Associations between PVS burden, TSS, and CSF opening pressure were analyzed. Interobserver agreement was assessed using Cohen's kappa statistics. Results: Basal ganglia PVS scores were significantly higher in pediatric IIH patients than in controls (p = 0.005), while no significant differences were observed in centrum semiovale or brainstem PVS scores. Centrum semiovale PVS scores differed according to TSS status; TSS-negative patients had lower scores than both TSS-positive patients and controls (Holm-adjusted p = 0.007 for both comparisons), whereas TSS-positive patients did not differ significantly from controls. No significant correlation was observed between CSF opening pressure and PVS scores in any evaluated region. Interobserver agreement for PVS grading was good for the centrum semiovale and basal ganglia and moderate for the brainstem. Conclusions: Pediatric IIH was associated with increased basal ganglia PVS burden, suggesting a regionally heterogeneous pattern. Pediatric IIH was associated with increased basal ganglia PVS burden, suggesting a regionally heterogeneous pattern. Centrum semiovale PVS burden differed according to TSS status, with lower scores in TSS-negative patients than in both TSS-positive patients and controls, whereas TSS-positive patients did not differ significantly from controls.

Title: Quantitative MRI Characterization of Fluid-Related Phenotypes in Pediatric Epilepsy: Deep Learning-Assisted Assessment of Enlarged Perivascular Space Burden, Regional Distribution, and Clinical Associations.
Abstract: Objective: To quantitatively characterize EPVS burden and regional distribution, together with CP and ventricular CSF structural imaging phenotypes, in pediatric epilepsy and to explore within-epilepsy clinical associations of EPVS measures differing from controls. Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study included 123 children with epilepsy and 108 controls aged 10-17 years. Enlarged perivascular space (EPVS), choroid plexus (CP), and ventricular cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) structural imaging phenotypes were quantitatively assessed using SHIVA-PVS, FreeSurfer, and 3D Slicer with expert visual quality control. Primary between-group comparisons used general linear models adjusted for age and sex, with estimated total intracranial volume additionally included for absolute volumetric measures, and multiple comparisons were controlled using the false discovery rate (FDR). Exploratory within-epilepsy clinical-association analyses were subsequently performed for EPVS measures showing FDR-significant between-group differences. Results: Global EPVS burden was higher in the epilepsy group than in controls (q < 0.01), with the most pronounced regional differences in the basal ganglia (BG; q < 0.001). Relative distribution measures showed higher BG burden and lower centrum semiovale (CSO) burden and CSO/BG ratios in epilepsy (q < 0.01). No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in the CP or ventricular CSF phenotypes. In exploratory within-epilepsy analyses, longer disease duration and drug resistance were associated predominantly with BG-EPVS measures, whereas associations with antiseizure medication burden were limited. Bilateral epileptiform activity was also associated with higher BG-EPVS burden after FDR correction (q < 0.05). Conclusions: Primary between-group analyses identified greater EPVS burden in pediatric epilepsy, with the most pronounced regional differences involving the BG. Exploratory within-epilepsy analyses identified associations between selected EPVS measures and specific clinical characteristics. These cross-sectional structural imaging findings characterize a regional EPVS phenotype for further longitudinal and multimodal investigation but do not establish an underlying glymphatic mechanism.

Title: Predictive Value of Left Atrial Strain Combined with Low-Voltage Substrate for Recurrence After Radiofrequency Catheter Ablation in Persistent Atrial Fibrillation.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: To evaluate associations of left atrial strain and low-voltage area (LVA) with recurrence after radiofrequency catheter ablation (RFCA) for persistent atrial fibrillation. Methods: This retrospective cohort included 66 patients undergoing first-time RFCA. Strain was measured before ablation and at 3 months, and voltage mapping quantified LVA. Recurrence after the 3-month blanking period was assessed during approximately 3 months of intermittent follow-up. Results: Recurrence was detected in 16 patients (24.2%). Preoperative left atrial reservoir strain (LASr) and contraction strain were lower in patients with recurrence. At 3 months, LASr-3mo and contraction strain remained lower, whereas LVA percentage was higher (11.50% vs. 3.00%; p < 0.001). LASr-3mo correlated negatively with LVA (r = -0.345; p = 0.005). In multivariable analyses, LASr-3mo (OR = 0.617; p < 0.001) and Delta LASr (OR = 0.461; p < 0.001) were inversely associated with recurrence, whereas LVA was positively associated (OR = 1.069; p = 0.044). The LASr-3mo plus LVA model showed promising apparent discrimination (apparent AUC = 0.923; bootstrap-corrected AUC = 0.913). Conclusions: LASr-3mo may contribute to postoperative risk reassessment. LVA remains an exploratory observational marker because voltage mapping influenced treatment selection. The cohort-derived 4.5% LVA cut-off and model performance require prospective external validation using standardized ablation protocols.

Title: Minute-Scale Sleep-Onset HRV as a Candidate Risk-Stratification Biomarker for Diabetic Retinopathy: An Exploratory Pilot Study.
Abstract: Background: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), yet DR screening coverage remains inadequate worldwide. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy typically precedes DR, and heart rate variability (HRV) provides a non-invasive autonomic measure; however, whether HRV can screen for DR remains unexplored. Methods: This pilot study investigated whether sleep-onset minute-scale HRV indices-SDANN1 (standard deviation of 1-min segment means of normal-to-normal intervals) and SDANN2 (2-min segments)-serve as candidate screening biomarkers. Using a public 24-h Holter ECG dataset of T2DM inpatients (N = 39; 11 DR-positive, 28 DR-negative), sleep-onset time-points from cardiopulmonary coupling analysis were used to extract 30 min of post-onset ECG. Results: SDANN1 was significantly lower in the DR group (median 23.6 vs. 44.8 ms, p = 0.028, d = 0.74), with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.731 (95% CI: 0.530-0.901). At the optimal threshold of ≤ 25 ms, the odds ratio was 8.1 (95% CI: 1.7-38.4), with DR prevalence of 58% in the high-risk versus 12.5% in the low-risk group. Among 12 candidates, only the SDANN family reached significance. Conclusions: sleep-onset minute-scale HRV shows promise as a candidate risk-stratification biomarker for DR; prospective longitudinal validation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts is required before any screening application.

Title: Arterial and Venous Thrombotic Events in Urological Malignancy-A Real-World Cohort Study from a Tertiary Urology Referral Center.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Cancer-associated thrombosis (CAT) increases morbidity and mortality in cancer patients. To describe CAT in urological malignancies and explore associated factors, timing, Khorana score performance and systemic inflammatory indices. Methods: This retrospective study included 1044 patients. Oncological, cardiovascular and laboratory data from medical records were compared by CAT status. Firth penalized logistic regression was used for sparse-event analyses. Results: Thirty-one patients (2.97%) developed CAT, including 17 arterial thrombotic events (ATE) and 14 venous thromboembolic events (VTE). Advanced stage was associated with CAT (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] per stage 1.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.21-2.17; p < 0.001) in the primary and sensitivity analyses. In an exploratory analysis, cardiovascular disease was associated with ATE (odds ratio [OR] 4.58, 95% CI 1.67-15.16; Benjamini-Hochberg [BH]-adjusted q = 0.031), although the small number of ATE precluded a reliable subgroup conclusion. Median time from cancer diagnosis to CAT was 3 months. The Khorana score did not show useful VTE discrimination in the systemic chemotherapy subgroup (77 patients; four VTE; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.437, 95% CI 0.127-0.746). The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) showed no useful discrimination (AUCs 0.487-0.513) or improvement of the clinical model (all BH-adjusted q = 0.963). Conclusions: Advanced stage was the most consistent correlate of CAT. Arterial and venous events occurred in similar proportions and were concentrated early after diagnosis. Exploratory analyses suggested a possible relationship between cardiovascular disease and ATE, whereas the Khorana findings were inconclusive and the inflammatory indices lacked discriminatory value. Larger prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings.

Title: Imaging and Management of Scoliosis-Related Low Back Pain in Adolescents and Adults.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Low back pain (LBP) is a clinically relevant symptom in adolescents and adults with scoliosis, but its relationship with curve magnitude is inconsistent, and curve measurement alone therefore cannot explain symptom burden or direct pain management. This narrative review examines imaging findings and clinically plausible mechanisms of scoliosis-related LBP, considered separately for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, adult idiopathic scoliosis, adult degenerative scoliosis and adult spinal deformity, and their implications for management. Methods: This narrative review was conducted and reported with reference to the SANRA quality domains. PubMed and the Cochrane Library were searched between June and July 2026, with database-specific search strings, search dates and record yields reported in full. Study selection was performed by the first author and reviewed by the co-authors, without independent duplicate screening or formal risk-of-bias assessment. Results: Curve magnitude is not a consistent independent predictor of pain burden, and pain distribution does not reliably follow curve laterality in adult degenerative scoliosis.
