BACKGROUND: The 2025 European Society of Cardiology/European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery Guidelines introduced a Class I recommendation for transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) in selected patients aged 70 years or older with tricuspid aortic stenosis and suitable anatomy, while surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) remains recommended in younger low-risk patients. In patients with long expected survival, this framework requires careful consideration of valve durability, future reintervention, and patient preferences. This expert review, developed by the Italian Cardiac Surgery Working Group, examines contemporary evidence and consensus recommendations from a lifetime-management perspective.
METHODS: We performed a narrative, evidence-based synthesis of randomized trials, trial-based meta-analyses, and propensity-matched real-world registries comparing transfemoral TAVI and SAVR, with primary emphasis on low-risk patients. Lower-intermediate-risk evidence was included only when directly relevant to lifetime management, durability, or reintervention.
RESULTS: Evidence suggests that treatment effects are time-dependent: early non-inferiority of TAVI may attenuate with longer follow-up, particularly in patients with substantial life expectancy. Randomized durability data remain limited, whereas propensity-matched real-world registries have suggested possible higher late mortality after TAVI in younger, lower-risk populations. Reintervention after a transcatheter-first strategy may be associated with increasing technical complexity and procedural risk over time.
CONCLUSIONS: This review supports appropriate application of current guidelines through a pragmatic framework for individualized, Heart Team-based decision-making. Transfemoral TAVI is often appropriate in patients with limited life expectancy or recognized high surgical risk when anatomically feasible. In patients with long expected survival, SAVR should retain a central role as an important reference strategy.

Title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists and Risk of Arrhythmias: A Network Meta-Analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Arrhythmias are often associated with comorbidities such as diabetes and obesity, which significantly influence their onset and progression. In this context, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have garnered attention for their potential benefits, with emerging evidence indicating that GLP-1 receptor activation might offer antiarrhythmic effects.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate the impact of all GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists on the incidence of new-onset arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation (AF).
METHODS: A comprehensive search of databases was conducted from inception to December 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) focusing on patients with diabetes or obesity receiving GLP-1 RAs or co-agonists. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. Interventions were ranked using the p-score cumulative rank, ranging from 0 (worst) to 1 (best).
RESULTS: A total of 94 RCTs involving 155,989 patients were included, comparing 12 GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists. Subcutaneous semaglutide emerged as the most effective intervention, significantly reducing AF incidence compared with placebo (RR 0.82; 95% CI: 0.68 to 0.99), and compared with tirzepatide (RR 0.57; 95% CI: 0.37 to 0.88). In contrast, dulaglutide was associated with an increased risk of AF, while lixisenatide was associated with a decreased risk in atrioventricular blocks. For AF, semaglutide presented a p-score of 0.7885, while tirzepatide and dulaglutide scored 0.1830 and 0.1750, respectively.
CONCLUSION: Among GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists, subcutaneous semaglutide is highlighted as the most effective intervention for reducing the risk of AF. Further studies focusing on arrhythmic outcomes are needed to confirm these findings.

Title: Association Between Epiretinal Membrane Geometry and Metamorphopsia.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the association between the geometric characteristics of epiretinal membranes (ERM) and metamorphopsia in patients with ERM.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 48 eyes with idiopathic ERM. En face swept-source optical coherence tomography and corresponding fundus photographs were used to determine the ERM extent. Geometric characteristics of ERM (centroid location, circularity, area, and perimeter) were quantified using ImageJ software. Inter-observer agreement for centroid-fovea distance was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). A multivariable logistic regression model was constructed including centroid-fovea distance, central macular thickness (CMT), and ectopic inner foveal layer (EIFL) presence after collinearity diagnostics. Metamorphopsia was evaluated using M-CHARTS (M(avg) > 0).
RESULTS: Metamorphopsia was documented in 36 of 48 eyes (75.0%). Centroid-fovea distance was significantly greater in eyes with metamorphopsia than in those without (0.938 ± 0.540 mm vs. 0.449 ± 0.203 mm, p < 0.001). Perimeter was significantly greater (p = 0.022) and circularity was significantly lower (p = 0.008) in eyes with metamorphopsia, whereas ERM area and BCVA did not differ. Inter-observer reproducibility for centroid-fovea distance was good (ICC = 0.770). In multivariable logistic regression, longer centroid-fovea distance (per 0.1-mm increase; adjusted OR = 2.40, 95% CI: 1.27-4.57, p = 0.007) and greater CMT (adjusted OR = 1.02, 95% CI: 1.00-1.04, p = 0.035) were independently associated with metamorphopsia. The ROC curve demonstrated good discriminative ability (AUC = 0.833). However, centroid-fovea distance was not correlated with metamorphopsia severity (R² = 0.026, p = 0.269).
CONCLUSIONS: The centroid-foveal distance is significantly associated with the presence, but not the severity, of metamorphopsia in eyes with ERM. These findings suggest that spatial displacement of the tractional center relative to the foveal center (FC) may contribute to the pathogenesis of metamorphopsia, whereas its severity is likely determined by additional microstructural and biomechanical factors. Our results provide further insight into the anatomical-functional correlation in eyes with ERM.

Title: Long-term Clinical Outcomes of Acute Zonal Occult Outer Retinopathy in a Tertiary Referral Center.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: To characterize the clinical features, multimodal imaging findings, and long-term visual outcomes of patients with acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) in a single-center cohort.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 34 eyes of 26 patients with AZOOR who were referred to a tertiary referral center between January 2015 and December 2023. Best-corrected visual acuity, fundus photography, fundus autofluorescence, optical coherence tomography (OCT), Humphrey 24-2 visual field examinations were conducted during the initial and final follow-up visits.
RESULTS: The mean follow-up duration was 50.8 ± 37.9 months (range, 14-138 months). Of these 26 patients, 24 (92.3%) underwent systemic treatment. Disruption of the outer nuclear layer and ellipsoid zone (EZ) was commonly noted at baseline. In contrast, the retinal pigment epithelium was relatively preserved. During follow-up, the proportion of eyes with intact EZ increased from 26.5% to 41.2%, although this change was not statistically significant (p = 0.065). EZ restoration was observed in five eyes. Visual acuity and visual field indices remained largely unchanged during follow-up.
CONCLUSION: In this cohort, patients diagnosed with AZOOR demonstrated heterogeneous long-term structural and functional outcomes. Although partial recovery of outer retinal structures was observed in some patients, visual impairment often persisted despite structural improvement. Long-term multimodal follow-up may therefore be important for evaluating disease progression and prognosis.

Title: Clinical Efficacy of Inferior Turbinate Outfracture Combined with Low-Temperature Plasma Radiofrequency Ablation in Obese Patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea-Hypopnea Syndrome Complicated with Nasal Obstruction.
Abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the long-term clinical efficacy of combined inferior turbinate outfracture and low-temperature plasma radiofrequency ablation on nasal ventilation, continuous positive airway pressure tolerance, sleep status and body mass index (BMI) in obese patients with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) complicated with bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy, whose BMI ≥28.0 kg/m2.MethodsThis single-center retrospective study enrolled a total of 40 obese OSAHS patients with bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy treated at the Department of Otorhinolaryngology, Liangxiang Hospital from August 2023 to August 2024. All subjects received combined inferior turbinate outfracture and low-temperature plasma radiofrequency ablation under general anesthesia. Outcome indicators including nasal airway resistance, apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), visual analogue scale (VAS) for nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) tolerance and BMI were detected before surgery, 1 month, 6 months and 1 year postoperatively. Polysomnography, anterior rhinomanometry and standardized scale assessment were performed uniformly at each follow-up time point. Intra-group comparisons between preoperative and postoperative data were analyzed by paired t-test; P < 0.05 was defined as statistically significant.ResultsAll 40 patients completed the 1-year standardized follow-up without loss to follow-up. Compared with preoperative baseline levels, nasal airway resistance, AHI, ESS scores and BMI were significantly decreased at 1, 6 and 12 months after surgery (all P < 0.05), while VAS scores reflecting nCPAP tolerance increased markedly (all P < 0.05). Nasal airway resistance remained stable at a low level within one year after operation. AHI and BMI were further reduced at postoperative 1 year compared with 1 month after surgery (P < 0.05), and ESS scores achieved the optimal improvement at postoperative 6 months.ConclusionObservations from this case series suggest that the combined inferior turbinate outfracture and low-temperature plasma radiofrequency ablation may represent a feasible minimally invasive surgical option for obese OSAHS patients with nasal obstruction, inferior turbinate hypertrophy and documented CPAP intolerance. Within this cohort, we observed postoperative reductions in nasal airway resistance, AHI, ESS scores and BMI, accompanied by improved self-reported nCPAP tolerance. However, we cannot quantify how much of these improvements stem from nasal surgery versus weight loss, CPAP use or other unmeasured factors. A reduction in BMI cannot be interpreted as evidence that surgery induces weight loss. The hypothesis of a positive therapeutic cycle remains speculative, as data regarding diet, exercise, weight-loss interventions and objective CPAP usage were not collected. No postoperative infection or active bleeding was observed in the present cohort; nevertheless, other potential complications were not systematically assessed, so the safety profile of this procedure cannot be fully determined. This surgical approach avoids the high perioperative risks of traditional extensive pharyngeal surgery and provides a potential observational reference for obese OSAHS patients with severe nasal stenosis.

Title: Hepatic steatosis in inflammatory bowel disease: practical questions and evidence-based answers.
Abstract: Hepatic steatosis is among the most frequent hepatobiliary abnormalities in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but its clinical interpretation is increasingly complex. This narrative review provides evidence-based guidance for gastroenterologists managing adults with IBD and hepatic steatosis. Cohort and meta-analytic evidence indicates that hepatic steatosis affects approximately one-quarter to one-third of patients with IBD, although estimates vary according to diagnostic method, population selection, disease phenotype, metabolic burden, and study design. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) provides a useful framework for patients with cardiometabolic dysfunction, but a steatosis-centered approach is more inclusive in IBD because it accommodates lean or undernourished patients, inflammation-associated phenotypes, ileal or bile acid-related mechanisms, alcohol overlap, medication-related vulnerability, and mixed presentations. The main clinical priority is not merely to detect liver fat, but to identify meaningful fibrosis, cardiometabolic risk, and modifiable contributors. Normal aminotransferases do not exclude steatosis or fibrosis. Screening should be risk-based rather than universal. Fibrosis-4 index can be used pragmatically for initial triage in stable adults, but its IBD-specific limitations require cautious interpretation; transient elastography is most useful as a secondary fibrosis assessment or as a combined first test when readily available. Follow-up should be driven by fibrosis and cardiometabolic risk rather than by IBD alone, and hepatology referral should be reserved for elevated liver stiffness, persistent or cholestatic liver-test abnormalities, portal-hypertension features, suspected alternative liver disease, discordant tests, or clinically significant hepatic dysfunction. Hepatic steatosis alone should not determine IBD drug selection, although liver dysfunction and treatment-specific hepatotoxicity may modify monitoring or therapeutic choices.

Title: [Patient Blood Management in Clinical Practice: A Multimodal Perioperative Approach].
Abstract: Patient Blood Management (PBM) is an evidence-based, multimodal approach to improve patient safety, reduce avoidable allogeneic blood transfusions, and preserve limited blood resources. A central component is the early detection and treatment of preoperative anemia, an independent risk factor for perioperative mortality, increased transfusion rates, and prolonged hospital stays.At Charité - University Medicine Berlin, a standardized PBM pathway integrates anemia screening into the preoperative assessment of patients with a relevant risk of bleeding and transfusion. Patients with anemia undergo further diagnostic evaluation followed by cause-specific treatment, particularly with intravenous iron, erythropoietin, or a combination of both. Treatment success is assessed by repeat hemoglobin measurement prior to surgery.Additional PBM measures include the targeted use of intraoperative cell salvage, standardized assessment of individual bleeding risk, and risk-adapted perioperative management of anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy. Together, these measures provide a structured, interdisciplinary approach to reducing perioperative blood loss and transfusion requirements while improving patient safety.
Publication Types: English Abstract; Journal Article; Practice Guideline

Title: Impact of Cardiac Dimensions and Patient Phenotype on Electrocardiographic Criteria for Left Bundle Branch Capture.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Electrocardiographic (ECG) criteria are commonly used to confirm left bundle branch (LBB) capture during conduction system pacing, but the influence of structural determinants on their performance remains uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: We aimed to assess the relationship of cardiac dimensions and patient phenotype with paced ECG parameters during confirmed LBB capture, and to determine whether ventricular size modifies the diagnostic performance of ECG-based criteria.
METHODS: Single-center prospective cohort including consecutive patients with LBB capture confirmed by differential capture. Associations between paced ECG parameters and clinical, phenotypic, and echocardiographic variables were tested using linear regression analysis. The effect of left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVEDD) on V6-RWPT diagnostic performance was evaluated across LVEDD strata, by generalized estimating equations, and by receiver-operating characteristic analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 307 patients with unequivocal LBB capture were included. LVEDD was independently associated with longer paced V6-RWPT, V1-RWPT, and paced QRS duration, but not with the V6-V1 interpeak interval. In contrast, patient phenotype was not independently associated with paced ECG parameters. Each 10-mm increase in LVEDD was associated with a 2.13-ms increase in paced V6-RWPT. The sensitivity of established V6-RWPT cutoffs decreased progressively with increasing LVEDD, and LVEDD significantly modified the relationship between V6-RWPT and LBB capture (interaction B = -0.003; P = 0.022). Receiver-operating characteristic analyses also showed lower discrimination in larger ventricles, particularly in diseased LBB.
CONCLUSIONS: Left ventricular size is an important determinant of paced ECG characteristics during LBB capture and influences the diagnostic performance of V6-RWPT. These findings support interpreting ECG criteria for LBB capture according to ventricular size.

Title: Patterns of Postdischarge Heart Failure, Ischemic, and Bleeding Events After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) have improved, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, ischemic events, and major bleeding remain clinical challenges in patients with severe aortic stenosis.
OBJECTIVES: The objective of the study was to evaluate the incidence, timing, and prognostic impact of these events after TAVR.
METHODS: This two-center retrospective registry included 988 patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent TAVR. Patients were grouped according to the first clinical event after discharge: HF hospitalization, ischemic events (myocardial infarction or ischemic stroke), major bleeding, or the event-free group. The timing of the first postdischarge event and all-cause mortality after the first event were evaluated.
RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 665 days after discharge, 165 patients (16.7%) experienced any of these events. As first events, HF hospitalization, ischemic events, and major bleeding occurred in 80 (8.1%), 32 (3.2%), and 53 (5.4%) patients, respectively, whereas 823 (83.3%) were in the event-free group. Among patients with a first postdischarge event, major bleeding occurred earliest among the 3 event groups. One-year all-cause mortality after the first event was high across groups (HF hospitalization, 31.5%; ischemic events, 30.4%; major bleeding, 25.4%).
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients who experienced a first postdischarge event after TAVR, major bleeding occurred earlier than HF hospitalization or ischemic events. Once a first postdischarge event occurred, subsequent all-cause mortality was high across the 3 event groups. These findings suggest that event timing should be considered and careful clinical reassessment may be warranted when a first postdischarge event occurs after TAVR.

Title: Trends in utilization of cervical cancer screening and screening-associated services in a multi-organizational research network in Chicago, Illinois, US.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: Chicago has a high degree of care fragmentation, with multiple large health systems and numerous safety-net systems. Fragmentation may be why the west and south areas of Chicago have high incidences of cervical cancer despite high self-reported screening rates. This study assesses utilization of cervical cancer screening-associated tests and procedures across seven health systems in Chicago between 2012 and 2022.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included females aged 15+ years enrolled in one or more health systems in the CAPriCORN network. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, geolocation, linear mixed-effects model, and Poisson regression. Proportions and trends in utilization by year of test modalities (cytology alone, cytology and human papillomavirus (HPV) test [cotest], HPV test alone, colposcopy, and cervical procedures [cone biopsy, loop electrosurgical excision procedure, and ablation]) were calculated and stratified by Chicago's six geographic zones. The time between screening utilization was compared by age, Chicago zone, and change in health system.
RESULTS: Of 1.20 million in the study cohort, 53.6% had only 1 screening test during the 11-year study period; 22.9% had 2 tests, and 22.9% had 3 or more. Individuals in Chicago who changed health systems between two consecutive screening tests had a longer median interval between tests compared with those who did not change (34 versus 15.4 months).
CONCLUSIONS: Over half of the cohort only had one screening test and may be underscreened. Switching health systems more than doubled the time interval between screening tests compared with patients who remained in the same system.

Title: Development and validation of prediction models for heart failure with improved ejection fraction.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Approximately 10-60% of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) patients may transition to heart failure with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF), a clinically meaningful phenotype associated with better prognosis. However, existing prediction tools demonstrate suboptimal discrimination and poor clinical utility. We aimed to develop and validate interpretable models for HFimpEF prediction by comparing logistic regression with ensemble machine learning.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 1,257 HFrEF patients from the First Affiliated Hospital of USTC (March 2015-October 2023), split into training (n = 1,006) and internal validation (n = 251) sets. External validation used data from 310 patients across eight hospitals in Anhui Province (January 2024-January 2025). HFimpEF was defined as LVEF increase ≥10% to >40%. Five models were developed: data-driven logistic regression (Model 1); literature-based logistic regression (Model 2) with 5 common predictors validated in both BIOSTAT-CHF and ASIAN-HF cohorts; random forest (Model 3) and XGBoost (Model 4), both tuned via 5-fold cross-validation; and a simplified ensemble (Model 5) that averaged the predicted probabilities of Models 1, 3, and 4, then calibrated the average via logistic regression. Performance was assessed using AUC for discrimination, Brier score with calibration plots for calibration, decision curve analysis for clinical utility, and DeLong's test for model comparisons; SHAP analysis was applied for interpretability of Models 3 and 4.
RESULTS: Median age was 65 years (IQR 53-73); 69.9% were male. Multivariable analysis identified seven predictors: age (OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.96-0.99), BMI (OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.00-1.09), systolic blood pressure (per 10 mmHg increase, OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.01-1.25), prior PCI (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.26-0.79), HDL-C (OR 2.48, 95% CI 1.36-4.50), FT3 (OR 1.21, 95% CI 1.02-1.45), and LVESD (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.87-0.99). In external validation, Model 5 showed superior discrimination (AUC 0.67 vs. 0.60 for Model 2, P = 0.004) but poorer calibration (Brier score 0.34). Model 1 demonstrated balanced performance (AUC 0.66, Brier score 0.23).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings indicate that ensemble learning methods provide a moderate enhancement in discrimination for HFimpEF prediction, while logistic regression models exhibit superior robustness and interpretability. We have developed an online tool (https://alslyy-wq.shinyapps.io/USTC-HF-HFimpEF-Prediction/) that integrates both methodologies to facilitate practical HFimpEF risk assessment.

Title: Mitral annular plane systolic excursion as a prognostic marker in critical illness: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiac dysfunction is common in critical illness, yet conventional indices such as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) may fail to detect early impairment. Mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE), a marker of longitudinal function, may provide prognostic information, but its role in critical illness remains uncertain.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies evaluating MAPSE in critically ill adults. Studies were included if MAPSE could be dichotomized using prespecified cutoffs (10 or 12 mm). The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included 28-30-day mortality and exploratory measures of cardiac function and organ support. Risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled. Risk of bias was assessed with QUIPS and certainty of evidence with GRADE.
RESULTS: Ten observational studies including 1313 patients were analyzed; 414 (31.5%) had reduced MAPSE. Most patients had sepsis or septic shock. Reduced MAPSE was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (37.7% vs 11.7%; RR 4.81; 95% CI 1.28-18.04; p = 0.02; I2 = 70.6%), with consistent effects across both cutoffs (p = 0.111) and adequate information size on trial sequential analysis. Reduced MAPSE was also associated with lower LVEF (MD -13.0%; 95% CI -20.6 to -5.4; p < 0.01; I2 = 94.6%), but not with 28-30-day mortality or exploratory outcomes. Certainty of evidence was low for in-hospital mortality and very low for secondary and exploratory outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Reduced MAPSE was associated with higher in-hospital mortality and may be a bedside marker of myocardial dysfunction. Given the limitations of the available evidence, MAPSE remains a hypothesis-generating marker requiring prospective validation.

Title: Stroke mimics in the emergency department: Prevalence, etiologies, and clinical predictors in patients with suspected acute stroke.
Journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stroke mimics present with acute neurological symptoms resembling stroke and remain a major diagnostic challenge in the emergency department (ED). Early differentiation from true stroke is important for timely treatment and appropriate resource utilization.
OBJECTIVE: To determine the prevalence, etiologies, and clinical predictors of stroke mimics among patients presenting to the ED with suspected acute stroke within 9 h of symptom onset.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults who presented to the ED of Srinagarind Hospital, Thailand, between January 2021 and December 2024. Eligible patients were aged ≥18 years, had suspected acute stroke within 9 h of symptom onset, and were triaged through the institutional Stroke Fast-Track protocol. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, presenting symptoms, physical examination findings, and neuroimaging results were extracted from electronic medical records. Attending neurologists determined the final diagnoses. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses identified factors independently associated with stroke mimics.
RESULTS: Among 1615 patients, 347 (21.5%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 19.5-23.5%) were diagnosed with stroke mimics. Seizure-related disorders were the most common etiology (13.8%), followed by cardiovascular and cerebrovascular non-stroke conditions (11.2%) and infectious or inflammatory diseases (10.1%). In multivariable analysis, younger age, male sex, a history of migraine, psychiatric disorders, and epilepsy, along with lower diastolic blood pressure and higher heart rate, were independently associated with stroke mimics. Presenting features independently associated with stroke mimics included altered consciousness (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.71; 95% CI, 1.25-2.33), seizure (aOR 2.68; 95% CI, 1.79-4.00), vertigo (aOR 1.85; 95% CI, 1.28-2.65), and fever (aOR 3.10; 95% CI, 1.36-7.12). Conversely, limb weakness and speech disturbance were independently associated with confirmed stroke.
CONCLUSION: Stroke mimics accounted for 21.5% of suspected acute stroke presentations in the ED. Altered consciousness, seizure, vertigo, and fever were independently associated with stroke mimics, whereas limb weakness and speech disturbance favored confirmed stroke.

Title: Evaluating Culturally Tailored Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) Training in Racial and Ethnically Diverse Communities.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is a critical determinant of survival following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). However, racial and ethnic minority populations in the United States are less likely to receive bystander CPR and experience disproportionately poorer outcomes.
STUDY OBJECTIVES: The objective of this study was to pilot and evaluate the feasibility of a culturally tailored hands-only CPR curriculum and assess changes in self-reported confidence and perceived difficulty of CPR among Indian American, Chinese American, and African American participants.
METHODS: We conducted a single-cohort pre-post study among three groups. Community-specific focus groups informed cultural adaptations to a standard emergency services hands-only CPR curriculum, and trainings were delivered at Hindu temples, Chinese language schools, and African American churches. Primary outcomes, measured by 10-point Likert scales, were changes in confidence in four main CPR skills and perceived difficulty of CPR.
RESULTS: The study included 104 participants: 47 (45%) Indian American, 23 (22%) Chinese American, and 34 (33%) African American participants. Confidence increased across the four main CPR skills, with the largest improvements observed in the connect an automated external defibrillator (AED) skill (+4.5; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.80-5.22). Perceived difficulty of CPR also decreased (-2.65; 95% CI: 1.97-3.33).
CONCLUSION: This pilot study provides preliminary evidence for the feasibility and acceptability of culturally tailored hands-only CPR training in community settings, with participants reporting improved confidence and reduced perceived difficulty of CPR after training. These exploratory findings warrant further evaluation in adequately powered comparative studies to determine whether cultural tailoring offers benefit beyond standard CPR instruction for racial and ethnic minority communities and can contribute to reducing disparities in cardiac arrest outcomes.

Title: Mesenchymal stromal cell-based therapies for obesity-associated metabolic complications: Mechanistic insights, translational evidence, and future perspectives.
Abstract: Obesity is a major global health challenge and a key driver of type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome. Although pharmacological therapies and bariatric surgery have improved both short- and long-term outcomes, with GLP-1 receptor agonists now demonstrating cardiovascular and heart-failure benefits beyond weight reduction (SELECT, SUMMIT), durable and broadly applicable treatments for all patients remain limited. In this context, mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC)-based therapies, particularly adipose-derived MSCs, have gained increasing attention due to their immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic regulatory properties demonstrated in preclinical models. Experimental studies suggest that MSCs influence adipose tissue remodeling, immune cell polarization, insulin sensitivity, and energy homeostasis predominantly through paracrine mechanisms, including the release of cytokines and extracellular vesicles, rather than long-term engraftment or differentiation. However, accumulating evidence indicates that obesity itself profoundly impairs endogenous MSC function through oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and epigenetic alterations, raising important concerns regarding the feasibility of autologous MSC-based approaches in obese individuals. Critically, no randomized controlled trial has evaluated MSC therapy for obesity with weight loss, body composition, or obesity-related clinical outcomes as primary endpoints; the available human evidence addresses glycemic control in type 2 diabetes and metabolic complications. In this review, we summarize current mechanistic insights, preclinical findings, and clinical data on MSC-based interventions for obesity-associated metabolic disorders, while critically discussing key biological, manufacturing, and regulatory challenges. Finally, we define the prerequisites for rational translation - standardized potency assays, obesity-specific early-phase trials with active comparators, objective body-composition endpoints, hemocompatibility testing, and long-term surveillance.

Title: CT-guided iodine-125 brachytherapy for advanced thymic epithelial tumors: a preliminary observational study.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to provide a preliminary description of the application of CT-guided iodine-125 (125I) seed implantation, a form of brachytherapy, in patients with advanced or recurrent thymic epithelial tumors (TETs).
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed seven patients with advanced or recurrent TETs who underwent CT-guided 125I seed implantation. Based on the extent of disease at presentation, one patient had widespread distant metastases, while the remaining six had localized lesions. Treatment planning was performed using a treatment planning system(TPS, Beijing Astro Technology Co., Ltd.) with a prescribed dose of 60-70 Gy. Follow-up evaluations included regular contrast-enhanced CT scans. Tumor response was assessed according to RECIST 1.1 criteria, and safety was evaluated using CTCAE v5.0.
RESULTS: A total of 12 lesions were treated across seven patients. All procedures were technically successful. Over a median follow-up of 46 months (range: 9-69 months),four patients (57.1%) attained a complete response (CR) and three patients (42.9%) attained a partial response (PR) at the patient level. Patient-level response was defined by composite assessment of all target lesions. At the lesion level, six lesions (50%) demonstrated a CR and six lesions (50%) demonstrated a partial response PR. Notably, lesion-level observations are statistically non-independent given that half of treated lesions derived from a single patient. Complications included pneumothorax in three patients (one of whom required drainage) and grade 1 radiation pneumonitis in one patient; all adverse events resolved without long-term sequelae. No severe radiation-related toxicities (e.g., pericarditis) were observed. In a descriptive subgroup excluding the patient with widespread metastases, four of six patients achieved CR and two achieved PR; no local progression was documented during available follow-up, but this finding remains descriptive and non-comparative.
CONCLUSION: CT-guided ¹²⁵I radioactive seed implantation appears feasible and well-tolerated in patients with advanced or recurrent TETs. The observed objective tumour responses and toxicity profile are hypothesis-generating but must be interpreted with caution given the very small sample size, heterogeneous cohort, non-independent lesion-level data, and lack of a control group. This preliminary study cannot establish durable local control or superiority over external beam radiotherapy. Further larger, prospective studies with standardized dosimetry and time-to-event endpoints are warranted.

Title: Circulating NOX2 and risk of cardiovascular events in the general population: results from the Moli-sani study.
Abstract: Oxidative stress plays a central role in atherosclerosis, yet prospective population-based evidence linking specific enzymatic sources of reactive oxygen species to cardiovascular disease (CVD) is limited. NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2) is a major source of vascular oxidative stress, but its prognostic value in the general population remains unclear. We conducted a case-cohort study nested within the Moli-sani prospective cohort, including a random subcohort of 1648 participants and 1283 incident CVD cases. Baseline serum NOX2-derived peptide (sNOX2-dp) levels were measured by ELISA. Associations with incident CVD were evaluated using Cox models adapted for the case-cohort design, with adjustment for major cardiovascular risk factors. Dose-response relationships were assessed using restricted cubic splines, and additional analyses examined whether adjustment for markers of low-grade systemic inflammation attenuated the association. Higher circulating NOX2 levels were associated with increased CVD risk after adjustment for major cardiovascular risk factors. Compared with the lowest quintile, risk estimates increased across NOX2 quintiles, reaching an HR of 1.70 in Q5 (P for trend = 0.0033). Additional adjustment for the INFLA-Score or C-reactive protein did not materially attenuate the association. In a large population-based cohort, elevated circulating NOX2 was associated with incident cardiovascular events after adjustment for traditional risk factors. The association was not materially attenuated by additional adjustment for the inflammatory markers measured in this study, supporting the potential value of NOX2-related oxidative stress as a marker of cardiovascular risk.

Title: Targeting pH during cardiac arrest and in the postresuscitation period.
Abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Cardiac arrest carries high mortality and morbidity, driven in part by a profound mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis arising from hypoperfusion during cardiopulmonary resuscitation and ischemia-reperfusion injury after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Severe acidosis impairs cardiovascular function, oxygen delivery, CO 2 transport, and cellular metabolism, potentially worsening outcomes. This review examines the physiological rationale and current evidence for pH-targeted therapies in cardiac arrest.
RECENT FINDINGS: Sodium bicarbonate remains the most studied buffer, but randomized trials and observational studies have largely failed to demonstrate improved survival or neurological outcomes. Its efficacy depends critically on adequate ventilation to eliminate generated CO 2 , a frequently overlooked variable. Sodium lactate has emerged as a promising alternative, offering buffering capacity alongside utility as an oxidizable energy substrate, with encouraging experimental data, though clinical evidence remains preliminary. Key gaps persist regarding optimal timing, dosing, and the interaction between buffer administration and ventilatory strategy.
SUMMARY: Despite limited support for routine bicarbonate use, pH-targeted interventions retain strong physiological plausibility, and remains a promising field for future research.

Title: A Comparison of Game-Based Learning and Peer-Assisted Learning in Cardiovascular Physiology among First-Year Medical Students: A Randomized Controlled Crossover Trial.
Abstract: Direct comparisons between game-based learning and peer-assisted learning (PAL) in cardiovascular physiology remain limited despite growing emphasis on active learning in medical education. This randomized controlled crossover trial compared a novel educational board game, CardioLeague (Group A), with PAL (Group B) among first-year MBBS students. Thirty-six students who had completed cardiovascular physiology lectures were randomized 1:1 into two groups (n = 18 each). Knowledge was assessed via multiple-choice questionnaire at pre-test, immediately after intervention (post-test 1), one week later (post-test 2), and after crossover to the alternate method (post-test 3). Four participants in Group A and two in Group B were lost to follow-up before post-test 2 (n = 30 thereafter). Learner perception was assessed with an 18-item Likert-scale questionnaire (Cronbach's α = 0.960). Both groups showed significant within-group knowledge gains after their initial intervention (Group A: 13.39 ± 4.82 to 16.56 ± 4.05, P = 0.0024**; Group B: 15.17 ± 5.73 to 17.83 ± 4.74, P = 0.0236*), with no significant between-group difference at any assessment point (all P > 0.05; Cohen's d = -0.29 to 0.22). Knowledge scores declined significantly in both groups by post-test 3 (P < 0.0001***), consistent with expected forgetting. Learner perception favored CardioLeague over PAL across most domains, including engagement (4.61 ± 0.45 vs. 3.84 ± 0.70, P < 0.001***) and overall conclusion ratings (4.48 ± 0.98 vs. 3.56 ± 1.00, P = 0.009**). These findings indicate that no statistically significant difference in knowledge gains was detected between CardioLeague and PAL, while CardioLeague was associated with greater learner engagement and satisfaction.

Title: Right Ventricular Afterload Across the Pulmonary Hypertension Spectrum.
Journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
Abstract: Right ventricular (RV) performance is the major determinant in pulmonary hypertension (PH). RV afterload is typically assessed using pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and pulmonary arterial (PA) compliance, overlooking the dynamic component of pulsatile load. Characteristic impedance serves as a measurement of the opposition to pulsatile flow in the proximal arteries. Combined post- and precapillary PH (CpcPH) represents a growing and therapeutically challenging subgroup whose hemodynamic profile remains incompletely characterized. Our aim was to comprehensively describe RV afterload components across the PH spectrum and to evaluate their associations with RV morphology and function. We applied the time-domain method reported in literature to calculate characteristic impedance in a prospective cohort of 78 patients with PH undergoing right heart catheterization and cardiac magnetic resonance. PVR, PA compliance, and characteristic impedance were assessed and compared across precapillary PH (PAH and CTEPH), isolated post-capillary PH (IpcPH), or CpcPH. IpcPH exhibited higher compliance (2.3 mL/mmHg [1.9-3.4]) and lower impedance and PVR (84.5 [63.8-112.2] and 186.0 dyn.s.cm-5 [139.4-208.0] respectively). CpcPH showed intermediate values (1.8 mL/mmHg [1.0-2.7]; 120.4 [88.3-177.7] and 384.8 dyn.s.cm-5 [257.5-627.9]) between IpcPH and precapillary PH (1.4 mL/mmHg [1.1-2.1], 182.5 [123.4-231.4] and 524.1 [367.9-714.5] dyn.s.cm-5), with values closer to the precapillary end of the spectrum. We concluded that CpcPH occupies an intermediate hemodynamic phenotype within the PH spectrum, with some patients showing substantial overlap in afterload components with PAH and CTEPH patients. We observed that characteristic impedance provided complementary information on RV afterload beyond conventional metrics, supporting its integration into multimodal hemodynamic assessment.

Title: Orthostatic and exercise intolerance in postacute sequelae of COVID-19 occur with intact sympathetic neural control and preserved cardiac reserve.
Journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
Abstract: Postacute sequelae of COVID-19 syndrome (PASC) is widely attributed to dysautonomia, although sympathetic outflow has rarely been measured directly. We tested whether exercise and orthostatic intolerance in PASC reflect impaired cardiac reserve or abnormal muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) and its reflex control. Adults with PASC (n = 35; symptoms >3 mo, no significant comorbidity) and age- and sex-matched recovered controls (n = 12) underwent cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), echocardiogram, resting and exercise cardiac MRI, and peroneal microneurography recordings of MSNA in supine position and during graded head-up tilt to 60°. Participants with PASC had lower peak oxygen uptake ([Formula: see text]) indexed to lean mass (43.0 ± 7.8 vs. 52.2 ± 8.2 mL/lean body mass kg/min, P = 0.009) and whole body mass (26.1 ± 7.5 vs. 34.9 ± 10.2 mL/kg/min, P = 0.006), lower heart rate reserve (84 ± 25 vs. 98 ± 13 beats/min, P = 0.019), and impaired ventilatory efficiency. Cardiac structure and biventricular contractile reserve were normal. Supine MSNA burst frequency, burst incidence, sympathetic baroreflex gain, and neurovascular transduction did not differ between groups, and MSNA and mean arterial pressure increased similarly during tilt (time P < 0.0001; group × time P = 0.78). Despite these findings, 12 of 29 participants with PASC (41%) terminated the tilt protocol due to orthostatic symptoms or presyncope (Kaplan-Meier P = 0.0178). Eight participants (27%) met postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) criteria and had lower MSNA than non-POTS participants (P = 0.045). Orthostatic intolerance occurred despite normal recruitment of MSNA and maintained arterial pressure and exercise intolerance despite preserved contractile reserve. Symptoms are therefore unlikely to originate in the efferent sympathetic limb or myocardium and more likely reflect afferent reflex dysregulation or impaired cerebral perfusion.NEW & NOTEWORTHY Muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA), sympathetic baroreflex gain, and neurovascular transduction were intact in people with postacute sequelae of COVID-19 syndrome (PASC), and MSNA was recruited normally during head-up tilt. However, 41% of participants could not complete the tilt. Biventricular contractile reserve was likewise preserved. Symptoms that track neither sympathetic outflow nor systemic pressure localize the disturbance upstream, to afferent reflex control, or downstream to the cerebral circulation.

Title: Bridging the Atlantic: converging paths, diverging approaches: a comparative review of the 2025 European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society focused update and the 2026 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association guideline on dyslipidaemia management.
Abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: The global burden of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) drives lipid-lowering strategies, now undergoing their biggest transformation since statins. In 2025 and 2026, the two most influential guideline bodies, the European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) and the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), both released updated guidance that reflects evolving clinical evidence. This review provides a detailed, head-to-head examination of their recommendations, highlighting areas of convergence, divergence, and the clinical implications for practitioners on both sides of the Atlantic.
RECENT FINDINGS: The 2025 Focused Update of the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the Management of Dyslipidaemias builds incrementally on an established framework, incorporating new trial data within its existing risk-stratified, target-driven model. In contrast, the 2026 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidaemia represents a comprehensive rewrite, introducing a novel risk calculator, reinstating explicit LDL-C targets for all risk categories, and endorsing a more flexible, individualized selection of nonstatin therapies.
SUMMARY: Both documents embrace the 'lower is better' and 'strike early and strong' paradigms, yet they differ profoundly in how they apply these principles. The review distinguishes the ESC/EAS's structured, stepwise approach from the ACC/AHA's flexible, individualized paradigm (Graphical abstract).

Title: Exploring cardiac kinetic energy in children with atrial septal defects: a case-control study.
Journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
Abstract: Kinetic energy (KE) of intracardiac blood flow constitutes an important part of the heart's energy expenditure and can be quantified using four-dimensional (4-D) flow cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). Pediatric patients with atrial septal defect (ASD) have volume-loaded right ventricles and underfilled left ventricles due to left-to-right shunting, which could make ASD a useful model to study such altered ventricular loading conditions in congenital heart disease to explore related pathophysiological changes to KE. To characterize ventricular KE in children with ASD before and after treatment, we matched patients to controls. We recruited 22 patients with ASD (8 males, median/[IQR]: 8.5/[5-12] yr) and performed repeat CMR in 16/22 (72.7%) at means ± SD: 7.7 ± 1.7 mo following treatment. Left ventricular (LV) and right ventricular (RV) KE were assessed by 4-D flow CMR. Results were compared with 11 controls. Before treatment, RV peak diastolic KE was higher in patients with ASD compared with controls (P = 0.02) and normalized afterward (P = 0.42) with abolishment of diastolic ASD streaming. Indexed for ventricular volume at the time of peak KE (iKE), RV peak systolic and peak diastolic iKE decreased among repeatedly assessed ASD after treatment (both: P < 0.01), suggesting altered RV energetics not only attributable to RV volume changes. After treatment, RV iKE was comparable between patients and controls (systolic: P = 0.18; diastolic: P = 0.87). Within the ASD group, LV peak systolic KE increased with increased LV volumes after treatment (P < 0.01), whereas LV peak diastolic KE did not change (P = 0.09). How the different RV and LV peak diastolic KE responses reflect different diastolic ventricular remodeling warrants further investigation.NEW & NOTEWORTHY During systole, RV peak KE among patients with ASD decreased after treatment independent of peak RV volumes, whereas LV peak systolic KE increased after ASD treatment due to improved LV filling conditions. During diastole, RV peak KE is higher than normal and reflects both the large ventricular blood volume and the streaming shunt volume from the ASD and normalizes after treatment.

Title: Acute ventilatory and hemodynamic responses to nasal versus oral breathing during normoxia, hypoxia, and hypercapnia.
Journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
Abstract: Nasal breathing is considered the primary respiratory route, yet its effects on resting cardiorespiratory function under altered inspired gas composition remain unclear. We compared ventilatory and hemodynamic responses during nasal, oral, and free breathing at rest. Twenty-one young adults completed 6-min trials of each breathing pattern during normoxia and normobaric hypoxia [fraction of inspired oxygen ([Formula: see text]) = 0.12]; a randomized subsample of 11 also completed normoxic hypercapnia [fraction of inspired carbon dioxide ([Formula: see text]) = 0.05]. Gas exchange, cardiac hemodynamics (transthoracic bioimpedance), and cardiovagal baroreflex sensitivity (BRS) were measured continuously, and each stressor was compared with its own same-day normoxic baseline. We hypothesized that nasal breathing would blunt these responses. In normoxia, breathing pattern had no consistent effect, although oral breathing lowered BRS relative to free breathing in one of the two normoxic trials (14 ± 6 vs. 19 ± 10 ms/mmHg; P = 0.047). In hypoxia, oral breathing elicited a higher respiratory frequency than free breathing (15.7 ± 2.8 vs. 14.9 ± 2.8 breaths/min; P = 0.008) and shortened expiratory time (P = 0.005), whereas nasal breathing attenuated the hypoxic rise in heart rate (70 ± 13 vs. 74 ± 13 beats/min; P = 0.018). In hypercapnia, oxygen consumption ([Formula: see text]) was lower during nasal than free breathing (324 ± 69 vs. 360 ± 58 mL/min; P = 0.026), and oral breathing increased diastolic blood pressure compared with free breathing (75 ± 5 vs. 72 ± 5 mmHg; P = 0.038). Breathing route had minimal consequences at rest in normoxia but became physiologically relevant under chemoreflex stress, where nasal breathing lowered oxygen consumption and heart rate whereas oral breathing produced less favorable cardiovascular responses. Maintaining nasal breathing may thus support cardiorespiratory function at altitude and during hypercapnia.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study is the first to compare nasal, oral, and free breathing during normoxia, hypoxia, and hypercapnia. Although breathing mode had negligible effects at rest in normoxia, nasal breathing was associated with changes in cardiorespiratory responses to chemoreflex stress: it attenuated the hypoxic rise in heart rate. Moreover, during hypercapnia, nasal breathing was associated with a lower [Formula: see text]. Conversely, oral breathing was associated with a lower cardiovagal baroreflex sensitivity. Overall, these findings suggest that nasal breathing may represent a simple strategy to support cardiorespiratory function under chemoreflex stress.

Title: Systematic Scoring Differences in Large Language Model-Based Clinical Benchmarking Reveal Evaluator-Dependent Divergence: Controlled Evaluation Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Large language model (LLM) benchmarking in clinical medicine is increasingly reliant on LLM-based assessment frameworks; in these systems, one AI scores the outputs of another. This practice relies on the assumptions of evaluator neutrality and rubric consistency. These assumptions have not been empirically tested in clinical fields.
OBJECTIVE: In this study, we aim to directly examine these assumptions by using the PARM (Planning-Action-Reflection-Memory) framework as a theoretical lens to characterize endovascular device selection and clinical reflective reasoning as a clinical field.
METHODS: We developed a scoring rubric (C1-C6) with 40 clinical vignettes and 6 criteria across 5 endovascular fields (peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic venous insufficiency, coronary in-stent restenosis [ISR], and cerebrovascular/neuroendovascular; 8 vignettes per field). Four LLMs were evaluated as clinical decision support systems: GPT-4o (M1), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (M2), Gemini 1.5 Pro (M3), and Llama 3.3 70B (M4). Two LLMs served as independent raters with the same evaluation criteria: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (rater 1) and GPT-4o (rater 2). The rater identity was intentionally disclosed; the primary research question concerned rater scoring behavior rather than the absolute performance of the model. Human assessment was intentionally excluded because its inclusion would have shifted the study question from rater disagreement to rater accuracy, a distinct and secondary question. Interrater reliability was measured using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC 2,1) two-way random effects modeling.
RESULTS: The combined ICC(2,1) was 0.153 (95% CI 0.007-0.295). In this exploratory study, the low ICC was not distributed randomly: the magnitude of score differences varied across models (M2 Δ=+5, M4 Δ=+31, M1 Δ=-46, and M3 Δ=-158 points). Scoring behavior analysis identified 2 intrinsically consistent but mutually inconsistent criterion-interpretation models. Rater 1's scores were most consistent with the reasoning quality approach (partial credit to clinical competence independent of vignette context). Rater 2's scores were most consistent with the context fidelity approach (near-zero scores for wrong vignette responses independent of reasoning quality). Contrary to the self-preference hypothesis, both raters placed the other higher-performing model above their own. Under rater 1, C6 (PARM reflection) was the lowest-scoring criterion across all 4 models, whereas rater 2 showed greater model-dependent variation in C6 scoring.
CONCLUSIONS: AI raters used in LLM-based clinical benchmarking do not behave as interchangeable scoring tools. Their scoring behavior is most consistent with model-specific criterion interpretation patterns that systematically produce different outcomes. The observed low interrater reliability requires interpretation rather than simply being ignored: it reflects structured, direction-specific disagreement concentrated in models with context-tracking failures, not random inconsistency. PARM reflection showed a notable yet evaluator-dependent scoring pattern that warranted further investigation, rather than being interpreted as an evaluator-independent deficit.

Title: Coronary artery calcium scoring and coronary computed tomography angiography in familial hypercholesterolemia: current evidence and future directions.
Abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Familial hypercholesterolemia is a prevalent genetic disorder characterized by lifelong elevated LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C), resulting in increased risk of premature atherosclerosis and cardiovascular events. General and familial hypercholesterolemia-specific risk scores (SAFEHEART-RE, Montreal-FH, and FH risk score) are insufficient to capture the interindividual variability in cardiovascular risk. Current guidelines and consensus statements recognize the potential value of coronary computed tomography in familial hypercholesterolemia, although specific guidance on timing and modality remains limited. This review evaluates the evidence and role of coronary artery calcium scoring (CACS) and coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) for improved cardiovascular risk stratification and therapeutic guidance.
RECENT FINDINGS: Although elevated CACS is highly prevalent among patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) and homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH), younger familial hypercholesterolemia patients may exhibit exclusively noncalcified plaque, and because most are treated with statins, which may increase coronary calcification, CACS should be interpreted with caution. CCTA provides comprehensive assessment of plaque burden, stenosis, and high-risk features, which are associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. CCTA may support therapy intensification by identifying patients with substantial coronary plaque burden, while the absence of detectable atherosclerosis should not justify withholding guideline-recommended lipid-lowering therapy (LLT).
SUMMARY: CCTA may provide additional information on atherosclerotic burden in familial hypercholesterolemia. In HeFH, evidence is currently insufficient to support routine CCTA screening at specific ages or intervals. CCTA at approximately 30 years of age in men and 40 years of age in women may represent a proposed strategy requiring prospective evaluation. In children with HoFH, screening is recommended at least once after the age of 3. Follow-up imaging should be individualized according to clinical indication, imaging findings, treatment response and radiation-associated risks.

Title: Characterizing implementation strategies and behavior change techniques used by Rhode Island Health Equity Zones to prevent chronic disease.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic diseases are highly prevalent and driven in part by modifiable behaviors including diet and physical activity. Most US adults do not meet behavioral guidelines. Rhode Island (RI)'s 14 Health Equity Zones (HEZs) address chronic disease through place-based efforts to support healthier behaviors statewide.
PURPOSE: To characterize the strategies used by the RI HEZs to implement programs to improve nutrition access and opportunities for physical activity.
METHODS: Annual process evaluations from RI HEZs were reviewed using retrospective content analysis to categorize HEZ implementation efforts related to improving diet and physical activity. Activities were coded using the established Behavior Change Technique (BCT) Taxonomy v1, and Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) strategies.
RESULTS: In each HEZ, 0-62 BCTs and ERIC strategy instances were used to increase physical activity or improve nutrition access. Coding identified 30 out of 93 BCTs and 33 out of 73 ERIC strategies. The most frequently coded BCTs were: Restructuring the social environment (n = 40), social support (practical) (n = 35), instruction on how to perform a behavior (n = 33), adding objects to the environment (n = 22), and restructuring the physical environment (n = 12). The most frequently coded ERIC strategies were: promote network weaving (n = 49), build a coalition (n = 23), access new funding (n = 20), develop resource sharing agreements (n = 18), and tailor strategies (n = 14). HEZs used BCTs and ERIC strategies primarily to implement programs to reduce food insecurity, increase access to nutritious foods, and support physical activity opportunities.
CONCLUSIONS: HEZs utilized social-driven BCTs and ERIC strategies to provide accessible nutrition and physical activity programming. Results inform strategies for future community-driven chronic disease prevention efforts.

Title: A Classification of Safety Risks in Medical AI.
Abstract: AbstractIn clinical practice, patient safety is paramount, guided by the principle "first, do no harm." For medical AI to become a core component of clinical care, safety cannot be determined by its performance or accuracy alone, but by whether or not it protects patients from harm. However, consequences of medical AI models - used either independently or in combination with clinicians - may result in harms that can emerge years after the initial AI-enabled diagnosis or intervention, are difficult to attribute to the original AI model, and are irreversible (e.g., serious morbidity or mortality). We propose a four-level clinical safety classification for medical AI. S1 refers to narrow, testable uses; S2 to decision support that clinicians can review before acting; S3 to uses in which important harms may appear only after follow-up and therefore require surveillance and outcome monitoring before wider rollout; and S4 to high-risk autonomous actions that should be prohibited or allowed only under exceptional safeguards. Using a real-world prospective study of DeepDR-LLM, an integrated image-language system that combines a large language model with image-based deep learning for primary diabetes care and diabetic retinopathy screening, we illustrate how the same AI function may remain classified as S2 when used as clinician-reviewed decision support, become S3 when safety depends on referral completion and follow-up outcomes, or approach S4 if used to bypass clinical judgment. We propose multiwindow postdeployment surveillance that captures near-term signals, scheduled follow-up checkpoints, and long-horizon monitoring beyond 12 months through registry or claims linkage and postimplementation surveillance studies, strengthening medicine's core commitment to "first, do no harm - both now and in the future."

Title: From Technical Performance to Clinical Readiness: A Phase-Based Framework for Evidence Standards in Clinical Artificial Intelligence.
Abstract: AbstractClinical AI is moving rapidly from technical development to patient care, yet evidence standards remain inconsistent. Many studies emphasize model discrimination and retrospective validation, while fewer assess calibration, transportability, prospective clinical impact, implementation readiness, or postdeployment safety. We propose a phase-based framework for evidentiary maturity in clinical AI, using cardiovascular AI as a representative use case. The framework spans model development and representation learning, internal validation, external validation, prospective evaluation of decision impact and implementation readiness, and postdeployment monitoring. Each phase is linked to a core question, expected evidence, and the type of claim that can reasonably be supported. By aligning claims with phase-appropriate evidence, this framework is intended to help investigators, reviewers, regulators, health systems, and clinicians distinguish technical feasibility from clinical readiness and identify when additional prospective evaluation, monitoring, or governance is needed.

Title: TRIALSCOPE - A Framework for Clinical Trial Simulation from Real-World Data.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The rapid digitization of real-world data presents an unprecedented opportunity to optimize health care delivery and accelerate biomedical discovery. However, these data are often found in unstructured forms, such as clinical notes in electronic medical records (EMRs), and are typically plagued by confounders, making it challenging to generate robust real-world evidence (RWE). Therefore, we present TRIALSCOPE, a framework designed to distill RWE from population-level observational data at scale.
METHODS: TRIALSCOPE leverages biomedical language models to structure clinical text at scale, employs advanced probabilistic modeling for denoising and imputation, and incorporates state-of-the-art causal inference techniques to address common confounders in treatment effect estimation.
RESULTS: Extensive experiments were conducted on a large-scale dataset of over 1 million cancer patients from a single large health care network in the United States. TRIALSCOPE was shown to automatically curate high-quality structured patient data, expanding the dataset and incorporating key patient attributes only available in unstructured form. The framework reduces confounding in treatment effect estimation, generating comparable results with randomized controlled lung cancer trials. In addition, we demonstrate simulations of unconducted clinical trials - including a pancreatic cancer trial with varying eligibility criteria - using a suite of validation tests to ensure robustness. Thorough ablation studies were conducted to better understand key components of TRIALSCOPE and establish best practices for RWE generation from EMRs.
CONCLUSIONS: TRIALSCOPE was able to extract cancer treatment data from EMRs, overcoming limitations of manual curation. We were also able to show that TRIALSCOPE could reproduce the results of lung and pancreatic cancer clinical trials from the extracted real-world data.

Title: TARGET-AI: A Foundational Approach for the Targeted Deployment of Artificial Intelligence Electrocardiography in the Electronic Health Record.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) applied to electrocardiograms (ECGs) offers promise for structural heart disease (SHD) screening, yet clinical integration remains challenged by high false-positive rates and a lack of tailored deployment strategies.
METHODS: We developed TARGET-AI, a multimodal approach that integrates longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) with ECGs to define patient phenotypes and support targeted SHD screening opportunities. TARGET-AI uses an EHR foundation model applied to 118 million events from 159,322 individuals, to generate temporal patient-level embeddings and identify screening candidates, and a contrastive vision-language model trained on 754,533 ECG image-echocardiogram report pairs, to detect distinct SHD subtypes with tunable characteristics. We evaluated this in 5198 individuals referred for a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) within 90 days of an ECG (temporal validation) and in geographically distinct cohorts, including 33,518 UK Biobank participants undergoing protocolized ECG and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and an inpatient cohort of 3628 patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-IV database with ECG-TTE pairs. We compared discrimination metrics between targeted and untargeted strategies, with bootstrap-derived 95% confidence intervals excluding zero considered significant.
RESULTS: The TARGET-AI ECG model discriminated 26 SHD subtypes, including left ventricular systolic dysfunction (area under the receiver operating curve [AUROC] of 0.90), severe aortic stenosis (AUROC of 0.85), and elevated right ventricular systolic pressure (AUROC of 0.82). Compared with untargeted screening, targeted screening in the temporal validation set (n=5198) was associated with a significant increase in F1 scores (median: 0.25; range: 0.09 to 0.75) and a decrease in the number of false positives (median: -303; range: -715 to -77) across 26 SHD labels. Similar results were seen in the UK Biobank (n=33,518; median change in false positives: -819 [range: -3521 to -459] across seven SHD labels) and MIMIC-IV (n=3628; median false-positive change: -255 [range: -716 to -86] across five SHD labels) participants.
CONCLUSIONS: TARGET-AI may guide the targeted deployment of AI-ECG for SHD screening across health systems. (Funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute of the National Institutes of Health and others.).

Title: Silent Validation of a Longitudinal Model for Predicting Delayed Cerebral Ischemia in Real Time after Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Longitudinal prediction of delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is crucial for timely interventions. Machine learning models for DCI risk prediction and stratification may support clinical decision-making, but safety concerns and regulatory constraints have precluded real-time bedside validation. We utilized the ICU (intensive care unit) Cockpit information technology infrastructure to establish a live data stream enabling real-time model predictions that were evaluated by independent research physicians in a silent validation framework, benchmarking algorithmic recommendations without influencing treatment decisions.
METHODS: We deployed a DCI algorithm validated on historical data in a live environment on running data streams of actual patients. Three independent physicians not involved in patient care reviewed real-time model outputs from day 2 through day 14 after SAH onset. With algorithm support, these physicians estimated DCI probability, decided on further diagnostic orders (computed tomography angiography with perfusion) and/or recommended the intervals for repetitive neurologic assessments (increased, 1-2 hourly; standard, ≥3 hourly). Researchers' decisions were compared with actual clinical decisions and the occurrence of DCI.
RESULTS: Out of 63 aneurysmal SAH patients enrolled, 17 developed DCI (27%). A total of 794 assessments were made. The number of increased neurologic assessment orders was 466 with algorithm support and 629 without (a reduction of 163; 25.91%). Although the number of true positives and false negatives for DCI prediction was similar with and without the algorithm, false positives were reduced by 164 (P<0.01). Additional diagnostic orders were 128 with algorithm support and 153 without (reduction of 25; 16.34%).
CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that continuous, real-time risk estimates can be generated without disrupting standard care, and that clinicians - when supported by an algorithm - may safely reduce unnecessary investigations without compromising DCI event detection. In addition, silent validation showed potential to optimize monitoring strategies and reduce clinician workload without reducing diagnostic accuracy. (Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation [project nos. 407540-167195 and 325230_200568].).

Title: Effect of diet-induced plasma ceramide on human in vivo microvascular endothelial function.
Journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
Abstract: Elevated plasma ceramides and microvascular endothelial dysfunction are separately implicated in the incidence of cardiovascular disease. Exogenous exposure and endogenous accumulation of ceramide causes microvascular endothelial dysfunction in isolated human microvessels ex vivo; however, the impact of increased plasma ceramide on in vivo human microvascular function is unknown. We measured peripheral microvascular endothelial function in young, healthy adults before and after increasing plasma ceramide levels via high-fat meal. We hypothesized that acute increases in plasma ceramide would induce peripheral microvascular dysfunction. Twenty-three healthy adults (12 males and 11 females) participated in this double-blind, randomized controlled, crossover trial. In vivo microvascular function and perfusion were assessed with laser Doppler flowmetry (LDF) using local heating and incident dark-field microscopy imaging, respectively. Plasma ceramides were quantified and microvascular function was assessed at baseline and 2 and 4 h post ingestion of a meal rich in long (LCT)- or medium (MCT)-chain fatty acids. Acute consumption of a LCT meal increased (P < 0.001) circulating ceramide concentrations in female participants only. Nitric oxide-dependent and maximal dilation, assessed via LDF, were similarly reduced after the intake of either a MCT or LCT meal, with no sex differences observed. No change in microvascular density and perfusion was observed after the consumption of either meal. Results suggest that an acute increase in plasma ceramide is not sufficient to further impair postprandial microvascular function, as both meals similarly reduced microvascular function despite ceramide elevations occurring only after the LCT meal. Future studies should investigate how repeated elevations in ceramide levels affect microvascular function.NEW & NOTEWORTHY Acute consumption of a long-chain fatty acid-rich meal increased circulating ceramides in a sex-specific manner, with elevations observed only in females. Despite this, in vivo microvascular endothelial function was similarly impaired after both medium- and long-chain fatty acid-rich meals, with no differences observed between sexes. Further studies are needed to define the role of ceramide-induced microvascular dysfunction and the long-term cardiovascular impact of repeated exposure.

Title: Generating Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Images from Electrocardiograms - A Multicenter Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) requires early and accurate diagnosis to improve outcomes. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides gold-standard functional and structural insights but remains limited by accessibility and complexity. Electrocardiogram (ECG) is widely available but lacks CMR's granularity. We propose CardioNets, a deep learning framework that translates 12-lead ECG into CMR-aligned functional parameters and synthetic images, enabling scalable, low-cost cardiac assessment.
METHODS: CardioNets aligns the ECG with CMR-derived latent representations via crossmodal contrastive learning, then generates CMR images from the ECG using masked autoregressive modeling. The study utilized 159,819 samples from the U.K. Biobank (UKB), the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) IV ECG database, and two external clinical datasets for model development and evaluation. The performance in cardiac measurement regression and disease detection was evaluated against ECG-only and CMR-based baseline models, and the synthesized CMR image quality was compared with state-of-the-art methods. A reader study compared CardioNets with physicians using ECG and clinically acquired CMR images.
RESULTS: In the UKB dataset, CardioNets improved cardiac measurement regression (R2=0.310; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.304 to 0.315) compared with the best ECG baseline (R2=0.269; 95% CI, 0.265 to 0.272; P<0.0001). For cardiomyopathy detection, CardioNets achieved an area under the receiver operator curve (AUROC) of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.836 to 0.944), outperforming the best ECG baseline (AUROC=0.867; 95% CI, 0.812 to 0.921; P<0.01), and demonstrating performance comparable to a CMR-based model (AUROC=0.906; 95% CI, 0.890 to 0.922; P=0.514). In MIMIC-IV for pulmonary hypertension detection, CardioNets (AUROC=0.879; 95% CI, 0.853 to 0.903) outperformed the best ECG baseline (AUROC=0.853; 95% CI, 0.824 to 0.881; P<0.001). Synthesized CMR images by CardioNets achieved a structural similarity index measure of 0.205 (95% CI, 0.202 to 0.208), outperforming the state-of-the-art method (0.122; 95% CI, 0.120 to 0.125; P<0.0001). In the reader study, CardioNets achieved an accuracy of 0.874 (95% CI, 0.800 to 0.923), outperforming participating readers.
CONCLUSIONS: CardioNets translates ECGs into CMR-level insights, improving CVD detection performance and enabling scalable accessibility. Prospective studies are warranted to validate clinical deployment. (Funded by the National Key Research and Development Program of China and others.).

Title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Auscultation to Identify Left Ventricular Dysfunction - Development and External Validation in Prospective Multicenter Studies.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular dysfunction (LVD) is common and associated with adverse prognosis, even in asymptomatic individuals. Early treatment improves outcomes, underscoring the need for efficient strategies to identify patients who may benefit from echocardiographic evaluation. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an AI auscultation method to detect LVD among patients referred for clinically indicated echocardiography.
METHODS: In this prospective, multicenter study, adult patients referred for echocardiography were enrolled to undergo digital auscultation at four standard auscultation sites with simultaneous single-lead ECGs. LVD was defined as a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) less than or equal to 40% on concurrent echocardiography. An ensemble model combining a transformer-based network and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network was trained on multicenter data and externally validated. The model's performance was compared with a seven-cardiologist reader substudy and clinical logistic regression models incorporating clinical variables, single-lead ECG-derived features, and B-type natriuretic peptide levels.
RESULTS: The multicenter training cohort included 2359 patients (mean age, 69.7±13.5 years; 40.4% female; 8.9% with reduced LVEF). The external validation cohort of 964 patients (mean age, 68.6±15.4 years; 38.9% female; 7.6% with reduced LVEF) was obtained from another independent multicenter registry. The four-site AI auscultation outperformed ECG-only models and the clinical logistic models, achieving an area under the receiver operator curve (AUROC) of 0.926 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.911 to 0.939) in the training cohort. In the external validation cohort, AUROC was 0.904 (95% CI, 0.876 to 0.930) and sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 86.3%, 74.2%, and 75.1%, respectively. In a 100-patient reader substudy, AI auscultation outperformed cardiologist consensus in accuracy (82.0% vs. 62.0%; P=0.004). Model performance was consistent across prespecified subgroups. The simplified two-site auscultation model retained high accuracy in the external validation cohort (AUROC, 0.903; 95% CI, 0.878 to 0.927).
CONCLUSIONS: AI auscultation accurately detected LVD among patients referred for clinically indicated echocardiography, supporting its potential as a scalable and accessible pre-echocardiographic risk-enrichment tool. Further validation is warranted before broader screening applications. (Funded by AMI Inc. and the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science KAKENHI program [grant number 25K19371].).
Publication Types: Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Validation Study

Title: Changes in Anthropometric, Metabolic, and Micronutrient Features Among Patients with Severe Obesity Awaiting Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Due to high demand for metabolic and bariatric surgery, patients often face significant waiting periods before undergoing the procedure. This study aimed to investigate trends in weight and metabolic changes among patients with severe obesity awaiting surgery, given the potential impact of preoperative metabolic changes on perioperative outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included patients with severe obesity who had been waiting for metabolic and bariatric surgery for at least six months. Weight, body composition analysis parameters, and biochemical tests were recorded every six to eight weeks for these candidates.
RESULTS: Among the 2926 patients studied, the average age was 39.7 years, with 74.8% being women. The mean weight was 124.65 kg, while the mean BMI was 46.14 kg/m². Seventy-five percent of the patients had obesity-related comorbidities. Adjusted models based on generalized estimating equations (GEE) approach showed that weight, FBS, insulin, and TG have an increasing trend over time. Male sex was associated with significantly higher weight (+25.78 kg), FBS (+4.11 mg/dL), insulin (+8.47 µIU/mL), TG (+15.39 mg/dL), SGPT (+17.59 IU/L), and SGOT (+6.93 IU/L), as well as lower HDL (-3.89 mg/dL), and a small but statistically significant increase in BUN.
