TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT07175727 (clinicaltrials.gov).

Title: Cavotricuspid Isthmus Ablation Using a Variable Loop Pulsed Field Ablation Catheter: A Single-Center Descriptive Analysis.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation is frequently performed concomitant with pulmonary vein isolation (PVI). Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as the preferred energy source for PVI, but it is unclear whether CTI ablation can be performed with PFA catheters.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed data from patients who underwent PVI and CTI ablation using a variable-loop PFA catheter for feasibility, efficacy, and safety.
RESULTS: Twenty-three patients (mean age 65 years, 57% male) were included in this analysis. Systemic intravenous nitroglycerin was administered to all subjects to prevent vasospasm. Acute CTI block could be documented in all patients at the end of the ablation procedure without complications and with low fluoroscopy exposure. We observed one symptomatic recurrence of possible typical atrial flutter during a mean follow-up of 218 days.
CONCLUSION: CTI ablation using a variable-loop PFA ablation catheter was feasible, efficient, and safe in the acute setting. Prospective studies with larger patient numbers are needed to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of this approach.

Title: Network Meta-Analysis of Static Cold Storage Versus Dynamic Organ Preservation for Liver Transplantation.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Donor organ scarcity and increasing use of extended-criteria donors have driven the development of dynamic preservation methods to improve outcomes following liver transplantation. Hypothermic machine perfusion (HMP) and normothermic machine perfusion (NMP), controlled oxygenated rewarming (COR), and ischemia-free liver transplantation (IFLT) are dynamic preservation methods that have been compared with traditional static cold storage (SCS). However, no randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have directly compared HMP with NMP. The aim of the present study is to conduct a network meta-analysis (NMA) of RCTs to compare the effects of available dynamic preservation strategies on clinical outcomes.
METHODS: Electronic databases were systematically searched for RCTs evaluating dynamic preservation methods in human liver transplantation. Eligibility criteria included reporting of at least one of the following primary outcome measures: early allograft dysfunction (EAD), biliary complications, and graft survival. A random-effects Bayesian NMA with a non-informative prior was conducted.
RESULTS: Thirteen RCTs were included with a total of 1888 recipients and assessed 5 interventions. IFLT had the highest probability of being the best-ranked treatment for EAD and biliary complications, but these findings were based on a single RCT. HMP (7 RCTs) ranked higher than NMP (4 RCTs) across all primary outcomes, whereas NMP ranked higher than SCS for EAD and biliary complications. Subgroup analysis of extended criteria brain-dead donors was consistent with overall findings.
CONCLUSIONS: Dynamic preservation modalities were associated with improved outcomes compared with SCS. HMP ranked higher than NMP across the primary outcomes. However, these comparisons were predominantly indirect and do not establish superiority of HMP over NMP.

Title: DAPAgliflozin-Related Cardiac REverse Remodeling by 2D and 3D Echocardiography in OptiMally Treated HFrEF Patients: The DAPA-REM Study.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors promote cardiac reverse remodeling in heart failure (HF), yet data integrating two-dimensional and three-dimensional echocardiography (2DE and 3DE, respectively) in optimally treated HFrEF populations are limited. This study aimed to evaluate heart chambers size and function by 2D/3DE after dapagliflozin initiation, and to explore whether baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) or myocardial fibrosis on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) influence reverse remodeling.
METHODS: Seventy-five patients with LVEF ≤40% on guideline-directed therapy were prospectively enrolled. Echocardiographic and clinical data were collected at baseline and 6-month follow-up (6MFU) after introduction of dapagliflozin 10 mg daily. Sub-analyses were performed according to eGFR (<45 vs. ≥45 mL/min/1.73 m2) and extent of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on CMR.
RESULTS: After 6MFU, left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes reduced, and LVEF increased as assessed by both 2DE (respectively: 88[72-122] vs. 92[79-122]mL/m2, 58[42-80] vs. 57[48-88]mL/m2, 36.6±8.8 vs. 34.5±7.7%; p < 0.001) and 3DE (respectively: 100[79-140] vs. 108[90-136]mL/m2, 64[46-82] vs. 69[55-93]mL/m2, 37.4±8.7 vs. 34.4±7.9%; p < 0.001). No significant association between eGFR and the magnitude of LV reverse remodeling was detected, while CMR analyses suggested a possible inverse correlation between LGE burden and improvement in 2D LVEF. LV diastolic function improved (grade≥2 diastolic dysfunction: 4.7% vs. 18.7%; p = 0.015), along with systolic pulmonary artery pressure (25[23-29] vs. 27[24-29]mmHg; p = 0.037).
CONCLUSION: In optimally treated HFrEF patients, LV size and systolic and diastolic function significantly improved during the 6MFU following dapagliflozin initiation. No significant differences in the magnitude of LV reverse remodeling were detected according to eGFR or LGE burden.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT05770167.
KEY LEARNING POINTS: What is already know Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors improve clinical outcomes in heart failure across a wide spectrum of left ventricular ejection fraction, with evidence of cardiac reverse remodeling. Dapagliflozin has been shown to reduce left ventricular and left atrial volumes, improve biventricular systolic function, and lower filling pressures, independent of diabetes status and baseline renal function. What this study adds In clinically stable HFrEF patients on fully optimized guideline-directed medical therapy, significant left ventricular reverse remodeling and improvement in systolic and diastolic function within 6 months after introduction of dapagliflozin was observed, as consistently demonstrated by both 2D and 3D echocardiography. A proportion of patients with baseline LVEF ≤35% crossed the 35% threshold at 6-month follow-up. This observation is hypothesis-generating and may warrant further investigation regarding the potential implications of reverse remodeling for subsequent device-therapy assessment. Exploratory analyses did not detect a statistically significant association between baseline renal function and the magnitude of cardiac reverse remodeling. In the CMR subgroup, preliminary data suggest that the extent of LGE burden might inversely correlate with improvement in 2D LVEF.

Title: Outcome-specific associations of remnant cholesterol with myocardial infarction and stroke across traditional risk factor burden.
Abstract: Remnant cholesterol (RC) is considered a contributor to residual cardiovascular risk, but whether its associations with specific cardiovascular outcomes vary according to the burden of traditional cardiovascular risk factors (CVRFs) remains uncertain. We investigated the associations of RC with myocardial infarction (MI) and stroke in relation to cumulative CVRF burden. We conducted a prospective analysis of 84,806 participants from the Kailuan cohort (baseline 2006) without prior cardiovascular disease. CVRF burden was categorized as 0, 1, 2, or ≥ 3 according to current smoking, overweight (BMI ≥ 24 kg/m²), hypertension, and diabetes. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for incident MI and stroke through 2021, and interaction terms were used to assess potential effect modification by CVRF burden. During a median follow-up of 15 years, 1,690 MI and 6,416 stroke events occurred. Compared with the lowest quartile, the highest RC quartile was associated with higher risks of MI (HR, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.37-1.83) and stroke (HR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.11-1.28). In supplementary subtype analyses, the stroke association was mainly observed for ischemic rather than hemorrhagic stroke. The RC-MI association appeared stronger across higher CVRF-burden categories (highest vs. lowest quartile HRs: 1.16, 1.52, 1.67, and 1.80 for 0, 1, 2, and ≥ 3 CVRFs, respectively), whereas the corresponding stroke association was attenuated (HRs: 1.44, 1.29, 1.21, and 1.03). After noncardiovascular death was treated as a competing event, the stroke interaction was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (P for interaction=0.21). In this large prospective cohort, RC was associated with higher risks of both MI and stroke, with stronger and more consistent associations observed for MI. The pattern of association differed across levels of CVRF burden, suggesting that the clinical interpretation of RC may benefit from outcome-specific and risk-context-specific assessment.

Title: The retrieved venous thrombus as a translational platform: a methodologic roadmap for venous immunothrombosis.
Abstract: Percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy is now widely used for iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) across several device platforms, and every procedure yields intact human thrombus that is routinely discarded. Whether this material can be developed into a translational resource linking thrombus biology to clinical outcome has not been systematically addressed. A narrative, non-systematic review was performed. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library were searched (January 2010 to August 2026) for studies addressing the biology, histopathology and translational analysis of mechanically retrieved venous thrombi, supplemented by reference-list, trial-registry and congress hand-searching. Published venous series remain small and largely confined to descriptive histology, disconnected from longitudinal outcomes. Intra-thrombus biology could address venous-specific questions that peripheral biomarkers and imaging alone cannot: post-thrombotic syndrome, incomplete recanalization, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and cancer-associated thrombosis. A device-agnostic framework is proposed, comprising structured intra-procedural sampling at the level of the case rather than the anatomical region, centralized specimen processing under harmonized quality standards, a tiered analytic pipeline anchored on quantitative immunohistochemistry, paired peripheral-biomarker collection, pre-specified hypotheses with feasibility-based sample sizes, and biobank infrastructure embedded in existing trial platforms. The equivalent programme in arterial thrombectomy supplies transferable methodology, subject to explicit boundary conditions. The retrieved venous thrombus is among the more underused translational specimens in vascular medicine. A standardized, registry-embedded characterization framework could accelerate progress toward precision venous thrombosis medicine.

Title: Fully biodegradable ventricular septal defect occluders: from biomaterials to clinical translation.
Abstract: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most prevalent congenital heart disease (CHD), which is approximately 20% of all congenital cardiac defects. Although transcatheter closure of VSD is a favorable alternative to traditional open-heart surgery, conventional nitinol-based occluders carry permanent risks of atrioventricular conduction disturbances, device erosion, and nickel allergy, which precluded regulatory approval in the United States for perimembranous VSD. Fully biodegradable occluders represent an attractive solution, offering equivalent closure efficacy while eliminating the long-term risks due to a permanent metallic implant. Owing to favorable endothelization-degradation kinetics, biocompatibility, and mechanical performance, polydioxanone (PDO) and poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) have emerged as the superior framework and membrane materials, respectively. Clinical evidence from case series, retrospective cohort studies, and a multicenter randomized controlled trial suggests high procedural success and favorable short- to mid-term safety, with a low incidence of conduction disturbances following biodegradable VSD occluder implantation. In 2022, the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) of China has granted regulatory approval for the MemoSorb® device, which represents the first clinical available fully biodegradable VSD occluder. This review focuses on biomaterials science, structural design principles, preclinical animal studies, and the emerging clinical evidence of fully biodegradable VSD occluder.

Title: Association between perioperative statin-ezetimibe therapy and reoperation following arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: A TriNetX database study.
Journal: Daru : journal of Faculty of Pharmacy, Tehran University of Medical Sciences
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hyperlipidemia (HLD) impairs tendon healing and is associated with increased revision risk following arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR). While statins may partially mitigate this effect, residual dyslipidemia may impair healing. Ezetimibe, through inhibition of intestinal cholesterol absorption, has demonstrated favorable effects on tendon healing in preclinical studies.
OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated whether perioperative statin-ezetimibe therapy is associated with improved postoperative outcomes following ARCR compared with statin monotherapy and patients without HLD.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX Research Network. Adult patients undergoing ARCR were stratified into three cohorts based on HLD status and perioperative (± 6 months) lipid-lowering therapy: (1) documented HLD treated with statin-ezetimibe prescriptions, (2) patients without documented HLD or lipid-lowering therapy prescriptions, and (3) documented HLD treated with statin monotherapy prescriptions. Primary comparisons were predefined between cohort 1 and cohorts 2 and 3. Propensity score matching (1:1) adjusted for demographics and comorbidities. Tear size and presence of fatty atrophy and fatty infiltration were not adjusted for. Outcomes occurring within 5 years included revision rotator cuff repair (RCR), conversion to shoulder arthroplasty, and secondary shoulder arthroscopy.
RESULTS: After matching, 1,066 patients were included in cohorts 1 and 2 and 1,114 patients in cohorts 1 and 3. Compared with patients without HLD, statin-ezetimibe therapy demonstrated similar rates of revision RCR (5.4% vs. 6.4%; RR 0.853; p = 0.358), conversion to shoulder arthroplasty (RR 1.227; p = 0.470), and secondary arthroscopy (RR 0.846; p = 0.260). Compared with statin monotherapy, statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower rates of revision RCR (5.6% vs. 8.0%; RR 0.697; p = 0.023) and secondary shoulder arthroscopy (7.3% vs. 9.6%; RR 0.757; p = 0.048), while arthroplasty rates remained similar (RR 1.261; p = 0.400).
CONCLUSION: Among patients with HLD undergoing ARCR, perioperative statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower reoperation rates compared with statin monotherapy and postoperative outcomes comparable to patients without HLD. These findings support further investigation of intensified lipid-lowering therapy, while accounting for tear size and fatty infiltration.

Title: Predictors of in-hospital venous thromboembolism in patients undergoing primary total hip arthroplasty.
Journal: European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie
Abstract:
PURPOSE: This study evaluated the national inpatient incidence, patient characteristics, and independent predictors of VTE following primary THA.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed using the National Inpatient Sample from 2016 to 2022. Adult patients undergoing primary THA were identified using ICD-10 procedure codes. The primary outcome was in-hospital VTE, defined as deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism during the index admission. Survey-weighted analyses were used to generate national estimates, compare baseline characteristics, and identify independent predictors of VTE using multivariable logistic regression. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.
RESULTS: Among 855,645 weighted inpatient primary THA admissions, 1660 patients developed in-hospital VTE, corresponding to an incidence of 0.19%. Patients with VTE were older (P < 0.001) and more frequently covered by Medicare (P < 0.001), treated at large hospitals (P = 0.009), and treated at urban teaching hospitals (P = 0.013). They also had a greater prevalence of comorbidities, including autoimmune disease, coagulopathy, congestive heart failure, deficiency anemia, peripheral vascular disease, pulmonary circulation disorders, and moderate renal failure (all P < 0.001), as well as chronic pulmonary disease (P = 0.001) and obesity (P = 0.003). On adjusted analysis, the strongest predictors of VTE were paralysis (OR 9.79, P < 0.001), lymphoma (OR 4.35, P = 0.001), other neurologic disorders (OR 4.30, P < 0.001), and pulmonary circulation disorders (OR 3.50, P < 0.001). Additional independent predictors included peripheral vascular disease (OR 2.19, P < 0.001), autoimmune disease (OR 2.01, P < 0.001), congestive heart failure (OR 1.83, P = 0.022), coagulopathy (OR 1.80, P = 0.035), deficiency anemia (OR 1.65, P = 0.002), hypothyroidism (OR 1.45, P = 0.007), and obesity (OR 1.35, P = 0.018).
CONCLUSION: In-hospital VTE following primary THA was uncommon but concentrated among medically complex patients. Improved risk stratification may guide perioperative counseling, surveillance, and individualized thromboprophylaxis for higher-risk patients.

Title: A randomized study comparing plant sterol- and soluble fiber-enriched soymilk with plain soymilk in adults with elevated LDL cholesterol.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lowering low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is an effective strategy to reduce coronary heart disease risk. Plant sterols/stanols, soluble fiber, and soy protein have each shown LDL-C-lowering effects. This study compared the effects of plant sterol-and soluble fiber-enriched soymilk (SFSM) versus plain soymilk (SM) on LDL-C over 8 weeks.
METHODS: A total of 242 adults aged ≥ 18 years with hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C > 130 mg/dL), either untreated or receiving stable lipid-lowering therapy were randomized to receive either plain soymilk (SM; n = 119) or plant sterol- and soluble fiber-enriched soymilk (SFSM; n = 123), with two 180-mL packs consumed daily for 8 weeks. Three participants discontinued the assigned intervention during the study (SM, n = 1; SFSM, n = 2); all three attended the week-2 visit and contributed post-baseline laboratory data, but had no week-8 measurements. Both products provided 5 g soy protein per 180-mL serving; SFSM additionally contained 1 g free plant sterol and 5 g inulin (soluble fiber), with a total dietary fiber content of 5.8 g per serving, corresponding to daily intakes of 2 g free plant sterol and 11.6 g total fiber. Fasting plasma glucose and lipid profiles were measured at baseline and at weeks 2, 4, 6, and 8. Dietary intake and physical activity were monitored throughout the study. The intention-to-treat analysis included all 242 randomized participants.
RESULTS: At week 8, SFSM group had a greater reduction in LDL-C than the SM group, with an adjusted between-group treatment effect of 5.5 mg/dL (95% CI 0.6 to 10.4, p = 0.028), favoring SFSM, after adjustment for baseline lipid values. No significant between-group differences were found in fasting plasma glucose, HDL-C, triglycerides, total cholesterol/HDL-C ratio, total energy intake, total fat intake, cholesterol intake, water consumption, or physical activity; however, fiber intake increased significantly more in the SFSM group.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the LDL-C-lowering benefit of plant sterol-and soluble fiber-enriched soymilk compared with plain soymilk over 8 weeks; however, secondary and subgroup findings should be interpreted cautiously because they were exploratory in nature. Trial registration Clinical Trials Registry Identifier: (NCT02459314) Retrospectively registered on May 15, 2015; first posted June 2, 2015. The study was conducted from April 2013 to April 2014. The original protocol date 22 October 2012 is provided as supplementary material.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Randomized Controlled Trial; Comparative Study

Title: Heart rate variability and cortisol responses to acute low- and moderate-intensity exercise in stress-related exhaustion.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: Exercise is commonly recommended to support stress regulation and mental health, yet it remains unclear whether these benefits translate to conditions characterized by prolonged stress and fatigue. The aims were to examine whether autonomic and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis responses to a single exercise bout differ between individuals with stress-related exhaustion and healthy controls, and whether responses vary by exercise intensity.
METHODS: In a randomized, counterbalanced crossover design, 30 individuals with stress-related exhaustion (93.3% women; age 46.3 ± 5.89) and 29 healthy controls with a comparable age and sex distribution (93.1% women; age 45.5 ± 5.47) completed two 22-min cycling sessions at workloads corresponding to 40% (low intensity) and 55% (moderate intensity) of estimated maximal oxygen uptake (V̇O₂max) on separate occasions. Heart rate variability (HRV; RMSSD, SD2/SD1, LF/HF) and salivary cortisol were assessed pre-exercise, post-exercise, and 30 min post-exercise, with HRV also assessed during exercise.
RESULTS: Compared with controls, individuals with stress-related exhaustion showed lower RMSSD overall, with the most apparent between-group differences observed during the post-exercise period. Within the exhaustion group, moderate- compared with low-intensity exercise was associated with lower RMSSD and higher SD2/SD1 and LF/HF, whereas no intensity effects were observed in controls. No between-group differences were observed in HRV during exercise. Cortisol analyses suggested overall group-related differences, without clear differences across time points.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest altered physiological stress-system regulation in stress-related exhaustion and highlight the post-exercise period and exercise intensity as important considerations when tailoring exercise recommendations for this population. The study was retrospectively registered on 05/30/2024 at Clinical Trials.gov, with trial registration number NCT06429423.

Title: Variation and temporal trends in Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Group billing for carotid endarterectomy across Vascular Quality Initiative centers.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hospitals use Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Group (MS-DRG) coding to bill for each admission, with higher payment provided for those with complications or comorbidities (CCs) or major CCs (MCCs). We analyzed variation in MS-DRG coding for carotid endarterectomy (CEA) across Vascular Quality Initiative (VQI) centers to identify opportunities for improvement.
METHODS: We matched CEA cases in the VQI registry with Medicare claims data from 2013 through 2023. A multivariable stepwise logistic regression model was created to identify variables associated with CC or MCC billing (with odds ratios [ORs]). We examined variations in CC or MCC billing percentages among centers and applied a multivariable model to compare observed-to-expected (O:E) CC or MCC billing rates to adjust for patient differences. Billing trends over time were analyzed using linear regression.
RESULTS: Among 75,064 primary CEA admissions for Medicare beneficiaries, 39.5% were billed with CCs or MCCs (31.1% CCs, 8.4% MCCs) and 60.5% without. Eleven VQI clinical variables that indicated CCs were significantly associated with CC or MCC billing: dialysis dependence (OR, 22.30), postoperative neurological events (OR, 5.25), length of stay >2 days (OR, 4.98), pre-existing heart failure (OR, 4.08), any postoperative complication (OR, 3.70), reoperation (OR, 3.65), preoperative neurological event (OR, 1.70), higher American Society of Anesthesiologists class (OR, 1.50), urgent/emergent procedure (OR, 1.28), postoperative intravenous blood pressure management (OR, 1.27), and institutional transfer (OR, 1.16). Across 371 VQI centers, CC or MCC billing rates varied 5.6-fold, ranging from 15% to 84% of admissions. After risk adjustment, observed-to-expected ratios still demonstrated 4.2-fold variation, from 0.45 to 1.90 across centers. The observed rate of CC or MCC billing increased over time, from 35.5% in 2015 to 46.1% in 2023 (P < .001). In contrast, the expected adjusted rates predicted by the model remained stable (P = .269). A discrete inflection point was identified between 2016 and 2017, after which higher billing rates persisted (P < .001).
CONCLUSIONS: Substantial variation exists for MS-DRG billing for CEA across VQI centers. Billing rates for CCs or MCCs increased from 2013 through 2023. These findings suggest potential underbilling at some centers and overbilling at others. Leveraging Medicare-linked VQI registry data and the proposed model could help to improve coding and billing accuracy, optimize reimbursement, and reduce Medicare audit risk.

Title: Early-Life Predictors of Obesity and High Blood Pressure Comorbidity at Midlife: Findings From the 1958 National Child Development Study (NCDS).
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early-life exposures can increase the risk of both obesity and high blood pressure in adulthood. In this paper, we identify exposures across five pre-hypothesised childhood domains, explore them as predictors of obesity and high blood pressure comorbidity using the 1958 National Child Development Study (NCDS), and discuss these results in comparison to a similar approach using another birth cohort (1970 British Cohort Study (BCS70)).
METHODS: The analytical sample included 9150 participants. The outcome was obesity (BMI of ≥ 30) and high blood pressure (blood pressure > 140/90 mm Hg) comorbidity at age 44. Domains included: 'prenatal, antenatal, neonatal and birth', 'developmental attributes and behaviour', 'education and academic ability', 'socioeconomic factors' and 'parental and family environment'. Stepwise backward elimination selected variables for inclusion for each domain, and predicted risk scores of obesity-high blood pressure for each cohort member within each domain were calculated. We performed multivariable logistic regression analysis including domain-specific risk scores, sex and ethnicity to assess how well the outcome could be predicted taking all domains into account. In additional analysis, we included potential adult factors.
RESULTS: Including all domain-specific risk scores, sex and ethnicity in the same prediction model the area under the curve was 0.70 (95% CI 0.67-0.72). The strongest domain predictor was the socioeconomic factors domain (OR 1.28 95% CI 1.19-1.38), similar to the BCS70 results. The parental and family environment domain was not a significant predictor (OR 1.08 95% CI 0.94-1.24) unlike the BCS70 results. After considering adult predictors, robust associations remained to the socioeconomic, education and academic abilities, development and behaviour, and prenatal, antenatal, neonatal and birth domains.
CONCLUSIONS: In the NCDS, some early-life course domains were significant predictors of obesity-high blood pressure comorbidity, supporting previous findings. Shared early-life characteristics could have a role in predicting obesity-high blood pressure comorbidity, particularly for those who faced socioeconomic disadvantage.

Title: Clinical Profiles and Early Outcomes of Living Kidney Donors With Pre-Existing Type 2 Diabetes.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: In 2022, Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network policy was revised to permit living kidney donation by carefully selected individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), which had previously been prohibited. Early evaluation is needed to understand adoption of this practice and short-term donor outcomes.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using U.S. national transplant registry data. Living kidney donors with and without pre-existing T2DM from July 26, 2022 through December 31, 2025 were compared. We examined prevalence, temporal trends, donor characteristics, and early post-donation outcomes. Five registry-captured chronic kidney disease risk factors at donation were assessed: insulin dependence, smoking, hypertension, body mass index ≥30 kg/m2, and proteinuria.
RESULTS: Among 21,827 donors, 46 (0.21%) had T2DM at donation. T2DM incidence increased from 7 donors in 2022 (0.11%) to 17 (0.26%) in 2025. T2DM donors were older than non-T2DM donors (median 54y vs. 45y; p < 0.001), and 87% of T2DM donors had ≥1 additional risk factor for CKD. No T2DM donors died, initiated dialysis, or were added to the transplant waiting list. Median most recent eGFR within 2 years was 61 vs. 66 mL/min/1.73m2 in donors with and without T2DM (p = 0.20). eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73m2, was more frequent in donors with T2DM (n = 4; 12% vs. n = 596; 4%; p = 0.03) and median 6-month eGFR-per-kidney gain was 11 vs.15 mL/min/1.73m2, (p = 0.12), and proteinuria was present in 12% of T2DM donors vs. 7% (p = 0.23).
CONCLUSIONS: Living kidney donation by individuals with T2DM is uncommon but increasing. Though differences in early outcomes for T2DM vs. non-T2DM donors were not statistically significant, these null findings are based on small sample sizes and should not be interpreted as evidence of long-term safety. Careful donor selection and longer-term follow-up are needed to better define donor risk.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Research Support, N.I.H., Extramural

Title: Screening for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in type 2 diabetes patients using the fibrosis-4 score in medina-retrospective study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a global health problem closely linked to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and advanced fibrosis. The fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index is a standard noninvasive tool for estimating fibrosis risk. This study aimed to describe the demographics, metabolic parameters, comorbidities, and T2DM duration of patients in Medina and to screen for MASLD using the FIB-4 score.
METHODS: At King Salman Diabetic Center, Medina, Saudi Arabia, a cross-sectional study was conducted among 280 T2DM patients aged >35 years. Data were gathered from electronic medical records. FIB-4 levels were calculated and categorized as low (<1.3), intermediate (1.3-2.67), or high (>2.67) risk. Statistical analysis was performed with IBM SPSS Statistics 30, with p < 0.05 considered significant.
RESULTS: A total of 87.9%of the 280 participants had low-risk FIB-4 scores, 11.4% had intermediate risk scores, and 0.7% had high risk scores. Individuals with FIB-4 ≥ 1.3 were predominantly male (64.7% vs. 43.5%, p = 0.0271) and older (median age: 56 vs. 52 years, p = 0.009). The risk groups were not significantly different in terms of body mass index (BMI) and lipid profiles, glycemic control, hypertension, or diabetes duration.
CONCLUSION: A significant proportion of T2DM patients had intermediate- or high-risk FIB-4 scores. These findings endorse the need for screening for liver fibrosis in T2DM patients, particularly those at increased risk. Early detection and appropriate management are essential to prevent progression to advanced liver disease.

Title: Rhythm-specific regional variation in neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a nationwide registry study in Japan.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Regional variation in outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has been reported worldwide; however, whether its magnitude differs by initial cardiac rhythm remains unknown. This study aimed to evaluate prefecture-level variation in neurological outcomes after OHCA according to initial cardiac rhythm.
METHODS: This retrospective observational study included adult patients with atraumatic OHCA registered in the All-Japan Utstein Registry from 2019 to 2023. Patients were categorized as presenting with a shockable rhythm, pulseless electrical activity (PEA), or asystole according to the initial cardiac rhythm. Mixed-effects logistic regression models were fitted separately for each rhythm group, with favorable neurological outcome at 1 month (defined as a Cerebral Performance Category of 1-2) as the dependent variable and prefecture as a random effect. Prefecture-level variation was quantified using the median odds ratios (MORs).
RESULTS: Among 616,519 participants, 46,575 had a shockable rhythm, 142,073 had PEA, and 427,871 had asystole. Favorable neurological outcomes occurred in 22.3%, 2.7%, and 0.2% of patients, respectively. The MORs were 1.19 for shockable rhythm, 1.31 for PEA, and 1.65 for asystole, indicating progressively greater prefecture-level variation across rhythm categories.
CONCLUSIONS: The magnitude of prefecture-level variation in favorable neurological outcomes differed by initial cardiac rhythm categories and was greatest among patients with asystole. The mechanisms underlying these regional differences remain unclear. Future investigations of regional and healthcare system characteristics may help identify potentially modifiable factors associated with disparities in OHCA outcomes.

Title: Temporal trends in bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation and favourable neurological outcome among older patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest stratified by bystander-patient relationship and age: a JCS-ReSS study.
Abstract:
AIM: To describe temporal trends in bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and favourable neurological outcomes among older patients with bystander-witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) according to bystander-patient relationship and age.
METHODS: A total of 322,943 patients aged ≥65 years with bystander-witnessed OHCA of cardiac origin were enrolled from the All-Japan Utstein Registry (2005-2022). Patients were stratified by age (65-74, 75-89, and ≥90 years) and bystander type (family member, friend/colleague/passerby, or other). Temporal trends in the proportions of bystander CPR and favourable neurological outcome at 1-month, defined as Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) 1-2, were assessed using the Cochran-Armitage test.
RESULTS: During the study period, the annual proportions of bystander CPR and CPC 1-2 in family member-witnessed OHCAs significantly increased across all age groups (all p for trend <0.001). However, bystander CPR remained at approximately 50% in all age groups. In other-witnessed OHCAs, bystander CPR also significantly increased across all age groups (all p for trend <0.001). However, CPC 1-2 significantly increased only in those aged 65-74 years (p for trend <0.05), with no significant temporal trend in older groups. Among those aged ≥90 years, bystander CPR increased to approximately 80%, whereas CPC 1-2 remained at approximately 1%, with no significant temporal trend.
CONCLUSIONS: Temporal trends in bystander CPR and CPC 1-2 varied according to bystander-patient relationship and age. Further investigation is warranted to identify the factors underlying the observed differences in bystander CPR and favourable neurological outcomes.

Title: Not All Brain Bleeds Are Equal: An Etiology-First Framework for Stroke Prevention After Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
Abstract: Stroke prevention after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) requires balancing cardioembolic protection against recurrent cerebral bleeding. Randomized evidence indicates that direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) substantially reduce ischemic stroke compared with no anticoagulation but may increase recurrent ICH in susceptible patients. Importantly, previous ICH does not represent a uniform biological risk. Deep hemorrhage related to hypertensive arteriopathy, lobar hemorrhage associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), mixed small-vessel disease, and hemorrhage from a treatable cause have different recurrence profiles. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) markers, including cerebral microbleed distribution, cortical superficial siderosis, convexity subarachnoid hemorrhage, lacunes, and enlarged perivascular spaces, can help characterize cerebral bleeding vulnerability, although no single marker should determine treatment. This editorial proposes an etiology-first, MRI-informed framework for selecting among restarting a DOAC, considering left atrial appendage closure (LAAC), and withholding long-term antithrombotic therapy. LAAC is not a risk-free alternative because it carries procedural risks and generally requires short-term antithrombotic treatment. Until prospective trials validate phenotype-specific pathways, ICH etiology and MRI phenotype should inform multidisciplinary, individualized, and preference-sensitive decisions.

Title: Clinical Performance and Safety of the Optima Non-compliant Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Angioplasty Balloon in Contemporary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Multicenter Real-World Study.
Abstract: Background Non-compliant (NC) balloon catheters are widely used during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for lesion preparation and stent optimization because they allow controlled high-pressure dilation. However, real-world clinical data describing the procedural performance and short-term clinical outcomes of NC balloon catheters across diverse patient and lesion characteristics remain limited. This study evaluated the observed procedural performance, device performance characteristics, and short-term clinical outcomes associated with the use of the Optima NC non-compliant percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) balloon catheter (Translumina Therapeutics Private Limited, New Delhi, India) during routine PCI. Methods This multicenter, retrospective, single-arm observational study included patients aged ≥18 years who underwent PCI using at least one Optima NC PTCA balloon catheter at four cardiology centers in India between January and June 2024. Eligible patients had ≥80% coronary artery stenosis requiring PCI. The primary endpoint was procedural success, defined as successful balloon delivery, inflation, and retrieval without major procedural complications, together with achievement of final Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) grade III flow. Secondary endpoints included device success, operator-assessed device performance characteristics, and clinical outcomes through three months of follow-up. Results Of 216 patients screened, 196 (90.7%) were included in the final analysis, and 20 (9.3%) were excluded because of incomplete clinical or procedural information. The mean age was 59.20 ± 11.74 years, and 151 (77.0%) patients were male. Acute coronary syndrome was present in 191 (97.45%) patients, and multivessel disease in 111 (56.63%). The left anterior descending artery (LAD) was the most frequently treated vessel (112 (57.14%) patients). Procedural success was achieved in 193/196 (98.5%) procedures, while final TIMI grade III flow was achieved in 196/196 (100%) procedures. Device success was achieved in 193/196 (98.5%) procedures. No major adverse cardiac events (MACE) were reported during the index procedure or at discharge. During follow-up, one myocardial infarction (0.51%) was reported at one month, while one target lesion failure (TLF) (0.51%) and one cardiac death (0.51%) were reported at three months. Conclusion In this multicenter real-world cohort, the Optima NC PTCA balloon catheter demonstrated high observed procedural and device success, with favorable operator-assessed performance and few clinical events during short-term follow-up. Given the retrospective single-arm design and absence of a comparator, these findings are descriptive and do not establish comparative efficacy, superiority, or long-term safety. Prospective comparative studies with larger populations and longer follow-up are warranted to further characterize the clinical performance of the device.

Title: Understanding veteran perspectives surrounding implantable cardioverter- defibrillator decision-making.
Journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: In 2018, the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) mandated the use of evidence-based shared decision-making (SDM) tools for cardiovascular decisions, including implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) implantation for primary prevention in patients with systolic heart failure. Military Veterans are a unique population with experiences including combat, and heightened rates of anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder. Understanding Veteran perspectives on ICD decision-making processes is necessary to inform the Veteran Health Administration's (VHA) ICD care model.
STUDY OBJECTIVE: To understand factors influencing Veterans' ICD decision-making, semi-structured interviews were conducted with Veteran patients with an ICD (Implanters), those referred for consideration (Deliberators), and those who declined (Decliners).
METHODS: Interviews explored experiences with being offered an ICD, understanding of the device, and factors influencing personal decisions. Data were analyzed using content and thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Interviews with 13 participants revealed four primary themes that guided ICD decision-making: (1) desire for information and involvement in personal decisions, (2) quality of life values, (3) views of spirituality (4) Decliners and Deliberators accepted natural death and expressed desire to not intervene medically to prolong life.Participants valued consultation with providers and personal networks, yet ultimately prioritized autonomy. The role of mental health experiences and cohort-level differences on decision-making was inconclusive.
CONCLUSION: Participants' ICD implantation decision-making were influenced by considerations around quality of life, spiritual beliefs, and reluctance to invasively interfere with disease progression. These insights highlight the importance of personalized patient-provider interactions and the need for decision-support tools tailored to VHA Veteran care.

Title: Insights into morbidity and mortality in Gaucher disease: a cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gaucher disease (GD) is a rare lysosomal disorder classified, on the basis of neurological involvement, into type 1 (GD1, non-neuronopathic) and types 2 (GD2) and 3 (GD3) (neuronopathic). Data on morbidity and mortality in Latin American cohorts remain scarce.
AIMS: To characterise morbidity and mortality patterns in a Brazilian GD cohort.
METHODS: Retrospective cohort study at a single GD referral centre in Porto Alegre, Brazil (2003-2023; n = 53; GD1 = 45, GD2 = 4, GD3 = 4). Diagnosis was molecularly confirmed by Sanger and massive parallel sequencing of GBA1. Comorbidities and causes of death were retrieved by chart review; survival was estimated by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results: Median follow-up was 15 years. In GD1, comorbidities were predominantly psychiatric (71%), metabolic/endocrinological (69%) and cardiovascular (60%). Nine patients (17%) died: four GD1 patients (median age 65 years; three from malignancy, one from sepsis), all four GD2 patients (median age 5 months; respiratory or hepatic failure, sepsis) and one GD3 patient (Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy at 27 years).
CONCLUSIONS: The phenotype-specific mortality pattern - malignancy as the leading cause of death in GD1, uniform early death in GD2 reflecting the disease's neurological trajectory rather than a failure of enzyme replacement therapy, and neurological death in GD3 - underscores the substantial burden of oncological, cardiovascular, metabolic and neurological comorbidities in this population and supports systematic multidisciplinary surveillance as a routine component of GD care in Brazil, even in resource-limited settings.
TAKE-HOME MESSAGE: Adult patients with Gaucher disease type 1 require close clinical monitoring for oncological, cardiovascular, metabolic and psychiatric comorbidities. Gaucher disease type 2 remains a devastating disease with a poor prognosis under current therapies.

Title: Artificial Intelligence for Automated Continuous Quantification of Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction From Standard Adult Transthoracic Echocardiography: A Systematic Review.
Abstract: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) guides diagnosis and treatment across cardiovascular disease, but its measurement from transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is operator-dependent and subject to observer variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods that estimate a continuous LVEF value have proliferated. This systematic review aimed to summarise how closely they agree with reference measurements at the group and individual-patient level. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and protocol registration on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO: CRD420261419064), we searched MEDLINE and Embase (via Ovid), Scopus, and IEEE Xplore from January 2015 to 10 September 2026, with forward and backward citation searching, for peer-reviewed journal articles of AI-derived continuous LVEF from standard adult TTE that reported an error or agreement metric against a reference standard. Risk of bias was assessed with a tailored Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Results were summarised as unweighted study-level medians without pooling. We included 108 studies. Most were retrospective (86 of 108), and 34 reported an external or independent test cohort as their main result. EchoNet-Dynamic or CAMUS were used in 54 studies. Systematic bias was small (median absolute bias: 1.5 EF percentage points, interquartile range: 0.5 to 3.4; 68 studies). Typical average error was moderate (median mean absolute error: 4.9 points, 62 studies). The median width of the study-specific 95% limits of agreement was 26 points (interquartile range: 22 to 30; 66 studies). Only 10 of 66 studies (15%) had limits within ±10 points, the usual gap between clinical LVEF decision thresholds. The limits were similarly wide when external results were used wherever available (median width: 26.3 points) and somewhat narrower in studies at low risk of bias (23.6 points). AI methods reproduce reference LVEF with small systematic bias, but individual-patient disagreement in most studies exceeds the difference between clinical LVEF categories and the agreement expected between two expert readers. On current evidence, automated LVEF is better suited to assistive use with expert oversight than to stand-alone measurement, pending prospective, externally validated evaluation.

Title: CardioCLIP: sequential multimodal prediction of echocardiographic abnormalities and natriuretic peptide elevation from electrocardiogram and chest radiographs.
Abstract:
AIMS: Diagnostic reasoning in clinical practice is inherently sequential and multimodal, with physicians integrating heterogeneous examinations under constraints such as missing data and variable test order. However, most multimodal machine learning models assume simultaneous availability of all modalities and fail to reflect this workflow.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We propose CardioCLIP, a sequential multimodal framework that embeds electrocardiograms (ECGs) and chest X-rays (CXRs) into a shared pathological representation space. The model consists of (i) a self-supervised embedding stage aligning ECG-CXR pairs from the same patient and day, and (2) a gated recurrent unit-based prediction stage that estimates clinical indicators as data are sequentially observed. The model was trained on 9458 patients from a single tertiary centre and evaluated for B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and E/e'. External validation was conducted using MIMIC-IV.CardioCLIP achieved strong cross-modal alignment and improved discrimination for selected echocardiographic abnormalities and natriuretic peptide elevation (AUC: 0.90 for BNP > 100 pg/mL, 0.87 for LVEF < 50%, and 0.80 for E/e' > 15). It also showed discrimination for subsequent severe BNP elevation (BNP > 400 pg/mL within 3 years) with an AUC of 0.79. External validation in MIMIC-IV showed an AUC of 0.89 for N-terminal pro-BNP elevation, supporting potential transportability for this endpoint.
CONCLUSION: CardioCLIP demonstrated the feasibility of order-flexible sequential multimodal prediction. By leveraging routinely acquired ECG and CXR data, it may provide a non-invasive adjunct for identifying echocardiographic abnormalities and natriuretic peptide elevation in cardiovascular care, subject to prospective clinical validation.

Title: Disparities in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and severe maternal morbidity: Evidence from a statewide birth cohort.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) complicate 15% of pregnancies nationally and are a major contributor to severe maternal morbidity (SMM). We aimed to characterize temporal trends and demographic disparities in HDP incidence and evaluate the association between HDP and SMM in a statewide cohort.
METHODS: This study is a descriptive and regression-based analysis of a retrospective cohort of Wisconsin births from 2017 to 2023. Data were obtained from the Wisconsin Hospital Association (WHA). Subtypes of HDP were identified using ICD-10 codes. Incidence rates of HDP per 10,000 births and average annual percent changes (AAPC) were estimated using Poisson regression and examined across demographic variables. Outcomes measured included SMM incidence, AAPCs, and SMM indicators by HDP.
RESULTS: Among 388,250 pregnancies, the incidence of nearly all HDP subtypes rose from 2017 to 2023. Severe pre-eclampsia had the highest AAPC (11.8%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 10.6%-13.0%). HDP incidence was highest in urban areas, though the AAPC in preeclampsia was greater in rural areas (8.7%; 95% CI, 7.1%-10.3%; p = 0.004). Black patients experienced higher incidences of HDP, with significant differences in AAPC for HDP overall, chronic hypertension, and severe preeclampsia (p < 0.001). Patients with HDP had higher SMM rates compared to those without, though the AAPC in SMM did not differ by HDP status.
CONCLUSION: These findings highlight a growing burden of HDP in Wisconsin, with an increase in severe preeclampsia incidence and disparities by geography and race. Targeted interventions in rural areas and for Black patients are needed to improve disparities in HDP incidence and reduce SMM across Wisconsin.

Title: Enhanced structural reverse remodeling following LVAD support in patients with TTN truncating variants.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Myocardial recovery sufficient for left ventricular assist device (LVAD) explantation remains uncommon. Titin truncating variant (TTNtv)-associated cardiomyopathy demonstrates favorable reverse remodeling with medical therapy, but its remodeling potential during durable mechanical unloading is unknown.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, single-center study of adults undergoing HeartMate 3 LVAD implantation from 2016-2025. Patients were categorized as TTNtv-associated cardiomyopathy, other genetically characterized nonischemic cardiomyopathy (NICM), or ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM). The primary endpoint was absolute change in left ventricular end-systolic volume index (LVESVI) during LVAD support. Multivariable and sensitivity analyses evaluated potential confounding and influential observations.
RESULTS: Among 51 patients, 7 had TTNtv-associated cardiomyopathy, 9 other NICM, and 35 ICM. TTNtv patients were younger than other NICM and ICM patients (40.5±15.8 vs 45.8±11.0 vs 67.4±9.3 years; P<0.001). Mean LVESVI decreased by 87.7±71.8 mL/m² in TTNtv patients compared with 30.4±28.3 mL/m² in other NICM and 32.6±30.6 mL/m² in ICM (P=0.039). Compared with ICM, TTNtv status remained associated with greater LVESVI reduction after adjustment for baseline LV end-diastolic diameter (β=-47.2 mL/m²; 95% CI, -75.9 to -18.4; P=0.002). Findings were directionally consistent across sensitivity analyses addressing age, post-LVAD guideline-directed medical therapy, follow-up duration, cardiomyopathy substrate, and influential observations. TTNtv patients more frequently met volumetric reverse remodeling criteria (85.7% vs 22.2% vs 57.1%; P=0.044).
CONCLUSIONS: TTNtv-associated cardiomyopathy was associated with greater structural reverse remodeling during LVAD support, particularly LVESVI reduction. Although limited by the small TTNtv cohort and potential residual confounding, these hypothesis-generating findings suggest that genetic substrate may contribute to myocardial remodeling during mechanical unloading.

Title: Acute eGFR Changes With Finerenone Examined in a Prespecified Analysis of FINE-ONE.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist finerenone reduces urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) in people with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). This prespecified analysis evaluated acute changes in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) with finerenone and their impact on safety.
METHODS: Adults with T1D and CKD (n = 242; eGFR ≥ 25-< 90 ml/min per 1.73 m2; UACR ≥ 200 to < 5000 mg/g) receiving stable renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibition were randomized 1:1 to finerenone or placebo. The primary outcome was acute change in eGFR (from baseline to month 1), termed "eGFR dip." Reversibility of eGFR change was assessed from end of the treatment (month 6) to follow-up (month 7). Change in eGFR was assessed across eGFR dip subgroups (eGFR > 0 to ≤ 10% decline, > 10% decline, and ≥ 0% increase) and prespecified characteristics (baseline eGFR, UACR, history of cardiovascular disease [CVD], and diuretic use).
RESULTS: Mean acute eGFR decline at month 1 was greater with finerenone (-2.78 ml/min per 1.73 m2 [95% confidence interval [CI], -4.15 to -1.40]) versus placebo (-0.78 ml/min per 1.73 m2; [95% CI, -2.22 to 0.66]); treatment difference was -1.99 ml/min per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -3.97 to -0.01 [P = 0.049]). Placebo-corrected eGFR increased during the washout period across the groups. Acute eGFR changes did not differ according to prespecified characteristics. The incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) was comparable across eGFR dip subgroups in both the treatment groups. Greater declines in eGFR were associated with greater reductions in UACR at month 3.
CONCLUSION: In people with T1D and CKD, finerenone induced an acute eGFR dip that was well tolerated without unexpected safety signals.

Title: Short-term indoor fine particulate matter exposure impedes cognitive performance and autonomic nervous system in adults.
Abstract: Evidence suggests short-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) air pollution can impact health, yet its wider cognitive effects and underlying mechanisms are unknown. In this randomized single-blind crossover lab-based study, 90 working-age adults were exposed to two stable indoor PM2.5 conditions generated by candle-burning: low concentration (1.70 μg/m3, representing clean air) achieved via an air purifier, and high concentration (31.22 μg/m3, representing global average exposure) using a sham filter in the purifier. Participants' cognitive performance across various domains was assessed, alongside heart rate variability (HRV) and electrodermal activity (EDA) to appraise potential mediating mechanisms of autonomic nervous activity on cognition. Higher PM2.5 exposure resulted in lower HRV and poorer cognitive performance in attention and memory, but not in coordination or reasoning. Decreased HRV partly mediated declines in some cognitive functions. The findings could have broader implications for workforce productivity beyond direct effects on ill health.

Title: The effects of the arts and arts therapies on mental health outcomes of children and young people: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: There is growing evidence on the positive effects of the arts and arts therapies for mental health (MH) outcomes. This review aims to fill a research gap by establishing the evidence on the effects of arts-based interventions on selected MH outcomes for children and young people (CYP).
METHODS: Our systematic review and meta-analysis included randomised controlled trials with CYP aged 5-24 years receiving any type of arts-based intervention. Five databases (CINAHL, Embase.com, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between 1/1/2005 and 18/5/2025. Two reviewers independently screened all records and assessed risk-of-bias using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB2) and certainty using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE). Data were initially extracted using the AI-assisted review tool Elicit and independently verified by two reviewers. All data were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, and effect estimates for MH outcomes are summarised as Standardised Mean Differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic, with pre-specified subgroup and sensitivity analyses conducted to explore possible sources of inconsistency. This study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251015352).
FINDINGS: One hundred trials across 29 countries involving CYP aged 5-24 years with a range of health conditions, alongside healthy populations, were included in this review. Based on studies with some concerns or high risk-of-bias, arts-based interventions were found to reduce individuals' depression (1.06 SMD lower [95% CI 0.45-1.67, n = 1655, I 2 = 97%]), anxiety (0.75 SMD lower [95% CI 0.57-0.94, n = 3898, I 2 = 87%]), and increase individuals' wellbeing (0.53 SMD higher [95% CI 0.26-0.80, n = 538, I 2 = 49%]) and quality of life (0.54 SMD higher [95% CI 0.25-0.83, n = 441, I 2 = 53%]) on average post-intervention. Certainty of results relating to wellbeing and quality of life was low due to imprecision and concerns about risk of bias, and very low for depression and anxiety due to additional inconsistency associated with high heterogeneity. Findings relating to anxiety were further supported by biomarker data (blood pressure and heart rate) with moderate certainty.
INTERPRETATION: This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis of evidence from randomised controlled trials assessing the effects of a wide variety arts-based interventions on the mental health of CYP. Although the strength of any conclusions is limited by heterogeneity, imprecision and bias of the studies assessed, average effects were similar to those typically reported for established non-arts-based psychosocial interventions, including talking therapies. These findings advance our understanding of arts-based therapeutic strategies for CYP's MH. Further high-quality trials, with larger sample sizes and standardised outcome measures and timepoints, are needed to improve the certainty of evidence in this area.
FUNDING: UKRI.

Title: Age-specific trends in poisoning-related out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Japan: a retrospective nationwide registry study.
Abstract:
AIM: Poisoning-related out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) may have distinct age-specific trends. We examined temporal changes in its proportion among all OHCA, population-based incidence, and neurological outcomes in Japan.
METHODS: In this retrospective nationwide registry study, we analyzed adults aged ≥18 years OHCA treated by emergency medical services (EMS) in the Japanese Utstein registry from 2013 to 2023. Age-specific logistic regression estimated annual trends in the proportion of poisoning-related OHCA, adjusted for age and sex. Poisson regression with age-group population as the exposure estimated incidence trends. Neurological outcome trends were examined secondarily.
RESULTS: Among 1,400,951 adults with OHCA treated by EMS, 3723 (0.27%) had poisoning-related OHCA. In adults aged 18-29 years, the adjusted odds of poisoning-related OHCA increased (odds ratio per year, 1.027; 95% CI, 1.001-1.054), whereas population-based incidence showed a nonsignificant upward trend (incidence rate ratio, 1.020; 95% CI, 0.995-1.046). All-cause OHCA incidence declined among adults aged 18-29 years (incidence rate ratio, 0.991; 95% CI, 0.983-0.9997). The poisoning proportion decreased at ages 50-64 and ≥65 years; poisoning incidence declined significantly only at ≥65 years. Favorable neurological outcome after poisoning-related OHCA showed no clear improvement (adjusted odds ratio per year, 0.998; 95% CI, 0.949-1.050).
CONCLUSION: Poisoning-related OHCA became increasingly prominent among young adults but declined among older adults. Although the incidence increase in young adults was not statistically significant, its upward direction, declining all-cause OHCA incidence, and lack of clear neurological outcome improvement suggest increasing clinical importance of poisoning-related OHCA in young adults.

Title: In-hospital medication administration prior to in-hospital cardiac arrest: a matched case-control study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Limited research has examined medication administration in patients with in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). We aimed to identify and describe in-hospital medications administered 24 h prior to IHCA compared with matched controls.
METHODS: This study was a registry-based, matched, case-control study including patients who were hospitalized in the Central Denmark Region from 2017 to 2022. Patients with IHCA were matched with hospitalized controls on age, sex, length, and period of admission. The index time was defined as the time of IHCA for cases, and a corresponding index time was assigned to matched controls. Medication administrations within 24 h prior to index time were identified and divided into 21 groups based on ATC codes, e.g. QTc-prolonging drugs. New medication administrations were defined as no prior redeemed prescription for the same ATC code within 2 years.
RESULTS: A total of 1976 cases and 19,716 controls met the study criteria and were included in the study. Among cases, the most frequently administered medication groups were antithrombotic agents (43% of cases), antibiotics (42%), and diuretics (35%), whereas for controls the groups were antibiotics (33% of controls), antithrombotic agents (33%), and opioids (24%). Overall, cases were administered a median of 11 (IQR: 0-20) medications within 24 h prior to the index time as compared to 5 (IQR: 0-14) medications for controls.
CONCLUSION: Medications administered in-hospital within 24 h prior to IHCA differed from those in matched controls and were characterized by a higher proportion of newly initiated treatments. These findings may help form new hypotheses on strategies on prevention of IHCA.

Title: Hemodynamic and Functional Outcomes of Rate-Adaptive and Physiologic Pacing in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise intolerance and poor quality of life remain challenges in HFpEF, driven by chronotropic incompetence and left atrial dysfunction. We evaluated whether rate-adaptive/accelerated pacing (RAAP), targeting these mechanisms, improves hemodynamic, functional, and patient-reported outcomes.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Outcomes included NT-proBNP, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ) score, 6-min walk distance (6MWD), E/e', and E/A. Within-group pre-post changes and comparisons with usual care were synthesized separately. Effects are reported as mean differences (MD) or odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).
RESULTS: Eight reports involving 380 patients were included with myPACE overlap handled by one report per cohort per analysis. Within-group, RAAP was associated with reductions in NT-proBNP (MD -462.58 pg/mL; 95% CI -891.37 to -33.79), E/A (MD -1.01; -1.19 to -0.83), and E/e' (MD -3.18; -5.65 to -0.72), and improvements in 6MWD (MD +74.10 m; 36.34 to 111.86) and MLHFQ score (MD -17.40 points; -33.06 to -1.74). Compared with usual care, associations favored RAAP for NT-proBNP (MD -108.51 pg/mL; -118.31 to -98.70), 6MWD (MD +73.36 m; 32.23 to 114.48), MLHFQ score (MD -16.52 points; -24.15 to -8.89), and AF burden (MD -6.13; -7.88 to -4.37). MACE also favored RAAP in an exploratory analysis (OR 0.47; 0.23 to 0.93), whereas peak VO2 did not differ significantly.
CONCLUSIONS: RAAP was associated with favorable changes in hemodynamic and functional outcomes. These findings support further evaluation of individualized rate modulation in adequately powered randomized trials.

Title: Repeated self-directed CPR testing enhances compression depth: evidence from a large retrospective cohort.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-quality chest compressions are critical to survival after cardiac arrest, yet CPR skills decline after conventional training. Low-dose, high-frequency (LDHF) training may sustain competence, but large-scale longitudinal evidence from self-directed stations remains limited.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of healthcare professionals completing at least two manikin-based CPR assessments between June 2023 and April 2026. Automated testing was performed using a self-directed manikin-based simulation station without real-time feedback. Mixed-effects models assessed associations of interval and test-day number with compression depth, rate, recoil, and guideline compliance. Sensitivity analyses modeled test-day number categorically and adjusted depth models for age and recorded sex.
RESULTS: Among 2558 participants (6232 tests), mean depth increased from 49.8 ± 9.2 mm on test day 1 to 52.5 ± 7.6 mm on test day 2 and remained within guideline targets thereafter; rate and recoil were stable. Interval had a negligible association with depth (0.027 mm per 30 days, p = 0.027) that was attenuated after demographic adjustment (p = 0.101). Per 30 days, interval was weakly associated with depth compliance, but not rate or combined compliance. Later test-day number was associated with higher depth (1.59 mm per test day, p < 0.001), with consistent categorical and adjusted findings.
CONCLUSION: Later test-day number was consistently associated with higher depth, whereas interval explained little variation. Although the observational design cannot establish station effectiveness or an optimal refresher interval, this study provides one of the largest longitudinal descriptions of repeated self-directed CPR assessment in certified healthcare professionals.

Title: Community Health Worker Coaching, Food Insecurity, and Physical Activity in the Healthy Food First Trial: A Causal Mediation and Longitudinal Analysis.
Abstract: To evaluate whether change in food insecurity (ΔFI) mediated the effect of a community health worker (CHW) intervention on physical activity (PA) among food insecure (FI) hypertensive adults, we conducted a secondary analysis of the Healthy Food First randomized clinical trial of food insecure adults with hypertension recruited from 364 North Carolina clinical sites. Participants were randomized to CHW coaching or no coaching within a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design. FI was measured at baseline and 12 months; total PA (MET-min/week) at 12 and 18 months. Mediation models estimated indirect (ACME), direct (ADE), and total effects (ATE) of CHW assignment on 12-month PA through ΔFI. Generalized estimating equations evaluated repeated PA by CHW assignment. CHW assignment was not associated with PA, and ΔFI did not mediate the relationship. Effects were small (ACME = 16.2; 95% CI -62.6, 121.8; ADE = -214.1; 95% CI -871.7, 484.5; ATE = -197.9; 95% CI -855.6, 500.8 MET-min/week). The proportion mediated was near zero (-8.2%; 95% CI -142%, 124%). GEE analyses similarly showed no association (B = 363.7 MET-min/week; SE = 302.8; P = 0.23). Modest improvements in FI alone may be insufficient to increase PA without additional PA supports. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05048836.

Title: Association between family member bystander CPR and survival for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Bystander CPR is associated with higher likelihood of survival in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Whether family member-administered bystander CPR is associated with higher survival is not fully understood, even though family members are often present when arrests occur at home and are best positioned to initiate CPR.
METHODS: Within the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) registry, we conducted a retrospective cohort study. Using multivariable mixed-effect logistic regression, we examined the association between family member (FM) and non-family member (non-FM) bystander CPR, as compared to those not receiving bystander CPR, with a primary outcome of survival to hospital discharge and secondary outcome of favorable neurological survival (survival without severe neurological deficits).
RESULTS: We identified 824,960 non-traumatic OHCAs between 2013 and 2024. Mean age was 62.2 ± 17.1 years and 35.6% were female. Overall, 78,139 (9.5%) people survived to hospital discharge. Compared to those with no bystander CPR (7.3%), higher survival rates occurred in those receiving FM-bystander CPR (9.6%; adjusted OR: 1.31 [95% CI: 1.29-1.34], p < 0.001) and non-FM bystander CPR (17.3%; adjusted OR: 1.58 [95% CI: 1.55-1.62], p < 0.001). When directly comparing the two bystander groups, those with non-FM bystander CPR had higher rates of survival than those with FM bystander CPR (adjusted OR: 1.21 [95% CI: 1.18, 1.24], p < 0.001). A similar pattern was observed with the outcome of favorable neurological survival.
CONCLUSION: Both non-FM and FM-bystander CPR were associated with higher survival outcome rates compared to no bystander CPR while non-FM CPR was associated with higher survival compared to FM-CPR.

Title: Pre-stroke frailty in patients with first-ever acute stroke: Its associations with stroke subtype and impact on activities of daily living.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Few studies have examined frailty in patients with first-ever stroke who were independent in activities of daily living (ADLs) prior to onset. This study aimed to investigate the characteristics of pre-stroke frailty and its impact on ADLs at discharge.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, 152 patients aged ≥65 years with first-ever stroke admitted to the stroke unit of a university hospital were enrolled. Pre-frailty/frailty was assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS). Associations between frailty status and clinical characteristics were evaluated. Multivariate regression analysis identified independent predictors of the Barthel Index (BI) at discharge.
RESULTS: Pre-frailty/frailty was present in 35.5% of patients, and was associated with higher rates of atrial fibrillation (p = 0.043) and cardioembolic stroke (p = 0.001). Compared with the robust group, the pre-frailty/frailty group had significantly lower BI scores at both admission and discharge, as well as more extended hospital stays. Both groups, however, demonstrated significant improvement in BI at discharge (p < 0.001). Multivariate analysis revealed that NIH Stroke Scale score (p < 0.001), stroke type (p = 0.010), and CFS score (p = 0.044) independently predicted BI at discharge.
CONCLUSION: Pre-stroke frailty is associated with a higher risk of cardioembolic stroke and poorer functional status during hospitalization. Nevertheless, patients with frailty still achieved significant ADL improvement with rehabilitation, underscoring the importance of active rehabilitation strategies in this population.

Title: Latest findings on complications following trans- catheter aortic valve replacement: A literature review.
Journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Severe aortic stenosis (As) is the most common valvular heart disease in developed countries, and transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has expanded across surgical risk groups. However, procedure-related complications remain clinically important, and their reported incidence and management have evolved with newer-generation devices and techniques. This review summarizes major TAVR complications, including their incidence and pathophysiology, risk factors, clinical impact, prevention and management, and outlines remaining knowledge gaps.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A structured narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted for studies published between 2012 and 2026, including randomized trials, registries, cohort studies, and systematic reviews.
RESULTS: Major complications reviewed included Stroke, Delirium, Conduction disturbances (CD) and Arrhythmias, Bleeding/Vascular(access) site injuries/Paravalvular leak (PVL), Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), Structural valve degeneration and thrombosis, Infective Endocarditis (IE) and Coronary Obstruction (CO).
CONCLUSIONS: TAVR complications remain multifactorial, and their incidence and management continue to shift with device evolution and procedural experience. Optimized patient selection, procedural refinement, frailty assessment, and individualized antithrombotic strategies remain important areas for improving outcomes.

Title: Stage at Presentation and Clinical Characteristics of Breast Cancer Patients at the Butaro Cancer Centre of Excellence, Rwanda: A Retrospective Chart Review.
Abstract: Background Breast cancer is the leading cancer among women in sub-Saharan Africa, where late-stage presentation contributes to poor outcomes. Understanding the risk-factor profile, comorbidity burden, and functional status of patients at presentation is essential to guide early-detection and management strategies in resource-limited settings. Methods We conducted a retrospective chart review of patients who underwent surgery for breast cancer at the Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence (BCCOE), Rwanda, between 2018 and 2023. From 422 patients identified, 300 charts were selected through simple random sampling and reviewed using a pretested REDCap tool drawing on electronic and paper-based records. Data was analyzed in IBM SPSS Statistics (version 29), and disease was staged according to the AJCC TNM system. Results The mean age at presentation was 50.8 years (SD = 11.8; range 28-82); 98% of patients were female, 94% had health insurance, and 74% were farmers. At least one risk factor was present in 65% of patients, with alcohol consumption (55.3%) and tobacco smoking (21.7%) the most common modifiable factors, followed by family history (5.3%) and nulliparity (3.7%). Comorbidities were frequent, affecting 60.3% of patients; hypertension (25.7%) and HIV/AIDS (7.0%) predominated. Most patients had good functional status at diagnosis (ECOG 0, 81.5%; ECOG 1, 16.4%). Of 281 staged patients (19 of 300 lacked complete TNM staging data), Stage III (38.4%) and Stage II (37.0%) were most common, and late-stage disease (Stage III-IV) accounted for 47.3% of cases. Conclusion Breast cancer patients at BCCOE are diagnosed at a younger age than the global average and carry a high burden of modifiable risk factors and comorbidities. The substantial proportion presenting at late stage may complicate treatment and compromise survival, emphasizing the need for strengthened awareness and early-detection efforts. By centering on a rural referral hospital, this study adds to the limited literature on breast cancer presentation in Rwanda.

Title: Frequency of late gadolinium enhancement-negative cardiac magnetic resonance imaging at initial presentation with metabolically active treatment-naïve cardiac sarcoidosis.
Journal: European heart journal. Imaging methods and practice
Abstract:
AIMS: The 2024 American Heart Association statement recommends fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) for patients with high clinical suspicion of cardiac sarcoidosis even without late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), but this recommendation has been challenged. We determined the frequency of LGE-negative CMR at first presentation of clinically manifest, metabolically active, treatment-naïve cardiac sarcoidosis.
METHODS AND RESULTS: In this single-centre sub-study of the prospective Cardiac Sarcoidosis Multi-Center Prospective Cohort Study, we analysed 46 consecutive treatment-naïve patients with de novo clinically manifest cardiac sarcoidosis and core-laboratory-defined abnormal cardiac and extracardiac FDG uptake, imaged within a 6-month interval, before immunosuppression. Four of 46 patients had no LGE on CMR (8.7%; exact 95% CI, 2.4-20.8%). All four presented with advanced atrioventricular conduction disease and none had ventricular tachycardia; three of four started immunosuppressive therapy. Compared with LGE-positive patients, LGE-negative patients had preserved left ventricular ejection fraction and lower cardiac inflammatory burden (left ventricular maximum standardized uptake value 3.9 ± 0.9 vs. 9.6 ± 5.2; P = 0.037).
CONCLUSION: An LGE-negative phenotype can occur in clinically relevant, treatment-naïve, FDG-avid cardiac sarcoidosis. These findings suggest considering FDG-PET in selected patients with high clinical suspicion of cardiac sarcoidosis, even when CMR shows no LGE.

Title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation.
Journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models.
RESULTS: Participants had a mean age of 73.8 ± 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume.
